title: TACET: Context-Appropriate Acoustic-Social Navigation for Quadrupeds
summary: Quadruped robots entering hospitals, care homes, and quiet offices must be context-appropriate not only in where they move but in how loudly they move: a legged robot's locomotion noise, dominated by foot-ground impacts, is itself a social variable. Prior social navigation respects human space but treats the robot as acoustically uniform, while quiet-locomotion methods reduce noise to an operator-specified, context-blind level. We present TACET, a context-appropriate acoustic-social navigation method that infers social context from the robot's egocentric view and decides both where it walks and how loudly, coupling a slow fine-tuned vision-language reasoner to a fast reactive controller through a single compact behavior token, <gait, speed, social_cost>. The same token conditions both a social costmap (where to go) and a quiet locomotion policy (how loudly to move), while a structured out-of-view memory keeps recently seen people in the reasoner's context after they leave the camera view. On a real quadruped, context-conditioned locomotion lowers locomotion noise by up to 9.3 dBA at matched speed, and across our scenarios the full method keeps personal-space compliance at 100% with low acoustic intrusion (<=2.9 dBA), jointly improving spatial and acoustic performance in the evaluated scenarios. The project page is available at https://rcilab.khu.ac.kr/tacet/.

AI.tldr: TACET is a context-appropriate acoustic-social navigation method for quadruped robots that infers social context from egocentric vision and jointly decides where to walk and how loudly, using a single behavior token <gait, speed, social_cost>.
AI.motivation: Quadruped robots entering hospitals, care homes, and quiet offices must be not only spatially but also acoustically appropriate, since locomotion noise dominated by foot-ground impacts is itself a social variable. Prior social navigation treats the robot as acoustically uniform, while quiet-locomotion methods reduce noise to an operator-specified, context-blind level.
AI.method: TACET couples a slow fine-tuned vision-language reasoner to a fast reactive controller through a single compact behavior token, <gait, speed, social_cost>. The same token conditions both a social costmap (where to go) and a quiet locomotion policy (how loudly to move), while a structured out-of-view memory keeps recently seen people in the reasoner's context after they leave the camera view.
AI.result: On a real quadruped, context-conditioned locomotion lowers locomotion noise by up to 9.3 dBA at matched speed. Across the scenarios, the full method keeps personal-space compliance at 100% with low acoustic intrusion (<=2.9 dBA).
AI.conclusion: TACET jointly improves spatial and acoustic performance in the evaluated scenarios, enabling context-appropriate acoustic-social navigation for quadruped robots. The project page is available at https://rcilab.khu.ac.kr/tacet/.

title: GOTT: Object-centric Dexterous Manipulation with a Reusable Cross-Embodiment Primitive
summary: Foundation models and large-scale human data provide rich sources of manipulation intent, but translating this intent into multi-fingered robot behavior remains difficult. Dexterous hands still lack a reusable low-level primitive that reliably establishes contact across tasks and embodiments. We propose GOTT, a reach-acquire-move framework built around a single cross-embodiment contact-acquisition primitive. Given a robot-agnostic object trajectory and a reach specification, GOTT first brings the hand near a task-relevant contact region. The shared closed-loop primitive then establishes stable contact from this approximate initialization, and a pose-conditioned controller tracks the desired object motion. Reach specifications may come from future-aware planning, external models, or human demonstrations, while the primitive and tracking backend remain unchanged. Simulation and real-world experiments show that GOTT is able to establish robust contact across diverse objects, arm-hand platforms, and seen and unseen hand morphologies. It also consistently improves end-to-end task success over open-loop grasp execution.

AI.tldr: GOTT is a reach-acquire-move framework for multi-fingered dexterous manipulation, centered on a single cross-embodiment contact-acquisition primitive that reliably establishes stable contact and tracks object motion across diverse objects, arm-hand platforms, and hand morphologies.
AI.motivation: Foundation models and large-scale human data offer rich manipulation intent, but translating this intent into multi-fingered robot behavior is hard. Dexterous hands lack a reusable low-level primitive that reliably establishes contact across tasks and embodiments.
AI.method: GOTT decomposes manipulation into reach, acquire, and move. Given a robot-agnostic object trajectory and a reach specification, it first brings the hand near a task-relevant contact region. A shared closed-loop contact-acquisition primitive then establishes stable contact from this approximate initialization, and a pose-conditioned controller tracks the desired object motion. Reach specifications can come from future-aware planning, external models, or human demonstrations, while the primitive and tracking backend remain unchanged.
AI.result: Simulation and real-world experiments show that GOTT establishes robust contact across diverse objects, arm-hand platforms, and seen and unseen hand morphologies. It also consistently improves end-to-end task success over open-loop grasp execution.
AI.conclusion: GOTT provides a reusable, cross-embodiment contact-acquisition primitive that decouples high-level manipulation intent from low-level dexterous control, enabling robust contact establishment and improved task success across embodiments.

title: MOSAIC-SV: Real-Time Adaptive Identification of Vessel Dynamics for the Control and Deployment of Aquatic Robots
summary: Model-based control of an aquatic robotic platform depends on a hydrodynamic model that is costly to identify and specific to the hull, payload, and conditions it was measured in. Here, we present MOSAIC-SV, a deployable real-time adaptive dynamics identification and control system that identifies a control-sufficient dynamics model from a spec-sheet engineering prior, without dedicated identification trials, and re-estimates it at every control step of a closed-loop mission while the controller plans on it. A physically admissible unscented Kalman filter re-estimates hydrodynamic, disturbance, and actuator parameters at every control step of the closed-loop mission; while a command-dependent consider projection withholds corrections the current command cannot attribute between actuator effectiveness and external force; and a model predictive path integral controller plans on the current estimate. In simulation on a CyberShip II plant, MOSAIC-SV recovers the transit performance of the calibrated model under static mismatch and transient changes, and stays within 20% of its own transit time at the unscaled prior when its inertia or damping prior is wrong by an order of magnitude. In on-water field trials on the Blue Robotics BlueBoat, a twin-thruster catamaran, MOSAIC-SV transits at least 25% faster and predicts its own motion with at least 56% less error than its frozen engineering prior, including under an unmodeled payload. The same MOSAIC-SV system concept was also feasibly deployed on a 6.3-tonne dual outboard monohull.

AI.tldr: MOSAIC-SV is a deployable real-time adaptive dynamics identification and control system for aquatic robots that learns a control-sufficient hydrodynamic model from a rough engineering prior and updates it online during closed-loop missions.
AI.motivation: Model-based control of aquatic robotic platforms requires hydrodynamic models that are costly to identify and highly specific to hull, payload, and operating conditions. This motivates a system that can avoid dedicated identification trials and adapt online without a costly bespoke model.
AI.method: MOSAIC-SV combines a physically admissible unscented Kalman filter that re-estimates hydrodynamic, disturbance, and actuator parameters at each control step; a command-dependent consider projection that withholds corrections the current command cannot attribute between actuator effectiveness and external force; and a model predictive path integral controller that plans on the current estimate. It starts from a spec-sheet engineering prior and updates during closed-loop operation.
AI.result: In CyberShip II simulations, MOSAIC-SV matches calibrated-model transit performance under static mismatch and transient changes, and stays within 20% of its unscaled-prior transit time when inertia or damping priors are off by an order of magnitude. On-water BlueBoat trials show at least 25% faster transits and at least 56% lower motion prediction error than a frozen engineering prior, including with an unmodeled payload. The concept was also feasibly deployed on a 6.3-tonne dual outboard monohull.
AI.conclusion: MOSAIC-SV enables real-time adaptive hydrodynamic identification and control from a spec-sheet prior without dedicated identification trials, improving transit performance and prediction accuracy across simulation and field trials, and demonstrating feasibility on a much larger vessel.

title: Sparse Calibration-Based Personalization of Kernel-Based Gait Phase and Speed Estimation Using Wearable IMUs
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, The 26th International Conference on Control, Automation, and Systems (ICCAS 2026)
summary: This paper presents sparse calibration-based personalization for kernel-based gait phase and walking speed co-estimation from wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs). A 28-speed reference library was constructed from bilateral thigh and shank trajectories in a 20-subject locomotion dataset. Rather than directly applying population-average kernels, the method combines a user-specific baseline estimated from three calibration speeds with a principal-component (PC) model of baseline-centered kinematic deviations. Offline validation showed that personalized kernels reduced phase error relative to the population kernel. In a single-participant online pilot evaluation, the personalized kernels produced numerically lower mean phase and speed errors and ran in real time on embedded hardware. However, the speed effect was not significant, and pairwise phase differences did not remain significant after multiple-comparison correction. The pilot evaluation establishes wearable implementation feasibility while indicating reference-to-online dataset mismatch and the need for larger-cohort validation.

AI.tldr: A sparse calibration-based personalization method for kernel-based gait phase and walking speed co-estimation from wearable IMUs is proposed, using a 3-speed user baseline plus a PC model of kinematic deviations; personalized kernels reduced phase error offline and ran in real time online, but speed gains and phase significance were limited.
AI.motivation: Population-average kernels are not well matched to individual users, degrading gait phase and walking speed estimation accuracy from wearable IMUs. A lightweight personalization approach is needed that requires only sparse calibration while remaining feasible for real-time embedded operation.
AI.method: A 28-speed reference library was built from bilateral thigh and shank trajectories in a 20-subject locomotion dataset. Instead of applying population-average kernels directly, the method combines a user-specific baseline estimated from three calibration speeds with a principal-component (PC) model of baseline-centered kinematic deviations, yielding personalized kernels for co-estimation of gait phase and walking speed.
AI.result: Offline validation showed personalized kernels reduced phase error relative to the population kernel. In a single-participant online pilot, personalized kernels gave numerically lower mean phase and speed errors and ran in real time on embedded hardware. However, the speed effect was not significant, and pairwise phase differences did not remain significant after multiple-comparison correction.
AI.conclusion: The pilot confirms wearable implementation feasibility of sparse calibration-based personalization, while revealing reference-to-online dataset mismatch and the need for larger-cohort validation to establish robust benefits.

title: Training Numerical Intelligence via Auto-Diagnosis and Skill Discovery
summary: AI agents are becoming increasingly capable of generating scientific code, but generating code is not the same as improving the algorithms behind it. For numerical solvers, execution feedback can expose poor performance, but rarely reveals its underlying cause and how to address it. We introduce Auto-Diagnosis and Skill Discovery (ADSD), a framework that links numerical diagnosis to reusable solver self-improvement. ADSD follows a diagnosis-first paradigm that first explains why a solver performs poorly, then uses this diagnosis to guide the discovery of appropriate numerical methods. The resulting knowledge is packaged into reusable solver skills, turning solver improvement from trial-and-error editing into a structured process of diagnosis, discovery, and implementation. Across four challenging numerical domains--power flow equation, AC optimal power flow control, stiff ordinary differential equations, and heterogeneous diffusion PDEs--ADSD consistently improves solver accuracy, robustness, and efficiency. On GOC-500 power flow, for example, ADSD reduces mean solver error by nearly $71\times$, with improvements further transferring to unseen grid topologies and operating regimes.

AI.tldr: ADSD is a diagnosis-first framework that links numerical diagnosis to reusable solver self-improvement, enabling agents to move beyond code generation toward structured discovery of better numerical methods.
AI.motivation: AI agents can generate scientific code but cannot reliably improve the underlying algorithms. For numerical solvers, execution feedback exposes poor performance but rarely reveals the root cause or how to fix it, so improvement remains trial-and-error.
AI.method: ADSD follows a diagnosis-first paradigm: it first explains why a solver performs poorly, then uses that diagnosis to guide discovery of appropriate numerical methods. The resulting knowledge is packaged into reusable solver skills, converting solver improvement into a structured process of diagnosis, discovery, and implementation.
AI.result: Across four challenging numerical domains—power flow equations, AC optimal power flow control, stiff ODEs, and heterogeneous diffusion PDEs—ADSD consistently improves solver accuracy, robustness, and efficiency. On GOC-500 power flow, it cuts mean solver error by nearly 71x, with gains transferring to unseen grid topologies and operating regimes.
AI.conclusion: Linking numerical diagnosis to reusable skill discovery enables structured, transferable solver self-improvement beyond mere scientific code generation.

title: REDIRECT: A 1% Fix for Bad Robot Habits
summary: Robots can acquire bad habits from a few defective moments in otherwise useful teleoperation. In mixed-quality robot data, normal and problematic demonstrations share most task behavior and differ only at a local action continuation. Full retraining is costly, while fine-tuning on clean data alone offers limited recovery under a small update budget. We ask whether the local difference can instead be fixed with only 1% of the full-training sample-backward budget. Using only episode-level retained/problematic labels, REDIRECT localizes the branch, assigns a coherent retained continuation to the original observations around it, and anchors shared behavior, without frame-level annotations or additional interaction. Across three randomized ManiSkill tasks and three seeds, REDIRECT raises the mean success rate from 68.2% to 90.3%, recovering 88.8% of the clean-retraining gap versus 22.1% for matched-compute fine-tuning. On a PiPER arm, it recovers 86.7-92.9% of the clean-only gap across cup insertion and towel folding. Local robot habits can therefore be repaired by spending the update budget on the behavioral difference rather than relearning shared behavior.

AI.tldr: REDIRECT repairs local "bad habits" in mixed-quality robot teleoperation data by spending only 1% of the full-training sample-backward budget on the local behavioral difference, using only episode-level labels; it substantially outperforms matched-compute fine-tuning across simulated and real tasks.
AI.motivation: Robots can acquire bad habits from a few defective moments in otherwise useful teleoperation. In mixed-quality data, normal and problematic demonstrations share most task behavior and differ only at a local action continuation. Full retraining is costly, and fine-tuning on clean data alone gives limited recovery under a small update budget. The question is whether the local difference can be fixed without frame-level annotations or additional interaction.
AI.method: Using only episode-level retained/problematic labels, REDIRECT localizes the branch point, assigns a coherent retained continuation to the original observations around it, and anchors shared behavior. It requires no frame-level annotations and no additional interaction.
AI.result: Across three randomized ManiSkill tasks and three seeds, REDIRECT raises the mean success rate from 68.2% to 90.3%, recovering 88.8% of the clean-retraining gap versus 22.1% for matched-compute fine-tuning. On a PiPER arm, it recovers 86.7-92.9% of the clean-only gap across cup insertion and towel folding.
AI.conclusion: Local robot habits can be repaired by spending the update budget on the behavioral difference rather than relearning shared behavior.

title: REACT: Physically and Chemically Consistent Reconstruction of Marine Active Tracers
summary: Reconstructing global sea surface pH from sparse observations is critical for monitoring ocean acidification and understanding marine carbon cycling. Traditional assimilation and inverse models are physically grounded but costly for large-scale reconstruction. Recent black-box and physics-guided AI models improve efficiency, but are mainly designed for passive tracers, where the reconstructed variable is also the transported inventory. In contrast, pH is an active carbonate tracer: it is the prediction target, while dissolved inorganic carbon (DIC) is the conserved carbon inventory. This mismatch can produce low pH error while violating carbonate closure and source-free carbon conservation. To address this, we introduce \textbf{REACT}, a carbon-first reconstruction framework that decouples transport, active correction, and chemical decoding. REACT transports a latent carbonate state with a conservative advection--diffusion solver, captures non-conservative carbon-cycle variations with a source module, decodes the corrected state into pH, and constrains the output through carbonate equilibrium. This design keeps pH as the target while enforcing consistency on the underlying carbon state. On simulation data, REACT reduces pH NRMSE by (14.7%) and chemical consistency error by (24.0%) over the best baseline. Cross-temporal-scale evaluations show robustness against error accumulation from coarse to fine temporal scales, and ablation studies validate the effectiveness of each component.

AI.tldr: REACT is a carbon-first framework that reconstructs global sea surface pH by transporting a latent carbonate state (conserving DIC), correcting non-conservative carbon-cycle variations, and decoding to pH under carbonate equilibrium constraints—reducing pH NRMSE by 14.7% and chemical consistency error by 24.0% over the best baseline.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing global sea surface pH from sparse observations is essential for monitoring ocean acidification and understanding marine carbon cycling. Traditional assimilation/inverse models are physically grounded but computationally expensive for large-scale reconstruction, while recent AI models (black-box and physics-guided) are efficient but mainly target passive tracers, where the reconstructed variable equals the transported inventory. pH, however, is an active carbonate tracer—the prediction target—while DIC is the conserved carbon inventory. This mismatch allows low pH error while violating carbonate closure and source-free carbon conservation.
AI.method: REACT decouples three stages: (1) transports a latent carbonate state via a conservative advection–diffusion solver; (2) captures non-conservative carbon-cycle variations with a source module (active correction); (3) decodes the corrected state into pH and constrains outputs through carbonate equilibrium. This keeps pH as the target while enforcing consistency on the underlying carbon state.
AI.result: On simulation data, REACT reduces pH NRMSE by 14.7% and chemical consistency error by 24.0% relative to the best baseline. Cross-temporal-scale evaluations demonstrate robustness against error accumulation from coarse to fine temporal scales, and ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component.
AI.conclusion: By reformulating pH reconstruction as a carbon-first problem that separates transport, active correction, and chemical decoding, REACT improves both accuracy and physical/chemical consistency over prior AI-based reconstruction models.

title: SUAVE: Unified Video-Action Models via Masked Diffusion
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) inherit strong semantic grounding from pretrained vision-language backbones but are typically optimized for predicting actions rather than future observations. They can see and act, but they do not imagine the future before acting. World action models (WAMs) built on video diffusion backbones can imagine but treat language as frozen conditioning on a continuous latent space. Unified models bring these modalities into one architecture, but they either decode autoregressively, one token at a time, or keep video continuous with an auxiliary action head. In this work, we present SUAVE, a Single vocabulary Unified Action-Video modEl in which a masked diffusion transformer generates video and actions conditioned on language, with all three modalities represented as discrete tokens in a shared sequence. Choosing which tokens to mask at inference turns the same network into a world model, a robot policy, or a video-action model. For action-free co-training, the action positions of unlabeled video are filled with mask tokens and excluded from the loss. Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate two findings. First, a single SUAVE model predicts long-horizon video and acts as a policy, competitive with dedicated world models and specialized action policies on static and dynamic manipulation tasks. On a real robot, our model generates subgoal images and an action chunk spanning one second of motion in 1,030 ms on an RTX 5090 GPU, sustaining closed-loop control at 2.5 actions per second. Second, pretraining on robot video and co-training on human video substantially improves policy performance and zero-shot robustness to distribution shift. Together, these results show that masked diffusion is a practical and versatile foundation for unified video-action modeling.

AI.tldr: SUAVE is a single-vocabulary unified action-video model built on a masked diffusion transformer that represents video, actions, and language as discrete tokens in one shared sequence, enabling the same network to act as a world model, policy, or video-action model by choosing which tokens to mask at inference.
AI.motivation: VLAs predict actions without imagining future observations; video-diffusion world action models imagine but treat language as frozen conditioning on a continuous latent space; existing unified models either decode autoregressively token-by-token or keep video continuous with an auxiliary action head. These limitations motivate a unified architecture that jointly models video and actions in a shared discrete space.
AI.method: SUAVE uses a masked diffusion transformer to generate video and actions conditioned on language, with all three modalities as discrete tokens in a shared sequence. Inference-time token masking switches the network between world model, robot policy, and video-action model roles. For action-free co-training, action positions of unlabeled video are filled with mask tokens and excluded from the loss.
AI.result: A single SUAVE model predicts long-horizon video and acts as a policy, competitive with dedicated world models and specialized action policies on static and dynamic manipulation tasks. On a real robot, it generates subgoal images and a one-second action chunk in 1,030 ms on an RTX 5090 GPU, sustaining closed-loop control at 2.5 actions per second. Pretraining on robot video and co-training on human video substantially improve policy performance and zero-shot robustness to distribution shift.
AI.conclusion: Masked diffusion provides a practical and versatile foundation for unified video-action modeling.

title: Proxy Confidence: Auditing Black-Box LLM Agents with a Surrogate's Log-Probabilities
summary:
A deployed LLM agent emits tool calls, queries, and code that can be silently wrong -- by the time the error surfaces, the action has run. Frontier chat APIs hide the model's token probabilities; the agent's stated confidence barely beats chance on the mistakes that matter; and resampling does not help, since frontier models are highly repetitive, reproducing the same call across samples.
  We recover the missing signal from a low-cost open-weight surrogate run in parallel. It reads the same context, schema, and proposed action as the agent, then scores the call from its own log-probabilities through a family of complementary readouts: teacher forcing and request-PMI weigh the likelihood of each argument value, a discriminative verdict judges the call as a whole, and tool-choice competition tests the function against its siblings. One principle says which to trust: a generative likelihood localizes wrong argument values, while the verdict catches holistically wrong calls. When the error type is unknown, an ensemble is the low-regret default. The readout is training-free, needs no access to the agent's internals, and costs one prefill pass alongside the tool call.
  On difficult coding tasks it reaches AUROC 0.825 where the actor's stated confidence is near chance (0.598), and the generative readouts beat it by +0.07 to +0.28 across three further actors. Against self-consistency it gains +0.14 to +0.19 on near-deterministic actors, at 1/K the cost. The signal drives two deployment modes: a real-time gate escalating the least-trustworthy calls for review (+0.05 to +0.30 accepted-action accuracy at 50% coverage), and confidence feedback, returning the tool result with the score so the agent adapts its next step -- lifting task success on live-execution benchmarks (+0.119 and +0.137, p <= 1e-4) and beating a random-value control where step errors are silent (+0.078, p = 0.003).

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a training-free, low-cost method to detect silently wrong tool calls from LLM agents by running a small open-weight surrogate model in parallel that scores the proposed call via multiple log-probability readouts, improving error detection and downstream task success.
AI.motivation: Deployed LLM agents can emit silently wrong tool calls, queries, or code, and errors are only visible after execution. Frontier chat APIs hide token probabilities, the agent's stated confidence is barely above chance on critical mistakes, and resampling is ineffective because frontier models are highly repetitive, reproducing the same erroneous call.
AI.method: A low-cost open-weight surrogate model is run in parallel, reading the same context, schema, and proposed action. It scores the call using its own log-probabilities through complementary readouts: teacher forcing and request-PMI for per-argument likelihood, a discriminative verdict for holistic call correctness, and tool-choice competition against sibling functions. A generative likelihood localizes wrong argument values while the verdict catches holistically wrong calls; an ensemble is used when error type is unknown. The approach is training-free, requires no access to the agent's internals, and costs one prefill pass.
AI.result: On difficult coding tasks, the method reaches AUROC 0.825 versus the actor's near-chance stated confidence of 0.598. Generative readouts beat stated confidence by +0.07 to +0.28 across three further actors. Against self-consistency, it gains +0.14 to +0.19 on near-deterministic actors at 1/K the cost. A real-time gate escalating least-trustworthy calls improves accepted-action accuracy by +0.05 to +0.30 at 50% coverage. Confidence feedback lifting task success by +0.119 and +0.137 (p <= 1e-4) and beating a random-value control where step errors are silent (+0.078, p = 0.003).
AI.conclusion: Recovering error signals from a parallel open-weight surrogate via log-probability readouts provides an effective, cheap, and training-free way to detect silently wrong agent actions, supporting real-time escalation and confidence feedback that improve downstream task success.

title: Return-to-Home Feasible Micro-Aerial Vehicle Exploration for 3D Gaussian Splatting Reconstruction
comment: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on INTELLIGENT ROBOTS & SYSTEMS 2026
summary: Micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) enable rapid indoor 3D reconstruction for inspection and time-critical situational awareness, but must operate under strict flight-time budgets and safety constraints that require explicit return-to-home (RTH) feasibility with a conservative margin. We present a topology-first active reconstruction framework that decouples high-fidelity rendering from navigation. A dense 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) map is optimized as the reconstruction target, while a lightweight Truncated Signed Distance Field (TSDF)/occupancy scaffold supports conservative collision checking and online construction of a sparse 3D Voronoi skeleton roadmap. Since directly extracting roadmaps from TSDF geometry can be unstable under noisy and incomplete online fusion, we validate nodes and edges using carved free-space consistency and dense visibility checks, which suppress behind-wall phantom structure and stabilize planning. Viewpoints are selected on the roadmap using a flight-time-budget-aware objective and a lightweight receding-horizon lookahead to improve non-myopic exploration behavior. We evaluate on photorealistic indoor simulation benchmarks (ReplicaCAD, Gibson, and HM3D), reporting reconstruction coverage/error, RTH success, and computational cost. Results demonstrate improved or competitive performance relative to recent GS-based baselines under identical flight-time budgets.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a topology-first active 3D reconstruction framework for micro aerial vehicles that decouples high-fidelity rendering from navigation, using a 3D Gaussian Splatting map as the reconstruction target while a lightweight TSDF/occupancy scaffold supports conservative collision checking and a sparse Voronoi skeleton roadmap for planning under flight-time budgets.
AI.motivation: MAVs can rapidly perform indoor 3D reconstruction for inspection and time-critical situational awareness, but they operate under strict flight-time budgets and safety constraints. This requires explicit return-to-home (RTH) feasibility with a conservative margin, which existing approaches may not adequately address.
AI.method: A topology-first active reconstruction framework decoupling high-fidelity rendering from navigation. A dense 3DGS map serves as the reconstruction target, while a lightweight TSDF/occupancy scaffold supports conservative collision checking and online construction of a sparse 3D Voronoi skeleton roadmap. Nodes and edges are validated via carved free-space consistency and dense visibility checks to suppress behind-wall phantom structure and stabilize planning. Viewpoints are selected on the roadmap using a flight-time-budget-aware objective and a lightweight receding-horizon lookahead for non-myopic exploration.
AI.result: Evaluation on photorealistic indoor simulation benchmarks (ReplicaCAD, Gibson, HM3D) reports reconstruction coverage/error, RTH success, and computational cost. The method demonstrates improved or competitive performance relative to recent GS-based baselines under identical flight-time budgets.
AI.conclusion: The topology-first framework achieves improved or competitive reconstruction performance versus recent GS-based baselines while satisfying flight-time budgets and conservative RTH feasibility, validating the decoupling of rendering from navigation for MAV-based indoor reconstruction.

title: SGAnalog: An End-to-End Circuit Benchmark from Open-Source Silicon Tapeouts
comment: Accepted at the AI for Chip Design Workshop at NeurIPS 2026
summary: Existing analog integrated circuit design benchmarks make two questions hard to answer: whether a model has learned transferable circuit skills rather than recalled familiar examples, and whether its output works under defined process and test conditions. We introduce a benchmark built from human-designed, open-source circuits associated with Tiny Tapeout manufacturing shuttles. The collection contains 273 topologically distinct top-level designs. Every source is retrieved at the revision recorded for its shuttle submission and processed in a fixed containerized environment. The pipeline exports each eligible schematic image and its SPICE netlist from the same source file, giving transcription an exact structural reference. Commit dates support model-specific training-cutoff analysis, while author testbenches provide the simulation context for sizing. The benchmark evaluates schematic-to-netlist transcription and device sizing. Across seven models on a fixed set of 66 transcription tasks, the strongest model reaches 56.1% exact graph isomorphism, and six of seven models drop sharply from the small to the medium tier. For one frontier model, removing author-chosen labels reduces exact matches while preserving aggregate structural F1, suggesting that labels can aid connectivity tracing. On the 17 sizing tasks, the leading model converges on all 17 proposals and reaches 91.2 out of 100 against the human reference, while the two newest Claude models refuse 4 and 11 of the same prompts they transcribe without objection; a proposal without sizes scores zero. The two tasks produce different model rankings, exposing distinct visual and design capabilities and, in one family, a policy rather than capability limit.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a benchmark of 273 human-designed, Tiny Tapeout-associated analog circuits, retrieved at shuttle-submission revisions and processed in a fixed containerized environment, which jointly evaluates schematic-to-netlist transcription and device sizing to test transferable circuit skills and manufacturability-aware correctness.
AI.motivation: Existing analog IC design benchmarks cannot readily answer whether a model has learned transferable circuit skills rather than recalled familiar examples, nor whether its output works under defined process and test conditions. The work aims to close this gap by building a provenance-controlled, structurally verifiable benchmark from real manufacturing-taped designs.
AI.method: A benchmark was constructed from human-designed open-source circuits associated with Tiny Tapeout manufacturing shuttles, comprising 273 topologically distinct top-level designs. Each source is retrieved at the revision recorded for its shuttle submission and processed in a fixed containerized environment. The pipeline exports each eligible schematic image and its SPICE netlist from the same source file, providing an exact structural reference for transcription. Commit dates enable model-specific training-cutoff analysis, while author testbenches supply the simulation context for sizing. Two tasks are evaluated: schematic-to-netlist transcription and device sizing.
AI.result: Across seven models on 66 fixed transcription tasks, the strongest reaches 56.1% exact graph isomorphism, and six of seven models drop sharply from the small to the medium tier. For one frontier model, removing author-chosen labels lowers exact matches while preserving aggregate structural F1, indicating labels can aid connectivity tracing. On 17 sizing tasks, the leading model converges on all 17 proposals and scores 91.2/100 against the human reference, whereas the two newest Claude models refuse 4 and 11 of the same prompts they transcribe without objection; a proposal without sizes scores zero. The two tasks yield different model rankings.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark exposes two distinct competencies—visual transcription and design/sizing capability—that rank models differently, with one family showing a policy rather than capability limit on sizing prompts. Provenance-controlled, revision-pinned circuits with paired schematic/netlist export and author testbenches provide a rigorous basis for assessing transferable circuit skill and simulation-context correctness.

title: A Biomimetic Gaze Control to Restore Head-Neck Movements
summary: Powered neck exoskeletons are developed to restore head-neck motions for those with neck muscle weakness. Current methods using hand-held input devices to control these robotic systems are unintuitive or non-viable for these populations. Alternatively, the eyes coordinate with the head to accomplish many daily tasks. Therefore, movements of the eyes can be a useful signal to control the neck exoskeletons without needing to use the hands. However, previous control models lack biobehavioral basis as well as means to personalize the control behavior, causing unnatural head-neck movements. This paper presents a novel eye-tracking controller design leveraging the vestibulo-ocular reflex to emulate natural eyehead coordination. Personalization tools were also designed, consisting of sliders to allow users to adjust the parameters of this controller. Here, we present the technical design and validation of this system in human users. Compared to the previous eye-tracking model, the new controller provides natural head motions personalized to the user through more natural velocity profiles and a 24 percent average increase of accurate motion intent detection. This system provides a powerful platform for studying eye-tracking controllers in the context of personalization and preference, and ultimately restoring the lost head-neck mobility in patient populations.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an eye-tracking controller for powered neck exoskeletons that leverages the vestibulo-ocular reflex to emulate natural eye-head coordination, with personalization sliders; it yields more natural velocity profiles and a 24% average increase in motion intent detection accuracy over prior work.
AI.motivation: Powered neck exoskeletons can restore head-neck motion for people with neck muscle weakness, but current hand-held input controls are unintuitive or non-viable for these users. Eyes naturally coordinate with the head in daily tasks, making eye movements a useful hands-free control signal. However, previous eye-tracking control models lack biobehavioral basis and personalization, producing unnatural head-neck movements.
AI.method: A novel eye-tracking controller design that leverages the vestibulo-ocular reflex to emulate natural eye-head coordination. Personalization tools were also designed, consisting of sliders enabling users to tune the controller parameters.
AI.result: Technical design and validation in human users. Compared with the previous eye-tracking model, the new controller produced more natural velocity profiles and a 24 percent average increase in accurate motion intent detection, with head motions personalized to the user.
AI.conclusion: The system provides a powerful platform for studying eye-tracking controllers in the context of personalization and preference, and ultimately for restoring lost head-neck mobility in patient populations.

title: MLLMs Fail to Refuse when Using Tools Agentically
summary: Agentic multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have recently pushed the frontier of visual reasoning by calling tools such as zooming and tagging. Despite the recent strong success of agentic MLLMs, this work uncovers a critical safety failure in the tool-use paradigm: agentic tool-using MLLMs become less capable of refusing harmful requests. Our experiments confirm that, across three popular safety benchmarks, all the top open- and closed-weight MLLMs we test exhibit significantly lower safety in tool-using settings than in non-tool settings, with a relative refusal failure rate increase of up to 68.7%. Based on analysis of 100,000+ responses, including extended experiments, we also propose two possible reasons for this safety degradation.

AI.tldr: Agentic multimodal LLMs that use tools (e.g., zooming, tagging) show markedly degraded safety refusal compared to non-tool settings, with refusal failure rate increasing up to 68.7% across three safety benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Agentic MLLMs have advanced visual reasoning via tool use, but this work identifies a critical safety gap: tool-using MLLMs become less able to refuse harmful requests than in non-tool settings.
AI.method: Empirical evaluation of top open- and closed-weight MLLMs across three popular safety benchmarks, comparing tool-using vs. non-tool settings, with analysis of over 100,000 responses and extended experiments to identify causes.
AI.result: All tested top MLLMs exhibit significantly lower safety in tool-using settings, with a relative refusal failure rate increase of up to 68.7%.
AI.conclusion: Tool use introduces a critical safety failure in agentic MLLMs, and the authors propose two possible reasons for this safety degradation based on their large-scale response analysis.

title: Reward-DAgger: Robot-Gated Interactive Imitation Learning with General-Purpose Progress-Based Reward Models
summary: Recent advances in robot learning have enabled generalist control policies capable of completing a wide range of tasks. However, their performance degrades when deployed in unseen environments, making it critical to detect failures and teach recovery behaviors. Existing runtime monitoring methods often require task- and policy-specific training or hyperparameter tuning, limiting cross-task deployment and introducing additional overhead during iterative policy updates. We present Reward-DAgger, a robot-gated interactive imitation learning framework that uses dense progress signals from a general-purpose reward model to determine when human intervention is needed. Our approach is agnostic to the underlying policy architecture, requires no access to policy internals, and can be applied across tasks without retuning the gating mechanism. Our results show that Reward-DAgger achieves a better failure-detection accuracy-latency tradeoff than existing runtime monitoring baselines. Across eight simulated and real-world tasks, Reward-DAgger consistently improves the downstream policy's autonomous success rate throughout interactive learning and achieves strong return on human effort, outperforming the baselines in most settings. Importantly, the same gating configuration is used across tasks without task-specific hyperparameter tuning, demonstrating transfer across tasks, environments, and policy architectures. Code and videos are available at https://liralab.usc.edu/reward-dagger.

AI.tldr: Reward-DAgger is a robot-gated interactive imitation learning framework that leverages dense progress signals from a general-purpose reward model to decide when human intervention is needed, achieving better failure-detection accuracy-latency tradeoffs and consistent success-rate improvements across tasks without task-specific tuning.
AI.motivation: Generalist control policies degrade in unseen environments, so detecting failures and teaching recovery behaviors is critical. Existing runtime monitoring methods require task- and policy-specific training or hyperparameter tuning, which limits cross-task deployment and adds overhead during iterative policy updates.
AI.method: Reward-DAgger uses dense progress signals from a general-purpose reward model to gate human intervention. The approach is agnostic to the underlying policy architecture, requires no access to policy internals, and can be applied across tasks without retuning the gating mechanism.
AI.result: Reward-DAgger achieves a better failure-detection accuracy-latency tradeoff than existing runtime monitoring baselines. Across eight simulated and real-world tasks, it consistently improves the downstream policy's autonomous success rate throughout interactive learning and achieves strong return on human effort, outperforming baselines in most settings. The same gating configuration transfers across tasks, environments, and policy architectures.
AI.conclusion: Reward-DAgger provides a task-agnostic, policy-agnostic gating mechanism for interactive imitation learning that improves failure detection and autonomous success rates while maximizing return on human effort, demonstrating transferability without task-specific hyperparameter tuning.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Model Decision-Making for Autonomous Driving Guided by Chinese Philosophical Wisdom
summary: Autonomous driving decision systems must balance safety, efficiency, and social norms in complex traffic interactions. Philosophical and ethical considerations have received limited attention in existing autonomous driving decision-making approaches based on numerical optimization, sequence prediction, and large language models (LLMs). We propose Chinese Philosophical Wisdom-Guided Driving (CPW-Drive), a closed-loop retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework that incorporates value guidance derived from Chinese philosophy into autonomous driving decision-making. Using Chinese Confucian thought as its knowledge source, CPW-Drive consolidates LLM-extracted keywords from relevant classical texts into driving-relevant value principles through manual screening and validation. It then contextualizes these principles through scenario-specific cases to form retrievable and reusable value guidance. We further propose Physics-aware Spatial Similarity Retrieval (PSSR), which compares vehicle layouts and velocity-extrapolated states to retrieve physically relevant historical cases. On Highway-env's multilane highway-driving task, CPW-Drive achieves success rates of 93.0%, 86.0%, and 72.0% across three traffic configurations. These results outperform the strongest baseline by 8.0, 22.5, and 25.0 percentage points, respectively. Across all configurations, CPW-Drive achieves the highest collision-free step count and maintains a low lane-change frequency. The results suggest that structured value guidance can improve simulated closed-loop safety and stability while introducing efficiency and latency trade-offs.

AI.tldr: CPW-Drive is a closed-loop RAG framework that injects Chinese philosophical value principles into autonomous driving decision-making, retrieving physically relevant historical cases via PSSR and outperforming the strongest baseline on multilane highway tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing autonomous driving decision approaches (numerical optimization, sequence prediction, LLMs) largely neglect philosophical and ethical considerations, leaving a gap in value-aligned, socially normative decision-making.
AI.method: The framework builds a value knowledge source from Chinese Confucian classical texts: LLM-extracted keywords are consolidated into driving-relevant value principles via manual screening and validation, then contextualized through scenario-specific cases into retrievable value guidance. A Physics-aware Spatial Similarity Retrieval (PSSR) module compares vehicle layouts and velocity-extrapolated states to retrieve physically relevant historical cases in a closed-loop RAG pipeline.
AI.result: On Highway-env's multilane highway task, CPW-Drive reaches success rates of 93.0%, 86.0%, and 72.0% across three traffic configurations, exceeding the strongest baseline by 8.0, 22.5, and 25.0 percentage points. It also achieves the highest collision-free step count in all configurations while maintaining low lane-change frequency, with trade-offs in efficiency and latency.
AI.conclusion: Structured value guidance from philosophical knowledge can improve simulated closed-loop safety and stability in autonomous driving, though at the cost of efficiency and latency.

title: Terrain-Dependent Intra-Cycle Leg Timing for Effective Locomotion on Granular Slopes
summary: Locomotion on granular slopes such as sand dunes remains a fundamental challenge for legged robots due to reduced shear strength and gravity-induced anisotropic yielding of granular media. Using a hexapedal robot on a tiltable granular bed, we systematically measure locomotion speed together with slope-dependent normal and shear granular resistive forces. While normal penetration resistance remains nearly unchanged with inclination, shear resistance decreases substantially as slope angle increases. Guided by these measurements, we develop a simple robot-terrain interaction model that predicts anchoring timing, step length, and resulting robot speed, as functions of terrain strength and slope angle. The model reveals that slope-induced performance loss is primarily governed by delayed anchoring and increased backward slip rather than excessive sinkage. By extending the model to generalized terrain conditions, we construct failure phase diagrams that identify sinkage- and slippage-induced failure regimes, enabling quantitative risk estimation for locomotion on granular slopes. This physics-informed framework provides predictive insight into terrain-dependent failure mechanisms and offers guidance for safer and more robust robot operation on deformable inclines.

AI.tldr: This paper studies legged-robot locomotion on granular slopes by measuring slope-dependent resistive forces on a hexapedal robot, builds a robot-terrain interaction model that predicts anchoring timing, step length, and speed, and constructs failure phase diagrams separating sinkage- and slippage-induced failure regimes.
AI.motivation: Locomotion on granular slopes like sand dunes is fundamentally challenging for legged robots because granular media exhibit reduced shear strength and gravity-induced anisotropic yielding, yet the underlying terrain-dependent failure mechanisms remain poorly understood.
AI.method: Using a hexapedal robot on a tiltable granular bed, the authors systematically measure locomotion speed along with slope-dependent normal and shear granular resistive forces. Guided by these measurements, they develop a simplified robot-terrain interaction model predicting anchoring timing, step length, and robot speed as functions of terrain strength and slope angle, then extend it to generalized terrain conditions to build failure phase diagrams.
AI.result: Normal penetration resistance stays nearly unchanged with inclination, whereas shear resistance decreases substantially as slope angle increases. The model shows that slope-induced performance loss is governed primarily by delayed anchoring and increased backward slip rather than excessive sinkage. The failure phase diagrams identify distinct sinkage- and slippage-induced failure regimes, enabling quantitative risk estimation.
AI.conclusion: This physics-informed framework provides predictive insight into terrain-dependent failure mechanisms and offers guidance for safer, more robust robot operation on deformable inclines.

title: LatentQuant: Preserving the Policy-Facing Latent Contract under NVFP4 VAE Quantization
summary: Recent world action models (WAMs) reuse pretrained video VAEs whose encoder latents directly condition downstream action policies. Quantization must therefore preserve not only reconstruction fidelity but also the policy-facing latent contract expected by the frozen policy. Direct NVFP4 leaves W4A4 quantization error uncompensated, whereas joint quantization-aware training (QAT) can recover reconstruction by moving this representation. On Wan2.1, joint QAT nearly matches FP32 VBench-7 (0.7403 versus 0.7409), yet LIBERO success collapses from 95.5% to 10.5%. Controlled decoder-only experiments show that activation quantize-dequantize operations alter the reconstruction signal and decoder Jacobian, redirecting the gradient returned to the encoder and inducing persistent latent drift. Based on this mechanism, we introduce LatentQuant, a two-stage NVFP4 QAT framework that first aligns the quantized encoder with its high-precision counterpart, then freezes it while adapting the decoder. Across Wan2.1 and Wan2.2, LatentQuant preserves near-baseline control and high reconstruction quality, achieving 95.75% success on LIBERO and 68.8% on RoboTwin. On NVIDIA B300 GPUs, NVFP4 execution achieves 1.17x-1.26x end-to-end VAE speedups over BF16 cuDNN.

AI.tldr: LatentQuant is a two-stage NVFP4 quantization-aware training framework for world action models that preserves both reconstruction quality and policy-facing latent contracts, achieving near-baseline control performance and end-to-end VAE speedups.
AI.motivation: World action models reuse pretrained video VAEs whose encoder latents directly condition downstream action policies, so quantization must preserve not only reconstruction fidelity but also the latent contract expected by the frozen policy. Direct NVFP4 leaves W4A4 quantization error uncompensated, while joint QAT can recover reconstruction by moving the representation but disrupts policy performance.
AI.method: LatentQuant is a two-stage NVFP4 QAT framework that first aligns the quantized encoder with its high-precision counterpart, then freezes the encoder while adapting the decoder. The design is motivated by controlled decoder-only experiments showing that activation quantize-dequantize operations alter the reconstruction signal and decoder Jacobian, redirecting gradients to the encoder and causing persistent latent drift.
AI.result: On Wan2.1, joint QAT nearly matches FP32 VBench-7 (0.7403 vs. 0.7409) but LIBERO success collapses from 95.5% to 10.5%. LatentQuant across Wan2.1 and Wan2.2 preserves near-baseline control and high reconstruction quality, reaching 95.75% success on LIBERO and 68.8% on RoboTwin, with 1.17x-1.26x end-to-end VAE speedups over BF16 cuDNN on NVIDIA B300 GPUs.
AI.conclusion: Aligning the quantized encoder before adapting the decoder mitigates latent drift and preserves the policy-facing latent contract, enabling efficient NVFP4 deployment of world action models without sacrificing control performance.

title: Autoware in Construction: Gap Analysis and LiDAR Perception Toward Off-Road Autonomous Driving
comment: 2026 IROS 5th Workshop on Future of Construction, 4 pages, 5 figures
summary: Autoware is an open-source autonomous driving software platform widely adopted by researchers and industry developers. Originally developed primarily for public-road applications, including passenger vehicles, taxis, and buses, Autoware is increasingly being extended to off-road environments such as construction and agricultural sites. Construction sites, however, differ fundamentally from public roads and challenge many assumptions underlying conventional autonomous driving systems. They are characterized by unstructured terrain, airborne dust, continuously evolving site conditions, and construction-specific objects. This paper presents lessons learned from ongoing efforts to extend an Autoware-based autonomous driving system to large dump trucks operating at construction sites. We identify gaps between public-road and off-road construction applications across the sensing, mapping, localization, perception, planning, and control modules of the Autoware stack. We then discuss potential solutions for addressing these gaps, with particular emphasis on ongoing LiDAR-based perception pipeline development and findings from field testing. Finally, we propose a roadmap toward end-to-end autonomous driving for construction vehicles.

AI.tldr: This paper shares lessons from extending the Autoware autonomous driving stack to large dump trucks in construction sites, identifying module-by-module gaps between public-road and off-road settings and proposing solutions and a roadmap toward end-to-end autonomy for construction vehicles.
AI.motivation: Autoware was designed for public-road applications (passenger vehicles, taxis, buses) but is increasingly being extended to off-road domains like construction and agriculture. Construction sites violate many assumptions of conventional autonomous driving due to unstructured terrain, airborne dust, evolving site conditions, and construction-specific objects. The authors aim to document what breaks when adapting Autoware to such environments and how to address it.
AI.method: The study is based on ongoing practical efforts to extend an Autoware-based system to large dump trucks at construction sites. The authors conduct a gap analysis across the Autoware stack—sensing, mapping, localization, perception, planning, and control—comparing public-road versus off-road construction requirements. They propose solutions with emphasis on an ongoing LiDAR-based perception pipeline development and field-testing findings.
AI.result: The paper identifies gaps between public-road and construction-site applications across all major Autoware modules. It reports on ongoing development of a LiDAR-based perception pipeline and presents findings from field testing of the adapted system on construction vehicles.
AI.conclusion: The authors propose a roadmap toward end-to-end autonomous driving for construction vehicles, framing their lessons learned as guidance for extending public-road autonomous driving software to off-road construction environments.

title: ROAR: Unifying Runs across Heterogeneous AI-Driven Research Systems
summary: Each run of an AI-driven research system (ADRS) is an expensive search over a vast solution space, and dependable evaluation requires many runs, making run data both costly to produce and valuable to retain for large-scale analysis. Yet this data remains fragmented: teams operate in isolation, ADRS frameworks emit results in different formats, and no shared infrastructure exists to aggregate or compare runs across problems and systems. We present ROAR, a solution for systematically unifying and analyzing heterogeneous ADRS outputs. ROAR addresses two challenges: reconciling heterogeneous ADRS outputs and enabling analytics across runs with different objectives and scoring functions. We achieve this through a relational schema and parsing layer that normalize heterogeneous ADRS outputs while preserving data lineage and temporal structure, and accommodating new systems without requiring schema modifications. From building a corpus of more than 900 runs from multiple ADRS, we show how pooled data can reveal properties of problem landscapes that are difficult to observe. Consistent with prior work, runs with identical configurations may converge to different scores. We find that many runs realize most gains early, and that the effectiveness of different strategies for incorporating prior solutions into the search process varies across problems. We further show that the pooled corpus is actionable and not merely analytical by using ROAR to configure ADRS runs. Together, these results illustrate how pooled ADRS data can expose problem-dependent structure in search behavior that is difficult to detect from any single system, team, or benchmark. Such cross-cutting insights are difficult to obtain while runs remain siloed; ROAR is the first infrastructure designed to unify them.

AI.tldr: ROAR is a relational schema and parsing layer that unifies heterogeneous AI-driven research system (ADRS) outputs, enabling pooled cross-system analytics; a 900+ run corpus reveals problem-dependent search structure and supports actionable run configuration.
AI.motivation: ADRS runs are expensive and require many repetitions for dependable evaluation, making run data costly yet valuable. However, this data is fragmented: teams work in isolation, frameworks emit incompatible formats, and no shared infrastructure exists to aggregate or compare runs across problems and systems.
AI.method: ROAR normalizes heterogeneous ADRS outputs via a relational schema and parsing layer that preserve data lineage and temporal structure and accommodate new systems without schema changes. It specifically addresses reconciling heterogeneous outputs and enabling analytics across runs with different objectives and scoring functions.
AI.result: From a corpus of over 900 runs across multiple ADRS, ROAR shows that pooled data reveals problem-landscape properties hard to observe otherwise: identical configurations may converge to different scores (consistent with prior work), many runs realize most gains early, and the effectiveness of strategies for incorporating prior solutions varies across problems. The corpus is also actionable, demonstrated by using ROAR to configure ADRS runs.
AI.conclusion: Pooled ADRS data can expose problem-dependent structure in search behavior that is difficult to detect from any single system, team, or benchmark. ROAR is the first infrastructure designed to unify such siloed runs and enable cross-cutting insights.

title: Bi-manual Stabilization of the Cervical Spine for Safe Physical Human-Robot Interaction in Rolling Maneuvers
summary: The neck, specifically the cervical spine, is a highly fragile and mobile part of the body with a high risk of catastrophic injury. Whether someone is injured on a battlefield, in a natural disaster, or in an athletic event, great care is always taken with the cervical spine when transporting, rolling, or moving the patient. In this work, we present an algorithm and adaptations for bi-manual robots to stabilize the cervical spine during rolling maneuvers. We investigate techniques to maximize grip strength within safety bounds and present a control approach for proper neck rotation. We found that with our approach, a bi-manual robot is capable of achieving human-level performance in maintaining target rotational alignments. The axial alignment for the robot with prediction was within .21 degrees of human novices.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an algorithm enabling a bi-manual robot to stabilize the cervical spine during rolling maneuvers, achieving axial alignment within 0.21 degrees of human novices.
AI.motivation: The cervical spine is fragile and highly prone to catastrophic injury, so extreme care is required when transporting, rolling, or moving patients in battlefield, disaster, or athletic contexts. Robotic assistance could help perform these delicate maneuvers safely.
AI.method: The authors develop an algorithm and adaptations for bi-manual robots to stabilize the cervical spine during rolling maneuvers. They investigate techniques to maximize grip strength within safety bounds and introduce a control approach for proper neck rotation.
AI.result: The bi-manual robot achieves human-level performance in maintaining target rotational alignments. With prediction, its axial alignment was within 0.21 degrees of human novices.
AI.conclusion: A bi-manual robot using the proposed approach can match human-level performance in cervical spine stabilization during rolling maneuvers, demonstrating the feasibility of robotic assistance for this high-risk task.

title: Teaching Agents to Code Reliably
summary: Autonomous coding agents solve repository issues by reading code, running commands, editing files, and submitting patches. Extra inference-time compute yields gains only when it produces a useful repair and supplies reliable evidence for choosing one. Three behaviors decide both, and we argue they are teachable rather than byproducts of scale, so a policy can carry them instead of a scaffold. Location diversity remains narrow, since attempts return to the same site and extra samples add no coverage. Edit diversity is left unexploited, since methodologies that differ resolve complementary issues no single run reaches. Verification misleads, since a test the agent writes for its own patch accepts many incorrect ones. Directing search by execution feedback and scoring each patch against its own reverted tree resolves 52.8% of SWE-bench Verified using 48.1% of the agent-steps an eight-sample baseline spends. Training moves these behaviors into the policy. On the 270 issues held out from SFT and RL training, weighted supervised fine-tuning raises pass@1 from 31.9% to 35.2% and pass@8 from 46.7% to 51.1%. A reinforcement objective then trains the verifier against gold-labeled repairs and incorrect variants, crediting the assertions that detect them. It raises pass@1 to 43.0% and pass@8 to 60.7%, lifts verifier precision from 26.8% to 41.7%, and more than halves false acceptance. Resolution improves on two of three out-of-distribution suites and verifier precision on all three, and the gains hold at 7B, 14B, and 30B against published coder baselines.

AI.tldr: Autonomous coding agents are bottlenecked by three teachable behaviors—narrow location diversity, unexploited edit diversity, and misleading self-written verification. The authors direct search with execution feedback and score patches against reverted trees, then move these behaviors into the policy via weighted SFT and a RL verifier objective, achieving 52.8% on SWE-bench Verified and large pass@1/pass@8 and verifier-precision gains across 7B–30B models.
AI.motivation: Extra inference-time compute only helps when it yields a useful repair and provides reliable evidence to select among candidates. Three failure modes undermine this: location diversity stays narrow (repeated attempts revisit the same site), edit diversity goes unexploited (complementary methodologies are ignored), and self-written verification misleads (agent-authored tests accept many incorrect patches). The authors argue these behaviors are teachable rather than emergent byproducts of scale, so they can be embedded in the policy instead of handled by an external scaffold.
AI.method: A search procedure guided by execution feedback that scores each patch against its own reverted tree. These behaviors are then trained into the policy: weighted supervised fine-tuning, followed by a reinforcement objective that trains the verifier against gold-labeled repairs and incorrect variants while crediting the assertions that distinguish them.
AI.result: The directed search resolves 52.8% of SWE-bench Verified using only 48.1% of the agent-steps of an eight-sample baseline. On 270 held-out issues, weighted SFT raises pass@1 from 31.9% to 35.2% and pass@8 from 46.7% to 51.1%. The RL verifier objective further raises pass@1 to 43.0% and pass@8 to 60.7%, lifts verifier precision from 26.8% to 41.7%, and more than halves false acceptance. Resolution improves on two of three out-of-distribution suites, verifier precision improves on all three, and gains hold at 7B, 14B, and 30B versus published coder baselines.
AI.conclusion: Location, edit, and verification behaviors are teachable policy capabilities, not scale-dependent byproducts. Directing search with execution feedback plus reverted-tree patch scoring improves efficiency, while SFT and RL verifier training transfer these behaviors into the policy, delivering consistent gains in resolution and verifier precision across model sizes and multiple out-of-distribution benchmarks.

title: Continual Humanoid Motion Learning
summary: Humanoid whole-body controllers can now track a diverse set of dynamic motions, but they are typically trained offline and then frozen, so teaching such a controller a new skill tends to erode the skills it already mastered. We study continual learning for humanoid whole-body motion, where a single controller must acquire skills from a sequential task stream without revisiting past data. We introduce Similarity-guided LoRA-PNN, a progressive neural network (PNN) policy that prevents catastrophic forgetting by construction while reusing knowledge across skills through lightweight low-rank adaptation. A two-level motion-similarity measure, built from dynamic time warping aggregated by optimal transport, decides which prior skill to build on and how much new capacity to allocate, yielding strong forward transfer and large efficiency gains. Across six sequentially learned skill categories, our similarity-guided LoRA policy attains the best forward transfer (0.125 vs. 0.079) and the highest average accuracy among all methods, while saving up to 94.5% of trainable parameters and 40.8% of training time. The resulting controller reaches 96.13% sim-to-sim transfer and is deployed on a physical Unitree G1. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/continual-humanoid-learning-35D3.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Similarity-guided LoRA-PNN, a progressive neural network policy for continual humanoid whole-body motion learning that avoids catastrophic forgetting via low-rank adaptation and motion-similarity-guided capacity allocation.
AI.motivation: Humanoid whole-body controllers can track diverse dynamic motions but are trained offline and frozen, so learning new skills erodes previously mastered ones. The paper targets continual learning for a single controller that acquires skills from a sequential task stream without revisiting past data.
AI.method: The authors propose Similarity-guided LoRA-PNN, a progressive neural network (PNN) policy that prevents catastrophic forgetting by construction while reusing knowledge across skills through lightweight low-rank adaptation (LoRA). A two-level motion-similarity measure, based on dynamic time warping aggregated by optimal transport, determines which prior skill to build on and how much new capacity to allocate.
AI.result: Across six sequentially learned skill categories, the similarity-guided LoRA policy achieves the best forward transfer (0.125 vs. 0.079) and the highest average accuracy among all methods, while saving up to 94.5% of trainable parameters and 40.8% of training time. The resulting controller reaches 96.13% sim-to-sim transfer and is deployed on a physical Unitree G1.
AI.conclusion: Similarity-guided LoRA-PNN enables efficient continual learning of humanoid whole-body motions, combining anti-forgetting by construction, strong forward transfer, parameter and training-time savings, and successful real-robot deployment.

title: Behavioral History Outperforms Descriptions of the Person for LLM Synthetic Personas
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as synthetic personas representing survey respondents. Their validity as substitutes for particular respondents depends on whether they reproduce individuals' decisions. We examine what information helps synthetic respondents predict each individual's later choices, using five conditions that add progressively richer information: no personal information, demographics, personality traits, cognitive scores, and finally the respondent's earlier survey choices as behavioral history. We use a two-wave panel of 845 US adults who completed measures of 14 behavioral biases (spanning risk, time preferences, overconfidence, and reasoning), so each respondent's earlier answers provide a human test-retest benchmark; in the behavioral-history condition, all items that score the target bias are withheld. At the population level, the average number of biases per respondent in every condition is close to the human average (7.1-8.1 biases, against 7.1 for humans). This aggregate similarity masks differences in variance: persona descriptions recover only 53-67% of human between-person variation, whereas adding behavioral history restores it to approximately the human level. At the individual level, description-based personas achieve only 7-12% of the informedness observed in human test-retest responses, while adding behavioral history raises this to 28%. The condition including behavioral history has the highest estimated informedness in all 17 demographic groups, whereas description-based conditions provide little or no information for some groups. Synthetic responses also exhibit stronger education- and income-related differences than human responses. For LLM synthetic personas, a respondent's past answers add more to individual-level prediction than a description of who they are.

AI.tldr: Synthetic personas from LLMs reproduce population-level averages of 14 behavioral biases but recover only 53-67% of human between-person variance and 7-12% of individual-level informedness; adding a respondent's prior survey answers as behavioral history raises variance to near-human levels and informedness to 28%, providing the most individual-level predictive information.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as synthetic survey respondents, and their validity as substitutes for specific individuals hinges on whether they reproduce those individuals' actual decisions. It is unclear which types of personal information (demographics, personality, cognition, or past behavior) enable synthetic respondents to predict an individual's later choices.
AI.method: Two-wave panel of 845 US adults measuring 14 behavioral biases (risk, time preferences, overconfidence, reasoning). Five nested information conditions: no personal information, demographics, personality traits, cognitive scores, and the respondent's earlier survey choices as behavioral history. In the behavioral-history condition, items scoring the target bias were withheld to avoid leakage. Synthetic responses were compared against human test-retest as a benchmark, with analyses of population averages, between-person variance, individual-level informedness, and 17 demographic groups.
AI.result: Population-level average number of biases matched humans closely in all conditions (7.1-8.1 vs. 7.1). Description-based personas recovered only 53-67% of human between-person variation, while behavioral history restored it to roughly human level. Individual-level informedness was 7-12% of human test-retest for description-based personas, rising to 28% with behavioral history. The behavioral-history condition had the highest estimated informedness in all 17 demographic groups, whereas description-based conditions gave little or no information for some groups. Synthetic responses showed stronger education- and income-related differences than human responses.
AI.conclusion: For LLM synthetic personas, a respondent's past answers contribute more to individual-level prediction than a description of who they are. Aggregate similarity can mask deficits in variance and individual-level accuracy, so validity claims should be assessed at the individual rather than population level.

title: Humanoid Rickshaw Pulling: Whole-Body Locomotion under Coupled Wheeled Loads
summary: Humanoid robots could transport payloads substantially heavier than themselves by pulling passive wheeled vehicles instead of carrying the load. This capability, however, creates a coupled locomotion problem: the robot must maintain persistent upper-body contact while adapting to unknown, configuration-dependent forces arising from the payload, vehicle, and terrain. We present a whole-body control framework for humanoid rickshaw pulling that tracks commanded vehicle motion while preserving balance and stable grasps under uncertain load dynamics. During training, a privileged teacher exploits vehicle states, interaction forces, and load properties. Its actions and latent are distilled into a history-conditioned student that implicitly infers coupled dynamics from proprioceptive responses, followed by reinforcement-learning fine-tuning. Comparisons with \emph{No History} and \emph{Only History} baselines show that the resulting policy achieves accurate vehicle tracking while reducing vehicle oscillation, torso tilt, and actuation cost. Behavioral analysis shows that Unitree G1 propels the rickshaw and generates gait-synchronized whole-body reactions that stabilize its lateral and roll motions. Moreover, pulling redistributes joint effort and yields a lower robot-normalized cost-of-transport proxy than unloaded walking over most tested load--speed conditions. On hardware, a single policy performs starting, sustained pulling, turning, and stopping with both rigid payloads and human passengers, handling a loaded rickshaw mass of up to 115~kg without load-specific retuning. These results demonstrate robust heavy-load transportation through coordinated and persistent humanoid--vehicle interaction.

AI.tldr: A whole-body control framework enables a Unitree G1 humanoid to pull a passive wheeled rickshaw with up to 115 kg load, using a privileged teacher distilled into a history-conditioned student policy plus RL fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Humanoid robots could transport payloads far heavier than themselves by pulling passive wheeled vehicles rather than carrying loads, but this creates a coupled locomotion problem: the robot must maintain persistent upper-body contact while adapting to unknown, configuration-dependent forces from the payload, vehicle, and terrain.
AI.method: The authors propose a whole-body control framework for humanoid rickshaw pulling that tracks commanded vehicle motion while preserving balance and stable grasps under uncertain load dynamics. A privileged teacher exploits vehicle states, interaction forces, and load properties during training; its actions and latent are distilled into a history-conditioned student that implicitly infers coupled dynamics from proprioceptive responses, followed by reinforcement-learning fine-tuning. Ablations compare against No History and Only History baselines.
AI.result: The policy achieves accurate vehicle tracking while reducing vehicle oscillation, torso tilt, and actuation cost. Behavioral analysis shows the Unitree G1 propels the rickshaw and generates gait-synchronized whole-body reactions stabilizing lateral and roll motion. Pulling redistributes joint effort and yields a lower robot-normalized cost-of-transport proxy than unloaded walking across most load-speed conditions. On hardware, a single policy performs starting, sustained pulling, turning, and stopping with rigid payloads and human passengers, handling up to 115 kg loaded rickshaw mass without load-specific retuning.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate robust heavy-load transportation achieved through coordinated and persistent humanoid-vehicle interaction, without load-specific retuning.

title: SkillScriptBench: Benchmarking Self-Evolution of Executable Agent Skill Packages Beyond Markdown
summary: Executable Agent Skills combine natural-language instructions and scripts into reusable packages for LLM agents, and revising them requires fixing errors without breaking correct behavior. Existing benchmarks do not systematically distinguish documentation repair, script repair, and preservation when evaluating skill self-evolution. We introduce SkillScriptBench, a 350-task benchmark designed to evaluate these capabilities separately. From a survey of over 35,000 GitHub-hosted Skill roots, we select 100 packages and construct 150 repair tasks. Each task pairs a package containing injected script faults with a maintenance request and executable checks of the required behavior.
