Qwen3.7-Plus with TCM retrieval served as the automated judge, alongside parallel blinded ratings by five senior TCM clinicians on a 600-case subset. Structural completeness was nearly saturated (99.3-100.0%), but normalized content scores ranged from 40.7% to 54.1%. The five general-purpose models averaged 50.0%, versus 41.3% for the two smaller TCM-specific models. Cross-block logic consistency ranged from 60.8% to 66.8% and correlated moderately with content across cases (Pearson's r = 0.515-0.656). Deficits were greatest in prescription generation, prescription analysis, and symptom-guided modification. In judge stress testing on 100 independent cases, perturbation detection rates across the three relations were 57%, 56%, and 31%, with contradictions detected more reliably than omissions. Separating component quality from cross-block consistency localizes failures missed by endpoint and completeness metrics and identifies where clinician oversight remains necessary.

AI.tldr: TCMClinicalReason-Bench, built from 2,000 multicenter EHR cases, shows LLMs produce structurally complete but poorly case-grounded TCM clinical reasoning, with content scores of 40.7-54.1% and weakest performance in prescription-related components.
AI.motivation: LLMs can generate clinical narratives insufficiently grounded in patient-specific evidence. In TCM, such errors propagate along the etiology-pathogenesis-syndrome-treatment-prescription chain, and existing endpoint or completeness metrics fail to detect fluent but unsupported conclusions.
AI.method: Built TCMClinicalReason-Bench from 2,000 multicenter EHR cases. Evaluated five general-purpose and two TCM-specific LLMs in zero-shot settings using an evidence-constrained rubric covering seven diagnostic/therapeutic components and three cross-block relations, with case-supported alternatives permitted. Automated judging used Qwen3.7-Plus with TCM retrieval, plus blinded parallel ratings by five senior TCM clinicians on a 600-case subset. Judge stress testing was performed on 100 independent cases.
AI.result: Structural completeness nearly saturated (99.3-100.0%), but normalized content scores were only 40.7-54.1%. General-purpose models averaged 50.0% vs 41.3% for TCM-specific models. Cross-block logic consistency was 60.8-66.8% and moderately correlated with content (r = 0.515-0.656). Largest deficits: prescription generation, prescription analysis, symptom-guided modification. Judge stress testing detection rates: 57%, 56%, 31% across the three relations, with contradictions detected more reliably than omissions.
AI.conclusion: Separating component quality from cross-block consistency exposes grounding failures obscured by endpoint and completeness metrics, localizing where clinician oversight remains necessary in TCM LLM deployment.

title: Lie Rarely, Lie Big: Stealthy Insider Attacks on LLM Robot Teams
summary: When a team of robots delegates planning and mutual trust to LLM agents, a single compromised robot can corrupt the shared outcome. We study this threat in a grounded task: a multi-robot survey in which measurements can be verified against the physical world, but every verification costs budget that would otherwise advance the mission. We treat the compromised robot as a stealthy adversary in the system-theoretic sense: it is limited not by an energy bound but by the team's own detectors. We then derive two bounds. First, the probability that the adversary's reports are verified is bounded below in terms of the degrees in the communication graph and the verification budget. Second, the map error caused by any stealthy adversary is bounded above by the value of a linear program over the adversary's bias distributions; its solution is an exchange rate between stealth budget and damage: below a critical verification level the worst stealthy attack tells rare, full-magnitude lies on the records least likely to be verified, and above it the better purchase is small biases hidden in the noise. In experiments where the honest robots are LLM agents, both bounds hold at the budget the attack actually spent. The experiments also show that which records an LLM robot re-checks is unbiased, but how much it re-checks is unpredictable.

AI.tldr: The paper studies security of LLM-agent-coordinated multi-robot teams where a compromised robot acts as a stealthy adversary constrained by the team's own verification detectors, deriving lower and upper bounds on verification probability and map error, and validating them with LLM-agent experiments.
AI.motivation: When robots delegate planning and mutual trust to LLM agents, a single compromised robot can corrupt the shared mission outcome. Verification against the physical world is possible but consumes budget that would otherwise advance the mission, creating a tradeoff between security and task progress that needs a formal treatment.
AI.method: The compromised robot is modeled as a stealthy adversary in the system-theoretic sense, limited not by an energy bound but by the team's detectors. The authors analyze a grounded multi-robot survey task and derive: (1) a lower bound on the probability that the adversary's reports are verified, expressed via communication-graph degrees and verification budget; and (2) an upper bound on map error caused by any stealthy adversary, given by the value of a linear program over the adversary's bias distributions, yielding an exchange rate between stealth budget and damage.
AI.result: Below a critical verification level, the worst stealthy attack consists of rare, full-magnitude lies placed on the records least likely to be verified; above that level, the better strategy is small biases hidden in the noise. In experiments with honest robots as LLM agents, both bounds hold at the budget the attack actually spent. Additionally, which records an LLM robot re-checks is unbiased, but how much it re-checks is unpredictable.
AI.conclusion: The work provides rigorous lower and upper performance bounds for stealthy attacks against LLM-agent multi-robot teams, characterizing an optimal attack structure that shifts with verification budget, and empirically confirms the bounds while revealing that LLM re-checking behavior is unbiased in target selection but unpredictable in volume.

title: On the Steering Dimensionality of Refusal in Language Models
summary: Existing activation steering methods often assume that a high-level concept can be mediated by a single steering direction. To support this, two complementary interventions should be achieved: additive steering should induce the target behavior, while directional ablation should suppress it. Yet behaviors may occupy richer activation geometries beyond a single direction, and semantically similar behaviors may be represented by distinct directions. In this work, we study how many directions can reliably control two different types of refusal behaviors: refusal triggered by the safety alignment and refusal in general contexts. Given the limited expressive capability of a single steering vector, we study the general setting of steering subspaces and introduce the notion of steering dimensionality as the minimum subspace dimensionality required to reliably control a behavior. We characterize sufficient steering subspaces that cover the full extent of the target behavior through both the (monotonic) improvement before the sufficient dimensionality, and the saturation beyond it. Empirically, we find that refusal triggered by safety alignment is 1-dim steerable, while multiple distinct steering directions can achieve comparable control. In contrast, refusal in general contexts exhibits substantially richer activation geometry where even 5-dim steering subspaces fail to reliably capture its full steerable variation. Our results reveal that the activation geometry underlying refusal is highly context-dependent and can be substantially more complex than a single linear steering direction.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how many steering directions are needed to control refusal behaviors, introducing "steering dimensionality" and finding that safety-alignment refusal is 1-dim steerable while general-context refusal requires far richer subspaces (even 5-dim fails).
AI.motivation: Existing activation steering methods assume a high-level concept can be mediated by a single steering direction, validated by additive steering (inducing behavior) and directional ablation (suppressing it). However, behaviors may occupy richer activation geometries than a single direction, and semantically similar behaviors may be represented by distinct directions, so this single-direction assumption is potentially too restrictive.
AI.method: The authors study two types of refusal behavior (safety-alignment-triggered refusal and general-context refusal) and generalize from single steering vectors to steering subspaces. They define steering dimensionality as the minimum subspace dimensionality needed to reliably control a behavior, and characterize sufficient steering subspaces via monotonic improvement before the sufficient dimensionality and saturation beyond it.
AI.result: Empirically, refusal triggered by safety alignment is 1-dim steerable, with multiple distinct steering directions achieving comparable control. In contrast, refusal in general contexts exhibits substantially richer activation geometry, where even 5-dim steering subspaces fail to reliably capture its full steerable variation.
AI.conclusion: The activation geometry underlying refusal is highly context-dependent and can be substantially more complex than a single linear steering direction, challenging the prevailing single-direction assumption in activation steering.

title: DNPush: Distributed Nonparallel Pushing Force Control of Multi-Robot Systems for Object Transportation
comment: 8 pages, 8 figures. Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters
summary: This letter proposes DNPush, a Distributed Nonparallel Pushing force controller for cooperative object transport without inter-robot communication. Each robot uses local force measurements, a preassigned force weight, and a locally expressed desired transport direction, without requiring an object model, contact locations, a CoM estimate, or moment arm magnitudes online. DNPush regulates nonparallel force magnitudes from local force direction misalignments through a reciprocal-sine law. Under the stated contact conditions, Lyapunov analysis with LaSalle's invariance principle proves convergence to a unique rotational equilibrium, where perpendicular force contributions cancel and the net torque from normal forces is zero. Object velocity converges to the desired transport direction, and suitable contact regions exist for convex polygons. Simulations isolate the reciprocal-sine scaling mechanism, five-robot coordination, and active rotational damping. Hardware experiments with soft tactile differential-drive robots achieve a velocity direction error of 0.61 deg +/- 0.79 deg over five trials with a fixed transport direction and demonstrate object transport through waypoints with three robots.

AI.tldr: DNPush is a communication-free distributed nonparallel pushing controller that uses local force measurements and a reciprocal-sine law to align cooperative transport, provably converging to the desired transport direction.
AI.motivation: Cooperative object transport typically needs inter-robot communication, an object model, contact locations, CoM estimates, or moment-arm knowledge, which are hard to obtain or maintain online in real deployments.
AI.method: Each robot exploits local force measurements, a preassigned force weight, and a locally expressed desired transport direction—no object model, contact locations, CoM estimate, or moment arm magnitudes online. Nonparallel force magnitudes are regulated from local force-direction misalignments via a reciprocal-sine law. Convergence is analyzed with Lyapunov analysis plus LaSalle's invariance principle.
AI.result: The analysis proves convergence to a unique rotational equilibrium where perpendicular force contributions cancel and net normal-force torque is zero; object velocity converges to the desired transport direction, and suitable contact regions exist for convex polygons. Simulations isolate the reciprocal-sine scaling mechanism, five-robot coordination, and active rotational damping. Hardware trials with soft tactile differential-drive robots achieve 0.61 deg +/- 0.79 deg velocity-direction error over five trials at a fixed direction, and three-robot transport through waypoints.
AI.conclusion: DNPush enables communication-free, model-free distributed cooperative transport with proven directional convergence, validated in simulation and hardware.

title: Spec2Game: Can LLMs Generate Complete Playable Games from Detailed Specifications?
summary: Generating an executable program does not necessarily mean that it correctly implements the behavioral requirements specified in natural language. To evaluate large language models' ability to realize detailed specifications as complete interactive programs, we introduce Spec2Game, a benchmark that requires models to generate complete Pygame projects from detailed natural-language game specifications. Spec2Game comprises 15 game families and 150 task instances, with one canonical task and nine controlled rule variants per family, spanning three levels of implementation complexity. Using source-code, runtime, and visual evidence, we evaluate generated projects along four dimensions---Executability, Specification Realization, Code Quality, and User-Facing Quality. Across 14 LLMs and 3,330 generated projects, we find that high executability does not imply faithful specification realization. Component-level analysis further shows that models perform substantially better on Game Element Modeling than on Rule and Mechanism Modeling or Goal and Termination Modeling, indicating that faithfully implementing game rules and termination logic remains a major challenge.

AI.tldr: Spec2Game is a new benchmark of 15 game families and 150 tasks that evaluates whether LLMs can turn detailed natural-language game specs into complete, correctly behaving Pygame programs.
AI.motivation: A program that runs is not necessarily a program that correctly implements the behavioral requirements described in natural language, so there is a need to test whether LLMs can realize detailed specifications as complete interactive programs rather than merely producing executable code.
AI.method: The authors build Spec2Game, requiring models to generate complete Pygame projects from detailed natural-language game specifications. It contains 15 game families and 150 task instances, each family having one canonical task and nine controlled rule variants across three complexity levels. Generated projects are assessed with source-code, runtime, and visual evidence along four dimensions: Executability, Specification Realization, Code Quality, and User-Facing Quality. The evaluation covers 14 LLMs and 3,330 generated projects.
AI.result: High executability does not imply faithful specification realization. Component-level analysis shows models perform substantially better on Game Element Modeling than on Rule and Mechanism Modeling or Goal and Termination Modeling.
AI.conclusion: Faithfully implementing game rules and termination logic remains a major challenge for LLMs, and executable code alone is insufficient evidence of correct specification realization.

title: PatternDex: Learning Interaction Patterns to Guide Reinforcement Learning of Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation of Articulated Objects
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Project page: https://patterndex.github.io/PatternDex/
summary: In this paper, we develop a method that enables bimanual dexterous hands to manipulate articulated objects with a high success rate without suffering from an embodiment gap. We observe that the correlation between hand motions and object motions is dictated by the object rather than the hands and can be learned from human-object demonstrations. Based on this observation, we propose PatternDex, a method that learns this correlation and represents it as a token sequence, which we call an interaction pattern. From this pattern, PatternDex estimates the wrist motions and contact points that fit the target robot, and then trains a reinforcement learning policy that exploits these estimates as guidance. Since the guidance fits the target embodiment, the policy explores only the actions that the target robot can execute and thus achieves high success rates. PatternDex also requires only simple fine-tuning to train a new robot, since it can reuse the learned interaction pattern. We evaluate PatternDex with bimanual dexterous hands on human demonstrations from the ARCTIC dataset. PatternDex achieves, on average, a 92.8% success rate with Allegro hands, while the state-of-the-art baseline achieves 52.2%. Also, it achieves success rates above 70% with three other robot hands after fine-tuning alone. Furthermore, we verify that the learned policy transfers well to a real-world task of opening a microwave. Videos and additional results are available at https://patterndex.github.io/PatternDex/

AI.tldr: PatternDex learns object-centric interaction patterns (token sequences) from human-object demonstrations to guide bimanual dexterous hands in manipulating articulated objects, achieving 92.8% success with Allegro hands vs. 52.2% for the SOTA baseline, and >70% with three other hands after fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Bimanual dexterous hands struggle to manipulate articulated objects due to the embodiment gap between human demonstrations and target robot hardware. Existing approaches suffer when transferring human-object interaction knowledge to robots with different hand morphologies.
AI.method: The key observation is that hand-object motion correlation is dictated by the object, not the hands, and can be learned from human-object demonstrations. PatternDex learns this correlation and encodes it as a token sequence called an interaction pattern. From this pattern, it estimates wrist motions and contact points that fit the target robot, then trains a reinforcement learning policy using these estimates as guidance. Because the guidance fits the target embodiment, the policy explores only executable actions. The learned pattern can be reused, requiring only simple fine-tuning to train a new robot.
AI.result: Evaluated on human demonstrations from the ARCTIC dataset with bimanual dexterous hands, PatternDex achieves on average 92.8% success with Allegro hands, versus 52.2% for the state-of-the-art baseline. It achieves above 70% success with three other robot hands after fine-tuning alone. The learned policy also transfers well to a real-world microwave-opening task.
AI.conclusion: PatternDex overcomes the embodiment gap for bimanual dexterous manipulation of articulated objects by leveraging object-centric interaction patterns, enabling high success rates, efficient transfer across robot hands via fine-tuning, and real-world deployment.

title: CADForge: Agentic Single-View CAD Reconstruction with Explicit Geometry Reasoning
summary: Reconstructing editable parametric CAD models from a single-view image is of great practical value for modern manufacturing, yet remains challenging due to incomplete geometric observations and complex inter-part relationships. To address it, we propose CADForge, an agentic framework that progressively converts a single image into CadQuery programs. CADForge decomposes an object into CAD-meaningful components and performs explicit geometric reasoning for each component, a process that first identifies CAD-relevant constraints and then translates them into precise modeling parameters through mathematical code. The inferred parameters then drive component-wise synthesis of executable CadQuery programs, with a review agent evaluating the resulting geometry and providing targeted feedback for iterative refinement. To further improve robustness and efficiency, CADForge incorporates a failure-guided toolkit construction mechanism to distill accumulated experience into tools, and maintains a compact parametric CAD memory for retrieving modeling context on demand. Experiments on diverse single- and multi-part objects show that CADForge consistently outperforms existing baselines in reconstruction fidelity and perceptual quality, demonstrating an effective approach to accurate single-view CAD reconstruction.

AI.tldr: CADForge is an agentic framework that converts a single-view image into editable parametric CAD models by decomposing objects into CAD-meaningful components, performing explicit geometric reasoning, and synthesizing executable CadQuery programs with an iterative review-and-refine loop.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing editable parametric CAD models from a single-view image is highly valuable for modern manufacturing but remains challenging due to incomplete geometric observations and complex inter-part relationships in single-view settings.
AI.method: CADForge progressively converts a single image into CadQuery programs. It decomposes an object into CAD-meaningful components and performs explicit per-component geometric reasoning: first identifying CAD-relevant constraints, then translating them into precise modeling parameters via mathematical code. The inferred parameters drive component-wise synthesis of executable CadQuery programs. A review agent evaluates the resulting geometry and provides targeted feedback for iterative refinement. Additionally, a failure-guided toolkit construction mechanism distills accumulated experience into reusable tools, and a compact parametric CAD memory retrieves modeling context on demand.
AI.result: Experiments on diverse single- and multi-part objects show CADForge consistently outperforms existing baselines in reconstruction fidelity and perceptual quality.
AI.conclusion: CADForge demonstrates an effective approach to accurate single-view CAD reconstruction, yielding editable parametric models with improved fidelity and perceptual quality over prior methods.

title: Flow Policies as Actions of Skill-Level World Models: Learned and Symbolic Abstractions for Long-Horizon Planning
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures, 1 table. Submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027. Project page: https://andreumatoses.github.io/research/flow-skill-wm
summary: Latent world models enable robots to plan by predicting the consequences of actions. Planning long tasks with control-rate actions requires many prediction steps, which enlarges the search space and accumulates error. Skill-level actions shorten these sequences, but a symbolic skill vocabulary requires domain knowledge and labeled demonstrations. We construct skill-level actions from the inputs of a flow-matching policy trained on demonstrations segmented into complete skills. The policy maps a noise seed and an observation, optionally with a code or label, to a complete skill execution, so one execution is one world-model transition. On this mechanism we propose four action abstractions with increasing task knowledge: a compressed seed, two discrete codes learned from the demonstrations, and a symbolic label. We evaluate them with a common world-model training procedure and planning framework on simulated block rearrangement tasks that require up to 14 sequential skills. The symbolic label succeeds in over 90% of the tasks that require up to six skills and degrades beyond. Without any label, an object-centric learned code matches it on single-skill tasks and retains half to three quarters of its success on tasks of two to five skills. Ablations attribute much of the label's advantage to its planner knowing which actions are applicable, rather than to the label itself. Beyond six skills the search, not the world model, limits success. Project page: https://andreumatoses.github.io/research/flow-skill-wm

AI.tldr: The paper builds skill-level action abstractions for latent world models by reusing a flow-matching policy trained on segmented demonstrations, yielding one skill execution per world-model transition, and compares four abstractions of increasing task knowledge on long-horizon block rearrangement.
AI.motivation: Planning at control rate requires many world-model prediction steps, which enlarges the search space and accumulates error, while symbolic skill vocabularies normally demand domain knowledge and labeled demonstrations.
AI.method: Skill-level actions are derived from the inputs of a flow-matching policy trained on demonstrations segmented into complete skills; the policy maps a noise seed and an observation (optionally with a code or label) to a full skill execution, so one execution equals one world-model transition. Four action abstractions with increasing task knowledge are proposed (compressed seed, two learned discrete codes, symbolic label) and evaluated under a common world-model training procedure and planning framework.
AI.result: On simulated block rearrangement tasks requiring up to 14 sequential skills, the symbolic label succeeds in over 90% of tasks needing up to six skills and degrades beyond. Without labels, an object-centric learned code matches it on single-skill tasks and retains half to three quarters of its success on two-to-five-skill tasks. Ablations show much of the label's advantage comes from the planner knowing which actions are applicable rather than from the label itself. Beyond six skills, search rather than the world model limits success.
AI.conclusion: Skill-level actions can be obtained from a demonstration-trained flow-matching policy without a hand-designed symbolic vocabulary, and task knowledge mainly helps through applicability-aware planning; for long horizons, the bottleneck shifts from world-model accuracy to the search procedure.

title: Dense Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning in a Unified Geometry State
summary: Geometry reasoning is naturally stateful: solving a problem repeatedly alternates between structural proposals and exact deductions. We formulate this process as dense neural-symbolic coupling, in which neural guidance and symbolic execution share a typed state and communicate through executable actions at every search step. Neural proposals contribute theorem instances, constructions, and algebraic bridges; the symbolic runtime applies registered rules, propagates exact constraints, and records provenance. A nested controller allocates computation first between neural and symbolic proposal sources and then among admitted actions. We instantiate the framework in OmniGeo, a single solver for plane, analytic, and solid geometry. With Claude Sonnet 4.6, OmniGeo reaches 94.2%, 88.5%, and 89.8% on FormalGeo7K, Conic10K, and SolidFGeo, respectively (90.8% macro average), and solves 21/30 IMO-AG-30 problems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dense neural-symbolic coupling framework for geometry reasoning where neural guidance and symbolic execution share a typed state and communicate via executable actions, instantiated as OmniGeo for plane, analytic, and solid geometry.
AI.motivation: Geometry reasoning is inherently stateful, alternating between structural proposals and exact deductions. Existing approaches likely treat neural and symbolic components separately rather than tightly coupling them across every search step.
AI.method: Formulates geometry solving as dense neural-symbolic coupling with a shared typed state. Neural proposals contribute theorem instances, constructions, and algebraic bridges; the symbolic runtime applies registered rules, propagates exact constraints, and records provenance. A nested controller allocates computation first between neural and symbolic proposal sources, then among admitted actions.
AI.result: Instantiated as OmniGeo, a unified solver for plane, analytic, and solid geometry. With Claude Sonnet 4.6, achieves 94.2% on FormalGeo7K, 88.5% on Conic10K, and 89.8% on SolidFGeo (90.8% macro average), solving 21/30 IMO-AG-30 problems.
AI.conclusion: Dense neural-symbolic coupling with a shared typed state and nested computation allocation enables a single unified geometry solver to achieve strong performance across plane, analytic, and solid geometry benchmarks.

title: Learning Task and Motion Plans from Real Demonstrations with Hybrid Flow Matching
comment: 9 pages, 9 figures, 1 table. Submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027. Project page: https://andreumatoses.github.io/research/hybrid-flow-planning
summary: Long-horizon mobile manipulation requires a task plan and the motion that executes it. Generative planners trained on demonstration produce both in one pass, requiring neither a symbolic domain nor search. To date, however, they have relied on thousands of scripted demonstrations of fixed-base arms and executed open loop. This paper presents a hybrid flow matching planner: a single network generates the symbolic plan with masked discrete flow matching and the motion trajectory with continuous flow matching. Unlike prior generative planners, we aim to learn from a much smaller set of demonstrations and to execute the plan in closed loop. Two properties of the data compensate for the small dataset. A demonstration resumed from any of its intermediate actions is itself a demonstration, which multiplies the training samples and enables replanning after every action. Objects of the same kind are interchangeable, which turns demonstrations of one goal into demonstrations of every permuted goal. Our base implementation produces valid plans on 68% of held-out scenes; a training and generation scheme for the discrete plan raises this to 76%, and replanning after every action raises the task completion rate from 40% to 53% in a kinematic simulation. The planner matches the task completion rate of motion-only flow matching policies while additionally providing the symbolic plan, and it outperforms previous hybrid diffusion formulations on both task completion and plan validity. We validate the planner on a real mobile manipulator. Videos and project page: https://andreumatoses.github.io/research/hybrid-flow-planning

AI.tldr: A hybrid flow matching planner generates both a symbolic plan (via masked discrete flow matching) and a continuous motion trajectory in one network, learning from a small demonstration set and executing in closed loop, validated in kinematic simulation and on a real mobile manipulator.
AI.motivation: Prior generative planners for long-horizon mobile manipulation require thousands of scripted demonstrations of fixed-base arms, execute open loop, and need neither symbolic domains nor search but scale poorly and cannot replan. This work aims to learn from far fewer demonstrations and to execute the plan in closed loop.
AI.method: The paper presents a hybrid flow matching planner: a single network produces the symbolic plan using masked discrete flow matching and the motion trajectory using continuous flow matching. Two data properties compensate for the small dataset: (1) a demonstration resumed from any intermediate action is itself a demonstration, multiplying training samples and enabling replanning after every action; (2) interchangeable objects of the same kind turn demonstrations of one goal into demonstrations of every permuted goal. A discrete-plan training and generation scheme further improves plan quality.
AI.result: The base implementation produces valid plans on 68% of held-out scenes; the discrete-plan training and generation scheme raises this to 76%. Replanning after every action raises task completion from 40% to 53% in kinematic simulation. The planner matches the task completion rate of motion-only flow matching policies while additionally providing the symbolic plan, and outperforms previous hybrid diffusion formulations on both task completion and plan validity. It is validated on a real mobile manipulator.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid flow matching enables a single network to jointly generate symbolic plans and motion trajectories from limited demonstrations, and closed-loop replanning after every action substantially improves task completion, providing a practical and effective approach for long-horizon mobile manipulation.

title: VIGIL: Verifier-Informed Gated Improvement Loop for Spreadsheet Question Answering
summary: Enterprise agents should improve from delayed feedback without allowing every correction to rewrite system behavior. We study continual harness learning for corpus-level spreadsheet question answering. Building on FiCo (Find-then-Compute), a static retrieval-and-execution backbone, we introduce VIGIL (Verifier-Informed Gated Improvement Loop). Within a question, VIGIL verifies and repairs diversely prompted Structured Query Language (SQL) candidates. Across episodes, delayed labels update only a contract calibrator and query/result-column selector. The base model, prompts, retriever, and recorded candidate pool remain fixed in the continual-learning protocol. With the gold workbook and expected type supplied, the ungated and dual-gated full-replay variants reach 82.4% and 82.0% forward accuracy over 79 documents, from a 75.8% static baseline. The dual gate has the larger retrospective gain (2.7 versus 2.3 points), and its 6.3-point forward gain has a 95% t-interval of 5.6-6.9. In a separate stricter split that excludes 16 documents and 380 questions from fitting and online promotion, the accuracy-only gate raises mean held-out accuracy across ten final harnesses from 80.3% to 86.7%. Calibrator-only adaptation gains 5.9 points, close to the combined 6.4-point gain. Yet three of 26 gate-approved updates reduce held-out accuracy relative to their incumbents, so replay-buffer non-regression does not imply held-out non-regression. MiMoTable and external-task case studies test within-task verification and reuse the same promote-or-retain discipline. Overall, the results support bounded, auditable harness adaptation while revealing where finite replay gates fail to generalize beyond their promotion buffers.

AI.tldr: VIGIL enables continual harness learning for spreadsheet QA by gating delayed-feedback updates, achieving 82.4% forward accuracy vs. a 75.8% static baseline while keeping the base model, prompts, retriever, and candidate pool fixed.
AI.motivation: Enterprise agents need to improve from delayed feedback, but allowing every correction to rewrite system behavior is risky. The paper seeks bounded, auditable adaptation for corpus-level spreadsheet question answering.
AI.method: Building on FiCo (Find-then-Compute), the authors introduce VIGIL (Verifier-Informed Gated Improvement Loop). Within a question, VIGIL verifies and repairs diversely prompted SQL candidates. Across episodes, delayed labels update only a contract calibrator and query/result-column selector, with the base model, prompts, retriever, and recorded candidate pool held fixed.
AI.result: With the gold workbook and expected type, ungated and dual-gated full-replay variants reach 82.4% and 82.0% forward accuracy over 79 documents, from a 75.8% static baseline. The dual gate shows a 2.7-point retrospective gain versus 2.3 points, and a 6.3-point forward gain (95% t-interval: 5.6–6.9). On a stricter split, the accuracy-only gate raises mean held-out accuracy from 80.3% to 86.7%. Calibrator-only adaptation gains 5.9 points versus 6.4 combined. Three of 26 gate-approved updates reduce held-out accuracy despite replay-buffer non-regression.
AI.conclusion: The results support bounded, auditable harness adaptation but reveal that finite replay gates do not guarantee generalization beyond their promotion buffers, since replay-buffer non-regression does not imply held-out non-regression.

title: Distributed Cascade Force Control of Soft-Tactile-Based Multi-robot System for Object Transportation
comment: 6 pages, 7 figures. Published in the 2024 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII)
summary: In this paper, we present a distributed cascade force control system (DCFC) for multiple robots with the aim of pushing a rigid object towards a desired moving target without their inter-robot communication. These mobile robots are equipped with 360-degree vision-based soft tactile sensors utilized to determine contact location and resultant impact force. By investigating the dynamics of moving rigid objects on the flat, we proposed a distributed cascade control. The inner loop control incorporates contact force and positioning, ensuring the robots' pushing contact and application of the desired force to the object. The outer loop control coordinates the robots to push the object in a desired direction without inter-robot communication, regardless of the unknown object mass. The stability and convergence of the system are verified using the Lyapunov stability theory. We also conducted simulation and real-word experiments to validate the performance of the proposed control method, and the experimental results showcase the successful coordination of multiple robots in pushing an object towards a moving desired direction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a distributed cascade force control (DCFC) system enabling multiple robots, without inter-robot communication, to push a rigid object toward a moving target using 360-degree vision-based soft tactile sensors.
AI.motivation: Coordinating multiple robots to push a rigid object toward a moving target typically requires inter-robot communication and knowledge of object mass, which is impractical. This work aims to achieve such coordination in a fully distributed manner despite unknown object mass.
AI.method: Each mobile robot is equipped with a 360-degree vision-based soft tactile sensor to determine contact location and resultant impact force. Based on analysis of moving rigid object dynamics on a flat surface, a distributed cascade control is designed: an inner loop for contact force and positioning, and an outer loop for coordinating pushing direction without inter-robot communication. Lyapunov stability theory is used to verify stability and convergence.
AI.result: Simulation and real-world experiments validate the proposed control method, demonstrating successful coordination of multiple robots in pushing an object toward a moving desired direction.
AI.conclusion: The DCFC system enables communication-free multi-robot pushing of a rigid object toward a moving target, with verified stability and convergence and experimental confirmation of coordinated performance.

title: LMBuild: Evaluating LLM Agents for Generating Buildable and Functional Structures
summary: LLM-based agents are increasingly capable of generating complex 3D structures, with the potential to reshape how objects are designed and realized in the physical world. Yet, producing elegant geometry is fundamentally different from producing objects that can be built and perform their intended functions. Existing evaluations largely focus on geometric quality while overlooking physical realizability. We introduce LMBuild, a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on generating buildable and functional structures. LMBuild represents generated objects as assembled structures comprising part decompositions, joints, materials, and sequences. To support reproducible evaluation, we provide a unified framework consisting of: (1) an interactive environment in which agents can use tools to retrieve, create, and place components to construct objects; (2) a curated benchmark that repurposes established CAD datasets and augments them with knowledge from Wikipedia; and (3) a evaluation framework covering structural soundness, functional affordance, design quality, and physical realization. Evaluations across 30 systems reveal several intriguing findings: (a) Soundness and alignment are no longer the primary bottlenecks for frontier closed-source models, while functional affordance and physical operability remain substantially more challenging; (b) stronger models more effectively create new components, whereas weaker models tend to rely on retrieval; and (c) providing functional specifications substantially improves part completeness, kinematics, and physical operability. These results show that generating real-world structures requires deeper reasoning about functional affordances, mechanics, and designing and creating novel components. We expect LMBuild to provide a foundation for measuring progress and incentivizing research toward agents that generate buildable and functional structures.

AI.tldr: LMBuild is a benchmark evaluating LLM agents on generating buildable, functional 3D structures (not just geometric quality), spanning part decompositions, joints, materials, and assembly sequences, with an interactive environment, a curated CAD+Wikipedia benchmark, and a 4-axis evaluation framework.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents can now generate complex 3D structures, but producing elegant geometry differs fundamentally from producing objects that can actually be built and function. Existing evaluations focus on geometric quality and neglect physical realizability, leaving a gap in measuring whether generated structures are buildable and functional.
AI.method: The authors introduce LMBuild, representing generated objects as assembled structures with part decompositions, joints, materials, and sequences. They provide a unified framework: (1) an interactive environment where agents use tools to retrieve, create, and place components; (2) a curated benchmark repurposing established CAD datasets augmented with Wikipedia knowledge; (3) an evaluation framework covering structural soundness, functional affordance, design quality, and physical realization. Evaluations span 30 systems.
AI.result: Three key findings: (a) soundness and alignment are no longer primary bottlenecks for frontier closed-source models, while functional affordance and physical operability remain substantially more challenging; (b) stronger models more effectively create new components, whereas weaker models rely on retrieval; (c) providing functional specifications substantially improves part completeness, kinematics, and physical operability.
AI.conclusion: Generating real-world structures requires deeper reasoning about functional affordances, mechanics, and the design and creation of novel components. LMBuild is expected to provide a foundation for measuring progress and incentivizing research toward agents that generate buildable and functional structures.

title: ExStereo: Lifting 2D Vision-Language-Action Models to 3D with Explicit Stereo Representations
summary: Three-dimensional perception is critical for robotic manipulation, particularly for high-precision tasks, as recovering metric depth and precise 3D object positions from monocular RGB observations is inherently ill-posed. However, many Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models rely solely on RGB observations for perception. Leveraging recent advances in foundation models for stereo matching, we introduce ExStereo, a stereo module that augments pre-trained 2D VLAs with 3D perception. ExStereo reconstructs scene geometry from stereo image pairs and renders multi-view observations as an explicit stereo representation for stereo feature extraction. The action tokens from the action expert selectively attend to the resulting stereo tokens through our proposed action-stereo cross-attention mechanism, enabling the policy to generate robot actions conditioned on 3D scene information. To learn robust 3D representations, we introduce a mid-training stage before task-specific post-training, using a self-supervised learning objective on large-scale stereo data. We validate our approach by fine-tuning two publicly available VLAs, $π_{0.5}$ and SmolVLA, and evaluate them in simulation and on a real-world bimanual PiPER platform. Across both settings, VLAs fine-tuned with ExStereo consistently outperform baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of stereo perception for robotic manipulation. Our project website is at: https://exstereo-vla.github.io/ExStereo/.

AI.tldr: ExStereo augments pre-trained 2D Vision-Language-Action models with a stereo perception module that reconstructs 3D scene geometry and injects it into the policy via action-stereo cross-attention, improving robotic manipulation in simulation and on a real robot.
AI.motivation: 3D perception is critical for high-precision robotic manipulation, but recovering metric depth and precise 3D object positions from monocular RGB is inherently ill-posed. Many VLA models rely solely on RGB observations, limiting their spatial precision.
AI.method: ExStereo is a stereo module that augments pre-trained 2D VLAs with 3D perception. It reconstructs scene geometry from stereo image pairs using foundation models for stereo matching and renders multi-view observations as an explicit stereo representation for feature extraction. Action tokens from the action expert selectively attend to stereo tokens through an action-stereo cross-attention mechanism. A self-supervised mid-training stage on large-scale stereo data precedes task-specific post-training to learn robust 3D representations.
AI.result: Fine-tuning two public VLAs ($\pi_{0.5}$ and SmolVLA) with ExStereo consistently outperforms baselines in both simulation and real-world evaluation on a bimanual PiPER platform.
AI.conclusion: Stereo perception is an effective way to equip 2D VLAs with 3D awareness for robotic manipulation, and ExStereo demonstrates consistent gains across simulated and real-world settings.

title: Language-Conditioned Token and Reasoning Efficiency in Large Language Models: A Paired Cross-Lingual Study Protocol
comment: 32 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Prospective paired study protocol; no confirmatory model outcomes are reported
summary: Large language models incur language-dependent representation and inference costs, but existing comparisons often conflate input language, assigned observable-trace language, and answer realization. We specify a prospective paired study that separates these interfaces while holding the semantic item, checkpoint, and answer oracle fixed. The initial design instantiates 240 exactly scored items rendered from templates in English and seven non-English languages, three distinct-lineage open-weight checkpoints, three trace-token budgets, 22 input- and trace-language conditions, a fixed answer reserve, and a separately counted delimiter: 47,520 initial core runs before prospective sample-size selection. RQ1-RQ3 estimate input and trace effects by intention-to-treat with failure-inclusive terminal accounting and test answer realization by cloning a sealed prefix and runtime-native KV state into eight crossed branches. Pre-freeze independent language review, fixed-form ASCII selectors, and code/surface/solver agreement constrain the realization test. H1-H5 share one Holm family and a global simultaneous component band. A secondary randomized experiment compares one-long-attempt and complete K-short-attempt policies at equal trace allowance under frozen seeds and oracle-blind aggregation; it is a full-policy contrast because answer capacity differs. Outcomes include exact token spans, correctness, latency, runtime-exposed memory, and qualified same-host operating-system-reported energy over prespecified hardware rails. The protocol separates tokenizer expansion, observable-trace cost, and answer-realization cost without treating visible traces as internal cognition or operating-system estimates as physical cross-device energy. No confirmatory model outcome is reported; result fields remain disabled until the frozen evidence ledger passes independent verification.

AI.tldr: A prospective paired-study protocol that disentangles three language interfaces (input language, assigned observable-trace language, answer realization) while holding semantic items, checkpoint, and answer oracle fixed; no confirmatory outcomes are reported yet.
AI.motivation: Existing cross-lingual comparisons of large language models conflate three distinct interfaces: the language of the input, the language assigned to the observable trace, and the language in which the answer is realized. This conflation prevents attributing language-dependent costs to tokenizer expansion, observable-trace cost, or answer-realization cost separately.
AI.method: A prospective paired design with 240 exactly scored template-rendered items (English plus seven non-English languages), three distinct-lineage open-weight checkpoints, three trace-token budgets, 22 input- and trace-language conditions, a fixed answer reserve, and a separately counted delimiter: 47,520 core runs prior to sample-size selection. RQ1-RQ3 use intention-to-treat estimation with failure-inclusive terminal accounting; answer realization is tested by cloning a sealed prefix plus runtime-native KV state into eight crossed branches. Constraints include pre-freeze independent language review, fixed-form ASCII selectors, and code/surface/solver agreement. H1-H5 share one Holm family with a global simultaneous component band. A secondary randomized experiment contrasts one-long-attempt versus complete K-short-attempt policies at equal trace allowance under frozen seeds and oracle-blind aggregation.
AI.result: No confirmatory model outcome is reported; result fields remain disabled until the frozen evidence ledger passes independent verification. Outcomes would include exact token spans, correctness, latency, runtime-exposed memory, and qualified same-host OS-reported energy over prespecified hardware rails.
AI.conclusion: The protocol separates tokenizer expansion, observable-trace cost, and answer-realization cost without treating visible traces as internal cognition or OS estimates as physical cross-device energy, providing a clean decomposition of language-dependent representation and inference costs.

title: Tackling Sim-to-Real Mismatch Through Sampling-Based Disturbance Observers: From Analytical Models to Learned World Models
comment: 15 pages, 14 figures, 7 tables. Project website: https://sampling-based-dob.github.io/
summary: Robotic controllers increasingly rely on analytical models, simulators, cost-query interfaces, and learned world models. However, physical deployment can deviate from nominal assumptions, and additional disturbances may arise even when the model itself is accurate. In control systems, disturbance observers (DOB) are widely used to estimate such unmeasured effects from nominal models and measured feedback. Classical DOB formulations are generally built around explicit plant models. This paper develops the sampling-based disturbance observer (SDOB), extending the DOB principle to a broader range of models, including simulators and learned world models, through state-rollout or cost-query interfaces. SDOB separates two observable channels: state-effect disturbances, for which the feedback state differs from its prediction, and cost disturbances, for which the same query state receives different costs as the perceived environment changes. Diverse simulation and real-robot experiments across traditional and learned models demonstrate the effectiveness of SDOB in compensating for sim-to-real mismatch and improving control performance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Sampling-based Disturbance Observer (SDOB), extending classical disturbance observer (DOB) principles beyond explicit plant models to simulators and learned world models via state-rollout or cost-query interfaces, enabling compensation for sim-to-real mismatch and improved control performance.
AI.motivation: Robotic controllers increasingly rely on analytical models, simulators, cost-query interfaces, and learned world models, but physical deployment often deviates from nominal assumptions, and additional disturbances can arise even when the model itself is accurate. Classical DOB formulations are typically limited to explicit plant models, restricting their applicability to these broader model classes.
AI.method: The authors develop the Sampling-based Disturbance Observer (SDOB), which extends the DOB principle to a wider range of models (including simulators and learned world models) through state-rollout or cost-query interfaces. SDOB separates two observable channels: state-effect disturbances (where feedback state differs from its prediction) and cost disturbances (where the same query state receives different costs as the perceived environment changes).
AI.result: Diverse simulation and real-robot experiments across both traditional and learned models demonstrate the effectiveness of SDOB in compensating for sim-to-real mismatch and improving control performance.
AI.conclusion: SDOB generalizes disturbance observation to model classes lacking explicit plant formulations, providing a practical mechanism to estimate and compensate unmeasured disturbances in robotic control under sim-to-real mismatch.

title: EnvDreamer: Large-Scale Multimodal-to-Environment Generation for Embodied AI
summary: Large datasets and high capacity models have accelerated progress in vision and language. This work introduces a platform aimed at bringing comparable gains to embodied learning, world models, and robotics. We present EnvDreamer, a framework that uses large language and vision language models to generate Unreal Engine 5 environments for embodied AI and robot training. EnvDreamer enables sampling of large, diverse, interactive, customizable, and validator passed virtual environments for training and evaluation across navigation, interaction, and manipulation. We illustrate the platform with a large set of generated scenes and simple baselines. Policies trained on EnvDreamer generated environments, without explicit mapping or human task supervision, achieve competitive results on multiple embodied benchmarks spanning navigation, rearrangement, and manipulation. EnvDreamer also supports image-conditioned reconstruction for real-to-sim studies. Finally, we release EnvDreamer-20k, a dataset of 20,000 validator passed environments with task programs, scene graphs, trajectories, and metadata to support reproducible benchmarking.

AI.tldr: EnvDreamer is a framework leveraging large language and vision-language models to automatically generate Unreal Engine 5 embodied AI environments, enabling scalable, diverse robot training and releasing a 20k-environment dataset.
AI.motivation: While large datasets and high-capacity models have driven rapid progress in vision and language, embodied learning, world models, and robotics have not benefited from comparable gains, largely due to a scarcity of large, diverse, and interactive training environments.
AI.method: The authors build EnvDreamer, a platform that uses large language and vision-language models to synthesize Unreal Engine 5 environments. It samples large, diverse, interactive, customizable virtual scenes, filtered through validators, supporting navigation, interaction, and manipulation tasks. It also supports image-conditioned reconstruction for real-to-sim transfer.
AI.result: Policies trained on EnvDreamer-generated environments, without explicit mapping or human task supervision, achieve competitive performance on multiple embodied benchmarks covering navigation, rearrangement, and manipulation. The platform is demonstrated with a large set of generated scenes and simple baselines.
AI.conclusion: EnvDreamer brings scalable, LLM/VLM-driven environment generation to embodied AI and robotics, and the authors release EnvDreamer-20k, a dataset of 20,000 validator-passed environments with task programs, scene graphs, trajectories, and metadata to support reproducible benchmarking.

title: GJK-CBF: Control Barrier Functions for Convex Rigid Body Collision Avoidance on SE(3)
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures. Demo video: https://youtu.be/eDvscHhGIj0. This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible. Code will be released upon publication
summary: Collision avoidance among convex bodies is a fundamental problem in robotics. Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) provide a practical framework for real-time safety filtering due to their computational efficiency. For general convex bodies, exact separation measures, such as distance or scaling factor, are typically computed through optimization. Existing CBF formulations often obtain the required gradient via differentiable optimization (diffOpt), adding computational overhead. In contrast, we leverage the Gilbert-Johnson-Keerthi (GJK) algorithm to obtain the current witness pair---the pair of points realizing the minimum distance or penetration depth---and formulate a CBF, termed GJK-CBF, whose gradient is constructed directly from the relative rigid-body motion of the witness pair, without resorting to diffOpt. This formulation applies to both 2D and 3D environments across a broad class of convex body pairs, provided that at least one in each one-to-one interaction is strictly convex. The proposed GJK-CBF is validated in various scenarios, including multi-robot position swapping in both 2D and 3D, navigation through a vertical slit in 3D, and its applicability to manipulators. The results demonstrate collision-free motion across all scenarios while reducing the conservativeness introduced by geometric approximations, particularly in narrow environments.

AI.tldr: GJK-CBF formulates a control barrier function for convex-body collision avoidance whose gradient is built directly from the GJK algorithm's witness points and relative rigid-body motion, avoiding differentiable optimization.
AI.motivation: Collision avoidance among convex bodies is fundamental in robotics. Existing CBF formulations for general convex bodies require the gradient of exact separation measures (distance or scaling factor), typically obtained via differentiable optimization (diffOpt), which adds computational overhead. The paper aims to eliminate this overhead.
AI.method: The authors use the Gilbert-Johnson-Keerthi (GJK) algorithm to obtain the current witness pair—the points realizing minimum distance or penetration depth—and construct a CBF (GJK-CBF) whose gradient is derived directly from the relative rigid-body motion of the witness pair, without diffOpt. The formulation covers 2D and 3D settings for a broad class of convex body pairs, requiring at least one strictly convex body in each one-to-one interaction.
AI.result: GJK-CBF is validated in multi-robot position swapping in 2D and 3D, navigation through a vertical slit in 3D, and manipulator applications. All scenarios achieve collision-free motion while reducing the conservativeness introduced by geometric approximations, especially in narrow environments.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging GJK witness points to construct the CBF gradient provides an efficient, diffOpt-free safety filter for convex-body collision avoidance, yielding collision-free behavior with less conservativeness in constrained spaces.

title: MOIRA: Mass-Oriented Indexing with Ragged Attention for Long-Context Decoding
summary: Long-context decoding is limited by memory bandwidth, because every output token reads the KV cache of every layer. Sparse decoding reduces this cost by reading only part of the KV cache. We observe that the number of pages a query needs varies widely across KV heads, layers and steps. Fixed budgets are simple, but they are sized for demanding cases and tuned per workload; adaptive budgets follow this variation more flexibly, but existing designs pay for it with extra selection cost or training. At the kernel level, FlashAttention-3 (FA3) and FlashInfer are designed for rows of similar length: with page lists whose length differs per KV head, they either pad the lists (forfeiting much of the sparse saving), leave thread blocks unbalanced, or rely on a host-side plan that runs outside the CUDA graph. We propose MOIRA, a training-free sparse decode path in vLLM whose budget adapts per KV head and per layer. For every request, layer, KV head and step, a coverage rule keeps the smallest set of pages whose estimated attention mass reaches a fraction $γ$. A new kernel, self-planning attention, lets each thread block derive its own share of the work from the list lengths, so the whole decode step stays inside the CUDA graph. On an H200, at RULER's 128k context, MOIRA with $γ=0.99$ matches dense accuracy while reading about 30% of the pages and reduces the time per output token (TPOT) by 2.2-2.5$\times$ relative to dense FA3; with $γ=0.98$ it reduces TPOT by 2.7$\times$ and stays within the noise of dense. Under high serving load it raises throughput by up to 51%. These results suggest that a budget adapted per head and layer, paired with a kernel that keeps such budgets inside the CUDA graph, makes sparse decoding both flexible and fast.

AI.tldr: MOIRA is a training-free sparse decoding method in vLLM that adapts the KV cache page budget per KV head and per layer, paired with a self-planning attention kernel that keeps the whole decode step inside the CUDA graph, achieving up to 2.7x lower TPOT and 51% higher throughput on H200 at 128k context.
AI.motivation: Long-context decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound because every output token must read the KV cache of every layer. Sparse decoding mitigates this by reading only part of the KV cache, but the number of pages a query needs varies widely across KV heads, layers, and steps. Fixed budgets are simple but sized for worst cases and tuned per workload; existing adaptive budgets add extra selection cost or training overhead. At the kernel level, FA3 and FlashInfer assume rows of similar length, so with variable page-list lengths per KV head they either pad lists (losing sparse savings), leave thread blocks unbalanced, or rely on a host-side plan outside the CUDA graph.
AI.method: MOIRA is a training-free sparse decode path integrated into vLLM with a per-KV-head and per-layer adaptive budget. For each request, layer, KV head, and step, a coverage rule keeps the smallest set of pages whose estimated attention mass reaches a fraction gamma. A new self-planning attention kernel lets each thread block derive its own share of work from the page-list lengths, keeping the entire decode step inside the CUDA graph without padding, load imbalance, or host-side planning.
AI.result: On an H200 at RULER's 128k context, MOIRA with gamma=0.99 matches dense accuracy while reading about 30% of the pages and reduces TPOT by 2.2-2.5x relative to dense FA3. With gamma=0.98 it reduces TPOT by 2.7x and stays within the noise of dense accuracy. Under high serving load, throughput increases by up to 51%.
AI.conclusion: A budget adapted per KV head and per layer, combined with a kernel that keeps such budgets inside the CUDA graph, makes sparse decoding both flexible and fast, matching dense accuracy while substantially cutting memory traffic, TPOT, and improving serving throughput.

title: $R^2$-WAM: Repair-and-Reject Post-Training for World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) emerge as a promising foundation for policy refinement by predicting the consequences of sampled actions. However, visually plausible predictions can mislead policy refinement if they fail to reflect the input actions. To address this mismatch, we introduce $R^2$-WAM, a two-stage repair-and-reject post-training framework that first improves the consistency of predicted futures with input actions, then uses these futures to select inferior action samples for negative fine-tuning. The repair stage grounds imagination in observed robot behavior through a kinematic alignment score that measures agreement between predicted and demonstrated motion, enabling the predicted video to faithfully reflect its input actions. Using the repaired video model, the rejection stage compares imagined outcomes of sampled and demonstrated actions, selectively applying negative fine-tuning to samples whose predicted task progress falls below the demonstrated reference by a prescribed margin. Together, the two stages extend video prediction from representation learning to consequence-based policy refinement without additional environment interaction or changes to the inference procedure. $R^2$-WAM achieves 93.8% average success on RoboTwin 2.0 across clean and randomized settings. On the long-horizon real-world Fold Shirt task, it achieves 87.5% average success, compared with 0% for Fast-WAM.

AI.tldr: R²-WAM is a two-stage repair-and-reject post-training framework that makes video-based action prediction faithful to input actions and uses it for consequence-based policy refinement without extra environment interaction.
AI.motivation: World Action Models can refine policies by predicting action consequences, but visually plausible predictions may not actually reflect the input actions, misleading the refinement process. The paper addresses this mismatch between predicted futures and the actions that produced them.
AI.method: A two-stage repair-and-reject post-training framework. The repair stage grounds imagination in observed robot behavior via a kinematic alignment score measuring agreement between predicted and demonstrated motion, so predicted video faithfully reflects input actions. The rejection stage uses the repaired video model to compare imagined outcomes of sampled versus demonstrated actions, selectively applying negative fine-tuning to samples whose predicted task progress falls below the demonstrated reference by a prescribed margin. No additional environment interaction or inference changes are required.
AI.result: 93.8% average success on RoboTwin 2.0 across clean and randomized settings. On the long-horizon real-world Fold Shirt task, 87.5% average success versus 0% for Fast-WAM.
AI.conclusion: The two stages extend video prediction from representation learning to consequence-based policy refinement, improving action-consistent imagination and enabling effective negative fine-tuning of inferior action samples.

title: From Latent Space to Jacobian Space: Measuring, Evading, and Training Against Safety-Content Accessibility
summary: Output-only safety monitoring sees only the end of a model's computation, yet the model computes its answer before emitting it: what it is internally poised to say is safety-critical. Jacobian-space (J-space) readouts, linear maps from hidden states to the output vocabulary via the model's input-output Jacobian, have been proposed as a window on behaviorally accessible internal content, and a first safety protocol (JADR) showed that danger recognition is readable there. What remains unknown is how this accessible content relates to the latent-space safety geometry studied by representation engineering, and how safety training shapes it. We introduce two quantitative bridges: (i) a transport-amplification profile $A_\ell$, measuring how strongly a latent safety direction is carried toward output space by each layer's Jacobian, and (ii) a paired base-vs-tuned protocol that attributes accessibility to training provenance. Across four small model pairs (135M to 1.5B, three lens-fit seeds), tuned checkpoints concentrate recognition in upper-middle layers, and at 0.5B DPO installs refusal while J-space recognition drops to chance: training can widen the accessibility gap exactly where behavioral safety looks best. A deployment audit closes the loop: monitor-aware GCG-style suffixes suppress the prompt-side monitor at zero behavioral cost at every scale; only a learned monitor rung resists its own adaptive re-attack; the training-time defense fails its re-attack at every penalty weight; steering shows the amplification profile is descriptive, not causal; and continuous-prefix optimization fails where discrete search succeeds. Safety monitoring, training, and evaluation must operate on accessibility itself, not on outputs alone.

AI.tldr: The paper bridges J-space accessibility (Jacobian readouts) and latent safety geometry via a transport-amplification profile A_ℓ and a paired base-vs-tuned protocol, showing safety training can widen the accessibility gap (e.g., DPO at 0.5B installs refusal while J-space recognition drops to chance), and that prompt-side monitors are suppressible at zero behavioral cost while only a learned monitor resists adaptive re-attack.
AI.motivation: Output-only safety monitoring observes only the model's emitted answer, but the model computes its answer before emitting it, so its internally accessible content is safety-critical. J-space readouts (linear maps from hidden states to the output vocabulary via the input-output Jacobian) were proposed as a window onto this internal content, and JADR showed danger recognition is readable there. However, it remained unknown how this accessible content relates to the latent-space safety geometry studied by representation engineering, and how safety training shapes it.
AI.method: Two quantitative bridges: (i) a transport-amplification profile A_ℓ measuring how strongly a latent safety direction is carried toward output space by each layer's Jacobian; (ii) a paired base-vs-tuned protocol attributing accessibility to training provenance. Evaluated across four small model pairs (135M–1.5B) with three lens-fit seeds, plus a deployment audit including monitor-aware GCG-style suffixes, learned-monitor re-attack, training-time defense under varying penalty weights, steering, and continuous-prefix vs. discrete search.
AI.result: Tuned checkpoints concentrate recognition in upper-middle layers; at 0.5B, DPO installs refusal while J-space recognition drops to chance, so training can widen the accessibility gap exactly where behavioral safety looks best. In the deployment audit, monitor-aware GCG-style suffixes suppress the prompt-side monitor at zero behavioral cost at every scale; only a learned monitor rung resists its own adaptive re-attack; the training-time defense fails its re-attack at every penalty weight; steering shows the amplification profile is descriptive, not causal; and continuous-prefix optimization fails where discrete search succeeds.
AI.conclusion: Safety monitoring, training, and evaluation must operate on accessibility itself—the internally poised content—rather than on outputs alone. The transport-amplification profile and paired base-vs-tuned protocol provide the bridges needed to analyze this gap.

title: PreAct-Nav: Agentic Reasoning Before Action for Urban Navigation
summary: Urban navigation requires embodied agents to pursue long-horizon goals through local decisions based on egocentric observations. However, existing agentic navigation methods often struggle to translate distant goals into coherent local decisions in large-scale physical environments. Their reliance on linguistic reasoning over transient observations or limited history constrains anticipation of the consequences of actions and future conditions, despite the importance of such foresight for navigating long and complex urban routes. To bridge this gap, we propose PreAct-Nav, an agentic navigation framework that equips frozen policies with anticipatory reasoning for robust urban navigation. Our central idea is to anchor local decisions in persistent medium-horizon subgoals, assess the consequences of predicted actions before execution, and continually update the reasoning context using actual outcomes. At its core, a navigation memory module maintains the active subgoal and relevant experience across decisions, translating distant goals into actionable intermediate objectives. We further introduce a predictive world sandbox that uses an action-conditioned world model (AC-WM) to forecast world dynamics conditioned on candidate movements. A vision-language model (VLM) reasoner interprets these predictions under the current subgoal to retain or revise actions. After execution, real observations are used to assess outcomes, correct inconsistent assumptions, and update memory to continue or reformulate the subgoal. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that the proposed PreAct-Nav improves action selection through memory updates and visual prediction, with more pronounced gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.

AI.tldr: PreAct-Nav is an agentic navigation framework that adds anticipatory reasoning to frozen policies by anchoring local decisions in medium-horizon subgoals, simulating action consequences via an action-conditioned world model, and refining a navigation memory with real outcomes, yielding improved urban navigation especially on long and turn-heavy routes.
AI.motivation: Urban navigation demands long-horizon goal pursuit via local, egocentric decisions. Existing agentic methods fail to translate distant goals into coherent local decisions in large-scale physical environments because they rely on linguistic reasoning over transient observations or limited history, which limits foresight about action consequences and future conditions—foresight that is essential for long, complex urban routes.
AI.method: PreAct-Nav equips frozen policies with anticipatory reasoning. It (1) anchors local decisions in persistent medium-horizon subgoals, (2) evaluates predicted action consequences before execution, and (3) updates reasoning context with actual outcomes. A navigation memory module maintains the active subgoal and relevant experience across decisions. A predictive world sandbox uses an action-conditioned world model (AC-WM) to forecast world dynamics under candidate movements. A VLM reasoner interprets these predictions under the current subgoal to retain or revise actions. After execution, real observations assess outcomes, correct inconsistent assumptions, and update memory to continue or reformulate the subgoal.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations show that PreAct-Nav improves action selection through memory updates and visual prediction, with more pronounced gains on longer routes and routes with more turns.
AI.conclusion: Anchoring decisions in persistent medium-horizon subgoals, screening actions via an AC-WM sandbox, and closing the loop with real-outcome memory updates enables frozen policies to achieve more robust, foresightful urban navigation, scaling better to long and complex routes.

title: Bidirectional Preference Synthesis: Learning Prompt-Conditioned Preferences from Boundary Failures
summary: Correction-based offline preference pipelines commonly treat model failures only as rejected responses under the original prompt. This supervision is incomplete for boundary failures: responses that violate the given instruction yet coherently satisfy a nearby intent or constraint setting. We introduce Bidirectional Preference Synthesis (BPS), a data-construction method for standard Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) that makes this missing prompt dependence explicit. For each validated boundary failure, BPS keeps the conventional forward pair under the original prompt and adds a reverse pair under a synthesized achieved prompt, so the same response is rejected where it is wrong and chosen where it is right, without changing the DPO objective, training a reward model, or requiring online sampling. On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, BPS preserves original-side pairwise ranking while raising achieved-side ranking accuracy from 6.8% to 62.3% on held-out crossed anchors, with a similar shift under a Kimi-K2.6 cross-teacher probe. A blind human audit supports the intended reverse preference direction, and downstream evaluations show the clearest separation from Forward-DPO in multilingual multi-turn instruction following, with consistent capability-retention patterns on agentic, tool-use, and code checks.

AI.tldr: BPS is a data-construction method for DPO that adds reverse preference pairs under synthesized "achieved" prompts to explicitly capture prompt dependence in boundary failures, improving achieved-side ranking without changing the DPO objective or requiring online sampling.
AI.motivation: Offline correction-based preference pipelines typically treat model failures only as rejected responses under the original prompt. This supervision is incomplete for boundary failures: responses that violate the given instruction yet coherently satisfy a nearby intent or constraint setting, since the missing prompt dependence is never made explicit.
AI.method: Bidirectional Preference Synthesis (BPS): for each validated boundary failure, keep the conventional forward pair under the original prompt and add a reverse pair under a synthesized achieved prompt, so the same response is rejected where wrong and chosen where right. BPS works with standard DPO without altering the objective, training a reward model, or requiring online sampling.
AI.result: On Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, BPS preserves original-side pairwise ranking while raising achieved-side ranking accuracy from 6.8% to 62.3% on held-out crossed anchors, with a similar shift under a Kimi-K2.6 cross-teacher probe. A blind human audit supports the intended reverse preference direction; downstream evaluations show the clearest separation from Forward-DPO in multilingual multi-turn instruction following, with consistent capability-retention on agentic, tool-use, and code checks.
AI.conclusion: Making prompt dependence explicit via bidirectional preference pairs yields a lightweight, DPO-compatible data-construction fix for boundary failures, improving achieved-side ranking and downstream instruction following while retaining general capabilities.

title: Nudge Before You Push: Physics-Aware Navigation via Tactile Probing
summary: Visually identical containers can conceal loads that require different handling decisions. We present TANav, which uses a brief nudge to measure push resistance for navigation under a site-defined handling boundary. TacPhys reads the force sequence, with optional RGB-D and kinematics, into a mass estimate for push authorization. A repeated-patrol planner weighs probe and route costs, requests a second contact when useful, and reuses observations across visits. In simulation, TacPhys approaches a resistance-only Bayes reference and reduces missed pushes from 28.7% to 5.5% relative to peak-force thresholding at comparable low-risk operating points. In repeated-patrol simulation, TANav recovers 90% of the oracle's path saving, more than halves human interventions relative to always-detour, and reduces boundary violations from 4.3% to 2.9% relative to RGB-D-only probing. On a quadruped manipulator with a Hall-array fingertip, offline zero-shot MAE is 0.28-1.07 kg on containers up to 2.82 kg. Force-rise calibration at 3 kg gives 93.5% pooled offline accuracy (86.4% on non-cube episodes); a separate raw-peak rule gives 15 of 20 correct online decisions on unseen boxes.

AI.tldr: TANav uses a brief nudge to measure push resistance, with TacPhys estimating mass from the force sequence (plus optional RGB-D/kinematics) to authorize pushes, and a repeated-patrol planner that trades probe vs. route cost, requests second contacts, and reuses observations.
AI.motivation: Visually identical containers can hide loads requiring different handling decisions, so vision alone cannot determine whether a push is safe.
AI.method: A brief nudge measures push resistance under a site-defined handling boundary. TacPhys reads the force sequence, with optional RGB-D and kinematics, into a mass estimate for push authorization. A repeated-patrol planner weighs probe and route costs, requests a second contact when useful, and reuses observations across visits.
AI.result: In simulation TacPhys approaches a resistance-only Bayes reference and cuts missed pushes from 28.7% to 5.5% vs. peak-force thresholding at comparable low-risk operating points.
