In repeated-patrol simulation TANav recovers 90% of the oracle's path saving, more than halves human interventions vs. always-detour, and reduces boundary violations from 4.3% to 2.9% vs. RGB-D-only probing. On a quadruped manipulator with a Hall-array fingertip, offline zero-shot MAE is 0.28-1.07 kg on containers up to 2.82 kg; force-rise calibration at 3 kg yields 93.5% pooled offline accuracy (86.4% on non-cube episodes), and a separate raw-peak rule gives 15/20 correct online decisions on unseen boxes.
AI.conclusion: Probing push resistance via a brief nudge enables reliable mass estimation and safer, more efficient navigation under a handling boundary, validated in simulation and on real hardware.

title: Suppressing Pressure, Amplifying Evidence: Self-Guided Attention Steering to Mitigate Sycophancy and Stubbornness
summary: Reliable language models should resist unsupported user pressure while effectively using objective contextual information. However, models may exhibit sycophancy by yielding to unsupported user pressure or contextual stubbornness by failing to update their answers when relevant contextual information warrants revision. Evaluating interventions for these failures separately can obscure whether mitigating one failure exacerbates the other. To assess this trade-off, we introduce CoPE-Bench with six conditions per question: a neutral baseline, correct or incorrect user pressure, contextual information consistent with or conflicting with the neutral answer, and a joint condition combining incorrect claims with conflicting contextual information. To regulate the influence of user pressure and contextual information, we propose SPAE (Suppressing Pressure, Amplifying Evidence), a training-free framework that uses the model's own judgments to identify relevant tokens, suppressing user pressure and amplifying contextual information through token-level attention steering. On average across five backbones, SPAE reduces pressure following by 18.8 percentage points and increases joint-condition updating by 5.5 percentage points relative to the strongest baseline in the main comparison. In two-turn dialogue, it improves joint-condition updating by an average of 13.2 percentage points over the strongest prompting baseline. The source data and codes can be found at https://github.com/03Grant/sycophancy-and-stubbornness.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CoPE-Bench to jointly evaluate sycophancy (yielding to unsupported user pressure) and contextual stubbornness (ignoring relevant context), and proposes SPAE, a training-free attention-steering framework that suppresses pressure tokens and amplifies evidence tokens, reducing pressure following and improving updating.
AI.motivation: Reliable language models should resist unsupported user pressure while incorporating objective contextual evidence. However, they can exhibit two opposing failures—sycophancy toward user pressure and stubbornness against contextual evidence. Evaluating these separately can hide whether fixing one worsens the other, so a joint trade-off assessment is needed.
AI.method: The authors build CoPE-Bench with six conditions per question: neutral baseline, correct/incorrect user pressure, context consistent/conflicting with the neutral answer, and a joint condition combining incorrect claims with conflicting context. They then propose SPAE (Suppressing Pressure, Amplifying Evidence), a training-free framework leveraging the model's own judgments to identify relevant tokens and performing token-level attention steering to suppress user pressure and amplify contextual information.
AI.result: Averaged over five backbones, SPAE reduces pressure following by 18.8 percentage points and increases joint-condition updating by 5.5 percentage points versus the strongest baseline in the main comparison. In two-turn dialogue, it improves joint-condition updating by 13.2 percentage points on average over the strongest prompting baseline.
AI.conclusion: Jointly evaluating sycophancy and contextual stubbornness reveals their trade-off, and token-level attention steering via SPAE effectively balances resistance to unsupported pressure with appropriate contextual updating, also generalizing to multi-turn dialogue.

title: RobotUse: Allocating Computation, Context, and Decisions
comment: 18 pages, 10 figures, 11 tables. Project page: https://robotuse-team.github.io/
summary: Robot agents must connect their intended actions to observed outcomes while retaining the context needed to revise their choices over repeated attempts. Existing interfaces often leave these choices inside predefined tools or require agents to manage detailed execution code and its growing history. We introduce RobotUse, a robot agent harness that organizes computation, context, and decisions around specifying and revising physical actions. Agents visually select targets and poses, while the backend handles geometry, motion planning, and control. Subagents retain detailed interactions within each subgoal and return the information needed for subsequent decisions. Continual harnessing lets agents learn from execution by updating a persistent playbook. On RoboLab, RobotUse achieves 45% task success, outperforming CaP-X by 6.7 percentage points while maintaining compact decision contexts and reducing reliance on predefined action abstractions. Furthermore, we show that RobotUse learns from real-world execution despite imperfect feedback and transfers what it learns to subsequent tasks. Project page is available at https://robotuse-team.github.io/.

AI.tldr: RobotUse is a robot agent harness that organizes computation, context, and decisions around specifying and revising physical actions via visual target/pose selection, with a backend handling geometry, planning, and control; subagents preserve detailed interaction history, and continual harnessing updates a persistent playbook. It reaches 45% task success on RoboLab, beating CaP-X by 6.7 points.
AI.motivation: Robot agents need to connect intended actions to observed outcomes while keeping enough context to revise choices over repeated attempts, but existing interfaces either bury these choices inside predefined tools or force agents to manage detailed execution code and ever-growing history.
AI.method: RobotUse is a harness that organizes computation, context, and decisions around specifying and revising physical actions. Agents visually select targets and poses while the backend handles geometry, motion planning, and control. Subagents retain detailed interactions within each subgoal and return information needed for subsequent decisions. Continual harnessing enables learning from execution by updating a persistent playbook.
AI.result: On RoboLab, RobotUse achieves 45% task success, outperforming CaP-X by 6.7 percentage points while maintaining compact decision contexts and reducing reliance on predefined action abstractions. It also learns from real-world execution despite imperfect feedback and transfers that learning to subsequent tasks.
AI.conclusion: RobotUse shows that structuring a robot agent around action specification/revising, subagent-bounded context, and a persistent playbook yields higher task success with compact contexts and less dependence on predefined abstractions, and supports real-world learning and transfer.

title: ShadowMiner v1 - An Experience Report on Implementing and Measuring a Problem-and-Hypothesis Discovery Engine
summary: ShadowMiner v1 is a system that automatically discovers research problems and generates hypotheses from AI papers. It is a nine-stage pipeline. It structures documents into a knowledge graph and finds graph gaps in it - structural blind spots in research. These graph gaps are included in the LLM generation prompt. Each generated hypothesis is then verified by checking whether it is already covered by existing research, scoring its quality, and checking that the facts it relies on are accurately drawn from its sources. This report does not propose a new generation or evaluation technique. It describes our experience of implementing and applying ideas from prior work, and measuring whether each one actually contributed.

AI.tldr: ShadowMiner v1 is a nine-stage pipeline that automatically discovers research problems and generates hypotheses from AI papers by structuring documents into a knowledge graph, detecting structural "graph gaps," and feeding them into an LLM prompt, with each hypothesis verified for novelty, quality, and factual grounding.
AI.motivation: The paper reports on implementing and applying ideas from prior work to build a system for automated research problem discovery and hypothesis generation, and measuring whether each component actually contributed. It explicitly does not aim to propose new generation or evaluation techniques.
AI.method: A nine-stage pipeline: documents are structured into a knowledge graph; graph gaps (structural blind spots in research) are identified; these gaps are included in the LLM generation prompt; each generated hypothesis is then verified by checking whether it is already covered by existing research, scoring its quality, and checking that its underlying facts are accurately drawn from the sources.
AI.result: The paper describes experience implementing and applying prior-work ideas, measuring whether each one actually contributed.
AI.conclusion: ShadowMiner v1 integrates existing ideas into a working system rather than introducing novel generation or evaluation methods; its contribution is an empirical account of which inherited components proved useful.

title: DiVeR: Decision-Critical Verifier Learning for VLA Test-Time Scaling
summary: Scaling robot data and model capacity has improved Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, but further progress is constrained by the high cost of robotic data. Verifier-guided test-time scaling offers an efficient alternative by sampling multiple action candidates and selecting the one most likely to lead to task success at inference time. Existing classification-based verifiers learn from trajectory-level outcomes but treat all visited states equally, even though their value for candidate discrimination can vary across a trajectory. At many states, plausible actions are similar and provide limited discrimination signal, while only a sparse set of decision-critical states admits meaningfully different actions that can substantially affect downstream outcomes. To address this, we propose DiVeR, which estimates decision criticality from the dispersion of sampled action representations. DiVeR then uses this signal to reweight verifier learning toward states where action selection is most consequential, without requiring step-level annotations or additional environment interaction. Across LIBERO, RoboCasa, and real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 robot, DiVeR consistently improves task success through more effective verifier-guided action selection, while adding negligible verifier inference overhead.

AI.tldr: DiVeR reweights verifier learning for VLA policies toward decision-critical states, identified via the dispersion of sampled action representations, improving verifier-guided test-time action selection without step-level annotations or extra environment interaction.
AI.motivation: Scaling robot data and model capacity for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies is limited by the high cost of robotic data. Verifier-guided test-time scaling is an efficient alternative, but existing classification-based verifiers learn from trajectory-level outcomes and treat all visited states equally, even though their discrimination value varies. At many states, plausible actions are similar and yield weak discrimination signal; only a sparse set of decision-critical states admits meaningfully different actions that substantially affect downstream outcomes.
AI.method: DiVeR estimates decision criticality from the dispersion of sampled action representations. It then uses this criticality signal to reweight verifier learning toward states where action selection is most consequential, without requiring step-level annotations or additional environment interaction.
AI.result: Across LIBERO, RoboCasa, and real-world experiments on a Franka Research 3 robot, DiVeR consistently improves task success through more effective verifier-guided action selection, while adding negligible verifier inference overhead.
AI.conclusion: DiVeR addresses the uniform treatment of states in verifier learning by focusing on decision-critical states identified through action representation dispersion, delivering consistent gains in verifier-guided action selection at minimal inference cost, without step-level annotations or extra environment interaction.

title: Functionally Equivalent or Not? Graph-Grounded Differential Surrogate Execution for Code Equivalence
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables, accepted by NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on AI for Verifiable Coding
summary: Determining whether two programs are functionally equivalent is central to code modernization, patch validation, refactoring, and code-generation evaluation. Yet the usual signals are incomplete: tests cover only finite inputs, textual similarity confuses implementation with behavior, and unconstrained LLM judgments are difficult to audit. Direct execution is often impossible when a program depends on an obsolete, licensed, unavailable, or unsafe environment. We introduce FEAgent, a selective equivalence assessor agent that combines typed program-graph evidence with differential surrogate execution. FEAgent first aligns public interfaces and behaviorally relevant graph anchors, then issues bounded queries over call-flow, control-flow, data-flow, type, import, and effect relations. Next, a branch-aware generator agent proposes discriminating inputs, and two blinded LLM surrogates independently predict source and target observables. Every claim and predicted divergence is recorded in an evidence ledger. A deterministic reconciler then returns EQUIVALENT, INEQUIVALENT, or UNCLEAR rather than forcing a verdict when paths are uncovered or evidence conflicts. We evaluate FEAgent on function-level equivalence and repository-level bug patches, where the existing oracle is a benchmark label or a passing test suite. Every disagreement with that oracle is adjudicated by direct execution, revealing errors in benchmark labels and behavioral divergences missed by unit-test-only scoring. On EquiBench, execution confirms FEAgent's disagreements with published labels on 216 of 1,200 evaluated pairs (18.0%); on SWE-bench Verified, 94 of 331 test-passing agent patches (28.4%) diverge from the reference patch. FEAgent thus serves as an audit layer between testing and formal verification, keeping its evidence reviewable and its uncertainty explicit without claiming a proof of equivalence.

AI.tldr: FEAgent is a selective agent that assesses program functional equivalence by combining typed program-graph evidence with differential surrogate execution, returning EQUIVALENT, INEQUIVALENT, or UNCLEAR verdicts while logging all evidence in an auditable ledger.
AI.motivation: Determining functional equivalence is central to code modernization, patch validation, refactoring, and code-generation evaluation, but existing signals are incomplete: tests cover only finite inputs, textual similarity conflates implementation with behavior, and unconstrained LLM judgments are hard to audit. Direct execution is often infeasible due to obsolete, licensed, unavailable, or unsafe environments.
AI.method: FEAgent aligns public interfaces and behaviorally relevant graph anchors, then issues bounded queries over call-flow, control-flow, data-flow, type, import, and effect relations. A branch-aware generator proposes discriminating inputs, and two blinded LLM surrogates independently predict source and target observables. All claims and predicted divergences are recorded in an evidence ledger, and a deterministic reconciler outputs EQUIVALENT, INEQUIVALENT, or UNCLEAR rather than forcing a verdict when paths are uncovered or evidence conflicts.
AI.result: Evaluated on function-level equivalence and repository-level bug patches. On EquiBench, execution confirmed FEAgent's disagreements with published labels on 216 of 1,200 pairs (18.0%); on SWE-bench Verified, 94 of 331 test-passing agent patches (28.4%) diverge from the reference patch, revealing errors in benchmark labels and behavioral divergences missed by unit-test-only scoring.
AI.conclusion: FEAgent acts as an audit layer between testing and formal verification, keeping its evidence reviewable and its uncertainty explicit without claiming a proof of equivalence.

title: A Unified Dynamics Framework for Reinforcement Learning and Classical Control of a Six-DOF Pipeline-Tracking ROV in NVIDIA Isaac Sim
summary: Reinforcement learning controllers for underwater vehicles are usually trained against one physics representation and deployed against another, so reported performance does not always describe behavior outside training. This paper presents a pipeline-tracking architecture for a six-degree-of-freedom remotely operated vehicle (ROV) in which one Universal Scene Description (USD) scene supplies the real BlueROV2-Heavy mass, added-mass, damping, buoyancy, and thruster parameters to both halves of the system: a vectorized NumPy implementation of Fossen's marine-craft equations, and an interactive NVIDIA Isaac Sim deployment applying the identical equations as PhysX forces at every step. The Coriolis-centripetal term is the primary dynamics model in both branches; a controlled ablation on PPO and TRPO shows that including it does not destabilize either algorithm and modestly improves tracking, about 19 percent lower standoff RMS error for TRPO. Five reinforcement learning algorithms, PPO, soft actor-critic, TD3, DDPG, and TRPO, are trained against one environment, reward, and randomized evaluation harness through a checkpoint-compatibility layer scoring any policy with the same code. The pipeline is extended with six classical baselines, PID, sliding-mode, fuzzy logic, feedback linearization, model predictive control, and an adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system, driven by the same guidance geometry and thruster allocation as the learned policies. Under Coriolis-enabled dynamics, PPO, TRPO, and feedback linearization reach the strongest combination of 100 percent success and competitive accuracy; PID, fuzzy control, and the neuro-fuzzy baseline also reach 100 percent success with looser tracking; DDPG and TD3 each show a specific, explainable failure mode rather than a general weakness of off-policy learning; and classical control remains a strong baseline against the best learned policies.

AI.tldr: A unified USD-based pipeline-tracking architecture for a 6-DOF BlueROV2-Heavy allows five RL algorithms and six classical controllers to be trained and deployed with identical physics; PPO, TRPO, and feedback linearization achieve 100% success with the best accuracy, while classical control remains a strong baseline.
AI.motivation: RL controllers for underwater vehicles are typically trained against one physics representation and deployed against another, so reported performance may not describe behavior outside training. The work aims to close this train-deploy gap by sharing a single physics source of truth across both the training and deployment branches, and to fairly compare learned and classical controllers under identical conditions.
AI.method: A single Universal Scene Description (USD) scene supplies the real BlueROV2-Heavy mass, added-mass, damping, buoyancy, and thruster parameters to both a vectorized NumPy implementation of Fossen's marine-craft equations and an interactive NVIDIA Isaac Sim deployment applying the identical equations as PhysX forces at each step. The Coriolis-centripetal term is used as the primary dynamics model in both branches, with a controlled ablation over PPO and TRPO. Five RL algorithms (PPO, SAC, TD3, DDPG, TRPO) are trained against one environment, reward, and randomized evaluation harness, scored through a checkpoint-compatibility layer using the same code. Six classical baselines (PID, sliding-mode, fuzzy logic, feedback linearization, MPC, ANFIS) use the same guidance geometry and thruster allocation as the learned policies.
AI.result: Including the Coriolis-centripetal term does not destabilize either algorithm and modestly improves tracking, yielding about 19% lower standoff RMS error for TRPO. With Coriolis-enabled dynamics, PPO, TRPO, and feedback linearization achieve the strongest combination of 100% success and competitive accuracy; PID, fuzzy control, and the neuro-fuzzy baseline also reach 100% success but with looser tracking; DDPG and TD3 each exhibit a specific, explainable failure mode rather than a general weakness of off-policy learning; classical control remains a strong baseline against the best learned policies.
AI.conclusion: Sharing a single USD physics description across the NumPy training environment and Isaac Sim deployment enables consistent, comparable evaluation of RL and classical controllers. Coriolis-enabled dynamics benefit tracking without harming stability. Learned and classical controllers perform comparably at the top end, indicating that classical control remains a strong baseline and that off-policy failures observed are algorithm-specific rather than fundamental.

title: Do Tool Calls Execute as Intended? Measuring and Repairing Intent-Execution Correspondence in LLM Agents
summary:
Agents built on large language models (LLMs) build and run software through tool calls. A call reaches its program through several hops, and any hop can change the call without notice. When the changed call fails, the agent retries a correct call, which costs users time and money. Benchmarks and failure analyses do not see the change, because they read the call and its result but not what a hop received. We define intent-execution correspondence (IEC) as the property that the executed action matches the action the emitted call denotes under the tool contract. Our protocol observes what each hop received without executing the call, and names the first hop that changed it by the receiver's own parser. IntAct then delivers the call in a form that this hop cannot alter, or refuses the call. We build IEC-Bench from the changes observed in real-world use, with chains of dependent calls under the execution paths of 4 widely-used harnesses.
  In 47,828 shell calls within production sessions, Claude Code's Bash tool changes 12.0% of the calls that carry code, escape sequences, or long text. For 80.7% of the calls whose backslashes are changed, the wrong action runs without any reported error. All 10 measured harnesses change a call. Trajectory-based judgment attributes 95.1% of the production failures to the LLM, although the path caused more than half of them. On IEC-Bench, the path raises the token cost per passed task 2.4 times (up to 12.3 times). A hop that changes a call also hides the changes after it, so 55.1% of the failures on one path appear only after its first hop is repaired. IntAct, deployed in a commercial product, recovers 79.2% of the failures with a changed call. Harnesses should therefore be designed and tested hop-by-hop to ensure a correct call executes as intended or is refused.

AI.tldr: LLM agents' tool calls can be silently altered as they pass through intermediate "hops" before execution, a problem existing benchmarks miss. The authors define intent-execution correspondence (IEC), build a hop-by-hop observation protocol named IntAct, and create IEC-Bench. They find that 12.0% of Claude Code Bash calls carrying code/escapes/long text are changed, all 10 tested harnesses alter calls, and the path (not the LLM) causes over half of production failures. IntAct recovers 79.2% of changed-call failures in a commercial deployment.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks and failure analyses read only the emitted call and its result, not what each intermediate hop actually received. As a result, silent alterations along the execution path go undetected, failures are misattributed to the LLM, and agents waste user time and money on retries.
AI.method: The paper formalizes intent-execution correspondence (IEC): the executed action must match the action the emitted call denotes under the tool contract. A protocol observes what each hop received without executing the call and identifies, via the receiver's own parser, the first hop that altered it. IntAct then either delivers the call in a form that hop cannot alter or refuses the call. IEC-Bench is constructed from real-world observed changes, with chains of dependent calls under the execution paths of 4 widely-used harnesses.
AI.result: In 47,828 production shell calls, Claude Code's Bash tool changes 12.0% of calls carrying code, escape sequences, or long text; for 80.7% of calls with altered backslashes, a wrong action runs with no reported error. All 10 measured harnesses change calls. Trajectory-based judgment blames the LLM for 95.1% of production failures though the path causes more than half. On IEC-Bench, the path raises token cost per passed task 2.4x (up to 12.3x). A hop that changes a call also hides downstream changes, so 55.1% of failures on one path appear only after its first hop is repaired. IntAct recovers 79.2% of changed-call failures in a commercial product.
AI.conclusion: Harnesses should be designed and tested hop-by-hop to ensure a correct call either executes as intended or is refused. IntAct demonstrates a practical remedy by preventing or refusing altered calls, recovering most failures and substantially reducing misattribution of failures to the LLM.

title: FreeLoc: Online Floorplan Localization via Diffusion-Aided Pose Refinement
comment: Accepted at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026
summary: Floorplans provide compact and widely available geometric maps for indoor localization, but existing high-performing floorplan-based methods still convert them into dense scene-specific offline databases, tying accuracy, storage, and runtime to the sampling resolution of the discretized pose space. We present FreeLoc, an online RGB-based floorplan localization framework that treats the floorplan as a directly queryable geometric map. FreeLoc introduces an efficient online geometric querying and diffusion-aided refinement scheme, which retrieves plausible pose anchors through on-the-fly floorplan ray querying and refines them into accurate continuous pose estimates. For sequential localization, FreeLoc develops an online likelihood construction strategy that bridges single-frame localization and probabilistic temporal fusion by constructing likelihoods from coarse-sampled candidates and refined pose hypotheses, enabling histogram-filter-based temporal fusion without offline databases. Experiments demonstrate real-time online inference and state-of-the-art performance in both single-frame and sequential localization, while real-world results validate practical deployability in indoor robotic localization scenarios.

AI.tldr: FreeLoc is an online RGB-based indoor localization framework that queries the floorplan directly as a geometric map, avoiding dense offline databases while achieving real-time, state-of-the-art single-frame and sequential localization.
AI.motivation: Existing high-performing floorplan-based indoor localization methods convert floorplans into dense scene-specific offline databases. This ties accuracy, storage, and runtime to the sampling resolution of the discretized pose space, making them costly and inflexible.
AI.method: FreeLoc treats the floorplan as a directly queryable geometric map. It introduces an online geometric querying and diffusion-aided refinement scheme that retrieves plausible pose anchors via on-the-fly floorplan ray querying and refines them into continuous pose estimates. For sequential localization, it develops an online likelihood construction strategy that bridges single-frame localization and probabilistic temporal fusion, building likelihoods from coarse-sampled candidates and refined hypotheses, enabling histogram-filter-based temporal fusion without offline databases.
AI.result: Experiments show real-time online inference and state-of-the-art performance in both single-frame and sequential localization. Real-world results validate practical deployability in indoor robotic localization scenarios.
AI.conclusion: FreeLoc eliminates the need for dense offline databases in floorplan-based localization by directly querying the floorplan online, delivering accurate, real-time, and deployable indoor localization.

title: AgentPersonaBench: Benchmarking Persona-Driven User Simulation
summary: We introduce AgentPersonaBench (APB), a benchmark evaluating whether persona conditioning faithfully steers downstream agent behavior. While language models are increasingly deployed for persona-driven user simulation, existing benchmarks primarily evaluate conversational styling or self-reports rather than authentic behavioral fidelity. APB evaluates latent persona adherence one trait at a time, embedding each target trait within a complete synthetic profile without explicitly naming the trait or disclosing the test. Ground-truth adherence is verified strictly from observable actions across four interaction surfaces of increasing realism: survey, chat, web (interactive web environments), and app (desktop software environments). APB comprises 2,460 tasks spanning 867 traits, verified through automated audits and expert review. Our evaluation of 20 frontier model arms demonstrates that high-fidelity user simulation is already attainable: leading models achieve up to 84.7% full-pass adherence under unprompted conditions. At the same time, APB identifies clear behavioral boundaries: adherence drops across interaction modalities (only 37.9-64.3% pass all four surfaces), multi-attribute demands degrade retention, and competing model families exhibit pronounced behavioral divergence.

AI.tldr: AgentPersonaBench (APB) is a new benchmark that tests whether persona conditioning genuinely controls agent behavior, rather than just conversational style or self-reports, by checking latent trait adherence from observable actions across four increasingly realistic interaction surfaces.
AI.motivation: Language models are increasingly used for persona-driven user simulation, but existing benchmarks mostly measure conversational styling or self-reports instead of authentic behavioral fidelity. There is a need to evaluate whether latent persona traits truly steer downstream agent actions.
AI.method: APB evaluates latent persona adherence one trait at a time, embedding each target trait in a complete synthetic profile without naming the trait or revealing the test. Ground-truth adherence is verified strictly from observable actions across four interaction surfaces of increasing realism: survey, chat, web (interactive web environments), and app (desktop software environments). The benchmark includes 2,460 tasks spanning 867 traits, validated through automated audits and expert review, and is applied to 20 frontier model arms.
AI.result: Leading models achieve up to 84.7% full-pass adherence under unprompted conditions, showing high-fidelity user simulation is already attainable. However, adherence drops across interaction modalities, with only 37.9-64.3% passing all four surfaces; multi-attribute demands reduce retention, and competing model families show pronounced behavioral divergence.
AI.conclusion: APB reveals that while strong persona adherence is achievable, current models still face clear behavioral boundaries across modalities, multi-attribute settings, and model families, highlighting the need for more robust persona-conditioned agent evaluation.

title: Now You Feel It, Now You See Me: Digital-Twin-based Teleoperation Interface for Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Teleoperation is becoming increasingly important for collecting high-quality demonstrations to teach robots dexterous manipulation skills. For dexterous manipulation, bare-hand tracking provides a practical way to control robotic hands and demonstrate coordinated finger movements without gloves or exoskeletons. However, this type of teleoperation faces two key feedback limitations: a lack of force feedback and visual feedback of occluded region. The absence of force feedback hinders precise and safe manipulation, as operators must infer contact force visually rather than feel them directly. Occlusion by objects or other robot parts impairs the assessment of hand positions, approach distances, and pre-grasp configurations suited to the object's shape. To address these limitations, we propose a digital-twin-based augmented reality (AR) teleoperation interface that integrates bare-hand tracking, bimanual robotic hands, and virtual representations of the robot and task objects. The interface renders tactile measurements on robot hand meshes as visuo-force feedback. Furthermore, it offers a user-controlled virtual view panel or occlusion-aware transparency rendering to provide occlusion-mitigating visual feedback. We evaluated the interface through user studies involving Task 1 and Task 2, examining how force visualization and visual assistance support demonstration collection in tasks requiring careful force regulation and manipulation under occlusion.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a digital-twin-based AR teleoperation interface that combines bare-hand tracking, bimanual robotic hands, and virtual robot/task-object representations to compensate for the lack of force feedback and occlusion-limited visual feedback in dexterous manipulation demonstration collection.
AI.motivation: Teleoperation is increasingly important for collecting high-quality demonstrations of dexterous manipulation. Bare-hand tracking enables glove- and exoskeleton-free control of robotic hands with coordinated finger movements, but it suffers from two key feedback limitations: no force feedback (operators must visually infer contact forces, hindering precise and safe manipulation) and no visual feedback of occluded regions (occlusion by objects or robot parts impairs assessment of hand positions, approach distances, and shape-suited pre-grasp configurations).
AI.method: A digital-twin-based augmented reality (AR) teleoperation interface integrating bare-hand tracking, bimanual robotic hands, and virtual representations of the robot and task objects. It renders tactile measurements on robot hand meshes as visuo-force feedback, and provides either a user-controlled virtual view panel or occlusion-aware transparency rendering to deliver occlusion-mitigating visual feedback.
AI.result: User studies with Task 1 and Task 2 examined how force visualization and visual assistance support demonstration collection in tasks requiring careful force regulation and manipulation under occlusion.
AI.conclusion: The proposed AR teleoperation interface addresses the force-feedback and occlusion limitations of bare-hand tracking teleoperation, supporting demonstration collection for dexterous manipulation tasks that demand careful force regulation and manipulation under occlusion.

title: TrustMed-RL: Long-Horizon Reinforcement Learning for Evidence-Grounded Clinical Diagnosis
summary: Medical language models can produce correct diagnoses despite incomplete investigations and unsupported reasoning. To support long-horizon, evidence-grounded diagnosis, we introduce \textbf{TrustMed-RL}. Built from PubMed rare-disease cases and over 24,000 manually annotated image panels, it integrates interviews, examinations, testing, specialist consultation, and literature search through state-dependent actions. Our 8B vision--language policy, trained with clinically adapted GiGPO and coverage-adjusted diagnostic rewards, achieves 37.1\% diagnostic accuracy on 2,500 evaluation cases, outperforming all evaluated open-weight baselines and improving over supervised fine-tuning by 12.4 percentage points.. When success additionally requires acquiring at least 50\% of supporting test evidence, TrustMed-RL achieves 32.5\%, exceeding GPT-4o by 6.8 percentage points. Furthermore, it surpasses all evaluated baselines on MTMedDialog and multiple larger 27--32B models on AgentClinic. In physician review of 200 diagnostically accepted test-set trajectories, 83.0\% receive evidential-grounding scores of 4--5 out of 5. Physicians' assessments suggest that these diagnostic trajectories are trustworthy and aligned with human diagnostic reasoning.

AI.tldr: TrustMed-RL is an 8B vision-language policy for long-horizon, evidence-grounded medical diagnosis, trained with clinically adapted GiGPO and coverage-adjusted rewards on PubMed rare-disease cases with 24,000+ annotated image panels, reaching 37.1% diagnostic accuracy and outperforming open-weight baselines and GPT-4o under evidence requirements.
AI.motivation: Medical language models can produce correct diagnoses despite incomplete investigations and unsupported reasoning, indicating a lack of trustworthy, evidence-grounded diagnostic reasoning. The work aims to support long-horizon diagnosis where conclusions are grounded in acquired clinical evidence.
AI.method: TrustMed-RL is built from PubMed rare-disease cases and over 24,000 manually annotated image panels. It models diagnosis as state-dependent actions spanning interviews, examinations, testing, specialist consultation, and literature search. An 8B vision-language policy is trained with clinically adapted GiGPO and coverage-adjusted diagnostic rewards.
AI.result: TrustMed-RL achieves 37.1% diagnostic accuracy on 2,500 evaluation cases, surpassing all evaluated open-weight baselines and improving over supervised fine-tuning by 12.4 percentage points. When success also requires acquiring at least 50% of supporting test evidence, it achieves 32.5%, exceeding GPT-4o by 6.8 percentage points. It also surpasses all evaluated baselines on MTMedDialog and multiple larger 27–32B models on AgentClinic. In physician review of 200 diagnostically accepted test-set trajectories, 83.0% receive evidential-grounding scores of 4–5 out of 5.
AI.conclusion: Physician assessments suggest that TrustMed-RL's diagnostic trajectories are trustworthy and aligned with human diagnostic reasoning, supporting evidence-grounded long-horizon medical diagnosis.

title: PB-STDG: A Prediction-Based Short-Term Decentralized Greedy Guidance Algorithm for a Drone Road System
summary: In recent years, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) or drones have been increasingly adopted in urban environments for applications such as parcel delivery, infrastructure inspection, emergency response, and drone light shows. A non-negligible issue is how to manage the increasing number of drones operated by different entities, to enable them to cooperatively avoid potential collisions and determine conflict-free short-term flight paths in urban airspace. This paper presents a Prediction-Based Short-Term Decentralized Greedy (PB-STDG) guidance algorithm for a structured Drone Road System (DRS). PB-STDG extends the original STDG algorithm by introducing a prediction mechanism that enables drones to anticipate the decisions of neighboring drones using additional information shared in beacon packets, aiming to address the over-conservative behavior observed in the STDG algorithm. Several simulation scenarios are conducted to evaluate and compare the proposed algorithm with STDG. The results show that PB-STDG improves traffic efficiency while maintaining a safety level comparable to that of STDG.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes PB-STDG, a prediction-based decentralized greedy guidance algorithm for drones in a structured Drone Road System that anticipates neighbors' decisions to reduce over-conservative behavior while maintaining safety.
AI.motivation: The growing use of UAVs in urban airspace by multiple operators creates a need to manage increasing drone traffic, ensuring cooperative collision avoidance and conflict-free short-term flight paths. The existing STDG algorithm exhibits over-conservative behavior, reducing traffic efficiency.
AI.method: PB-STDG extends the original STDG algorithm by introducing a prediction mechanism. Drones anticipate the decisions of neighboring drones using additional information shared in beacon packets, within a structured Drone Road System (DRS).
AI.result: Simulation scenarios comparing PB-STDG with STDG show that PB-STDG improves traffic efficiency while maintaining a safety level comparable to STDG.
AI.conclusion: The prediction mechanism effectively mitigates the over-conservative behavior of STDG, offering a more efficient yet equally safe decentralized guidance solution for urban drone traffic management.

title: TimeNet: An Extensible Unified Data Infrastructure for Next-Generation Temporal Foundation Models
summary: Temporal Foundation Models (TFMs) aim to generalize across domains, datasets, and tasks. Yet, their development remains constrained by fragmented, task-specific data formats, annotations, and processing pipelines. We introduce TimeNet, an open-source data standard and scalable infrastructure that decouples temporal data from task definitions and represents signals, metadata, annotations, and supervision in a shared, extensible data model. TimeNet supports multimodal signals with regular, irregular, or ordinal time axes and expresses different task families (including classification, forecasting, temporal localization, question answering, generation, and editing) as reusable views over the same recordings. This shared representation enables heterogeneous time-series datasets to be combined for large-scale model training across domains, modalities, and tasks. We demonstrate TimeNet by transcoding datasets with 1.5M task instances spanning diverse domains, modalities, temporal scales, and forms of supervision, while retaining practical I/O performance relative to native formats. TimeNet enables an existing TFN training pipeline to support joint training on a configurable number of heterogeneous datasets through configuration changes alone. We show this capability by training TFM across multiple datasets and tasks, obtaining a 14% F1 score improvement compared with models trained on individual datasets. These results show that TimeNet provides the data and systems foundation needed to move beyond task- and dataset-specific TFMs toward models that can learn jointly across heterogeneous domains, modalities, temporal scales, and forms of supervision from a common data model.

AI.tldr: TimeNet is an open-source data standard and scalable infrastructure that decouples temporal data from task definitions, expressing signals, metadata, annotations, and supervision in a shared extensible model to enable joint training of temporal foundation models across heterogeneous domains, modalities, and tasks.
AI.motivation: Temporal Foundation Models aim to generalize across domains, datasets, and tasks, but their development is constrained by fragmented, task-specific data formats, annotations, and processing pipelines, preventing large-scale joint training on heterogeneous time-series data.
AI.method: TimeNet introduces a shared, extensible data model that represents signals, metadata, annotations, and supervision uniformly. It supports multimodal signals with regular, irregular, or ordinal time axes, and expresses task families (classification, forecasting, temporal localization, question answering, generation, and editing) as reusable views over the same recordings. This decouples temporal data from task definitions and enables combining heterogeneous datasets for large-scale training.
AI.result: The authors transcoded datasets with 1.5M task instances across diverse domains, modalities, temporal scales, and supervision forms while retaining practical I/O performance relative to native formats. An existing TFM training pipeline supported joint training on a configurable number of heterogeneous datasets through configuration changes alone, yielding a 14% F1 score improvement compared with models trained on individual datasets.
AI.conclusion: TimeNet provides the data and systems foundation needed to move beyond task- and dataset-specific TFMs toward models that learn jointly across heterogeneous domains, modalities, temporal scales, and forms of supervision from a common data model.

title: Recursive Self-Improvement of Visuomotor Policies through Local Recovery Supervision
summary: Visuomotor policies can execute familiar tasks yet lack the corrective behavior needed after their own mistakes. We present a framework for recursive self-improvement through local recovery supervision. Each round audits the current policy, generates corrective demonstrations at supported failure states, and uses them to update the policy that drives the next round of collection. An offline auditor locates unresolved failures using coarse and dense temporal evidence and specifies observable repair goals. A fixed multimodal agent acts as a tool-using teacher, generating recovery actions through observation, computation, execution, and feedback. The frozen student tests whether each teacher endpoint supports further progress. If continuation fails, the system restores that endpoint and extends the demonstration. Action-level quality assessment then defines continuous training windows with aligned observations, quality weights, and validity masks. Only the student is deployed. In a preliminary LIBERO-Goal study, recovery-augmented post-training achieves 88 successful episodes out of 100 validation scenes, compared with 78 for original-data continuation from the same $π_0$ checkpoint. An earlier BC-RNN study on robomimic Can improves success from 102/130 to 112/130 using 26 local recovery segments. Both comparisons match 2,000 additional optimization steps.

AI.tldr: A recursive self-improvement framework uses local recovery supervision—auditing failures, generating corrective demos at failure states via a tool-using teacher, and filtering them by action-quality—to improve visuomotor policies, yielding +10 successes on LIBERO-Goal and +10 on robomimic Can over matched baselines.
AI.motivation: Visuomotor policies can perform familiar tasks but lack corrective behavior after their own mistakes. Existing policies thus fail to recover from errors, and standard data continuation does not target the specific unresolved failure states.
AI.method: A recursive self-improvement loop via local recovery supervision. Each round: (1) an offline auditor locates unresolved failures using coarse and dense temporal evidence and specifies observable repair goals; (2) a fixed multimodal, tool-using teacher generates recovery actions through observation, computation, execution, and feedback; (3) the frozen student tests whether each teacher endpoint supports further progress—if continuation fails, the endpoint is restored and the demonstration extended; (4) action-level quality assessment defines continuous training windows with aligned observations, quality weights, and validity masks. The updated policy drives the next round's collection. Only the student is deployed.
AI.result: LIBERO-Goal (preliminary): recovery-augmented post-training achieves 88/100 successful episodes vs. 78/100 for original-data continuation from the same π0 checkpoint. robomimic Can (earlier BC-RNN study): success improves from 102/130 to 112/130 using 26 local recovery segments. Both comparisons use 2,000 additional optimization steps.
AI.conclusion: Recursive local recovery supervision improves visuomotor policies beyond standard data continuation at equal optimization budget, and the method is effective across different policy architectures (π0 and BC-RNN) and benchmarks (LIBERO-Goal and robomimic Can).

title: CORE-RL: Confidence-Oriented Reliability Evaluation of Black-Box Reinforcement Learning Policies
summary: The deployment of Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents in critical domains must be preceded with a pipeline to evaluate the alignment of the RL agent with complex multi-objective specifications and robustness under real-world environmental drift. However, to protect intellectual property, the RL agent may be delivered for evaluation as opaque executable or remote API, which makes traditional evaluation techniques based on the internals of the policies infeasible. To address this gap, CORE-RL: Confidence-Oriented Reliability Evaluation of black box RL policy is proposed in this paper. The CORE-RL pipeline introduces a Unified Reliability Metric that formally integrates early task termination and safety constraint violations, preventing unsafe policies from masking failures through premature episode halts. By subjecting the policy to a noise certification envelope of perceptual noise, actuation noise and change in environment dynamics, the pipeline computes the finite-sample Clopper-Pearson bounds on unified reliability metric and Hoeffdings' lower bound on reward and safety cost. The pipeline then defines safe operational design domain to report high-confidence certificates for safety and expected performance. Experiments on continuous control tasks demonstrate the CORE-RL pipeline's ability to automatically reject non-compliant policies and map the safe Operational Design Domain (ODD) of safety-aware policies. Thus CORE-RL provides an evaluation framework towards a quantitative, transparent and reproducible, statistical rationale necessary to safely evaluate, compare, and deploy black box RL solutions.

AI.tldr: CORE-RL is a black-box evaluation pipeline that quantifies RL policy reliability using a Unified Reliability Metric, statistical confidence bounds, and a safe Operational Design Domain, validated on continuous control tasks.
AI.motivation: Deploying RL in critical domains requires evaluating multi-objective alignment and robustness under environmental drift. However, IP protection often means the policy is delivered as an opaque executable or remote API, rendering internals-based evaluation techniques infeasible.
AI.method: CORE-RL introduces a Unified Reliability Metric that formally integrates early task termination and safety constraint violations to prevent unsafe policies from masking failures via premature halts. It applies a noise certification envelope (perceptual noise, actuation noise, and changed environment dynamics) and computes finite-sample Clopper-Pearson bounds on the unified reliability metric plus Hoeffding's lower bound on reward and safety cost, then defines a safe Operational Design Domain to report high-confidence certificates.
AI.result: Experiments on continuous control tasks show CORE-RL automatically rejects non-compliant policies and maps the safe Operational Design Domain of safety-aware policies.
AI.conclusion: CORE-RL offers a quantitative, transparent, reproducible, and statistically grounded evaluation framework for safely evaluating, comparing, and deploying black-box RL solutions.

title: VICON: Visual-Inertial-Contact based Hand-Object Tracking for Manipulation Datasets
summary: Learning dexterous manipulation benefits from human demonstration datasets that capture diverse and natural hand-object interactions. In particular, contact points and forces provide supervision on where and how strongly to interact, which cannot be fully captured by motion trajectories alone. However, methods for jointly capturing hand and object motion, contact points, and forces remain limited. Moreover, severe occlusion from hand-object interaction challenges accurate tracking of both hands and objects. To address these limitations, we present a Visual-Inertial-CONtact based hand-object tracking (VICON) framework. It holistically captures both hand and object motion along with contact information during manipulation, even under severe occlusion. First, we adopt a visual-inertial glove and an RGB-D camera for accurate hand tracking, and redesign the glove to incorporate contact sensing. Specifically, force-sensitive resistors (FSRs) are placed on the glove based on human grasp frequency to synchronously record contact states and calibrated normal forces. Second, without requiring pre-existing CAD models, we estimate object poses using RGB-D images and a mesh reconstructed from a monocular video. We propose factor-graph-based object trajectory estimation that fuses object-pose estimates weighted by visibility under hand-object occlusion, FSR measurements, and a hand-motion prior. Across 40 motion-capture sessions with five objects, VICON achieves a 2.5% failed-frame rate compared with 50.9-64.6% for the baselines, with median errors of 3.9 mm and 3.0 degrees under occlusion. Using VICON, we construct a dataset containing synchronized hand-object motion, contact points, and normal forces, and will publicly release an expanded dataset covering 10 object categories at https://github.com/VICON-dataset/dataset.

AI.tldr: VICON is a visual-inertial-contact framework that jointly captures hand and object motion plus contact states and normal forces during dexterous manipulation, even under severe hand-object occlusion, and releases a synchronized dataset.
AI.motivation: Dexterous manipulation learning needs human demonstration data containing contact points and forces, since motion trajectories alone cannot fully supervise where and how strongly to interact. Existing methods rarely capture hand motion, object motion, contact points, and forces jointly, and severe occlusion from hand-object interaction degrades tracking accuracy.
AI.method: VICON uses a visual-inertial glove redesigned with force-sensitive resistors (FSRs) placed according to human grasp frequency to record contact states and calibrated normal forces, plus an RGB-D camera for accurate hand tracking. Object poses are estimated without pre-existing CAD models via RGB-D images and a monocular-video-reconstructed mesh. A factor-graph-based object trajectory estimation fuses visibility-weighted object-pose estimates under occlusion, FSR measurements, and a hand-motion prior.
AI.result: Across 40 motion-capture sessions with five objects, VICON reaches a 2.5% failed-frame rate versus 50.9-64.6% for baselines, with median errors of 3.9 mm and 3.0 degrees under occlusion. The authors build a dataset of synchronized hand-object motion, contact points, and normal forces, and will release an expanded dataset of 10 object categories.
AI.conclusion: VICON jointly and robustly captures hand-object motion, contact points, and normal forces under severe occlusion, substantially outperforming baselines, and provides a public dataset to support dexterous manipulation research.

title: Asking Earns Nothing: Scoring the Decision to Act in BFCL Multi-Turn
summary: An agent that lacks the information it needs should ask rather than act, and the task definitions of agent leaderboards say so. BFCL multi-turn builds two of its four categories around a turn on which the model is supposed to ask, and its scorer never looks at that turn: the gold trajectory there is empty, the checker skips it, and the scripted user cannot answer, so asking earns nothing, guessing costs nothing on that turn, and asking twice loses the item. The benchmark also contains the control experiment for that decision. A should-ask item is a base item with one piece of information removed from one turn, so the same request appears twice at the same turn index, once complete and once not: on the first the model should make the call that changes the world, on the second it should ask. We score one decision per pair, whether the model attempted a world-changing call on that turn, read off the stored trajectories with no LLM judge; acting always and asking always both score 50. On the 223 pairs that pose this decision, gpt-5.4 attempts the call on 83.4% of the complete turns and holds back on 78.0% of the incomplete ones, the best decision accuracy of seven models at 80.7%; on the same items the official score ranks it sixth and puts first a model that lands in the middle here. One added line telling gpt-5.4 not to ask pushes it toward acting on both sides of the pair, so its decision accuracy shows no detectable change, while its official score rises by 13.5 to 23.5 points on the two should-ask categories and on the base twins; the opposite line, telling gemma-4-31B-it to ask first, improves its decision by 4.5 points and gains no official score. The score moves with the push toward action, not with the decision. We release the pairs, a turn-level scorer that runs on any BFCL output directory without an API key, and 31 manually verified bad items.

AI.tldr: BFCL multi-turn's should-ask categories are scored in a way that ignores the asking turn, so asking earns nothing and guessing costs nothing; a new paired-item scorer reveals the official score tracks the tendency to act, not the decision to ask.
AI.motivation: Agent leaderboards stipulate that an agent lacking needed information should ask rather than act, and BFCL multi-turn builds two of its four categories around such a turn. However, the scorer never evaluates that turn: the gold trajectory is empty, the checker skips it, and the scripted user cannot respond, so asking is unrewarded, guessing is free on that turn, and asking twice loses the item. The paper seeks to expose and quantify this measurement gap.
AI.method: The authors exploit a built-in control: a should-ask item is a base item with one piece of information removed from one turn, so the same request appears twice at the same turn index—once complete and once incomplete. For each pair they score a single decision: whether the model attempted a world-changing call on that turn, read off stored trajectories with no LLM judge. They also run prompt manipulations: adding one line telling gpt-5.4 not to ask, and the opposite line telling gemma-4-31B-it to ask first, comparing decision accuracy against official scores.
AI.result: On the 223 pairs posing this decision, gpt-5.4 attempts the call on 83.4% of complete turns and holds back on 78.0% of incomplete ones—80.7% decision accuracy, best of seven models—yet the official score ranks it sixth and puts first a model that lands mid-pack here. The added "do not ask" line pushes gpt-5.4 toward acting on both sides, leaving decision accuracy undetectably changed while official score rises 13.5–23.5 points on the two should-ask categories and base twins. The opposite "ask first" line improves gemma-4-31B-it's decision by 4.5 points with no official-score gain.
AI.conclusion: The official BFCL multi-turn score moves with the push toward action rather than with the quality of the ask-vs-act decision, meaning the should-ask categories fail to measure the behavior they claim to test. The authors release the paired items, a turn-level scorer that runs on any BFCL output directory without an API key, and 31 manually verified bad items.

title: Vela: Scaling Vision-Language-Action Models with Adaptive Action Curve Parametrization
summary: Most vision-language-action models represent future motion as fixed-rate action chunks, tying temporal resolution and prediction horizon to a fixed output budget. This pointwise representation wastes capacity on highly correlated neighboring actions, leaves temporal continuity and smoothness to be learned implicitly, and forces a tradeoff between long-horizon coverage and the local precision required for contact-rich manipulation. To address these limitations, we introduce Vela, a vision-language-action foundation model that represents future robot behavior as continuous trajectories. Vela combines a compact spline-based action representation with motion-dependent temporal support and a shared action interface for heterogeneous embodiments, allowing a fixed output budget to adapt its temporal resolution across motions. We pretrain Vela on large-scale multi-embodiment robot data and evaluate it on LIBERO-X, EBench, and two real-world long-horizon tasks, egg-cake cooking and potato shredding, obtaining promising results across simulation and physical manipulation. These results highlight the potential of continuous action representations as a foundation for future embodied foundation models. Project page and more results: https://clementine24.github.io/Vela/ .

AI.tldr: Vela is a vision-language-action foundation model that represents future robot motion as continuous spline-based trajectories with motion-dependent temporal support instead of fixed-rate action chunks, enabling adaptive temporal resolution under a fixed output budget and improving long-horizon, contact-rich manipulation across simulation and real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Most VLA models encode future motion as fixed-rate action chunks, which ties temporal resolution and prediction horizon to a fixed output budget. This pointwise scheme wastes capacity on highly correlated neighboring actions, leaves temporal continuity and smoothness to be learned implicitly, and forces a tradeoff between long-horizon coverage and the local precision needed for contact-rich manipulation.
AI.method: The authors propose Vela, a VLA foundation model representing future robot behavior as continuous trajectories. It combines (1) a compact spline-based action representation, (2) motion-dependent temporal support, and (3) a shared action interface for heterogeneous embodiments, so a fixed output budget adapts its temporal resolution across motions. Vela is pretrained on large-scale multi-embodiment robot data.
AI.result: Vela was evaluated on LIBERO-X, EBench, and two real-world long-horizon tasks (egg-cake cooking and potato shredding), achieving promising results across simulation and physical manipulation.
AI.conclusion: Continuous action representations show potential as a foundation for future embodied foundation models.

title: MERCI Cards: An LLM Evaluation and Deployment Framework for High-Stakes Domains
summary: As LLMs are increasingly deployed in high-stakes professional workflows, engineers and researchers require principled protocols to systematically track, monitor, and improve model performance across deployment cycles. We present a mathematical framework for iterative LLM evaluation and deployment, and demonstrate its application to AI systems used in criminal justice. Our framework formalizes LLM integration in high-stakes, high-risk, and resource-constrained domains across model selection, rubric design, evaluations and deployment via a weighted multi-objective optimization. We demonstrate that MERCI Cards can guide improvements of the system across deployment iterations, direct developer attention toward under-performing areas, and focus user attention on validation and error-correction in the LLM's outputs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a mathematical framework for iterative LLM evaluation and deployment in high-stakes settings, applying it to criminal justice AI systems via MERCI Cards.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly deployed in high-stakes professional workflows, engineers and researchers require principled protocols to systematically track, monitor, and improve model performance across deployment cycles.
AI.method: The framework formalizes LLM integration in high-stakes, high-risk, and resource-constrained domains across model selection, rubric design, evaluations, and deployment, formulated as a weighted multi-objective optimization.
AI.result: MERCI Cards can guide system improvements across deployment iterations, direct developer attention toward under-performing areas, and focus user attention on validation and error-correction in LLM outputs.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework and MERCI Cards provide a principled protocol for iterative LLM evaluation and deployment, demonstrated in criminal justice applications.

title: Safe Ergodic Control for Multi-Robot Systems via Quadratic Programming
summary: Ergodic control drives robots to spend time in each region in proportion to a spatial distribution of interest, making it well suited for dense spatiotemporal environmental monitoring. Existing safe ergodic controllers rely on offline trajectory optimization or hierarchical architectures, which limit real-time applicability and decouple the ergodicity objective from the safety constraint. This paper presents a quadratic programming (QP)-based controller that treats ergodicity and safety jointly. We first introduce a Gaussian-kernel ergodic metric that, unlike the classical indicator-based metric, is time differentiable. This allows the exponential decay of the metric to be imposed as a time-varying control barrier function (CBF) constraint, relaxed by a slack variable, alongside hard CBF constraints for region containment and inter-robot collision avoidance. We establish that the resulting QP remains feasible from any safe initial configuration and that, up to the slack term, the ergodic metric decays exponentially. Simulations show improved performance over baseline methods, and experiments with three aerial vehicles validate the work on real hardware.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a QP-based controller that jointly treats ergodicity and safety for dense spatiotemporal environmental monitoring, using a time-differentiable Gaussian-kernel ergodic metric enforced as a time-varying control barrier function constraint.
AI.motivation: Ergodic control is well suited for dense spatiotemporal environmental monitoring because it drives robots to spend time in each region proportionally to a spatial distribution of interest. However, existing safe ergodic controllers rely on offline trajectory optimization or hierarchical architectures, which limit real-time applicability and decouple the ergodicity objective from the safety constraint.
AI.method: The authors introduce a Gaussian-kernel ergodic metric that, unlike the classical indicator-based metric, is time differentiable. This enables the exponential decay of the metric to be imposed as a time-varying control barrier function (CBF) constraint, relaxed by a slack variable, alongside hard CBF constraints for region containment and inter-robot collision avoidance. The overall controller is formulated as a quadratic program (QP).
AI.result: The paper establishes that the resulting QP remains feasible from any safe initial configuration and that, up to the slack term, the ergodic metric decays exponentially. Simulations show improved performance over baseline methods, and experiments with three aerial vehicles validate the work on real hardware.
AI.conclusion: The proposed QP-based controller jointly handles ergodicity and safety in a single real-time formulation, providing feasibility guarantees and exponential ergodic metric decay, and is validated in simulation and on real aerial vehicles.

title: What Does a Harness Buy? Tokens, Mostly
summary: A coding agent is a language model wrapped in a harness: the system prompt, the tool set, and the context management that turn a chat model into something that can work inside a repository. Production harnesses ship releases daily, vendors advertise pass-rate gains from harness changes, and leaderboards mix harnesses freely. What is rarely measured is how much the harness itself moves the score when the model is held fixed. We run five models through three production harnesses, Claude Code, mini-SWE-agent, and OpenCode, on SWE-bench Verified, and rerun the same configurations to calibrate how much a score moves when nothing changes but the run. On 447 tasks and the two models we ran there, Claude Code and mini-SWE-agent, the heaviest and the lightest harness, are equivalent within five points. On a 45-task hard subset and five models, swapping the harness flips as many tasks as rerunning the same harness, 13% in both cases, and the tasks a harness wins in one run are not the tasks it wins in the next. The one harness effect that clears the noise is a loss, not a gain: OpenCode trails by up to 9 points on the large pool, and on one model half of that gap sits in runs its output cap cut short. What the harness does decide is the bill. With the same model, the same tasks, and one price list, cost per task differs by up to 3x across harnesses. The gap is set at the first call, by the preamble of system prompt and tool schemas each harness sends with every step, and scaled by the number of steps; per-step growth and per-call tool output differ far less. The provider's price for cached input scales the bill and does not reorder it. The rerun data also give the resolution a harness comparison needs: at the discordance we observe, 45 tasks catch a 13-point gap only half the time and no gap with 80% power, and 447 tasks resolve 5 points, still coarser than the gains many harness changes claim.

AI.tldr: Holding the model fixed, swapping production coding harnesses rarely moves SWE-bench Verified scores: the heaviest and lightest harness are equivalent within 5 points, and swapping harnesses flips as many tasks as rerunning the same one (13%). The robust harness effect is economic, not accuracy: identical models/tasks/prices yield up to 3x different per-task cost, driven by the system-prompt and tool-schema preamble sent every step.
AI.motivation: Harnesses (system prompt, tools, context management) ship daily and vendors advertise harness-driven pass-rate gains, while leaderboards mix harnesses freely, yet the harness's isolated contribution to score with the model held fixed is rarely measured. The paper aims to separate harness effect from run-to-run noise, quantify the resolution needed for valid harness comparisons, and characterize what the harness reliably controls.
AI.method: Five models run through three production harnesses (Claude Code, mini-SWE-agent, OpenCode) on SWE-bench Verified, with repeated identical reruns for noise calibration. Experiments span 447 tasks (two models) and a 45-task hard subset (five models). Comparisons cover task-flip rates between harness swaps vs. same-harness reruns, accuracy gaps, cost per task under one price list, and cost decomposition into first-call preamble (system prompt + tool schemas), per-step growth, and per-call tool output.
AI.result: On 447 tasks, Claude Code and mini-SWE-agent (heaviest vs. lightest) are equivalent within 5 points. On the 45-task subset, swapping harnesses flips 13% of tasks, identical to rerun flips, and winning tasks are not stable across runs. The only harness effect exceeding noise is a loss: OpenCode trails by up to 9 points on the large pool, with half the gap on one model attributable to output-cap truncation. Cost per task varies up to 3x across harnesses with fixed model/tasks/prices; the gap originates at the first call via each harness's preamble and scales with step count, while per-step growth and per-call tool output differ far less. Cached-input pricing scales but does not reorder the bill. Resolution analysis: at observed discordance, 45 tasks detect a 13-point gap only half the time and detect no gap at 80% power; 447 tasks resolve 5 points, still coarser than many claimed harness gains.
AI.conclusion: With the model fixed, harness choice is largely accuracy-neutral on SWE-bench Verified; measured harness "wins" are mostly run-to-run noise, the one reliable accuracy effect is a penalty (OpenCode, partly a truncation artifact), and no harness change is credibly superior below the multi-point resolution floor of standard benchmarks. The harness's real, deterministic effect is on cost, set by the recurring preamble and step count. Harness comparisons should rerun configurations for noise calibration and report effect sizes against achievable statistical resolution rather than headline pass-rate deltas.

title: CoDance: Learning Reactive and Compliant Human-Humanoid Interaction from Video
summary: Partnered human-humanoid interaction couples locomotion with continuous physical contact. A humanoid needs to coordinate with a person's motion while responding to interaction forces and maintaining stable and natural movement. We present CoDance, a framework for learning reactive and compliant human-humanoid interaction from video. We study partnered dancing as a challenging instantiation, where a humanoid coordinates its footsteps with a moving partner and maintains continuous two-hand contact. Given a single video of two human dancers, CoDance retargets their motions into a robot reference and a moving partner. We introduce a multi-link compliance augmentation that transforms the kinematic demonstration into force-aware training data by adapting the robot reference under structured forces at both hands. Policies trained on this data follow the observed partner while preserving the demonstrated locomotion style and responding compliantly to physical interaction. In simulation, the policies adapt their footsteps to changes in the partner and reproduce approximately 80% of the wrist displacement encoded by the augmented demonstrations. On a physical humanoid, CoDance enables sustained two-hand dancing with a human partner including repeated transitions between forward and backward motions.

AI.tldr: CoDance is a framework that learns reactive, compliant human-humanoid partnered dancing from a single video of two human dancers, using a multi-link compliance augmentation to produce force-aware training data, achieving sustained two-hand contact dancing in simulation and on a physical humanoid.
AI.motivation: Partnered human-humanoid interaction requires coupling locomotion with continuous physical contact: the humanoid must coordinate with a person's motion, respond to interaction forces, and maintain stable, natural movement. Partnered dancing is studied as a challenging instantiation of this problem.
AI.method: Given a single video of two human dancers, CoDance retargets their motions into a robot reference and a moving partner. It introduces a multi-link compliance augmentation that transforms the kinematic demonstration into force-aware training data by adapting the robot reference under structured forces applied at both hands. Policies trained on this data follow the observed partner while preserving the demonstrated locomotion style and responding compliantly to physical interaction.
AI.result: In simulation, the policies adapt their footsteps to changes in the partner and reproduce approximately 80% of the wrist displacement encoded by the augmented demonstrations. On a physical humanoid, CoDance enables sustained two-hand dancing with a human partner, including repeated transitions between forward and backward motions.
AI.conclusion: CoDance demonstrates that reactive and compliant human-humanoid interaction can be learned from video via force-aware data augmentation, enabling a physical humanoid to maintain continuous two-hand contact and coordinated locomotion with a moving human partner.

title: CRAFT: An Agentic Spreadsheet Form Filling System with Template Awareness
summary: Spreadsheet form filling requires agents to consolidate external evidence, ground values to precise cells, and preserve irregular template structure. Errors in early edits can overwrite labels or misalign fields, undermining later decisions. We propose CRAFT, a template-aware agent framework that connects reflective validation to constrained local repair. Instead of treating reflection as a free-form request to regenerate the workbook, CRAFT grounds detected errors to spreadsheet regions, restores corrupted template state when necessary, and re-grounds plausible writable slots before subsequent edits. A Rectangle-Aware Slot Grounder (RASG) proposes writable cells, while label-slot hints and protected regions constrain subsequent edits. We introduce FormFillBench, with 327 forms across Instruction-Only and Multi-File tracks. Compared with the strongest baselines, CRAFT improves pair accuracy by 8.51 and 23.38 percentage points on these tracks, respectively. Component-removal experiments support structural adjudication and slot re-grounding within the pipeline, and the framework retains its relative advantage among the methods evaluated with a second backbone. The code and benchmark FormFillBench are available at https://github.com/Glllllly/CRAFT.

AI.tldr: CRAFT is a template-aware agent framework for spreadsheet form filling that combines reflective validation with constrained local repair, and it is evaluated on the new FormFillBench benchmark.
AI.motivation: Spreadsheet form filling requires consolidating external evidence, grounding values to precise cells, and preserving irregular template structure. Early editing errors can overwrite labels or misalign fields, propagating and undermining later decisions.
AI.method: CRAFT connects reflective validation to constrained local repair rather than regenerating the whole workbook. It grounds detected errors to spreadsheet regions, restores corrupted template state, and re-grounds plausible writable slots before subsequent edits. A Rectangle-Aware Slot Grounder (RASG) proposes writable cells, while label-slot hints and protected regions constrain edits.
AI.result: On FormFillBench (327 forms; Instruction-Only and Multi-File tracks), CRAFT improves pair accuracy by 8.51 and 23.38 percentage points over the strongest baselines. Component-removal experiments support structural adjudication and slot re-grounding, and the framework retains its relative advantage with a second backbone.
AI.conclusion: Template-aware, locally constrained repair with error grounding is effective for spreadsheet form filling, and FormFillBench plus code are publicly released.

title: VAMPS: Visual and Motor Policies from Sampling-Based Planning
summary: Learning robot policies directly on physical systems remains difficult because data collection is costly and policy exploration can be unsafe. We introduce Visual and Motor Policies from Sampling-Based Planning (VAMPS), a framework that uses Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control to train reusable policies without human demonstrations. VAMPS supports two training modes. For one-step proprioceptive policies, it operates iteratively in simulation: the policy warm-starts MPPI, and the refined trajectories provide new supervision as the policy changes. A learned terminal value improves short-horizon planning, while an Implicit Q-Learning (IQL) critic guides the policy update. Iterative refinement outperforms training once on frozen MPPI data, and we transfer the learned locomotion policy to a Unitree Go2. For visuomotor policies, VAMPS operates directly from real-robot data. MPPI uses task-specific state estimates to plan and execute trajectories while recording RGB and sensor observations on a Flexiv Rizon 10S. Action Chunking with Transformers predicts action chunks, reducing the effective prediction horizon, and is trained offline on this fixed dataset. We demonstrate visuomotor pick-and-place and force-aware whiteboard erasing. In the latter task, the policy additionally observes the measured $6$-D wrench and desired normal force. These results show that VAMPS can learn policies either in simulation followed by hardware transfer or directly from autonomously collected real-robot data.

AI.tldr: VAMPS trains reusable robot policies from sampling-based MPPI planning without human demonstrations, supporting simulation-based one-step proprioceptive policies transferred to hardware and real-robot visuomotor policies trained offline.
AI.motivation: Learning robot policies directly on physical systems is difficult because data collection is costly and policy exploration can be unsafe. VAMPS aims to avoid human demonstrations by leveraging sampling-based planning to autonomously generate training supervision.
