AI.tldr: An open-weight LLM pipeline (gpt-oss-120B) with 150 hierarchical templates structured an entire multimodality radiology report archive (2,186,982 reports) without human oversight, achieving high content fidelity (macro STS 0.95-0.97, 88.7% of fields unchanged) at 1,258 reports/hour on one GPU.
AI.motivation: To develop and evaluate an open-weight LLM pipeline capable of converting an entire free-text radiology report archive into structured reports autonomously, without human oversight.
AI.method: Retrospective study. A pipeline with 150 hierarchically organized templates was developed at one center and tested at a second center on reports from 2010-2025. The open-weight gpt-oss-120B model selects a template via three constrained-decoding steps and fills it on one local GPU. Template selection was scored against expert labels on 914 randomly sampled reports across five modalities; structuring quality was assessed on 920 radiography and CT reports corrected field by field by five residents. The pipeline then processed the complete archive of the second center. Proportions are reported with Wilson 95% CIs.
AI.result: An optimal template set was selected for 74.4% of reports (680/914; 95% CI 71.5-77.1%) and an appropriate set for 82.3% (752/914; 95% CI 79.7-84.6%), with 87.7% for single-region and 54.1% for multi-region reports. Macro semantic textual similarity between output and corrected reference was 0.95 (radiography) and 0.97 (CT); residents left 88.7% of 24,638 fields unchanged; unsupported content was flagged in 1.0% and 1.5% of reports. Of 2,186,982 archive reports, 96.5% received structured output (2,401,544 structured reports) at 1,258 reports/hour on one GPU.
AI.conclusion: An open-weight LLM pipeline structured a complete multimodality report archive without human oversight with high content fidelity. Multi-region reports remained the main source of template errors.

title: Emergency Obstacle Avoidance Maneuvers in Differential-Drive Mobile Robots
summary: Emergency obstacle avoidance requires a mobile robot to brake or change its heading within the available distance. This paper investigates the dependence of maneuver performance and odometric error on approach speed for a differential-drive robot. A footprint-clearance analysis and a normalized wheel-motion index provide a kinematic description of five braking and turning maneuvers. The principal experiment comprises 540 block-randomized trials on tile, of which 539 are retained, at commanded approach speeds of 45, 55, and 65 cm/s. An overhead camera provides an independent pose reference. When encoder, gyro, and camera heading changes are evaluated over complete motion records, the mean encoder discrepancy increases by 4.7-5.1 degrees for the two reverse-spin maneuvers between the lowest and highest speeds; the arc and brake-assisted pivot change by less than 0.4 degrees. Larger encoder discrepancy is associated with lower avoidance success after adjustment for distance, speed, maneuver, day, and turn direction. Gyro discrepancies remain approximately 3 degrees for the reverse spins. Estimated reaction distances for 90% success and their uncertainty quantify the maneuver trade-offs. The results support speed-specific empirical characterization of emergency maneuvers and distinguish encoder error from recovery motion and measurement-window mismatch.

AI.tldr: Approach speed strongly affects the odometric accuracy of reverse-spin emergency maneuvers but not of arc or brake-assisted pivot maneuvers, and larger encoder discrepancy correlates with lower avoidance success.
AI.motivation: Emergency obstacle avoidance requires a mobile robot to brake or turn within the available distance, so maneuver performance and odometric error must be characterized as a function of approach speed to enable speed-specific emergency behavior.
AI.method: A footprint-clearance analysis and a normalized wheel-motion index kinematically describe five braking and turning maneuvers for a differential-drive robot. A principal experiment of 540 block-randomized tile trials (539 retained) at commanded approach speeds of 45, 55, and 65 cm/s uses an overhead camera as an independent pose reference, comparing encoder, gyro, and camera heading changes over complete motion records.
AI.result: Mean encoder discrepancy increases by 4.7-5.1 degrees for the two reverse-spin maneuvers from lowest to highest speed, whereas the arc and brake-assisted pivot change by less than 0.4 degrees. Gyro discrepancies remain approximately 3 degrees for the reverse spins. Larger encoder discrepancy is associated with lower avoidance success after adjustment for distance, speed, maneuver, day, and turn direction, and estimated reaction distances for 90% success quantify maneuver trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: The findings support speed-specific empirical characterization of emergency maneuvers and separate encoder error from recovery motion and measurement-window mismatch.

title: Decide, Ask, or Defer: Clinical LLMs under Incomplete Evidence
comment: Preprint. Accepted to the Main Track of the NeurIPS 2026 GenAI4Health Workshop
summary: Clinical LLMs must decide not only what diagnosis to produce, but also whether the available evidence is sufficient for autonomous decision making. Binary DECIDE/ABSTAIN formulations merge distinct non decision states and do not explicitly evaluate information acquisition. We introduce a DECIDE/ASK/DEFER formulation together with a blinded protocol that prevents models from using evidence completeness metadata. We evaluate Qwen, Gemini, and GPT on 200 matched clinical evidence states constructed from DDXPlus. The models show substantial differences in action selection under identical evidence, with disagreement in 137 of 200 states. For Qwen, a matched targeted versus random analysis shows that selected information changes the likelihood of a subsequent autonomous decision more clearly than diagnostic correctness. Its matched DECIDE/ABSTAIN baseline further reveals a safety autonomy tradeoff: the three action policy rescues some erroneous autonomous decisions but also removes some correct autonomous deci sions. These results show that separating information acquisition from clinician deferral exposes behavior that binary abstention hides, without yielding a uniformly improved decision policy.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a DECIDE/ASK/DEFER formulation with a blinded protocol that hides evidence-completeness metadata, evaluates Qwen, Gemini, and GPT on 200 matched clinical evidence states from DDXPlus, and shows that separating information acquisition from clinician deferral exposes behavior hidden by binary abstention, without uniformly improving the decision policy.
AI.motivation: Clinical LLMs must decide not only the diagnosis but also whether the available evidence suffices for autonomous decision making. Binary DECIDE/ABSTAIN formulations merge distinct non-decision states and fail to explicitly evaluate information acquisition, obscuring important behavioral distinctions.
AI.method: The authors propose a DECIDE/ASK/DEFER formulation together with a blinded protocol that prevents models from exploiting evidence-completeness metadata. They evaluate Qwen, Gemini, and GPT across 200 matched clinical evidence states constructed from DDXPlus, including a matched targeted-versus-random information analysis and a matched DECIDE/ABSTAIN baseline for Qwen.
AI.result: Models show substantial divergence in action selection under identical evidence, disagreeing in 137 of 200 states. For Qwen, selected information changes the likelihood of a subsequent autonomous decision more clearly than diagnostic correctness. The matched DECIDE/ABSTAIN baseline reveals a safety-autonomy tradeoff: the three-action policy rescues some erroneous autonomous decisions but also removes some correct ones.
AI.conclusion: Separating information acquisition from clinician deferral exposes model behavior that binary abstention hides, though it does not yield a uniformly improved decision policy.

title: FOCUS: Fine-Grained Open-Vocabulary Change Detection for Uncertainty-Aware Semi-Static Scenes
summary: Autonomous robots operating over long periods must keep their environmental memory up to date as the world changes between visits. In semi-static environments, an object may be replaced in place by a different but geometrically and semantically similar instance, making the identity change difficult to detect from geometry or coarse semantics alone. We present FOCUS, an uncertainty-aware framework for object-level change detection and map maintenance. We formulate semi-static memory maintenance as probabilistic inference that fuses geometric likelihood with appearance likelihood rendered from a 3D Gaussian map. A recursive three-state estimator maintains whether each mapped object is PERSISTED, REPLACED, or REMOVED. To account for imperfect 3DGS rendering, we model the rendered appearance evidence probabilistically rather than using it as a direct change score, with the model parameters automatically calibrated from a change-free replay of the initial mapping session. We evaluate our method on a new Isaac Sim warehouse benchmark with ambiguous in-place replacements and on the real-world TorWIC dataset. It improves object-level replacement F1 from 0.20 to 0.84 over a probabilistic baseline and transfers to real-world data without manual parameter retuning.

AI.tldr: FOCUS is an uncertainty-aware framework for object-level change detection and map maintenance in semi-static environments, fusing geometric and 3D Gaussian Splatting-rendered appearance likelihoods via a recursive three-state estimator to classify objects as persisted, replaced, or removed.
AI.motivation: Long-term autonomous robots must update environmental memory as the world changes. In semi-static environments, objects may be replaced in place by geometrically and semantically similar instances, making identity changes hard to detect from geometry or coarse semantics alone.
AI.method: The authors formulate semi-static memory maintenance as probabilistic inference, fusing a geometric likelihood with an appearance likelihood rendered from a 3D Gaussian map. A recursive three-state estimator tracks whether each mapped object is PERSISTED, REPLACED, or REMOVED. To handle imperfect 3DGS rendering, rendered appearance evidence is modeled probabilistically rather than used as a direct change score, with parameters auto-calibrated from a change-free replay of the initial mapping session.
AI.result: Evaluated on a new Isaac Sim warehouse benchmark with ambiguous in-place replacements and on the real-world TorWIC dataset, FOCUS improves object-level replacement F1 from 0.20 to 0.84 over a probabilistic baseline and transfers to real-world data without manual parameter retuning.
AI.conclusion: Fusing probabilistic geometric and 3DGS-rendered appearance evidence within a recursive three-state estimator enables robust object-level change detection and map maintenance in semi-static environments, generalizing from simulation to real-world data without manual tuning.

title: Label Agreement Does Not Measure Authorization
summary: Many groups now delegate label ontology and metadata harmonization to agentic LLM pipelines. We built one and audited it. Our aggregate scores looked healthy, but the pipeline kept failing in ways they did not show, so we set out to find what they hid. Label agreement asks whether a proposed label matches a reference. It does not ask whether the agent was entitled to propose it, whether the output was complete enough to act on, or whether the label moved when the evidence moved. We measured those three separately on COBRE and FBIRN, two schizophrenia and control neuroimaging cohorts from different consortia, and they come apart, from label agreement and from each other. Showing the agent an upstream proposal barely moves label agreement, 0.857 to 0.870, while agreement on the chosen action doubles, 0.409 to 0.830. Output that parses as JSON still drops a required field on 10% of one model's cases and 33% of the other's. And an agent that replays its first answer scores perfectly on original cases and zero once we change the evidence that decides them. Downstream, a row-order error that none of these metrics reports erases most of the diagnostic signal. So we measure these properties apart, pair each with a control, and gate commitment on the result, which makes failures visible and easy to route to a person. None of this prevents failure. Our reference labels are rule-derived, so agreement with them means consistency, not correctness. Code is available at https://github.com/amir-sbg/Label-Agreement-Does-Not-Measure-Authorization.

AI.tldr: An audited agentic LLM label-harmonization pipeline shows healthy aggregate label agreement while failing on three unmeasured properties—authorization, completeness, and evidence sensitivity—so the authors propose measuring them separately, each with a control, and gating commitment on the result.
AI.motivation: Label agreement, the dominant metric for ontology/metadata harmonization pipelines, only checks whether a proposed label matches a reference. It is silent on whether the agent was entitled to propose the label (authorization), whether the output was actionable/complete, and whether the label responds to changes in evidence. These hidden failure modes pass unnoticed behind good aggregate scores, so the authors set out to expose what aggregate scores conceal.
AI.method: The authors built and audited an agentic LLM labeling pipeline and measured three properties separately: (1) authorization of the proposal (including whether showing an upstream proposal changes behavior), (2) output completeness (whether parseable JSON still drops required fields), and (3) evidence sensitivity (whether labels move when the deciding evidence changes), evaluated on COBRE and FBIRN, two schizophrenia/control neuroimaging cohorts from different consortia. Each property is paired with a control, and downstream impact is probed via a row-order error invisible to the metrics.
AI.result: The three properties dissociate from label agreement and from each other. Providing an upstream proposal barely changes label agreement (0.857→0.870) but doubles agreement on the chosen action (0.409→0.830). JSON-parseable output still drops a required field in 10% of cases for one model and 33% for the other. An agent replaying its first answer scores perfectly on original cases but zero when the deciding evidence is changed. Downstream, an unreported row-order error erases most of the diagnostic signal.
AI.conclusion: Aggregate label agreement hides authorization, completeness, and evidence-sensitivity failures. Measuring these properties separately with paired controls and gating commitment on the outcome makes failures visible and routable to a human. This does not prevent failure, and since reference labels are rule-derived, agreement with them indicates consistency rather than correctness.

title: Spacecraft Rendezvous Trajectory Generation with Modular Constraints via Diffusion Model Composition
summary: Emerging mission classes such as on-orbit servicing, satellite inspection, and active debris removal require trajectory design methods that are adaptable to a variety of mission scenarios. We present a diffusion-based trajectory generation approach for rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) that enables flexible configuration of mission constraints. First, individual energy-based diffusion models are trained to satisfy distinct constraints such as approach cone and sensor line-of-sight from a set of optimized trajectories. Then, at inference time, the learned energy models can be composed with one another, or with an analytically defined energy field, to enforce specific constraint combinations. We validate this framework with the composition of a learned approach cone model and a learned sensor line-of-sight model, as well as a learned approach cone model and synthetic obstacle avoidance model, both of which yield constraint satisfaction rates that are within 1 percentage point of the single-constraint models or higher. These results indicate that our compositional diffusion framework can provide a modular approach to RPO trajectory design and enable reconfiguration for new constraint combinations without requiring model retraining.

AI.tldr: A compositional diffusion framework generates RPO trajectories by training separate energy-based diffusion models per constraint and composing them at inference, achieving constraint satisfaction within 1 percentage point of single-constraint models.
AI.motivation: Emerging mission classes (on-orbit servicing, satellite inspection, active debris removal) demand trajectory design methods adaptable to diverse mission scenarios with flexible constraint configuration.
AI.method: Train individual energy-based diffusion models to satisfy distinct constraints (approach cone, sensor line-of-sight) from optimized trajectories. At inference, compose learned energy models with each other or with analytically defined energy fields to enforce constraint combinations.
AI.result: Validation via composition of learned approach cone + learned sensor line-of-sight models, and learned approach cone + synthetic obstacle avoidance model, both yielding constraint satisfaction rates within 1 percentage point of or higher than single-constraint models.
AI.conclusion: The compositional diffusion framework offers a modular approach to RPO trajectory design, enabling reconfiguration for new constraint combinations without model retraining.

title: $\mathrm{TRIZ}^{a}$: Guiding Agent Evolution from Pattern Recognition to Solution Invention
summary: We propose $\mathrm{TRIZ}^{a}$ (TRIZ exponentiated by an agent), a general R\&D automation paradigm that combines TRIZ inventive theory with LLM-driven agent evolutionary search. TRIZ's 40 inventive principles and contradiction matrix provide structured, explainable directions for solution generation, replacing random or untyped mutation with theory-guided ideation. Functional information (FI), operationalized under a frozen reference contract, is combined with TRIZ Ideality to measure useful and harmful function on a commensurable information scale, while hard gates keep promotion distinct from metric improvement. We validate $\mathrm{TRIZ}^{a}$ in cybersecurity--an adversarial and rapidly evolving domain--on PowerDuck GOOSE, CICIoT2023, and CIC-DDoS2019. Under paired-rerun protocols with protocol fingerprinting and hard-gate validation, the legacy experiments yield absolute F1 improvements of $+2.88$, $+4.23$, and $+0.15$ percentage points, respectively. A completed 45-activity CICIoT2023 campaign further increases macro-F1 from $0.8325$ to $0.8483$, but does not pass its frozen promotion gate. Every result remains traceable from contradiction identification and TRIZ principle selection to code transformation, evaluation metrics, and promotion decision.

AI.tldr: TRIZ^a integrates TRIZ inventive theory with LLM-driven evolutionary agents to automate R&D, using the 40 inventive principles and contradiction matrix to guide ideation, and validates it in cybersecurity tasks.
AI.motivation: Conventional LLM-based automated R&D relies on random or untyped mutation for solution generation, which lacks structure and explainability. The paper aims to replace this with theory-guided ideation by combining TRIZ inventive theory with agent-based evolutionary search.
AI.method: TRIZ^a couples TRIZ's 40 inventive principles and contradiction matrix with LLM-driven agent evolutionary search. Functional Information (FI), operationalized under a frozen reference contract, is combined with TRIZ Ideality to measure useful and harmful function on a commensurable information scale. Hard gates separate promotion decisions from metric improvement.
AI.result: On PowerDuck GOOSE, CICIoT2023, and CIC-DDoS2019 under paired-rerun protocols with protocol fingerprinting and hard-gate validation, legacy experiments achieve absolute F1 gains of +2.88, +4.23, and +0.15 percentage points. A 45-activity CICIoT2023 campaign raises macro-F1 from 0.8325 to 0.8483 but fails its frozen promotion gate.
AI.conclusion: TRIZ^a provides a general, traceable R&D automation paradigm in which every result is traceable from contradiction identification and TRIZ principle selection to code transformation, evaluation metrics, and promotion decision. Notably, it demonstrates that metric improvement does not necessarily equate to passing the promotion gate.

title: Bayesian Data Augmentation for DNN Retraining with Binomial Outcomes in Vision-Based UAV Landing
summary:
In GPS-denied or cluttered urban environments, vision-based landing is essential for reliable UAV missions. Real-world landing sites are often unstructured and highly variable, requiring strong generalization by the perception system. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) trained with synthetic data augmentation offer a scalable solution for learning landing-site features across diverse vehicle and environmental states. However, computationally expensive DNN retraining, along with challenging performance validation via test flights, limits exhaustive model fine-tuning and necessitates an optimized retraining pipeline. In this work, we deploy a Bayesian data augmentation framework integrated with a photorealistic simulator featuring high-fidelity vehicle dynamics to iteratively retrain the helipad detector DNN, maximizing landing performance as the objective function.
  We validate our framework with experiments in a photorealistic simulator under different environmental conditions and vehicle states, demonstrating improved landing performance and tighter confidence intervals on predicted landing outcomes.

AI.tldr: A Bayesian data augmentation framework coupled with a photorealistic, high-fidelity-dynamics simulator iteratively retrains a helipad detector DNN to maximize UAV landing performance, yielding better landings and tighter confidence intervals.
AI.motivation: In GPS-denied or cluttered urban environments, vision-based landing is essential for reliable UAV missions, but real-world landing sites are unstructured and highly variable, demanding strong perception generalization. While DNNs trained with synthetic data augmentation scale well, expensive retraining and costly flight-based validation preclude exhaustive fine-tuning, motivating an optimized retraining pipeline.
AI.method: The authors deploy a Bayesian data augmentation framework integrated with a photorealistic simulator featuring high-fidelity vehicle dynamics, and use it to iteratively retrain the helipad detector DNN with landing performance as the objective function being maximized.
AI.result: Experiments in the photorealistic simulator under varied environmental conditions and vehicle states show improved landing performance and tighter confidence intervals on predicted landing outcomes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Bayesian augmentation-plus-simulation retraining pipeline improves helipad detection and landing outcomes, offering a scalable, validation-efficient alternative to exhaustive fine-tuning and test flights.

title: Recursive Improvement of a Differentiable Scientific Software Ecosystem
summary: Differentiable programming connects scientific computation with gradient-based inference, learning and design. Extending these capabilities across a heterogeneous software ecosystem requires specialized effort to implement derivatives, integrate interfaces and evaluate quality. AI coding agents can accelerate this transformation, but translating their capabilities into useful scientific software requires identifying research needs and evaluating how well implementations meet them. We present an environment for agent-driven evolution of differentiable scientific software that connects demand identification, development and quality evaluation. A unified differentiation interface exposes reusable derivative rules alongside existing numerical routines, allowing research tasks to share these capabilities. Research requirements guide development, with implementations assessed through independent derivative checks, workflow tests and performance evaluation. Validated software, research programs and tests become shared resources for subsequent studies. We construct and validate automatic differentiation extensions across 20 packages spanning physical, chemical and biological modeling, with research workflows demonstrating reuse across tasks. Benchmarks demonstrate computational savings over finite differences in gradient evaluation and complete parameter estimation. Research-driven revisions make previously unsupported workflows differentiable, correct derivatives of scientific observables and eliminate redundant computation. Quantum-control and thermal-design studies revise objectives in response to physical evaluation, improving designs while reusing existing derivatives. This work provides a practical approach to expanding differentiable programming across established scientific software and organizing AI agents around the recursive improvement of a shared computational ecosystem.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an environment for agent-driven evolution of differentiable scientific software that links demand identification, development, and quality evaluation, and validates it by building automatic differentiation extensions across 20 scientific packages.
AI.motivation: Differentiable programming bridges scientific computation with gradient-based inference, learning, and design, but extending it across a heterogeneous software ecosystem requires specialized work in implementing derivatives, integrating interfaces, and evaluating quality. AI coding agents can accelerate this, yet translating their capabilities into useful scientific software demands identifying research needs and assessing how well implementations meet them.
AI.method: A unified differentiation interface exposes reusable derivative rules alongside existing numerical routines so research tasks can share capabilities. Research requirements guide development, and implementations are assessed via independent derivative checks, workflow tests, and performance evaluation. Validated software, research programs, and tests become shared resources. The authors construct and validate automatic differentiation extensions across 20 packages spanning physical, chemical, and biological modeling.
AI.result: Research workflows demonstrate reuse across tasks. Benchmarks show computational savings over finite differences in both gradient evaluation and complete parameter estimation. Research-driven revisions make previously unsupported workflows differentiable, correct derivatives of scientific observables, and eliminate redundant computation. Quantum-control and thermal-design studies revise objectives based on physical evaluation, improving designs while reusing existing derivatives.
AI.conclusion: The work offers a practical approach to expanding differentiable programming across established scientific software and to organizing AI agents around the recursive improvement of a shared computational ecosystem.

title: Learning Coordinated Visuomotor Box-Pushing from Solo Demonstrations
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures. Accepted for presentation at the 2026 Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026)
summary: Multi-robot imitation learning, particularly in settings where visuomotor policies are deployed in a communication-free, onboard decentralised style, represents an attractive paradigm. However, its realisation remains insufficiently understood, largely due to the difficulty of collecting collective demonstrations, since a single operator cannot control many robots simultaneously. Meanwhile, unlike coupled collaborative manipulation, many coordinated tasks achieve system-wide efficiency primarily through minimising inter-robot interference. This structure motivates us to study whether data collected by a teleoperated single-robot can be leveraged for large-scale coordinated box-pushing as a testbed. We systematically investigate dataset creation strategies and lightweight policy architectures. In particular, experiments with up to 40 robots highlight the difficulty of acquiring effective coordination solely through passive observation of other operating robots, revealing a concrete bottleneck for multi-robot research.

AI.tldr: This paper studies whether single-robot teleoperated data can support large-scale communication-free, onboard decentralized multi-robot imitation learning, using coordinated box-pushing as a testbed, and identifies passive observation as a key bottleneck.
AI.motivation: Multi-robot imitation learning with communication-free, onboard decentralized visuomotor policies is attractive, but its realization is poorly understood because collecting collective demonstrations is hard—a single operator cannot control many robots simultaneously. The authors note that many coordinated tasks achieve system-wide efficiency mainly by minimizing inter-robot interference, which may allow single-robot data to suffice.
AI.method: The authors use large-scale coordinated box-pushing as a testbed and systematically investigate dataset creation strategies and lightweight policy architectures. They conduct experiments scaling up to 40 robots, including settings where robots passively observe other operating robots.
AI.result: Experiments with up to 40 robots show that effective coordination is difficult to acquire solely through passive observation of other operating robots, revealing a concrete bottleneck for multi-robot research.
AI.conclusion: Single-robot teleoperated data can be leveraged for large-scale coordinated box-pushing, but passive observation alone is insufficient for acquiring effective coordination, highlighting a key open challenge for communication-free decentralized multi-robot imitation learning.

title: Strong Helps Weak: Directional Cross-Modal Alignment Transfer in Multi-modal LLMs
summary: Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs) achieve strong modality understanding by pairing a large language model (LLM) with an encoder for a target modality such as vision, video, or audio. However, improving an MLLM's capability for a given modality typically requires additional training on large modality-specific datasets, incurring substantial data collection and compute costs. Model merging offers an alternative, but it is often infeasible for data-scarce, large per-sample size, or domain-specific modalities (\textit{e.g.}, audio and video), where same-modality model variants are rarely available. In this work, we characterize an intriguing asymmetric phenomenon: merging a well-aligned, data-rich source-modality MLLM into a data-scarce target-modality MLLM substantially improves the target on its own benchmarks. Our theoretical and empirical analyses show that this gain stems from enhanced alignment between modality-specific and textual tokens, induced by the stronger donor modality. Specifically, we derive a mutual-information lower bound that is monotonic in alignment-related quantities and strongly correlated with downstream MLLM performance. Building on this principle, we propose Directional Cross-modal Alignment Transfer (DCAT), a novel framework that transfers textual alignment from a strong, well-aligned source (donor) modality to a weak target (recipient) modality, boosting target-modality performance without further fine-tuning. We further show that the alignment-enhancing objective admits a closed-form weight-space solution computed from only a small calibration set. DCAT outperforms existing model-merging methods, offering an efficient path toward cross-modal alignment transfer. Project page with code is available at \url{https://seohoiki3215.github.io/DCAT_project_page}

AI.tldr: DCAT transfers textual alignment from a data-rich donor modality to a data-scarce target-modality MLLM via a closed-form weight-space merge, improving target performance without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Improving an MLLM's modality capability normally needs large modality-specific datasets. Model merging is an alternative but is infeasible for data-scarce, large per-sample, or domain-specific modalities (e.g., audio, video) where same-modality model variants are unavailable.
AI.method: The paper characterizes an asymmetric phenomenon: merging a well-aligned, data-rich source-modality MLLM into a data-scarce target-modality MLLM improves the target. It derives a mutual-information lower bound, monotonic in alignment-related quantities and correlated with downstream performance. Based on this, DCAT transfers textual alignment from a strong donor modality to a weak recipient, and the alignment-enhancing objective admits a closed-form weight-space solution computed from a small calibration set.
AI.result: The derived mutual-information lower bound strongly correlates with downstream MLLM performance. DCAT outperforms existing model-merging methods, transferring cross-modal alignment efficiently.
AI.conclusion: Cross-modal alignment transfer is an efficient path to boost data-scarce target-modality MLLM performance without further fine-tuning.

title: Dataset-Free Compliant Humanoid Loco-Manipulation with Dynamic Online Posture
summary: Most humanoid loco-manipulation controllers require human motion data to learn whole-body coordination and posture, leaving policies reliant on external sources to provide this data. We present OCLO (Online-posture Compliant LOco-manipulation), a humanoid loco-manipulation system trained without human motion data and commanded only through two end-effector targets. Because these targets do not uniquely determine whole-body posture, OCLO generates pelvis height and torso orientation online using an analytic reachability prior, further refined through policy-in-the-loop sampling with a task-agnostic cost. OCLO also learns whole-body compliance by displacing end-effector references according to measured forces through a spring-damper model, encouraging the legs, waist, and pelvis to yield to external loads. In simulation, using the reachability prior leads to a 77.8% success rate in acquiring the commanded reference, a vast improvement over the 37.8% success rate accomplished without the prior. Further, refinement reduces end-effector orientation error across all evaluated tasks. The same posture module improves a pretrained SONIC controller on four of five tasks. Without compliance training, policies tend to lose balance under disturbances rather than sacrifice tracking. On a Unitree G1, OCLO maintains balance under end-effector disturbances that cause its ablations to fail and performs seven loco-manipulation tasks, including crouched walking and picking up a box from a low surface. Project website: https://oclo-humanoid.github.io/

AI.tldr: OCLO is a humanoid loco-manipulation system trained without human motion data, commanded only by two end-effector targets, using an analytic reachability prior plus policy-in-the-loop sampling to generate posture online and learning whole-body compliance for disturbance robustness.
AI.motivation: Most humanoid loco-manipulation controllers rely on human motion data to learn whole-body coordination and posture, making policies dependent on external data sources. The paper aims to remove this dependency by deriving posture from task targets alone.
AI.method: OCLO takes only two end-effector targets as commands. Since these do not uniquely determine whole-body posture, pelvis height and torso orientation are generated online via an analytic reachability prior, refined through policy-in-the-loop sampling with a task-agnostic cost. Whole-body compliance is learned by displacing end-effector references according to measured forces via a spring-damper model, so legs, waist, and pelvis yield to external loads.
AI.result: In simulation, the reachability prior yields 77.8% success in acquiring the commanded reference versus 37.8% without it; refinement reduces end-effector orientation error across all tasks; the posture module improves a pretrained SONIC controller on four of five tasks. Without compliance training, policies lose balance under disturbances instead of sacrificing tracking. On a Unitree G1, OCLO maintains balance under disturbances that cause ablations to fail and performs seven loco-manipulation tasks, including crouched walking and picking up a box from a low surface.
AI.conclusion: A human-motion-data-free humanoid loco-manipulation system can achieve robust whole-body coordination and compliance by generating posture online from an analytic reachability prior with policy-in-the-loop refinement, validated in simulation and on real hardware.

title: Bounds, Decompositions and Null Behaviour of KRATOS: A Mathematical Specification of a Recognition-Comparability Diagnostic
summary: KRATOS is a group-structured bibliometric diagnostic that compares the distribution of documents (participation) with the distribution of citation weight (recognition) over a fixed, finite universe of analytical groups. This note gives its complete mathematical specification and derives the properties that govern its interpretation. Beyond bounds and equality conditions for each component, we show that the recognition-alignment score depends on citation data only through ratios of group mean citation rates to the corpus mean; that the composition ceiling of the participation--recognition factor is an affine function of the total variation distance to the uniform reference; and that the factor itself satisfies Fréchet-type bounds in terms of this ceiling and a participation-weighted recognition score. We establish an exact logarithmic decomposition of the composite index, an ordering between the primary and a reciprocal-symmetric recognition score, invariance properties, and closed-form first and second moments of the recognition ratios under global and stratified permutation nulls. These results explain why composite orderings can be sensitive to small groups, heavy-tailed citation distributions and metadata reassignment. All results are verified numerically with an accompanying script. The specification concerns measurement structure only; it does not define a measure of epistemic change or justice.

AI.tldr: KRATOS is a group-structured bibliometric diagnostic that compares document participation against citation recognition over a fixed universe of groups. This note provides its full mathematical specification and derives interpretive properties: bounds, equality conditions, ratio-based dependence on citation data, an affine composition ceiling tied to total variation distance from uniformity, Fréchet-type bounds, an exact logarithmic decomposition, ordering between primary and reciprocal-symmetric recognition scores, invariance properties, and closed-form permutation-null moments.
AI.motivation: Composite bibliometric indices can produce orderings that are unstable with respect to small groups, heavy-tailed citation distributions, and metadata reassignment, yet their mathematical structure is often left implicit. The paper motivates a complete formal specification of KRATOS so that its interpretive behavior—separating participation from recognition—can be derived rather than assumed.
AI.method: The paper formally specifies KRATOS over a fixed, finite universe of analytical groups. It compares the document distribution (participation) with the citation-weight distribution (recognition), then derives analytic properties: component bounds and equality conditions; reduction of the recognition-alignment score to ratios of group mean citation rates to the corpus mean; an affine representation of the participation–recognition factor's composition ceiling in terms of total variation distance to the uniform reference; Fréchet-type bounds relating the factor to this ceiling and a participation-weighted recognition score; an exact logarithmic decomposition of the composite index; ordering between primary and reciprocal-symmetric recognition scores; invariance properties; and closed-form first and second moments of recognition ratios under global and stratified permutation nulls. Results are verified numerically with an accompanying script.
AI.result: The recognition-alignment score depends on citation data only through ratios of group mean citation rates to the corpus mean. The composition ceiling of the participation–recognition factor is affine in the total variation distance to the uniform reference. The factor satisfies Fréchet-type bounds in terms of that ceiling and a participation-weighted recognition score. Additional results include an exact logarithmic decomposition of the composite index, an ordering between the primary and reciprocal-symmetric recognition score, invariance properties, and closed-form first and second moments of recognition ratios under global and stratified permutation nulls. Numerical verification supports all derivations.
AI.conclusion: KRATOS is fully specified as a measurement structure, and its analytic properties explain why composite orderings can be sensitive to small groups, heavy-tailed citation distributions, and metadata reassignment. The specification concerns measurement structure only and does not define a measure of epistemic change or justice.

title: Benchmarking Generative Trajectory Models for Active-Inference Control
comment: Accepted at the 7th International Workshop on Active Inference (IWAI 2026). 16 pages, including appendix and references; 4 figures. Code: https://github.com/lyeeonardo/generative-trajectory-benchmark
summary: Learning from trajectory demonstrations offers a route to active-inference control of complex systems whose dynamics are difficult to model explicitly. We introduce generative active-inference control (GenAIF), in which one generative trajectory model learns from demonstrations and measured action interventions to supply a goal-conditioned policy distribution and a state-to-observation likelihood mapping. From this control design, we derive three model requirements: (i) useful action proposals, (ii) accurate prediction under imposed actions, and (iii) probabilistic observation evidence for belief updating and expected information gain. We benchmark diffusion, autoregressive Transformers, conditional variational autoencoders (CVAEs), and flow matching in a MuJoCo manipulation task with multiple physical conditions. Diffusion delivers the strongest control across the tested dynamics, while CVAE combines comparable short-horizon prediction with much faster inference. Correct conditioning is decisive, and trajectory reuse offers further computational savings. With the same frozen models, a hidden-dynamics experiment demonstrates prompt belief adaptation after an unannounced tilt change; subsequent instability identifies sustained inference as a remaining challenge. These findings support the use of shared generative trajectory models to connect action proposal, controlled prediction, and observation evidence within GenAIF.

AI.tldr: GenAIF learns a single generative trajectory model from demonstrations and action interventions to provide a goal-conditioned policy and state-to-observation likelihood for active-inference control; diffusion gives the best control, CVAE gives fast inference at comparable short-horizon accuracy, and correct conditioning is decisive.
AI.motivation: Active-inference control of complex systems typically requires explicit dynamics models that are hard to obtain. Learning directly from trajectory demonstrations offers an alternative, but it is unclear which generative model class best supplies the ingredients active inference needs.
AI.method: Introduce Generative Active-Inference Control (GenAIF), where one generative trajectory model learns from demonstrations and measured action interventions to provide a goal-conditioned policy distribution and a state-to-observation likelihood mapping. Derive three model requirements: (i) useful action proposals, (ii) accurate prediction under imposed actions, and (iii) probabilistic observation evidence for belief updating and expected information gain. Benchmark diffusion, autoregressive Transformers, CVAEs, and flow matching on a MuJoCo manipulation task under multiple physical conditions.
AI.result: Diffusion delivers the strongest control across tested dynamics; CVAE combines comparable short-horizon prediction with much faster inference. Correct conditioning is decisive, and trajectory reuse yields additional computational savings. With frozen models, a hidden-dynamics experiment shows prompt belief adaptation after an unannounced tilt change, while subsequent instability reveals sustained inference as an open challenge.
AI.conclusion: Shared generative trajectory models can unify action proposal, controlled prediction, and observation evidence within GenAIF, supporting their use for active-inference control learned from demonstrations.

title: LatentIndex: Cross-Layer Sharing with Layer-Specific Selection for Sparse Attention
summary: Sparse attention reduces core-attention computation, but its indexers still incur repeated selection work and per-layer key-cache storage. Reusing selected indices across layers reduces this overhead but constrains multiple layers to the same token set. We introduce LatentIndex, which extends the latent-sharing principle of Multi-head Latent Attention across indexer layers. Each layer group constructs a shared latent cache from its first layer's hidden states, while layer-specific scoring enables independent token selection. Absorbing key decoders into queries enables direct scoring of the shared cache without reconstructing historical per-layer keys. We develop training-free calibration and investigate a training-aware instantiation of this principle. To balance quality and computation, a hierarchical selection (HS) variant lets followers independently refine a shared candidate set proposed by the anchor. With four-layer sharing, LatentIndex reduces logical indexer-cache storage by 61.1% on DeepSeek-V3.2. Across DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5, training-free LatentIndex improves head-wise attention-mass recall over IndexCache by up to 3.28 percentage points while maintaining RULER and LongBench performance close to native DSA. HS further achieves 2.30-2.72 times decode indexer speedups over DSA across 8K-128K contexts, retaining most of LatentIndex's recall. LatentIndex offers a new perspective on cross-layer indexing: sharing continuous representations rather than discrete selections enables efficient reuse while preserving layer-specific token selection.

AI.tldr: LatentIndex shares continuous latent caches across indexer layers (extending MLA's latent-sharing principle) to cut repeated indexer selection and per-layer key-cache storage, while preserving layer-specific token selection via hierarchical selection.
AI.motivation: Sparse attention reduces core-attention computation, but its indexers still incur repeated selection work and per-layer key-cache storage. Existing cross-layer index reuse constrains multiple layers to the same token set, degrading quality.
AI.method: LatentIndex: each layer group builds a shared latent cache from its first layer's hidden states; layer-specific scoring enables independent token selection. Key decoders are absorbed into queries to score the shared cache directly without reconstructing historical per-layer keys. Includes training-free calibration, a training-aware instantiation, and a hierarchical selection (HS) variant where followers refine a shared anchor candidate set.
AI.result: With four-layer sharing, logical indexer-cache storage drops 61.1% on DeepSeek-V3.2. Training-free LatentIndex improves head-wise attention-mass recall over IndexCache by up to 3.28 pp (DeepSeek-V3.2, GLM-5) while keeping RULER/LongBench near native DSA. HS yields 2.30-2.72x decode indexer speedups over DSA at 8K-128K contexts, retaining most recall.
AI.conclusion: LatentIndex offers a new perspective on cross-layer indexing: sharing continuous representations rather than discrete selections enables efficient reuse while preserving layer-specific token selection.

title: Virtual model control for compliant reaching under uncertainties
summary: Virtual Model Control (VMC) is an approach to design a controller for force-controlled robots in complex uncertain environments. While this method was primarily investigated for legged robot locomotion in the past, it can be more generally applicable to other types of robotic systems. This paper investigates the VMC framework for reaching tasks in a force-controlled robotic arm. We propose six different approaches to designing virtual models in order to achieve reaching tasks in environments with obstacles and uncertainties. A force-controlled 8 degree-of-freedom humanoid robot was used to validate the proposed approach in the real world. We conducted three experiments to test the performance of VMC controllers in terms of predictability, sensitivity to external force, and adaptability against known and unknown obstacles. Experimental analyses show that, even though the proposed approach needs to sacrifice accuracy and trajectory optimality, it enables us to design complex reaching motions under uncertainties, in an intuitive and extendable manner.

AI.tldr: This paper extends Virtual Model Control (VMC), previously used for legged locomotion, to reaching tasks in a force-controlled robotic arm, proposing six virtual-model designs validated on an 8-DoF humanoid robot across three experiments.
AI.motivation: VMC was primarily studied for legged robot locomotion, but it can be more generally applicable to other robotic systems. The authors aim to investigate whether the VMC framework can support reaching tasks in a force-controlled robotic arm operating in complex, uncertain environments with obstacles.
AI.method: The authors propose six different approaches to designing virtual models for achieving reaching tasks under obstacles and uncertainties. They validate the approach using a force-controlled 8 degree-of-freedom humanoid robot in real-world experiments, and run three experiments assessing predictability, sensitivity to external force, and adaptability against known and unknown obstacles.
AI.result: The experimental analyses show that although the proposed approach sacrifices accuracy and trajectory optimality, it enables the design of complex reaching motions under uncertainties in an intuitive and extendable manner.
AI.conclusion: VMC is a viable and generalizable framework for reachin

title: SEIS: Self-Evolving Inference Systems
summary: Inference systems determine how fast and how cheaply language models can be served, so making them faster has direct practical value. However, prior work focuses mostly on optimizing certain parts such as kernels or memory within the large system. In this work, we take a holistic approach and apply agentic self-evolution to optimize the whole system end-to-end. Our SEIS (Self-Evolving Inference Systems) autonomously optimizes the entire mini-sglang engine without human intervention through iterative sessions with inherited experiences and code changes. Serving Qwen3-0.6B on H100, the resulting engine reaches 3.27X the throughput of the original mini-sglang implementation and beats SOTA engines like vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and SGLang in the single-request workload. The correctness of the optimized inference engine by SEIS is tested in terms of numerical difference and downstream accuracy on math and long-context retrieval tasks. The code and session histories show that the speedup comes from redesigning the whole engine and that building on earlier sessions beats independent attempts. These results suggest that agentic self-evolution can optimize a complex system end-to-end. The evaluation also has to evolve with the engine, and letting agents evolve it is a natural next step.

AI.tldr: SEIS uses agentic self-evolution to autonomously optimize the entire mini-sglang inference engine end-to-end, achieving 3.27X throughput over the original and beating SOTA engines like vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, and SGLang on single-request workloads while maintaining numerical and downstream accuracy.
AI.motivation: Inference systems determine how fast and cheaply language models are served, giving direct practical value to speedups. However, prior work mostly optimizes isolated parts such as kernels or memory within the larger system, rather than the system as a whole.
AI.method: The authors take a holistic approach, applying agentic self-evolution to optimize the whole system end-to-end. Their SEIS (Self-Evolving Inference Systems) autonomously optimizes the entire mini-sglang engine without human intervention via iterative sessions that inherit prior experiences and make code changes.
AI.result: Serving Qwen3-0.6B on H100, the optimized engine reaches 3.27X the throughput of the original mini-sglang and beats SOTA engines (vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang) on the single-request workload. Correctness is validated via numerical difference and downstream accuracy on math and long-context retrieval tasks. Session histories show the speedup stems from redesigning the whole engine, and building on earlier sessions outperforms independent attempts.
AI.conclusion: Agentic self-evolution can optimize a complex system end-to-end. The evaluation itself must also evolve with the engine, making agent-driven evolution of the evaluation a natural next step.

title: When to Switch: Reliable Action-Chunk Extension for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models serve as unified policies for robotic manipulation, yet their expensive inference forces robots to pause between policy calls, resulting in stop-and-go execution that interrupts smooth motion and prolongs task completion. Extending the action chunk reduces policy calls and hence these pauses, but predicting farther into the future makes long-chunk execution unreliable. To understand where this unreliability arises, we analyze action errors within long chunks and find that they concentrate around transitions between manipulation subskills, growing sharply with chunk length. This suggests the importance of transition timing, i.e., when to switch subskills within a chunk. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RACE (Reliable Action-Chunk Extension), a framework that predicts the transition timing from an auxiliary one-step denoising pass and conditions action generation on it. By learning and conditioning on transition timing, RACE reduces errors at subskill transitions and enables reliable execution of longer action chunks. Across simulation benchmarks, RACE outperforms fine-tuning at the same chunk length; with 2x longer chunks, it surpasses recent state-of-the-art and efficient VLAs in success rate, and with 4x longer chunks, it remains competitive. On a real robot, RACE uses 4x longer chunks, which reduces the idle time caused by stop-and-go execution by about 5x, while achieving a higher success rate than fine-tuning with the same chunk length. Code and a real-robot demo are available at https://github.com/Seonghoon-Yu/RACE-VLA

AI.tldr: RACE extends action chunks in VLA models by predicting subskill transition timing via an auxiliary one-step denoising pass, conditioning action generation on it to reduce transition errors and enable reliable long-chunk execution.
AI.motivation: VLA models have expensive inference, forcing robots into stop-and-go execution between policy calls. Extending action chunks reduces calls/pauses but makes long-chunk execution unreliable.
AI.method: Analysis shows action errors concentrate at subskill transitions, growing sharply with chunk length. RACE predicts transition timing from an auxiliary one-step denoising pass and conditions action generation on it.
AI.result: RACE beats fine-tuning at same chunk length; with 2x longer chunks surpasses SOTA and efficient VLAs in success rate, remains competitive at 4x. On real robot, 4x longer chunks cut idle time ~5x with higher success rate than fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning on transition timing reduces subskill-transition errors, enabling reliable longer action chunks and smoother, more efficient robotic manipulation.

title: PermVLA: Factorization Order as a Regularizer for VLA Learning
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies commonly learn action chunks through a fixed left-to-right (LTR) factorization, although the same expert trajectory distribution admits many valid chain-rule factorizations. We identify factorization order as an overlooked regularization choice and introduce causally anchored permutation (CAP), which samples action reveal orders with a tunable chronological prefix. Its auxiliary objective trains one shared policy to predict actions from different known subsets of the same expert chunk, while deployment retains deterministic LTR control. We call this conditional-set augmentation: it creates multiple conditional prediction problems from one expert chunk without adding demonstrations. This discourages reliance on the single chronological prefix used by ordinary teacher forcing. Controlled experiments show that CAP consistently outperforms standard LTR training on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, with the same advantage appearing in cross-dataset CALVIN evaluation. A diagnostic that measures the expected squared difference between a chunk's joint log likelihood under two reveal orders verifies that CAP training internalizes agreement across reveal orders. These findings position sampled subset-conditioned auxiliary objectives as a general recipe for constructing VLA regularizers, illustrated by an extension to diffusion action generators.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies the fixed left-to-right (LTR) factorization used to learn action chunks in vision-language-action (VLA) policies as an overlooked regularization choice, and proposes causally anchored permutation (CAP), a subset-conditioned auxiliary objective that samples action reveal orders with a tunable chronological prefix, consistently improving over standard LTR training.
AI.motivation: VLA policies conventionally learn action chunks through a fixed left-to-right chain-rule factorization. However, the same expert trajectory distribution admits many valid factorizations, yet this design choice has been treated as fixed rather than as a tunable regularization knob. The authors argue that reliance on the single chronological prefix imposed by ordinary teacher forcing is a limitation worth addressing.
AI.method: Causally anchored permutation (CAP): samples action reveal orders with a tunable chronological prefix, yielding an auxiliary objective that trains one shared policy to predict actions from different known subsets of the same expert chunk. Deployment retains deterministic LTR control. The approach is framed as conditional-set augmentation, generating multiple conditional prediction problems from a single expert chunk without additional demonstrations. A diagnostic measures the expected squared difference between a chunk's joint log likelihood under two reveal orders. The recipe is extended to diffusion action generators.
AI.result: CAP consistently outperforms standard LTR training on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, with the same advantage observed in cross-dataset CALVIN evaluation. The diagnostic confirms that CAP training internalizes agreement across reveal orders.
AI.conclusion: Factorization order is an overlooked regularization choice in VLA policy learning. Sampled subset-conditioned auxiliary objectives constitute a general recipe for constructing VLA regularizers, as illustrated by CAP and its extension to diffusion action generators.

authors: Tommaso Van Der Meer Andrea Garulli
title: End-to-End Safe Social Navigation via Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning and Probabilistic Perception
comment: Accepted to the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS), 2026
summary: Autonomous social navigation requires balancing efficiency, physical safety, and social compliance. Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods provide a viable and effective solution but often rely on unrealistic assumptions, such as the knowledge of humans' position and velocity. In this paper, we introduce JESSI (JAX-based E2E Safe Social Interpretable navigation), a lightweight end-to-end RL framework that maps raw LiDAR scans directly to kinematically feasible control commands. JESSI enhances safety via Dirichlet-parameterized continuous action spaces and deterministic bounding, while an integrated attention-based perception module extracts probabilistic human states for interpretable, socially aware decision-making. Through extensive simulations and real-world deployment on a differential-drive robot, we demonstrate that jointly optimizing the RL policy with a supervised perception signal in a multi-task paradigm enhances social behavior. Ultimately, JESSI is able to balance high navigation success rates and superior social behaviors compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: JESSI is a lightweight end-to-end RL framework for safe social navigation that maps raw LiDAR scans directly to kinematically feasible control commands without assuming human position/velocity knowledge.
AI.motivation: Autonomous social navigation must balance efficiency, physical safety, and social compliance. Existing RL methods often rely on unrealistic assumptions, such as knowing humans' positions and velocities, which limits real-world applicability.
AI.method: JESSI (JAX-based E2E Safe Social Interpretable navigation) maps raw LiDAR scans directly to kinematically feasible control commands. Safety is enhanced via Dirichlet-parameterized continuous action spaces and deterministic bounding, while an integrated attention-based perception module extracts probabilistic human states for interpretable, socially aware decision-making. The RL policy is jointly optimized with a supervised perception signal in a multi-task paradigm.
AI.result: Through extensive simulations and real-world deployment on a differential-drive robot, jointly optimizing the RL policy with a supervised perception signal in a multi-task paradigm enhances social behavior. JESSI achieves a balance of high navigation success rates and superior social behaviors compared to state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: JESSI provides an end-to-end, interpretable, and safe social navigation solution that avoids unrealistic assumptions about human state knowledge and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both navigation success and social compliance.

title: Efficient Neural Surrogates for Linear Radiation Transport on the Lattice and Hohlraum benchmarks
summary: Linear radiation transport equations (RTEs) form the simulation foundations underpinning design and analysis tasks in nuclear engineering, inertial confinement fusion, medical imaging, and astrophysics, but resolving the high-dimensional phase space at engineering fidelity remains expensive enough that outer-loop workflows, such as design optimization, uncertainty quantification, and parameter sweeps, are routinely budget-bound on traditional solvers. Neural surrogates promise to relax this bottleneck by amortizing simulation cost across thousands of downstream queries, but the architectural choices and engineered inductive biases that make a surrogate accurate on one transport problem do not transfer straightforwardly across model families. We benchmark two parameter-matched neural surrogate architectures, the physics-attention Transolver and the multi-scale graph network Bi-Stride Multi-Scale MeshGraphNet (BSMS-MGN), as end-to-end approximations of the final-time particle concentration for the two-dimensional linear RTE on the canonical Lattice and Hohlraum benchmarks. An ablation across Fourier features and region-weighted training loss exposes strongly architecture-dependent inductive-bias preferences, indicating that design choices common to physics-informed surrogate workflows must be revisited per architecture rather than imported across model families, and that downstream utility depends on per-QoI sensitivity rather than a single field-level score. The model training recipe, training data, and evaluation pipeline are released alongside this paper to support reproduction, transfer to related transport problems, and evaluation as amortized forward-model components in larger outer-loop simulation workflows.

AI.tldr: The paper benchmarks two parameter-matched neural surrogate architectures (Transolver and BSMS-MGN) as end-to-end approximations of final-time particle concentration for the 2D linear radiation transport equation on Lattice and Hohlraum benchmarks, finding strongly architecture-dependent inductive-bias preferences.
AI.motivation: Linear RTEs underpin design and analysis in nuclear engineering, inertial confinement fusion, medical imaging, and astrophysics, but resolving the high-dimensional phase space at engineering fidelity is expensive, making outer-loop workflows (optimization, UQ, parameter sweeps) budget-bound. Neural surrogates promise to amortize simulation cost, but architectural choices and inductive biases that work for one transport problem do not transfer straightforwardly across model families.
AI.method: Benchmark two parameter-matched neural surrogate architectures—the physics-attention Transolver and the multi-scale graph network Bi-Stride Multi-Scale MeshGraphNet (BSMS-MGN)—as end-to-end approximations of the final-time particle concentration for the 2D linear RTE on the canonical Lattice and Hohlraum benchmarks. Perform an ablation across Fourier features and region-weighted training loss.
AI.result: The ablation exposes strongly architecture-dependent inductive-bias preferences, indicating that design choices common to physics-informed surrogate workflows must be revisited per architecture rather than imported across model families, and that downstream utility depends on per-QoI sensitivity rather than a single field-level score.
AI.conclusion: Design choices in physics-informed surrogate workflows should be revisited per architecture rather than transferred across model families, and downstream utility hinges on per-QoI sensitivity. The training recipe, data, and evaluation pipeline are released to support reproduction, transfer to related transport problems, and evaluation as amortized forward-model components in larger outer-loop workflows.

title: FreeSpeed: Training-Free Speed Control for Generative Robot Policies
comment: 37 pages, 21 figures, 14 tables. Project page: https://yuxuanhu9.github.io/FreeSpeed/
summary: Online control of execution speed is essential for deploying robot policies in real-world scenarios, as robots may need to speed up under time constraints or slow down to facilitate human interaction and improve safety. However, imitation-learned policies inherit the execution speed of their demonstrations, and test-time speed modification can introduce unrecoverable out-of-distribution observations, reducing task success. We observe that the directional inconsistency of action chunks reflects task-phase criticality, indicating how aggressively action step lengths can be modified while preserving task success. Based on this observation, we introduce FreeSpeed, a training-free module that post-processes action chunks from pretrained policies. FreeSpeed resamples each predicted chunk at the requested rate, then uses directional inconsistency between adjacent actions as the primary signal for rescaling. This signal adaptively determines how closely the execution speed can approach the requested speed, allowing flexible speed adjustment within the evaluated limits without compromising task success. Across three policy families and 50 simulated tasks, FreeSpeed supports online speed changes, with realized execution rates spanning 0.22x to 2.53x among settings that preserve per-task success. Across four real-world manipulation tasks, FreeSpeed achieves an average success rate of 94.0%, matching the frozen policy's 93.8%, while realizing execution rates from 0.38x to 1.97x.

AI.tldr: FreeSpeed is a training-free module that post-processes action chunks from pretrained robot policies to enable online execution-speed control, using directional inconsistency within chunks as a signal for how much speed can be adjusted without losing task success.
AI.motivation: Online control of execution speed is essential for deploying robot policies, as robots may need to accelerate under time constraints or decelerate for safe human interaction. However, imitation-learned policies inherit their demonstration speed, and naive test-time speed modification produces unrecoverable out-of-distribution observations that reduce task success.
AI.method: The authors observe that directional inconsistency of action chunks reflects task-phase criticality, indicating how aggressively action step lengths can be modified while preserving success. FreeSpeed resamples each predicted chunk at the requested rate, then uses directional inconsistency between adjacent actions as the primary signal for rescaling, adaptively determining how closely execution speed can approach the requested speed.
AI.result: Across three policy families and 50 simulated tasks, FreeSpeed supports online speed changes with realized execution rates from 0.22x to 2.53x among settings preserving per-task success. Across four real-world manipulation tasks, it achieves 94.0% average success versus the frozen policy's 93.8%, while realizing rates from 0.38x to 1.97x.
AI.conclusion: FreeSpeed enables flexible online speed adjustment within evaluated limits without compromising task success, and is training-free, requiring no retraining of the underlying policy.

title: A Tropical Geometry View of Forgetting: A Per-Unit Projector for Knowledge-Preserving Fine-Tuning
summary: Fine-tuning a language model on new text degrades what it already does. Replay-free projectors such as Adam-NSCL and GPM forbid one shared subspace of a layer's inputs in every row of the update. The tropical geometry of a ReLU layer shows why this is too coarse. In data space, the units' walls are tropical hypersurfaces whose cells are dual to the upper vertices of a zonotope; in weight space, each old token is a hyperplane, and the tokens cut out a polyhedron, the closure of the weights that keep every token on its side. An exact identity joins the two pictures: the squared change of the layer's output under any weight change splits into in-cell, open-to-closed and closed-to-open terms, and the first two live on the tokens each unit fires on. The identity names a gate-aware per-unit projector, and a budget-separation theorem prices exact protection: it costs a unit the rank of its own open tokens, while a shared subspace pays at least the rank of their union in every row. On OPT-1.3b, where 96% of (token, unit) pairs are closed, the projector forgets less than Adam-NSCL at all six matched budgets from 9 to 60 constrained directions per row, the gap widening from $1.1\times$ to $4.3\times$; with 1/5.5 of the directions it halves the forgetting of Adam-NSCL at GPM's energy threshold. On OPT-6.7b, it matches Adam-NSCL's forgetting at matched budget while learning more. As the theory predicts, the open/closed partition is the operative variable: open tokens beat random, sign-blind and anti-gate token sets on 18 of 18 seed-pairs. In pruning repair, every derivative-based local model of the output error at the dense weights is blind to pairs that open: the minimisers of the gate-weighted objective can leave the polyhedron, the objective's closed-form solution is 1.94 nats worse than no repair on OPT-1.3b, and a convex one-sided penalty bounds the escape.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that replay-free projectors like Adam-NSCL and GPM use too coarse a constraint (one shared subspace per row), and proposes a gate-aware per-unit projector derived from tropical geometry of ReLU layers. This projector forgets less than Adam-NSCL at matched budgets on OPT-1.3b (gap widening 1.1× to 4.3×) and matches it on OPT-6.7b while learning more, with the open/closed token partition confirmed as the operative variable.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning a language model on new text degrades existing capabilities. Replay-free projectors such as Adam-NSCL and GPM restrict one shared subspace of a layer's inputs across every row of the update. However, the tropical geometry of a ReLU layer shows that this single shared subspace is too coarse, because the structure of the layer depends on which units fire on which tokens.
AI.method: The authors use tropical geometry to analyze ReLU layers. In data space, unit walls are tropical hypersurfaces with cells dual to upper vertices of a zonotope; in weight space, each old token is a hyperplane and the tokens cut out a polyhedron (the closure of weights keeping every token on its side). They derive an exact identity splitting the squared change of the layer output under any weight change into in-cell, open-to-closed, and closed-to-open terms, where the first two live on the tokens each unit fires on. This yields a gate-aware per-unit projector and a budget-separation theorem pricing exact protection.
AI.result: On OPT-1.3b, where 96% of (token, unit) pairs are closed, the projector forgets less than Adam-NSCL at all six matched budgets (9 to 60 constrained directions per row), with the gap widening from 1.1× to 4.3×; with 1/5.5 of the directions it halves Adam-NSCL's forgetting at GPM's energy threshold. On OPT-6.7b, it matches Adam-NSCL's forgetting at matched budget while learning more. The open/closed partition is the operative variable: open tokens beat random, sign-blind, and anti-gate token sets on 18 of 18 seed-pairs. In pruning repair, every derivative-based local model of the output error at dense weights is blind to pairs that open; minimisers of the gate-weighted objective can leave the polyhedron, the closed-form solution is 1.94 nats worse than no repair on OPT-1.3b, and a convex one-sided penalty bounds the escape.
AI.conclusion: The gate-aware per-unit projector derived from tropical geometry enables more precise, efficient protection against forgetting than shared-subspace methods. The theory's predicted open/closed token partition is empirically the operative variable, and derivative-based local error models are fundamentally limited in pruning repair, motivating a bounded convex one-sided penalty.

title: The Unexpired Plan: A Free Monitor for Accelerated Diffusion Policies
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Project website (code and videos): https://yizhaojasper.com/unexpired-plan/
summary: Training-free acceleration of a diffusion policy is accepted when an internal similarity signal reports that the shortcut changed nothing. We price every monitor a control loop can afford in closed-loop success rather than feature distance, over $114$ accelerator configurations and four policy families: two accelerators each clear their own gate's bar and log every reuse as certified, while on one task one finishes every episode and the other none. A monitor is two designs, not one --- the statistic it reads, and what it does when that statistic fires. Published gates re-arm after every rejection, and under that response even an oracle handed every forward pass and the exact local action error loses twenty points; absorbing the same statistic costs one point, and most of its speed. What makes a response that never forgets affordable is a statistic that rarely fires, and what it must measure is deviation from the policy the accelerator replaced --- which a chunked policy has already paid for, its last plan not yet expired and free to read. Guarding every call this way cuts per-call compute by $1.55$--$3.09\times$, where any reference-requiring check at the same coverage would have to stop accelerating altogether. On three of our four families the schedule alone already holds the pre-stated $\pm2$-point margin. What the monitor is measurably worth shows in three places: on the fourth family, where it rescues the candidate selection landed on; on four configurations it did not select; and on a contact-rich fifth family, chosen where the schedule was expected to fail and run after every design choice was frozen, where no unmonitored arm at its speed holds the margin and the monitored one does.

AI.tldr: A training-free diffusion-policy acceleration is only "certified" when an internal similarity signal confirms the shortcut changed nothing; this work shows the monitor must be evaluated as two separate designs (the statistic and the response to it), and that a rarely-firing statistic measuring deviation from the replaced policy makes a never-forgetting response affordable.
AI.motivation: Accelerated diffusion policies are accepted based on internal similarity signals, but the paper argues this acceptance criterion and the monitor's design are under-examined; existing published gates re-arm after every rejection, which is costly, and the monitor has been treated as a single design rather than composed of a statistic and a response.
AI.method: Across 114 accelerator configurations and four policy families, the authors price each affordable monitor by closed-loop success rather than feature distance. They decompose the monitor into the statistic it reads and the action taken when it fires, comparing re-arming gates, absorbing responses, and reference-based checks. Their proposed statistic measures deviation from the policy the accelerator replaced, read for free from a chunked policy's not-yet-expired last plan, enabling a never-forgetting (absorbing) response.
AI.result: Under re-arming responses, even an oracle with every forward pass and exact local action error loses twenty points; absorbing the same statistic costs one point and most of its speed. The proposed guarded calls cut per-call compute by 1.55--3.09x, while any reference-requiring check at the same coverage would have to stop accelerating. Two accelerators each clear their own gate yet on one task one finishes every episode and the other none. On three of four families the schedule alone holds the +/-2-point margin; the monitor's worth shows on the fourth family, on four non-selected configurations, and on a contact-rich fifth family where no unmonitored arm at its speed holds the margin but the monitored one does.
AI.conclusion: Monitor design must be treated as two coupled decisions---statistic and response---and success should be measured in closed-loop success, not feature distance. A rarely-firing statistic that measures deviation from the replaced policy makes an affordable, never-forgetting response possible, delivering 1.55--3.09x per-call compute reduction and preserving stated margins where unmonitored acceleration fails.

title: MASBench: Benchmarking LLM-based Multi-Agent Collaboration under Partial Observability
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have progressively evolved into the core of autonomous agents. Building on this progress, LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) coordinate multiple agents into a synergistic team to accomplish complex tasks that exceed the capabilities of individual agents. The effectiveness of such systems depends not only on the agents themselves, but also on how collaboration mechanisms are designed and organized. Note that real-world collaboration is typically partially observable, where each agent can only access partial information about the environment due to physical or privacy-related constraints.
