However, many existing multi-agent benchmarks assume global observability, and leave limited support for systematically evaluating collaboration mechanisms. To bridge this gap, we introduce MASBench, a multi-agent collaboration benchmark designed under partially observable constraints. It is organized into three progressive task categories: Reasoning, Scheduling, and Game. Through this structure, we progressively evaluate three representative collaboration mechanisms: Protocol, Memory, and Routing. MASBench further provides deterministic evaluation metrics, including performance score, communication cost, and cost effectiveness, to characterize both collaboration outcomes and communication overhead. Experiments across diverse LLM backbones and mechanism configurations offer empirical guidance for effective MAS design. Code is available at: https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/MASBench

AI.tldr: MASBench is a benchmark for LLM-based multi-agent systems under partial observability, evaluating three collaboration mechanisms (Protocol, Memory, Routing) across Reasoning, Scheduling, and Game tasks with deterministic metrics.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems coordinate agents to solve complex tasks, and their effectiveness hinges on collaboration mechanisms. Real-world collaboration is typically partially observable due to physical or privacy constraints, yet most existing multi-agent benchmarks assume global observability and offer limited support for systematically evaluating collaboration mechanisms.
AI.method: MASBench organizes tasks into three progressive categories (Reasoning, Scheduling, Game) that progressively evaluate three collaboration mechanisms: Protocol, Memory, and Routing. It provides deterministic metrics including performance score, communication cost, and cost effectiveness. Experiments are conducted across diverse LLM backbones and mechanism configurations.
AI.result: Experiments across diverse LLM backbones and mechanism configurations yield empirical guidance for effective MAS design, characterizing both collaboration outcomes and communication overhead.
AI.conclusion: MASBench fills the gap of partial-observability multi-agent collaboration evaluation, offering structured mechanism assessment and actionable design guidance for LLM-based multi-agent systems.

title: Demonstration-Calibrated Port-Hamiltonian Retuning for Manipulation Policies
summary: Diffusion and VLA policies for manipulation are often deployed through downstream impedance controllers. The stiffness and damping gains of these controllers affect task success, yet are commonly inherited from data collection rather than selected for the deployed policy. Although empirical gain sweeps can improve performance, they require repeated evaluation rollouts. We introduce PHRetune, an offline method that derives controller gains for a frozen policy without evaluation rollouts or gain search. Our approach learns a port-Hamiltonian model from demonstrations to estimate the effort and energy associated with the policy's predicted actions. The policy is applied to recorded demonstration observations, and its predictions are assessed against demonstration-derived effort and energy budgets. From this comparison, we derive a single gain scale in closed form, adjusting the downstream controller while preserving the policy and its action representation. The gains are fixed before evaluation, without requiring a prior manipulator model, task rewards, policy retraining, or additional runtime computation. Across LIBERO suites, PHRetune improves Diffusion Policy success by up to 9.4 percentage points, with the derived gains achieving the highest observed success rates in empirical gain sweeps. On all four real-world manipulation tasks, PHRetuned Diffusion Policy outperforms the nominal policy, alternative gain-tuning methods, and a policy-retraining baseline. The same procedure improves success with SmolVLA and OpenVLA-OFT on every task, while reducing acceleration and jerk for both VLA backbones.

AI.tldr: PHRetune is an offline method that derives downstream impedance controller gains for a frozen diffusion or VLA manipulation policy by learning a port-Hamiltonian model from demonstrations and computing a closed-form gain scale, improving success without evaluation rollouts or gain search.
AI.motivation: Diffusion and VLA manipulation policies are deployed via downstream impedance controllers whose stiffness and damping gains strongly affect task success, but these gains are typically inherited from data collection rather than tuned for the deployed policy. Empirical gain sweeps can help but demand repeated evaluation rollouts, which is costly.
AI.method: PHRetune learns a port-Hamiltonian model from demonstrations to estimate the effort and energy associated with the policy's predicted actions. The frozen policy is applied to recorded demonstration observations, and its predictions are assessed against demonstration-derived effort and energy budgets. From this comparison, a single gain scale is derived in closed form, adjusting the downstream controller while preserving the policy and its action representation. Gains are fixed before evaluation, requiring no prior manipulator model, task rewards, policy retraining, or additional runtime computation.
AI.result: Across LIBERO suites, PHRetune improves Diffusion Policy success by up to 9.4 percentage points, with derived gains achieving the highest success rates observed in empirical gain sweeps. On all four real-world manipulation tasks, PHRetuned Diffusion Policy outperforms the nominal policy, alternative gain-tuning methods, and a policy-retraining baseline. The same procedure improves success with SmolVLA and OpenVLA-OFT on every task while reducing acceleration and jerk for both VLA backbones.
AI.conclusion: PHRetune offers an offline, rollout-free way to derive impedance controller gains for frozen diffusion and VLA policies, consistently improving success and motion smoothness across simulated and real-world tasks without gain search, retraining, or runtime overhead.

title: When Debate Helps: Proposal Supply and Verification-Aware Readout in Multi-Agent Reasoning
summary: Multi-agent debate can improve reasoning, yet often fails to beat simple majority voting. We argue that successful debate requires two distinct mechanisms: proposal supply must surface a correct answer, and readout must identify that answer when voting misses it. We formalize the first requirement through recoverable headroom, which measures cases where a correct proposal is available but the majority answer is wrong. For the second, we develop Latent Verification Debate (LVD), an accounting model in which candidate proposals receive answer-specific verification evidence before final generation. Controlled fixed-proposal interventions estimate this latent effect in equivalent peer-support units and show that correct evidence changes answer probabilities and generated decisions while proposal supply remains fixed. To improve proposal supply, we construct societies from neural-thicket agents using labeled and label-free coverage objectives. Across two backbones and matched-budget reasoning benchmarks, coverage-selected societies increase complementary proposal supply and improve aggregate accuracy in repeated stochastic evaluations. Round-level controls further show that interaction provides gains beyond applying the same finalizer directly to the initial proposals. These results identify proposal coverage and truth-sensitive evidence use as complementary conditions for debate to outperform voting. Code is available at https://github.com/Wang-ML-Lab/when-debate-helps.

AI.tldr: This paper argues debate beats majority voting only when two conditions hold—sufficient proposal supply (a correct answer is surfaced) and a truth-sensitive readout (the correct answer is identified even when the majority vote misses it)—and operationalizes these via recoverable headroom, Latent Verification Debate (LVD), and coverage-objective neural-thicket societies.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent debate often fails to outperform simple majority voting. The authors contend this is because prior work conflates two separate requirements for debate success: proposal supply (surfacing a correct answer) and readout (identifying that answer when voting fails), and neither is adequately isolated or measured.
AI.method: The authors formalize proposal supply via "recoverable headroom," cases where a correct proposal exists but the majority answer is wrong. For readout, they develop Latent Verification Debate (LVD), an accounting model where candidate proposals receive answer-specific verification evidence before final generation; controlled fixed-proposal interventions estimate this latent effect in equivalent peer-support units. To improve proposal supply, they build societies of neural-thicket agents using labeled and label-free coverage objectives.
AI.result: Correct verification evidence changes answer probabilities and generated decisions while proposal supply is held fixed. Across two backbones and matched-budget reasoning benchmarks, coverage-selected societies increase complementary proposal supply and improve aggregate accuracy under repeated stochastic evaluation. Round-level controls show interaction yields gains beyond applying the same finalizer directly to the initial proposals.
AI.conclusion: Proposal coverage and truth-sensitive evidence use are complementary, jointly necessary conditions for debate to outperform voting. Code is available at https://github.com/Wang-ML-Lab/when-debate-helps.

title: Human-in-the-Loop Neuro-Symbolic Drift Anticipation for Reliable Visual SLAM
summary: This paper introduces Hybrid DeepSEE (HDS), a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) neuro-symbolic framework for proactive drift anticipation in Visual SLAM (V-SLAM). While data-driven models offer predictive power, their "black-box" nature often yields physically inconsistent outputs in out-of-distribution (OOD) environments. To address this, HDS integrates neural drift risk estimation with symbolic constraint reasoning. By utilizing a Large Language Model (LLM) as a reasoning bridge, the framework translates qualitative human context into interpretable symbolic constraints. Building upon this architecture, we propose a superior drift anticipation framework that ensures enhanced reliability and consistency in Visual SLAM

AI.tldr: This paper proposes HDS, a Human-in-the-Loop neuro-symbolic framework for proactive drift anticipation in V-SLAM, combining neural drift risk estimation with symbolic constraint reasoning via an LLM reasoning bridge to improve reliability and consistency.
AI.motivation: Data-driven models for Visual SLAM drift anticipation offer predictive power, but their black-box nature often produces physically inconsistent outputs in out-of-distribution environments. There is a need for a framework that remedies this while maintaining interpretability and reliability.
AI.method: HDS integrates neural drift risk estimation with symbolic constraint reasoning in a Human-in-the-Loop neuro-symbolic setup. A Large Language Model serves as a reasoning bridge, translating qualitative human context into interpretable symbolic constraints, upon which a superior drift anticipation framework is built.
AI.result: The proposed framework yields enhanced reliability and consistency in Visual SLAM drift anticipation.
AI.conclusion: HDS constitutes a proactive, interpretable neuro-symbolic approach to drift anticipation that leverages human context through symbolic reasoning, positioning it as a superior and more trustworthy alternative to purely data-driven methods.

title: RAGStress: A controlled benchmark for evaluating retrieval-augmented generation under knowledge-base degradation
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is typically evaluated under the implicit assumption that the underlying knowledge base (KB) is clean, leaving the behaviour of RAG systems under realistic KB degradation poorly characterised. We introduce RAGStress, a controlled evaluation benchmark for stress-testing RAG systems under systematic KB corruption. The benchmark pairs four naturalistic corruption types (factual corruption, numeric typo, relevance poisoning, and contradiction injection) with three severity levels (subtle, moderate, and obvious) over a single-KB, metadata-filtered experimental design built from 57 MMLU subjects and 182,546 documents. Across 52,500 model-question-condition evaluations, RAGStress reveals that clean retrieval can mask robustness differences, semantic-fidelity corruptions are substantially more harmful than signal-utility perturbations, no-retrieval accuracy does not predict corrupted-retrieval robustness, and mixed-KB accuracy should not be treated as worst-case robustness. We document the benchmark's intended use, supported claims, and limitations, and provide an artifact bundle including generation scripts, corruption prompts, metadata schema, and evaluation code. RAGStress is intended as a controlled stress test for RAG robustness under KB corruption, not as a general model leaderboard.

AI.tldr: RAGStress is a controlled benchmark for evaluating RAG systems under systematic knowledge base corruption, revealing that clean retrieval masks robustness differences and that semantic-fidelity corruption is more harmful than signal-utility perturbation.
AI.motivation: RAG is usually evaluated assuming a clean knowledge base, so its behaviour under realistic KB degradation is poorly characterised.
AI.method: The benchmark pairs four naturalistic corruption types (factual corruption, numeric typo, relevance poisoning, contradiction injection) with three severity levels (subtle, moderate, obvious) in a single-KB, metadata-filtered design built from 57 MMLU subjects and 182,546 documents, run over 52,500 model-question-condition evaluations.
AI.result: Clean retrieval can mask robustness differences; semantic-fidelity corruptions are substantially more harmful than signal-utility perturbations; no-retrieval accuracy does not predict corrupted-retrieval robustness; mixed-KB accuracy should not be treated as worst-case robustness.
AI.conclusion: RAGStress is a controlled stress test for RAG robustness under KB corruption, not a general model leaderboard; the artifact bundle includes generation scripts, corruption prompts, metadata schema, and evaluation code, with documented intended use, supported claims, and limitations.

title: Bilinear Flow Policy: Distributional Extrapolation for Goal-Conditioned Visuomotor Imitation
summary: Goal-conditioned imitation learning (GCIL) with flow matching is a promising framework that can represent multimodal behaviors while adapting to diverse, user-specified goals, yet often fails when goals lie outside the demonstration support. To extrapolate to such unseen goals without collapsing multimodality - a problem we call distributional extrapolation - we introduce Bilinear Flow Policy (BFP), a generative visuomotor policy that combines transductive retrieval with a bilinear conditional flow. Given an unseen observation-goal pair, BFP retrieves an "anchor" training example and transductively reformulates the unseen pair as this familiar anchor plus a residual term. For this decomposition to guide action prediction, the residual must compactly encode how the current observation-goal pair differs from the anchor, and the anchor must be chosen so that this difference is predictive of the corresponding action distribution. BFP achieves this with pretrained visual features and a novel learned anchor-selection algorithm. The novel bilinear flow then models how the anchor and the residual jointly determine the multimodal action distribution. We prove that, for bilinear flow under suitable assumptions, action distribution error at unseen goals is bounded by the in-distribution flow-matching error up to problem-dependent factors. Across five manipulation tasks in simulation, BFP achieves 2.63x the out-of distribution success rate of a GCIL policy and 1.36x that of the strongest extrapolation-targeted baseline. On two real-world tasks, BFP improves over GCIL by 32%. Finally, our theory yields practical, pre deployment diagnostics for predicting which trained policies will extrapolate well and to which unseen goal.

AI.tldr: BFP is a goal-conditioned imitation learning policy that combines transductive retrieval with a bilinear conditional flow to extrapolate to unseen goals without collapsing multimodality.
AI.motivation: Goal-conditioned imitation learning with flow matching represents multimodal behaviors and adapts to user-specified goals, but fails when goals lie outside the demonstration support. The challenge is distributional extrapolation: reaching unseen goals while preserving multimodality.
AI.method: BFP retrieves an anchor training example for an unseen observation-goal pair and reformulates it as anchor plus residual. It uses pretrained visual features and a learned anchor-selection algorithm so the residual compactly encodes the difference and is predictive of action distribution. A novel bilinear flow models how anchor and residual jointly determine the multimodal action distribution.
AI.result: Theory bounds action distribution error at unseen goals by in-distribution flow-matching error under suitable assumptions. In simulation, BFP achieves 2.63x the out-of-distribution success rate of a GCIL policy and 1.36x the strongest extrapolation-targeted baseline across five manipulation tasks. On two real-world tasks, it improves over GCIL by 32%. The theory also yields pre-deployment diagnostics for predicting extrapolation performance.
AI.conclusion: BFP effectively addresses distributional extrapolation in GCIL by combining transductive retrieval and bilinear flow, with theoretical guarantees and strong empirical gains. The theory provides practical diagnostics for predicting which policies will extrapolate well and to which unseen goals.

title: Penumbra: Sample-Efficient Adversarial Search for Regulatory Obligations
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Self-Evolving Diversity-Driven Search for Robust AI Systems (EvoRobust) at NeurIPS 2026. Workshop papers are non-archival. 12 pages (4 content pages plus references and appendices)
summary: Agents are entering finance, healthcare and law, sectors where a violation leaves no lexical signature and carries real penalties. Whether an omission is material, or a disclosure sufficient, depends on what the response left out. Probing such an obligation means finding responses one minimal edit from flipping compliance, and every probe costs a generation and two adjudications, so the binding constraint on regulatory red-teaming is sample efficiency, not volume. We introduce Penumbra, an adversarial search that walks from a verified anchor under an expanding edit budget until a two-evaluator committee changes its verdict, and emits the two adjacent responses that straddle the change. Allocation is adaptive, and the objective is coverage of the defeat surface: distinct (obligation x defeat mode) cells resolved per candidate. At matched budget, adaptive allocation reaches uniform allocation's full-budget coverage on 59% of the candidates; at equal records it covers 1.43x the defeat modes of naive enumeration, and the gain is confined to the axis it targets. On 60 screened obligations of a financial advisory constitution, Penumbra returns 144 pairs, each a compliant and a violating response that the committee places on opposite sides of the boundary, differing by a handful of words where a model asked for both directly produces texts sharing almost nothing. A second constitution, for clinical triage, reproduces this on 18 obligations: 49 pairs at the same tightness, with the same modes hardest. Pairs like these show where an obligation's own terms stop deciding, which is what an agent deployed under it must be tested against, and the search finds them at a cost that scales with the boundary, not the text.

AI.tldr: Penumbra is an adversarial search method for regulatory red-teaming of AI agents that efficiently finds minimal-edit pairs of compliant and violating responses straddling a compliance boundary, using adaptive allocation to maximize coverage of the defeat surface.
AI.motivation: In finance, healthcare, and law, agent violations leave no lexical signature but carry real penalties; whether an omission is material or a disclosure sufficient depends on what a response left out. Probing such obligations requires finding responses one minimal edit from flipping compliance, and each probe costs a generation plus two adjudications, making sample efficiency—not volume—the binding constraint.
AI.method: Penumbra performs an adversarial search that walks from a verified anchor under an expanding edit budget until a two-evaluator committee changes its verdict, emitting the two adjacent responses that straddle the change. Allocation is adaptive, with the objective of covering the defeat surface: distinct (obligation x defeat mode) cells resolved per candidate.
AI.result: At matched budget, adaptive allocation reaches uniform allocation's full-budget coverage on 59% of candidates; at equal records it covers 1.43x the defeat modes of naive enumeration, with gains confined to the targeted axis. On 60 screened obligations of a financial advisory constitution, Penumbra returns 144 compliant/violating pairs differing by a handful of words (vs. models asked for both sharing almost nothing); a clinical triage constitution reproduces this on 18 obligations with 49 pairs at the same tightness and same hardest modes.
AI.conclusion: Penumbra's minimal-edit boundary pairs reveal where an obligation's own terms stop deciding—the exact condition an agent deployed under it must be tested against—and the search finds them at a cost that scales with the boundary, not the text.

title: DASH: A da Vinci Adapter for Serial-link and Humanoid Robots as an Accessible Platform for Surgical Robotics Research
summary: Robotic minimally invasive surgery offers well-documented clinical benefits, but the cost and infrastructure requirements of purpose-built platforms limit access in rural and lower-resourced facilities. Recent work has teleoperated general-purpose robots for laparoscopic tasks and in vivo procedures, but relied on handheld instruments coupled through passive linkages rather than native robotic actuation. Instead, we adapt da Vinci Classic and Xi instruments onto general-purpose robots that can integrate in clinical workflows. We present DASH, a da Vinci Adapter for Serial-link and Humanoid platforms, consisting of two types of adapters that require no modification to the instruments themselves. Each adapter is compatible with many robotic platform load capacities, engages the instrument's native latch, and wirelessly identifies inserted tools to load instrument-specific kinematics and coupling matrices. Teleoperated experiments demonstrate the efficacy of DASH and its benefits for enabling research access to surgical robotic platforms.

AI.tldr: DASH adapts da Vinci Classic and Xi instruments onto general-purpose (serial-link and humanoid) robots without modifying the instruments, enabling low-cost teleoperated surgical robotics research.
AI.motivation: Purpose-built surgical robotic platforms are costly and infrastructure-heavy, restricting access in rural and lower-resourced facilities. Prior teleoperation of general-purpose robots for laparoscopic and in vivo tasks relied on handheld instruments coupled via passive linkages rather than native robotic actuation, which limits capability.
AI.method: The authors present DASH (da Vinci Adapter for Serial-link and Humanoid platforms), comprising two adapter types that need no modification to the instruments. Each adapter fits many robotic platform load capacities, engages the instrument's native latch, and wirelessly identifies inserted tools to load instrument-specific kinematics and coupling matrices.
AI.result: Teleoperated experiments demonstrate the efficacy of DASH and its benefits for enabling research access to surgical robotic platforms.
AI.conclusion: DASH provides a practical means to integrate da Vinci instruments into general-purpose robots that can fit clinical workflows, expanding affordable research and potential clinical access to robotic minimally invasive surgery.

title: Not Self-Decidable: LLMs Cannot Draw the Boundary of What an Agent Verifier Can Check
comment: Accepted at the Who Verifies the Agents? Workshop at NeurIPS 2026. Workshop papers are non-archival. 21 pages (9 content pages plus references and appendices)
summary: A verifier for an agent faces rules of two kinds: the ones a fixed check can settle and the ones that require a judge. A team that derives its own checks fixes that split up front. Where the requirements come from outside, as in finance, healthcare and law, the agent enforces rules it did not write, so the split falls to runtime, recurring for every predicate of every rule on every action at a rate no reviewer can audit. Every escalation scheme assumes a model can make that decision itself, that it is self-decidable. Across six corpora, including the EU AI Act, FINRA guidance and a deployed credit agent, we collect roughly 22,000 labels from four models built by three labs. They agree almost perfectly where the answer is obvious and collapse on regulatory text; their errors run in opposite directions, so no model can be trusted as the conservative choice; and on the deployed agent's own rule-set they err together, over-claiming that a fixed check will do, the direction that never gets escalated. We introduce CoVer (corroborate-then-verify), which treats unanimity as a nomination, admitting a predicate only when the check synthesized for it survives intervention, reading fields the agent cannot write and holding under deterministic rewording. That gate rejects most of what corroboration wrongly admits, at a cost in coverage we report rather than tune away. The obvious alternative, agreement with a reference judge, certifies nothing: it climbs from 30% to 77% across calibration bands while the genuinely decidable share does not move, because a judge drawn from the population under indictment ratifies the blind spot it shares. Self-decidability is not a capability to elicit from a model but a boundary the verifier must construct.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that whether a rule predicate can be settled by a fixed check or needs a judge is not self-decidable by any model, and introduces CoVer, a corroborate-then-verify gate that constructs this boundary at runtime.
AI.motivation: In domains like finance, healthcare and law, agents enforce externally imposed rules, so the decidable-vs-judgeable split must be resolved at runtime for every predicate of every rule on every action. Existing escalation schemes assume a model can make that decision itself (self-decidability), an assumption the authors set out to test.
AI.method: Across six corpora (including the EU AI Act, FINRA guidance, and a deployed credit agent) the authors collect ~22,000 labels from four models built by three labs. They compare model corroboration, reference-judge agreement, and their proposed CoVer (corroborate-then-verify), which treats unanimity as a nomination and admits a predicate only when a synthesized check survives intervention, reads fields the agent cannot write, and holds under deterministic rewording.
AI.result: Models agree almost perfectly on obvious cases but collapse on regulatory text; their errors diverge in direction, so none is a conservative fallback. On the deployed agent's own rule-set they err together, over-claiming that fixed checks suffice—the direction that never escalates. CoVer rejects most of what corroboration wrongly admits, at a reported coverage cost. Reference-judge agreement certifies nothing: it rises from 30% to 77% across calibration bands while the genuinely decidable share stays flat, as judges ratify their shared blind spot.
AI.conclusion: Self-decidability is not a capability to be elicited from a model but a boundary the verifier must construct. CoVer operationalizes this construction, trading coverage for correctness rather than tuning the trade-off away.

title: Dynamics-Aware Adaptive Corridors with Feasibility-Perturbed Trust-Region SQP for Certified Nonholonomic Motion Planning
summary: Optimisation-based parking planners usually impose collision constraints only at the time samples, so a vehicle corner can cut an obstacle between samples, and no executable trajectory exists until the solver converges. We present a planner for car-like vehicles with reverse gear in which every iterate of the optimisation phase satisfies the discretised dynamics exactly and keeps the whole vehicle rectangle clear of obstacles between the samples. Each time interval receives one convex corridor that holds all vehicle corners at both ends and is shrunk by a sweep margin bounding how far the corner paths leave their chords. Separating half-planes give the corridors a direction out of obstacles when the initial guess is in collision; later, heading-aligned boxes are grown from the speed, curvature and step of the current iterate and rebuilt after accepted steps. A feasibility-perturbed trust-region sequential quadratic programming method projects each step onto the dynamics by feedback and verifies it exactly; the cost decreases monotonically, and once the corridors stop changing, limit points are Karush-Kuhn-Tucker points of the corridor-constrained problem or violate a constraint qualification. On 820 benchmark cases the planner succeeds in 818 without penetration (797 from the first initial guess), none of the 7103 evaluated optimisation-phase iterates is unusable, and it succeeds in 96.5% of the cases when 99% of the initial guesses intersect an obstacle. Its maneuvers take 0.7% longer in the median than those of a similarly certified exact-collision baseline. The guarantees hold for the planning model, not for a physical vehicle.

AI.tldr: A continuous-collision-safe optimisation-based parking planner guarantees that every iterate satisfies discretised dynamics exactly and keeps the full vehicle rectangle obstacle-free between samples, solving 818/820 benchmarks with none of 7103 iterates unusable.
AI.motivation: Collision constraints in optimisation-based parking planners are usually enforced only at time samples, so a vehicle corner can cut through an obstacle between samples. Moreover, no executable trajectory exists until the solver converges, making intermediate iterates unusable in practice.
AI.method: For car-like vehicles with reverse gear, each time interval is assigned one convex corridor containing all vehicle corners at both endpoints, shrunk by a sweep margin that bounds how far corner paths depart from their chords. Separating half-planes orient corridors out of obstacles when the initial guess is in collision; heading-aligned boxes are grown from the current iterate's speed, curvature and step, and rebuilt after accepted steps. A feasibility-perturbed trust-region SQP method projects each step onto the dynamics via feedback and verifies it exactly.
AI.result: The cost decreases monotonically; once corridors stop changing, limit points are KKT points of the corridor-constrained problem or violate a constraint qualification. On 820 benchmarks it succeeds in 818 without penetration (797 from the first initial guess), none of the 7103 evaluated iterates is unusable, and it succeeds in 96.5% of cases where 99% of initial guesses intersect an obstacle. Maneuvers are 0.7% longer in the median than an exact-collision baseline; guarantees hold for the planning model, not a physical vehicle.
AI.conclusion: Corridor-based continuous collision checking combined with feedback-projected SQP yields a parking planner whose every iterate is dynamically exact and collision-free between samples, with monotone cost decrease and KKT-convergence guarantees under unchanged corridors.

title: Learning to Clarify Underspecified Intents Under Limited Interaction
summary: AI assistants receive requests that leave out information needed for a good outcome, for example about users' preferences or goals. They must then either speculate or ask for more information before proceeding. We reconceptualize this as a value-of-information problem: the assistant should acquire information whose absence causes the greatest avoidable loss in user utility. This is rarely known ex ante; rather, assistants must predict it in order to optimally allocate limited user interactions. We instantiate this problem in image generation and derive a reinforcement learning framework using multi-turn simulated users to maximize utility recovery under uncertainty. In a preregistered study with 456 interactive sessions across 76 human participants, this helped users significantly better match reference images with significantly fewer questions, less total interaction time, and lower cost. This points toward a simple and scalable framework for training language model assistants to better disambiguate user intent by asking more informative questions.

AI.tldr: This paper frames an AI assistant's need to ask clarifying questions as a value-of-information problem: the assistant should seek the information whose absence causes the greatest avoidable loss in user utility, predicting this ex ante to allocate limited interactions optimally.
AI.motivation: AI assistants often receive under-specified requests missing information about users' preferences or goals. They must either speculate or ask for more information. This work reconceptualizes clarification as a value-of-information problem, since the assistant rarely knows ex ante which missing information matters most and must predict it to optimally allocate limited user interactions.
AI.method: The authors instantiate the value-of-information problem in image generation and derive a reinforcement learning framework that uses multi-turn simulated users to maximize utility recovery under uncertainty.
AI.result: In a preregistered study with 456 interactive sessions across 76 human participants, the framework helped users significantly better match reference images with significantly fewer questions, less total interaction time, and lower cost.
AI.conclusion: The work points toward a simple and scalable framework for training language model assistants to better disambiguate user intent by asking more informative questions.

title: What the Guard Misses, the Robot Executes: Implied Harm in VLA Instructions
comment: Under review at the SPAIS 2026 workshop (CoRL 2026)
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) act on instructions without being able to refuse, so screening harmful requests falls to monitors. We test whether these monitors catch ordinary robot tasks requested for harmful reasons, holding the task fixed while varying only how explicitly the intent is stated. $π_{0.5}$ completes the task at every level of explicitness, as often as for harmless controls. Text guards flag nearly every blunt request but few implied ones: up to 95% of implied-harm runs end with the task done and no flag raised, and up to 90% even after recalibrating on robot instructions. Monitoring the model's activations does not close this gap. Linear probes separate harmful from harmless instructions almost perfectly in the base language and vision-language models, but this separation weakens after robot training in two model families, most for implied harm.

AI.tldr: Text-based monitors fail to catch robot instructions whose harmful intent is only implied, even though π₀.₅ always executes them and activation probes degrade after robot training.
AI.motivation: VLAs execute instructions without refusal capability, so safety depends entirely on external monitors. The paper asks whether these monitors detect ordinary robot tasks requested for harmful reasons, isolating intent explicitness while holding the task fixed.
AI.method: The task is held constant while only the explicitness of the harmful intent is varied. The authors evaluate π₀.₅ task completion, text guards on both blunt and implied requests (including recalibration on robot instructions), activation-based monitoring, and linear probes on base language and vision-language models versus after robot training across two model families.
AI.result: π₀.₅ completes the task at every explicitness level as often as for harmless controls. Text guards flag nearly all blunt requests but few implied ones: up to 95% of implied-harm runs finish the task with no flag, and up to 90% even after recalibration. Activation monitoring does not close the gap. Linear probes separate harmful from harmless instructions almost perfectly in base LM/VLM, but this separation weakens after robot training in both families, most severely for implied harm.
AI.conclusion: Monitor-based safety for VLAs is fragile: implied-intent harmful requests evade text guards and activation monitoring, and robot training erodes the representational separation that probes rely on, especially for implied harm.

title: PyINE: A Framework for Scalable Elicitation and Oversight via Code Execution
summary: Reasoning models can remain capable of solving a task while still defaulting to cheaper but misleading shortcuts. This creates a central oversight problem: when a model gives an answer with plausible but incomplete reasoning, can an overseer determine whether that output should be trusted? To study this problem, we introduce PyINE, a framework for scalable elicitation and oversight using instrumented Python programs as a verifiable execution substrate. In PyINE, programs define task environments, execution traces provide authoritative labels for outcomes and intermediate facts, and task variants can be generated mechanically rather than through static human annotation. We instantiate the framework in PyINE-v1, a first release built from nearly one million deterministic execution traces and over 500,000 matched LLM-generated code variants used for counterfactual evaluation. Using standard RL with verifiable rewards on cue-varied tasks, we train a shortcut-following model that improves substantially at predicting execution outcomes while still making systematic errors when misleading human-facing cues conflict with the program's realized behavior. We then evaluate activation probes, trained text classifiers, prompted judges, and a lightweight debate protocol as overseers of this model. We find that performance pooled at the dataset level can hide weak coverage of the failures that matter most: cheap learned overseers often miss rare shortcut-driven errors, while stronger model-based checks are more balanced but substantially costlier and harder to turn into reliable thresholded decisions. PyINE-v1 turns this failure-mode coverage problem into a reusable experimental setting for developing oversight methods that are verifiable, failure-mode-aware, and cost-sensitive.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PyINE, a framework using instrumented Python programs as a verifiable execution substrate for scalable oversight, instantiated as PyINE-v1 with ~1M execution traces and 500K+ LLM code variants. It trains a shortcut-following reasoning model and evaluates several overseer types, finding that dataset-level aggregate performance masks poor coverage of rare shortcut-driven errors.
AI.motivation: Reasoning models can solve tasks while defaulting to cheaper but misleading shortcuts. This creates an oversight problem: given plausible yet incomplete reasoning, can an overseer decide whether an output should be trusted? Existing static human annotation and evaluation setups make it hard to study scalable, verifiable oversight with controlled failure modes.
AI.method: The authors propose PyINE, a framework where instrumented Python programs define task environments, execution traces provide authoritative labels for outcomes and intermediate facts, and task variants are generated mechanically. They build PyINE-v1 from nearly one million deterministic execution traces and over 500,000 matched LLM-generated code variants for counterfactual evaluation. Using standard RL with verifiable rewards on cue-varied tasks, they train a shortcut-following model, then evaluate activation probes, trained text classifiers, prompted judges, and a lightweight debate protocol as overseers.
AI.result: The trained shortcut-following model improves substantially at predicting execution outcomes yet still makes systematic errors when misleading human-facing cues conflict with the program's realized behavior. Evaluating overseers shows that dataset-level pooled performance can hide weak coverage of the most important failures: cheap learned overseers often miss rare shortcut-driven errors, while stronger model-based checks are more balanced but substantially costlier and harder to convert into reliable thresholded decisions.
AI.conclusion: PyINE-v1 reframes oversight evaluation as a failure-mode coverage problem, providing a reusable, verifiable, failure-mode-aware, and cost-sensitive experimental setting for developing oversight methods.

title: Transporting Unsecured Stacked Payloads with a Quadrupedal Robot via Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning
summary: Transporting unsecured payloads with legged robots over uneven terrain requires balancing locomotion performance and payload stability, since aggressive motion can destabilize the payload even when the robot remains stable. We study quadrupedal transportation of unsecured stacked boxes on an edgeless torso-mounted board without dedicated payload sensors or active carrier mechanisms. To address this trade-off, we propose Payload-Adaptive Multi-Objective Reinforcement learning for Transportation (PAMORT). PAMORT trains a multi-objective base policy conditioned on a preference vector that weights locomotion and payload-stability reward groups, then trains a weight adjuster on the frozen policy to adapt this preference online from proprioception. In simulation, PAMORT achieves comparable or better overall transportation success than a corresponding single-objective baseline across different payload configurations, including an unseen three-box stack, despite training only with two boxes. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 demonstrate zero-shot transfer to slopes and steps at or beyond the training difficulty, with mean success rates of 0.850 for PAMORT and 0.675 for the baseline across eight tasks. These results demonstrate robust unsecured-payload transportation with online adaptation of the locomotion--payload trade-off from proprioceptive information.

AI.tldr: PAMORT is a multi-objective RL framework for quadrupedal transport of unsecured stacked boxes, using a preference-conditioned base policy plus a learned weight adjuster for online adaptation from proprioception, achieving robust zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
AI.motivation: Transporting unsecured payloads over uneven terrain requires balancing locomotion performance against payload stability, since aggressive motion can destabilize the payload even when the robot itself stays stable. This trade-off is difficult to manage without dedicated payload sensors or active carrier mechanisms.
AI.method: PAMORT trains a multi-objective base policy conditioned on a preference vector weighting locomotion and payload-stability reward groups, then trains a weight adjuster on the frozen policy to adapt this preference online from proprioception. The setup uses an edgeless torso-mounted board with unsecured stacked boxes on a quadruped.
AI.result: In simulation, PAMORT matches or exceeds a single-objective baseline across payload configurations, including an unseen three-box stack, despite training only with two boxes. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 show zero-shot transfer to slopes and steps at or beyond training difficulty, with mean success rates of 0.850 (PAMORT) versus 0.675 (baseline) across eight tasks.
AI.conclusion: PAMORT enables robust unsecured-payload transportation by adaptively modulating the locomotion–payload trade-off online from proprioceptive information, generalizing to unseen payload configurations and challenging real-world terrain.

title: Toward a Locally Deployable Agentic Co-Scientist: Small-Model Planning for Early-Stage Drug Discovery
comment: 22 pages, 4 figures. Accepted at the AI for Drug Discovery Workshop, NeurIPS 2026
summary: Early-stage computational drug discovery requires coordinating heterogeneous scientific tools across multi-step workflows. We present a lightweight, tool-augmented framework in which a locally deployable compact language model plans calls to 18 modular tools. A Unified Molecular Schema maintains shared molecular records, while a plug-in interface supports tool replacement and extension. We construct 1,263 manually refined query-plan pairs through workflow-graph path coverage and apply LoRA fine-tuning to three compact model families. Under the query-level split, all fine-tuned models generate fully parseable and schema-compliant plans on 47 held-out cross-group queries. Llama 3.2-3B achieves a tool-selection F1 of 0.998, sequence exact match of 0.979, and argument F1 of 0.960. Under the stricter workflow-grouped split, which excludes identical ordered tool sequences across partitions, sequence exact match reaches 0.452 to 0.548, highlighting the remaining difficulty for compact models in generating complete workflow paths unseen during training. These results demonstrate the feasibility of compact, locally deployable planning while identifying compositional generalization as an important direction for further improvement.

AI.tldr: A lightweight framework using a locally deployable compact LLM to plan calls to 18 modular drug-discovery tools, fine-tuned with LoRA on 1,263 query-plan pairs, achieves near-perfect planning on in-distribution queries but reveals compositional generalization limits on unseen workflow paths.
AI.motivation: Early-stage computational drug discovery requires coordinating heterogeneous scientific tools across multi-step workflows, creating a need for planning systems that are both capable and locally deployable.
AI.method: The authors build a tool-augmented framework in which a compact language model plans calls to 18 modular tools. A Unified Molecular Schema maintains shared molecular records, and a plug-in interface enables tool replacement and extension. They construct 1,263 manually refined query-plan pairs via workflow-graph path coverage and apply LoRA fine-tuning to three compact model families, evaluated under query-level and workflow-grouped splits.
AI.result: Under the query-level split, all fine-tuned models produce fully parseable and schema-compliant plans on 47 held-out cross-group queries; Llama 3.2-3B attains tool-selection F1 of 0.998, sequence exact match of 0.979, and argument F1 of 0.960. Under the stricter workflow-grouped split, sequence exact match drops to 0.452–0.548.
AI.conclusion: Compact, locally deployable planning for drug discovery is feasible, but compositional generalization to complete workflow paths unseen during training remains difficult and is flagged as a key direction for future improvement.

title: Dual-Rate Force-Image Control with Model-Based Orientation Limits for Robotic Ultrasound
summary: Robotic ultrasound couples a high-rate contact-force loop with slower, delayed image feedback, so image-guided ultrasound probe rotation can perturb contact force before the resulting image response is observed. We derive a closed-form orientation-rate limit that bounds the modeled rotation-induced estimated-force excursion over a finite horizon while accounting for disturbance rejection by the fast force loop. The limit depends on local contact stiffness, force-loop gains, a conservative rotation-to-force gain bound, the excursion budget, and the prediction horizon. We implement this model in a dual-rate controller with timestamp-based delay reconstruction and joint-torque-based force estimation, and evaluate it on a curved gelatin phantom using paired controller comparisons and component ablations. Relative to unconstrained image guidance, the proposed rate-limited controller reduced first-second root-mean-square (RMS) estimated-force error by 0.40 N while increasing cue-convergence time by 0.94 s. A fixed rate cap near the analytically predicted ceiling produced no resolvable difference in force error and converged 0.32 s faster, indicating that the principal practical value of the model is the rate-design rule rather than online prediction. Delay reconstruction had no resolvable effect at the tested latency. A single-subject popliteal scan demonstrated feasibility, although the image cue was noise-limited on heterogeneous tissue.

AI.tldr: A closed-form orientation-rate limit is derived for robotic ultrasound that bounds rotation-induced contact-force excursion while respecting the fast force loop, then implemented in a dual-rate controller; on a gelatin phantom it cut first-second RMS force error by 0.40 N at the cost of 0.94 s slower cue convergence, showing the main value lies in the rate-design rule rather than online prediction.
AI.motivation: Robotic ultrasound couples a high-rate contact-force loop with slower, delayed image feedback. Image-guided probe rotation can therefore perturb contact force before the resulting image response is observed, creating a need to constrain orientation rate so that force excursions stay bounded.
AI.method: The authors derive a closed-form orientation-rate limit bounding the modeled rotation-induced estimated-force excursion over a finite horizon, accounting for disturbance rejection by the fast force loop. The limit depends on local contact stiffness, force-loop gains, a conservative rotation-to-force gain bound, the excursion budget, and the prediction horizon. It is implemented in a dual-rate controller with timestamp-based delay reconstruction and joint-torque-based force estimation, evaluated on a curved gelatin phantom via paired controller comparisons and component ablations.
AI.result: Versus unconstrained image guidance, the rate-limited controller reduced first-second RMS estimated-force error by 0.40 N while increasing cue-convergence time by 0.94 s. A fixed rate cap near the analytically predicted ceiling showed no resolvable difference in force error and converged 0.32 s faster. Delay reconstruction had no resolvable effect at the tested latency. A single-subject popliteal scan demonstrated feasibility, though the image cue was noise-limited on heterogeneous tissue.
AI.conclusion: The principal practical value of the model is the rate-design rule rather than online prediction; delay reconstruction offered no measurable benefit at the tested latency, and in vivo feasibility was shown but limited by noise on heterogeneous tissue.

title: Formalizing the Moral Evaluation of Speech Acts: Truthfulness, Lies and Ethical Dilemmas
comment: To appear in the Proceedings of the 27th International Conference on Principles and Practice of Multi-Agent Systems (PRIMA 2026). Kumamoto, Japan
summary: In life-or-death situations, a benevolent lie may appear more moral than telling the truth. Yet such lies can backfire, producing unintended and sometimes fatal consequences. This tension, famously disputed by Kant and Constant in 1797, applies not only to lying but to assertive speech acts in general, raising the question of which utterance should be chosen when moral stakes are high. We present a logical framework for the ethical evaluation of speech-act utterances based on agents' beliefs. Implemented in Answer Set Programming (ASP), the framework assesses utterances under deontologism, consequentialism, and principialism, and is illustrated on Sartre's The Wall (1939), a reworking of that controversy in which lying leads alternately to rescue and to death. Our setting is general by design: as two variants show, accommodating a new moral situation amounts to adjusting parameters, not rules.

AI.tldr: A logic-based framework evaluates the morality of assertive speech acts (e.g., lying vs. truth-telling) under deontologism, consequentialism, and principialism, implemented in Answer Set Programming and illustrated via Sartre's The Wall.
AI.motivation: In life-or-death situations, benevolent lies may seem more moral than truth yet can backfire with fatal results. This Kant–Constant controversy (1797) extends beyond lying to assertive speech acts in general, leaving open which utterance should be chosen when moral stakes are high.
AI.method: A logical framework for ethically evaluating speech-act utterances based on agents' beliefs, implemented in Answer Set Programming (ASP), assessing utterances under three moral theories.
AI.result: The framework is illustrated on Sartre's The Wall (1939), where lying alternately leads to rescue or death, and two variants show that accommodating a new moral situation requires only adjusting parameters, not rules.
AI.conclusion: The framework is general by design, offering a parameterizable, belief-based approach to the ethical evaluation of assertive speech acts across moral theories.

title: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Collision-Free Locomotion of an Underactuated Biped
summary: A bipedal robot cannot deviate from its path to avoid an obstacle without disturbing its balance, and this coupling is most severe on underactuated platforms such as the biped considered here, which has four actuated joints per leg and no hip or ankle roll. This paper presents a Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning (HRL) framework in which a High-Level (HL) policy observes the robot pose, 36 raycast proximity measurements, moving-obstacle states, and a receding-horizon local goal, and outputs a body-velocity command $(v_x, v_y, ω_{yaw})$ every ten control steps, while a velocity-conditioned Low-Level (LL) policy tracks each command through PD-controlled joint targets. Both policies are trained jointly with Soft Actor-Critic (SAC). Because the converged gait is task-agnostic, it is frozen and driven by classical planners over the same command interface, yielding three controlled baselines: SAC+A*, SAC+RRT*, and SAC+APF. Across 100 evaluation trials per method in randomized PyBullet environments, the proposed method reaches the goal in 98.0% of static and 88.0% of dynamic trials, against at most 78.0% and 68.0% for the planner hybrids, with path lengths within 4% of the A* reference, and ablations confirm that each observation channel and reward term contributes materially to this performance.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical RL framework with a high-level velocity-command policy and a frozen low-level gait controller achieves 98% static and 88% dynamic goal-reaching for a four-actuator-per-leg biped without hip/ankle roll, far surpassing SAC+A*/RRT*/APF planner hybrids.
AI.motivation: Bipedal robots cannot avoid obstacles without disturbing balance, and this coupling is worst on underactuated platforms such as the considered biped (four actuated joints per leg, no hip or ankle roll). Classical planners driving a fixed gait are therefore insufficient.
AI.method: A Hierarchical RL (HRL) framework is proposed. The High-Level (HL) policy observes robot pose, 36 raycast proximity measurements, moving-obstacle states, and a receding-horizon local goal, and outputs a body-velocity command (v_x, v_y, ω_yaw) every ten control steps. A velocity-conditioned Low-Level (LL) policy tracks each command via PD-controlled joint targets. Both policies are trained jointly with Soft Actor-Critic (SAC).
AI.result: Because the converged gait is task-agnostic, it is frozen and driven by classical planners over the same command interface, yielding three baselines: SAC+A*, SAC+RRT*, and SAC+APF. Over 100 evaluation trials per method in randomized PyBullet environments, the proposed method reaches the goal in 98.0% of static and 88.0% of dynamic trials, versus at most 78.0% and 68.0% for the planner hybrids, with path lengths within 4% of the A* reference.
AI.conclusion: Ablations confirm that each observation channel and each reward term contributes materially to performance, validating the proposed HRL framework and its jointly trained hierarchical policies.

title: Agentic discovery of blood biomarker from distilled private health records
summary: Routine complete blood counts (CBCs) could yield new biomarkers, but the private records needed to evaluate candidates cannot be shared with frontier language model agents that excel at discovery. We distilled the evidence held in the Clalit Health Services panel of over 5.4 million patients into a released scoring tool: for each of 13 immune-mediated diseases, a graph attention network was trained inside the data boundary to predict the case-control AUC of candidate CBC expressions, and only the trained weights were released. The tool grounds an agent's propose-score-refine loop in real-world data without exposing any patient data. In external validation, agent-discovered expressions improved on their literature-seeded starting points by a median of 4.18 AUC percentage points, and across three independent cohorts, reranking the candidates of three frontier research tools improved on their first choices in most comparisons, with gains that varied by cohort. The released scorer supports privacy-preserving biomarker hypothesis generation.

AI.tldr: The authors distilled 5.4M-patient CBC records into a released graph attention scoring tool that lets frontier LLM agents discover immune-disease biomarkers without accessing private data, yielding median AUC gains of 4.18 points over literature baselines.
AI.motivation: Routine CBCs may contain valuable biomarkers, but the private clinical records required to test biomarker candidates cannot be shared with frontier language-model agents, which are otherwise strong at scientific discovery. This creates a tension between the need for real-world data grounding and patient privacy.
AI.method: Evidence from the Clalit Health Services panel of over 5.4 million patients was distilled into a released scoring tool. For each of 13 immune-mediated diseases, a graph attention network was trained within the data boundary to predict the case-control AUC of candidate CBC expressions; only the trained weights were released. This scorer supports an agent's propose-score-refine loop without exposing patient data.
AI.result: In external validation, agent-discovered expressions improved on their literature-seeded starting points by a median of 4.18 AUC percentage points. Across three independent cohorts, reranking candidates from three frontier research tools improved on their first choices in most comparisons, with gains varying by cohort.
AI.conclusion: The released scorer enables privacy-preserving biomarker hypothesis generation, allowing frontier agents to discover and refine CBC-based biomarker candidates grounded in real-world data while keeping patient records private.

title: Mulligan: Performance-Guided Data Collection for Efficient On-Robot Learning
summary: Learning from human demonstrations is a reliable way to teach robots new tasks, but the gains from each additional demonstration shrink as the policy improves. Continued improvement can instead come from supervised deployment, where an operator places the objects and intervenes when the policy fails. We ask how to maximize improvement from a fixed budget of supervised episodes on high-precision manipulation tasks with wide ranges of object placements. We observe that failures can concentrate in a small subset of initial states, so uniform collection spends much of the operator's time on states the policy already handles. Mulligan makes the initial-state distribution a decision, starting each round's episodes at observed failures and untried states. To further improve data efficiency, we augment interactive imitation learning with a value function trained on all data, including failures that imitation discards. Across three real-world tasks evaluated on 2,550 held-out, blinded episodes and two simulated tasks, Mulligan outperforms uniform initial-state sampling at matched collection budgets, and combined with value-based action selection, HiL-IDQL+Mulligan, improves final real-task success by 10-34 percentage points. With operator interventions, the human-robot team completes 98% of collection episodes, remaining productive while the policy learns. Videos, code, and data are available at https://mulligan.page/.

AI.tldr: Mulligan replaces uniform initial-state sampling in supervised robot deployment by making the initial-state distribution a decision: each round's episodes start at observed failures and untried states, and it augments interactive imitation learning with a value function trained on all data (including discarded failures). It beats uniform sampling at matched budgets and, with value-based action selection (HiL-IDQL+Mulligan), raises real-task success by 10–34 points.
AI.motivation: Learning from human demonstrations yields diminishing returns as the policy improves. Supervised deployment (an operator places objects and intervenes on failures) is a scalable alternative, but a fixed budget of supervised episodes must be spent efficiently. Failures concentrate in a small subset of initial states, so uniform initial-state sampling wastes operator time on states the policy already handles.
AI.method: Mulligan treats the initial-state distribution as a decision: each round's episodes start at observed failures and untried states rather than uniform placements. It further augments interactive imitation learning with a value function trained on all collected data, including failures that imitation learning discards. Combined with value-based action selection, this yields HiL-IDQL+Mulligan.
AI.result: Evaluated on three real-world tasks (2,550 held-out, blinded episodes) and two simulated tasks, Mulligan outperforms uniform initial-state sampling at matched collection budgets. HiL-IDQL+Mulligan improves final real-task success by 10–34 percentage points. With operator interventions, the human-robot team completes 98% of collection episodes, remaining productive while the policy learns.
AI.conclusion: Targeting failures and untried states, and exploiting all data via a value function, maximizes policy improvement per supervised episode on high-precision manipulation with wide placement ranges. This makes supervised deployment more data-efficient and keeps the human-robot team productive throughout collection.

title: Dynamic Routing as a New Dimension for Test-time Versatility of LLMs
summary: Beyond scaling their parameters and data, large language models currently gain versatility on new problems along a single axis: the tokens they spend on chain-of-thought (CoT). We investigate whether dynamic routing programs, which execute a subset of the model's layers or iterate some of them, can open a second axis of test-time adaptation, complementary to CoT and free of any gradient update. Prior work showed that such programs exist and bring accuracy and efficiency gains on problems similar to those they were trained on; we ask whether they can also be identified rapidly, from a handful of demonstrations (3 or 10), by a strategy that transfers across models and tasks without training. First, we find that strategies that select programs by the probability they assign to the demonstrations' labels, arbitrated by the model's own confidence, bring consistent gains: on average over the 49 tasks of MMLU and substantially on four of seven models, and most of all on far out-of-distribution tasks such as ARC-AGI, where programs double the accuracy of a 7B model whose CoT fails. Second, on MMLU across the seven post-trained models, routing complements CoT in practice: the two succeed on different queries, and their composition exceeds CoT alone. Despite these gains, our analyses show that confidence-based selection leaves much of the potential untapped, in two places in particular: (1) in surfacing the routing potential that is already present early in pre-training but becomes harder to select after post-training, and (2) in making models robust to the refinements routing introduces, since unsuccessful routes tend to drive the residual stream out of the distribution that the following layers expect. Together, our results point to dynamic routing as a paradigm for extending the plasticity of existing and future LLMs in rapid test-time adaptation.

AI.tldr: Dynamic routing programs (executing subsets of layers or iterating them) can serve as a second axis of test-time adaptation alongside chain-of-thought, offering accuracy and efficiency gains that can be selected from just a few demonstrations without gradients.
AI.motivation: LLMs currently gain versatility on new problems along a single axis: tokens spent on chain-of-thought. The authors investigate whether dynamic routing programs could open a complementary second axis of test-time adaptation, free of gradient updates, and whether such programs can be rapidly identified from a handful of demonstrations by a strategy that transfers across models and tasks without training.
AI.method: The authors study dynamic routing programs that execute a subset of a model's layers or iterate some of them. They evaluate strategies that select programs by the probability they assign to demonstrations' labels, arbitrated by the model's own confidence, using few demonstrations (3 or 10), across 49 MMLU tasks, seven post-trained models, and far out-of-distribution tasks such as ARC-AGI. They further analyze where confidence-based selection leaves potential untapped.
AI.result: Confidence-arbitrated, label-probability-based program selection yields consistent gains: on average over 49 MMLU tasks and substantially on four of seven models, and most notably on far out-of-distribution tasks like ARC-AGI, where programs double the accuracy of a 7B model whose CoT fails. On MMLU, routing complements CoT: the two succeed on different queries, and their composition exceeds CoT alone. Analyses show confidence-based selection leaves potential untapped in two places: (1) routing potential present early in pre-training becomes harder to select after post-training, and (2) unsuccessful routes drive the residual stream out of distribution expected by following layers.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic routing constitutes a promising paradigm for extending the plasticity of existing and future LLMs in rapid test-time adaptation, complementing chain-of-thought, though confidence-based selection captures only part of its potential.

title: From Social Reasoning to Embodied Interaction: An Agentic Framework for Social Robots
summary: Natural face-to-face human--robot interaction requires a robot to understand an evolving social situation, decide when to engage, and express its intent through coordinated physical behavior. Yet existing approaches rarely close this loop: foundation-model agents provide increasingly capable multimodal reasoning and memory but remain largely disembodied, while expressive virtual agents do not face the physical constraints of real robots, and physical social robots typically address social reasoning and embodied expression only partially. We present ARISE, a unified framework that bridges Agentic Reasoning and Interactive Social Embodiment on the Sophia humanoid robot. ARISE integrates multimodal context understanding, long-term memory, and reactive and proactive interaction to determine when and what to communicate, and translates social intent into robot-native gestures coordinated with speech and mechanical facial expressions through streaming execution. Extensive evaluations on Sophia demonstrate strong perceived interaction quality, expressive and well-coordinated embodied behavior, and substantial latency reductions through streaming execution. These results highlight the importance of jointly reasoning about what to communicate, when to engage, and how to physically express social intent for natural interaction with humanoid robots. Project Page: https://robosocial.github.io/

AI.tldr: ARISE is a unified framework for the Sophia humanoid that closes the loop between agentic reasoning and embodied social interaction, jointly deciding what to say, when to engage, and how to express intent physically.
AI.motivation: Natural face-to-face human-robot interaction demands a robot that understands an evolving social situation, decides when to engage, and expresses intent through coordinated physical behavior. Existing work fails to close this loop: foundation-model agents are capable but disembodied, virtual agents ignore physical constraints, and physical social robots handle social reasoning and embodied expression only partially.
AI.method: ARISE bridges Agentic Reasoning and Interactive Social Embodiment on the Sophia humanoid robot. It integrates multimodal context understanding, long-term memory, and reactive plus proactive interaction to determine when and what to communicate, then translates social intent into robot-native gestures coordinated with speech and mechanical facial expressions via streaming execution.
AI.result: Extensive evaluations on Sophia show strong perceived interaction quality, expressive and well-coordinated embodied behavior, and substantial latency reductions achieved through streaming execution.
AI.conclusion: The results underscore the importance of jointly reasoning about what to communicate, when to engage, and how to physically express social intent for natural interaction with humanoid robots.

title: When Is Enough Enough in Self-Evolving LLM Systems?
summary: Self-evolving large language model (LLM) systems repeatedly propose, evaluate, and incorporate updates to prompts, skills, or other persistent artifacts. Despite their growing effectiveness, these systems typically operate under a predetermined iteration or compute budget, without a principled criterion to determine when further evolution is no longer worthwhile. This can lead to two undesirable consequences: unnecessary computation after performance has saturated and the risk of returning late updates that overfit or exploit the evaluation signal. These issues motivate us to study two fundamental questions: when should a self-evolving system stop, and what should it output once it stops? We address the first by formulating an online sequential testing problem and constructing an anytime-valid restart detector using the per-item paired evaluation outcomes already produced by self-evolving LLM systems. We address the second by formulating a change-point estimation problem and using the estimated transition to select an earlier artifact for output. The resulting procedure is plug-and-play and requires no modification of the underlying self-evolving algorithms. Across two self-evolving frameworks, three LLM model families, and five benchmarks, our method substantially reduces computation costs while maintaining comparable unseen-test performance. For example, on SearchQA with SkillOpt and DeepSeek V4 Flash, our method stops at round 4 rather than the full budget of 40, reducing token usage by 91.6% while achieving 82.43% unseen-test accuracy versus 82.00% under the full-budget run.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses when a self-evolving LLM system should stop iterating and what artifact to output upon stopping, via an anytime-valid restart detector and change-point-based artifact selection, cutting compute without hurting test performance.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving LLM systems iteratively update prompts, skills, or other persistent artifacts, but typically run under a fixed iteration/compute budget with no principled stopping criterion. This causes unnecessary computation after saturation and risks returning late, overfit, or evaluation-signal-exploiting updates. Two questions arise: when should such a system stop, and what should it output once it stops?
AI.method: The authors frame stopping as an online sequential testing problem and build an anytime-valid restart detector using the per-item paired evaluation outcomes already produced by self-evolving LLM systems. For output selection, they formulate a change-point estimation problem and use the estimated transition to pick an earlier artifact to return. The procedure is plug-and-play, requiring no modification to underlying self-evolving algorithms.
AI.result: Across two self-evolving frameworks, three LLM model families, and five benchmarks, the method substantially reduces computation while maintaining comparable unseen-test performance. On SearchQA with SkillOpt and DeepSeek V4 Flash, it stops at round 4 instead of the full budget of 40, reducing token usage by 91.6% while achieving 82.43% unseen-test accuracy versus 82.00% at full budget.
AI.conclusion: A principled, plug-and-play stopping and output-selection procedure for self-evolving LLM systems can largely cut computation costs while preserving or matching unseen-test accuracy, avoiding wasted iterations and overfit late updates.

title: A State Based Dispatch Controller for Hospital Delivery Robots with Shared Human and Infrastructure Resources
summary: Robot delivery studies can overstate transport capacity when travel to pickups and human support fall outside the modeled schedule. We formulate a location aware dispatch model that couples robot admission to transporter support and shared elevators, charging, and cleaning. The model replays 33,079 observed hospital requests; missing contents, deadlines, staffing, and completion times remain explicit scenario assumptions. Two full grids compare human dispatch, a resource aware controller, and a proximity and workload benchmark in 30 paired replications per scenario. An exploratory extension tests a simpler deadline admission rule under the same operating model. Pickup travel increases demand on a pooled elevator bank. In one high staffing case, raising assumed elevator capacity from two to four reduces human only lateness from 55.11\% to 3.18\%, exceeding the dispatch differences. Direct policy comparisons and robot coverage distinguish admission selectivity from system service. The analysis explains why a robot can pass a deadline admission test yet delay service through staff handoffs and shared facilities. Its contribution is a reproducible evaluation of coupled dispatch workflows, with a clear separation between admission, completion, and return to availability. The results are conditional comparisons, not estimates of hospital benefit or released clinical capacity.

AI.tldr: A location-aware dispatch model couples robot admission to human transporter support and shared hospital infrastructure, showing that pickup travel and elevator capacity dominate dispatch policy differences.
AI.motivation: Robot delivery studies can overstate transport capacity when travel to pickups and human support fall outside the modeled schedule. The paper aims to provide a reproducible evaluation that exposes these coupled workflows rather than isolated admission tests.
AI.method: Formulates a location-aware dispatch model coupling robot admission to transporter support and shared elevators, charging, and cleaning. It replays 33,079 observed hospital requests with explicit scenario assumptions for missing contents, deadlines, staffing, and completion times. Two full grids compare human dispatch, a resource-aware controller, and a proximity-and-workload benchmark across 30 paired replications per scenario, plus an exploratory extension testing a simpler deadline admission rule.
AI.result: Pickup travel increases demand on a pooled elevator bank. In one high-staffing case, raising assumed elevator capacity from two to four reduced human-only lateness from 55.11% to 3.18%, exceeding the differences attributable to dispatch policy.
AI.conclusion: Direct policy comparisons and robot coverage distinguish admission selectivity from system service. The analysis explains why a robot can pass a deadline admission test yet delay service through staff handoffs and shared facilities. Its contribution is a reproducible evaluation of coupled dispatch workflows, clearly separating admission, completion, and return to availability. Results are conditional comparisons, not estimates of hospital benefit or released clinical capacity.

title: Not All Answers Are Contextually Persuadable: Inference Dynamics in Large Language Models under Contextual Influence
comment: Published in the Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: At the core of modern prompting techniques is contextual sensitivity, the ability of large language models to adapt their predictions based on inference-time context. Despite its central role, inference behavior under strong contextual influence remains poorly understood, particularly at the level of internal inference dynamics. We introduce a theoretical framework for analyzing contextual influence through inference dynamics, enabling quantitative characterization of inference behavior beyond output-level answer changes. Our analysis shows that inference dynamics do not exhibit unbounded drift under repeated contextual assertions. Instead, predictive representations converge to stable, query-dependent regimes that fundamentally constrain whether contextual signals can alter a model's prediction. This leads to a surprising finding: Repeated contextual assertions do not act as accumulating evidence during inference and may therefore fail to alter a model's prediction even under unbounded repetition, while in other cases a prediction change becomes inevitable. We empirically validate our theoretical predictions, demonstrating strong alignment between theory and observed inference behavior. These contributions offer a principled pathway toward characterizing the limits of contextual influence during inference, providing practical implications for model development.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a theoretical framework for understanding how inference-time context shapes LLM predictions by analyzing internal inference dynamics, showing that contextual influence does not accumulate but converges to stable regimes, which constrains whether context can change predictions.
AI.motivation: Modern prompting relies on contextual sensitivity, yet inference behavior under strong contextual influence is poorly understood, especially at the level of internal inference dynamics rather than output-level answer changes.
AI.method: The authors introduce a theoretical framework that quantitatively characterizes contextual influence through inference dynamics, enabling analysis beyond simple output-level answer changes.
AI.result: Inference dynamics do not exhibit unbounded drift under repeated contextual assertions; instead, predictive representations converge to stable, query-dependent regimes. Repeated contextual assertions do not act as accumulating evidence and may fail to alter predictions even under unbounded repetition, while in other cases prediction change becomes inevitable. Empirical validation shows strong alignment between theory and observed behavior.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a principled pathway toward characterizing the limits of contextual influence during inference, with practical implications for model development.

title: How (and How Not) to Use Data Augmentation in VLA Post-Training
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 workshop RoboPAD. Code and videos at https://bramgrooten.nl/vla-augm/
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models currently demonstrate strong performance in a wide range of real-world robotics tasks.
