AI.method: CI-JEPA learns to predict ΔZ = Z_CF − Z between an original image and a modified counterpart, and assesses robustness via selective sensitivity (stronger responses to semantic changes than to nuisance changes). Experiments on Flowers102 use flower-center occlusion as a semantic intervention, with background blur and tint as nuisance interventions, evaluated through frozen-encoder linear probing.
AI.result: Frozen-encoder linear probing reaches a best validation accuracy of 78.14% versus 77.55% for pretrained ViT-B/16 and I-JEPA (a 0.59 pp gain). Mean L2 representation changes are 4.42 (center occlusion), 3.48 (background tint), and 2.83 (background blur), consistent with relative semantic selectivity rather than complete nuisance invariance.
AI.conclusion: The accuracy gain is complementary and does not establish improved robustness over baselines; the framework studies intervention-induced changes in JEPA representations but does not establish causal feature discovery or robustness to all visual changes.

title: Dual Variational Autoencoders for Efficient Sim-to-Real Transfer in Low-Cost Robotic Navigation
comment: 30 pages, 13 figures. Published in Image and Vision Computing under a CC BY 4.0 license
summary: Vision-based autonomous navigation for low-cost robots remains a fundamental challenge, primarily due to the significant gap between simulated training environments and real-world operational conditions. Direct policy transfer from simulation is often ineffective, while training exclusively on real data is impractical. We propose a hybrid transfer learning framework that effectively bridges the sim-to-real gap by combining domain randomization with feature-level domain adaptation. Our method employs a dual convolutional variational autoencoder architecture with a shared decoder, trained on an extensive set of 45225 simulated images and a minimal set of only 4556 real-world samples. This architecture learns a compact, common latent representation space that aligns the distributions of both domains. The adaptation process is further enhanced by two complementary data augmentation techniques designed to expand the limited real-world data. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that our method achieves an average success rate of almost 91% on image classification tasks for real-world indoor navigation, significantly outperforming both simulation-only and real-world-only training. We validate these findings through a direct, real-world deployment, where the proposed policy successfully guides a low-cost robot in a reactive exploration task. Furthermore, we validate the model's efficiency through a rigorous computational estimation, confirming its suitability for resource-constrained embedded platforms such as the Raspberry Pi 4 and NVIDIA Jetson Nano. This work presents a practical solution for developing effective and efficient navigation policies for low-cost robotic systems.

AI.tldr: A hybrid transfer learning framework combining domain randomization and feature-level domain adaptation closes the sim-to-real gap for low-cost robot navigation, achieving ~91% success on real-world indoor image classification.
AI.motivation: Vision-based autonomous navigation for low-cost robots is hindered by the sim-to-real gap: simulation-only policy transfer is ineffective, while real-data-only training is impractical. A practical method is needed to bridge the two domains under limited real-world data and constrained hardware.
AI.method: The authors propose a hybrid transfer learning framework that combines domain randomization with feature-level domain adaptation. It uses a dual convolutional variational autoencoder (VAE) architecture with a shared decoder, trained on 45225 simulated images and only 4556 real-world samples, to learn a compact shared latent space aligning both domain distributions. Two complementary data augmentation techniques expand the limited real-world data.
AI.result: The method achieves an average success rate of nearly 91% on real-world indoor navigation image classification, significantly outperforming simulation-only and real-world-only training. Real-world deployment successfully guided a low-cost robot in a reactive exploration task, and computational estimation confirmed suitability for embedded platforms such as Raspberry Pi 4 and NVIDIA Jetson Nano.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hybrid transfer learning framework offers a practical, efficient solution for developing effective navigation policies for low-cost, resource-constrained robotic systems.

title: Why, Where, How: Taxonomy-guided Error Grounding for Code Repair in NL2SQL
summary: SQL queries that large language models write from natural language questions can execute successfully yet produce incorrect results, so execution alone does not reveal what to fix. An error taxonomy says why the query is wrong, but not where to look or how to change it. Existing methods can guide SQL correction through feedback, error reports, or generated plans alongside an unmasked query. We introduce TEG(Taxonomy-guided Error Grounding), which turns a supplied diagnosis into a structured correction input for natural language-to-SQL (NL2SQL) correction. Type-specific rules map each error type to construct classes to reconsider and an edit operation to request. TEG masks the selected constructs in the query when applicable and states that operation in an edit instruction. TEG generates candidate corrections from this input, uses execution feedback to guide candidate selection, and repeats the process one annotation at a time for queries with several errors. On NL2SQL-BUGs, TEG reaches 47.3 single-error execution accuracy and 37.0 overall with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Across the model sizes and thinking modes evaluated in the main comparison, TEG outperforms all evaluated baselines on single-error queries, even when the baselines receive the same error-type annotations. With predicted types, TEG stays above direct LLM correction and ErrorLLM on single-error queries.

AI.tldr: TEG (Taxonomy-guided Error Grounding) converts a supplied SQL error diagnosis into a structured correction input by mapping each error type to construct classes and an edit operation, masking the selected query constructs and issuing an edit instruction, then iteratively generating and selecting candidate corrections via execution feedback.
AI.motivation: LLM-written SQL queries can execute successfully yet return incorrect results, so execution alone does not indicate what to fix. An error taxonomy explains why a query is wrong but not where to look or how to change it, and prior correction methods (feedback, error reports, generated plans with an unmasked query) provide weak grounding for targeted correction.
AI.method: Type-specific rules map each error type to construct classes to reconsider and an edit operation to request. TEG masks the selected constructs in the query when applicable and states the operation in an edit instruction. It generates candidate corrections from this input, uses execution feedback to guide candidate selection, and repeats one annotation at a time for queries with multiple errors.
AI.result: On NL2SQL-BUGs, TEG achieves 47.3 single-error execution accuracy and 37.0 overall with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Across evaluated model sizes and thinking modes, TEG outperforms all baselines on single-error queries, even when baselines receive the same error-type annotations. With predicted types, TEG remains above direct LLM correction and ErrorLLM on single-error queries.
AI.conclusion: Grounding an error diagnosis into construct-level masking plus a concrete edit operation provides more effective NL2SQL correction than taxonomy labels, feedback, or plans alone, with gains robust to annotation source and model configuration.

title: DexForge: High-Fidelity Physics-Informed Dexterous Retargeting
summary: Human demonstrations offer rich examples of precise dexterous manipulation and a promising source of robot training data. However, high-fidelity reproduction of demonstrated motions and hand-object interactions across robot embodiments remains challenging under physical constraints. We present DexForge, a differentiable physics-grounded framework for converting human video demonstrations into high-fidelity robot trajectories. We reconstruct spherical-Gaussian object models and hand-object motion from visual observations, then build a differentiable simulator combining efficient Gaussian collision detection with existing differentiable dynamics. Based on this simulator, DexForge combines contact-aware kinematic retargeting with force-aware dynamics retargeting: robot-adapted stable contacts guide kinematic reference construction and subsequent gradient-based control refinement for precise physical motion reproduction. Experiments on 130 DexYCB and HOT3D demonstrations across seven dexterous hands show success-rate gains of approximately 35-53 percentage points over the baseline, with object position and orientation tracking errors on successful trajectories reduced by approximately 34-67% and 71-78%, respectively. Further experiments demonstrate open-loop transfer to MuJoCo and real-robot execution. Our project page is available at https://wmz1226.github.io/DexForge/

AI.tldr: DexForge is a differentiable, physics-grounded framework that converts human video demonstrations into high-fidelity dexterous robot trajectories via contact-aware kinematic retargeting and force-aware dynamics retargeting.
AI.motivation: Human demonstrations provide rich examples of precise dexterous manipulation and a promising source of robot training data, but reproducing demonstrated motions and hand-object interactions across different robot embodiments with high fidelity under physical constraints remains challenging.
AI.method: The framework reconstructs spherical-Gaussian object models and hand-object motion from visual observations, then builds a differentiable simulator combining efficient Gaussian collision detection with differentiable dynamics. It performs contact-aware kinematic retargeting, where robot-adapted stable contacts guide kinematic reference construction, followed by force-aware dynamics retargeting using gradient-based control refinement for precise physical motion reproduction.
AI.result: On 130 DexYCB and HOT3D demonstrations across seven dexterous hands, DexForge achieves success-rate gains of roughly 35-53 percentage points over the baseline, and reduces object position and orientation tracking errors on successful trajectories by about 34-67% and 71-78%, respectively. Additional experiments show open-loop transfer to MuJoCo and real-robot execution.
AI.conclusion: DexForge enables high-fidelity, physics-consistent reproduction of human dexterous manipulation on robot embodiments, improving success rates and trajectory tracking accuracy while transferring to simulation and real hardware.

title: SharpDraft: Accelerating Long-Context Speculative Decoding with Cardinality-Aware Query Scaling
summary: Long-form reasoning makes inference expensive, and speculative decoding mitigates this cost by verifying multiple draft tokens in parallel. Its speedup, however, can fade as context grows and draft acceptance declines. We focus on attention-mass dilution: as softmax normalizes over more visible Keys, the mass concentrated on the highest-scoring Keys can decrease. We introduce SharpDraft, a training-free method that counteracts this effect through cardinality-aware Query scaling, without the computational overhead of online adaptation. Under explicit assumptions, we derive an exact top-$k$ mass correction and deploy a closed-form fixed-slope approximation. Across AIME-26, GPQA-Diamond, and LongGenBench Diary, SharpDraft achieves $2.59$-$3.19\times$ geometric-mean end-to-end speedups over target-only autoregressive decoding when applied to DFlash, PARD, and EAGLE 3.1. With DFlash, it improves decoding speed and outperforms full-parameter and LoRA-based online adaptation in end-to-end speedup, while matching the unmodified drafter's reported peak allocated GPU memory.

AI.tldr: SharpDraft is a training-free method that counteracts attention-mass dilution in speculative decoding via cardinality-aware Query scaling, achieving 2.59-3.19x end-to-end speedups across benchmarks and drafters.
AI.motivation: Speculative decoding accelerates long-form reasoning by verifying multiple draft tokens in parallel, but its speedup fades as context grows and draft acceptance declines. The paper identifies a root cause: attention-mass dilution, where softmax normalization over an increasing number of visible Keys reduces the mass concentrated on the highest-scoring Keys, degrading draft quality.
AI.method: SharpDraft is a training-free method that counteracts attention-mass dilution through cardinality-aware Query scaling without online adaptation overhead. Under explicit assumptions, it derives an exact top-k mass correction and deploys a closed-form fixed-slope approximation. It is applied to existing drafters (DFlash, PARD, EAGLE 3.1).
AI.result: Across AIME-26, GPQA-Diamond, and LongGenBench Diary, SharpDraft achieves 2.59-3.19x geometric-mean end-to-end speedups over target-only autoregressive decoding. With DFlash, it improves decoding speed, outperforms full-parameter and LoRA-based online adaptation in end-to-end speedup, and matches the unmodified drafter's reported peak allocated GPU memory.
AI.conclusion: SharpDraft addresses attention-mass dilution in speculative decoding through a simple, training-free Query-scaling correction, delivering substantial speedups and outperforming more expensive online adaptation methods at no additional memory cost.

title: Towards Robust Prehensile Manipulation in Open-Ended Environments
comment: 3 pages, 1 figure. Accepted at the 7th International Workshop on Intrinsically Motivated Open-ended Learning (IMOL 2025)
summary: We propose to use Quality-Diversity (QD) algorithms to solve robotic prehensile manipulation tasks in open-ended environments. Our approach enables the efficient discovery of a wide range robust grasp configurations, which serve as reliable starting points for generating diverse prehensile manipulation trajectories on articulated objects. The resulting diversity in manipulation behaviors enhances generalization and adaptability, enabling effective deployment continuously evolving open-world settings.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using Quality-Diversity (QD) algorithms for robotic prehensile manipulation in open-ended environments, efficiently discovering diverse and robust grasp configurations that seed varied manipulation trajectories on articulated objects.
AI.motivation: Robotic prehensile manipulation in open-ended environments requires both robustness and adaptability. Traditional optimization tends to converge on a single solution, failing to provide the diversity needed for generalization across continuously evolving settings.
AI.method: The authors apply QD algorithms to search the grasp configuration space, explicitly optimizing for both quality (robustness) and diversity of grasps. These robust grasp configurations are then used as reliable starting points to generate a diverse set of prehensile manipulation trajectories on articulated objects.
AI.result: The approach efficiently discovers a wide range of robust grasp configurations and yields diverse manipulation trajectories, increasing behavioral diversity across the task.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging QD for prehensile manipulation produces diverse, robust behaviors whose diversity enhances generalization and adaptability, supporting effective deployment in continuously evolving open-world settings.

title: LexiHorizon: Stabilizing Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Deep Search
summary: Deep search agents tackle complex knowledge tasks through iterative retrieval, multi-hop reasoning, and evidence synthesis across multiple sources. Existing approaches typically assume relatively stable retrieval systems and operate over short-horizon tool interaction. However, when retrieval is sensitive to query formulation, even a semantically appropriate query may fail to surface critical evidence because of mismatched entity names, aliases, or keyword combinations. Recovering from such failures requires repeated query reformulation and longer interaction trajectories. This setting poses a distinct training challenge, as the policy must sustain long-horizon query exploration while managing an expanding volume of retrieved content. We propose LexiHorizon, a framework for training search agents over long horizons that expands the trajectory context budget, manages accumulated retrieval content using a window over recent tool observations while preserving the reasoning history, and introduces an outcome-gated search-effort reward that provides a bounded bonus for tool invocations to trajectories with nonzero answer reward. Experiments on XBench, WebWalkerQA, and BrowseComp-ZH show that the resulting 9B model consistently outperforms both its base model and MiroThinker-1.7-mini, with maximum absolute gains of 8.7 and 23.8 percentage points, respectively. These results suggest that combining an extended context budget with reasoning-preserving context management benefits long-horizon deep search agents.

AI.tldr: LexiHorizon trains deep search agents for long-horizon retrieval by extending the trajectory context budget, managing retrieved content with a sliding window while preserving reasoning history, and adding an outcome-gated search-effort reward. A 9B model outperforms its base and MiroThinker-1.7-mini on three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing deep search agents assume stable retrieval systems and short-horizon tool interaction. When retrieval is sensitive to query formulation, semantically appropriate queries can fail to surface critical evidence due to mismatched entity names, aliases, or keyword combinations. Recovering requires repeated query reformulation and longer interaction trajectories, creating a training challenge: sustaining long-horizon query exploration while managing expanding retrieved content.
AI.method: LexiHorizon expands the trajectory context budget; manages accumulated retrieval content via a window over recent tool observations while preserving reasoning history; and introduces an outcome-gated search-effort reward giving a bounded bonus for tool invocations only to trajectories with nonzero answer reward.
AI.result: On XBench, WebWalkerQA, and BrowseComp-ZH, the resulting 9B model consistently outperforms both its base model and MiroThinker-1.7-mini, with maximum absolute gains of 8.7 and 23.8 percentage points respectively.
AI.conclusion: Combining an extended context budget with reasoning-preserving context management benefits long-horizon deep search agents.

title: Visual Swarm Navigation via Deep Reinforcement Learning and Evolutionary Hybrid Design
comment: 46 pages, 21 figures. Published in Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence under a CC BY 4.0 license
summary: Swarm robotics presents a robust and cost-effective paradigm for advanced automation in complex, dynamic environments, such as those encountered in search and rescue or environmental monitoring. A fundamental challenge for this field is the data-driven design of decentralized controllers capable of generating emergent collective behaviors. This paper proposes a novel, AI-driven hybrid methodology for the automatic synthesis of swarm robotic controllers for autonomous visual navigation. This approach synergistically combines multi-agent reinforcement learning with neuro-evolutionary strategies, specifically leveraging implementations of the cross-entropy method and the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy to optimize a pre-trained individual navigation policy. The underlying deep architecture is engineered for low-cost, resource-constrained platforms, utilizing a compact neural network that relies exclusively on monocular camera imagery. This vision-based design emphasizes computational and energy efficiency, a critical requirement for practical swarm deployments. Experiments, performed in a high-fidelity physics simulator, demonstrate that the resulting controllers enable robust and scalable collective exploration of diverse indoor environments. The controller trained using our cross-entropy method achieves superior exploration coverage, visiting 36.20% more regions compared to the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy. Critically, our best vision-based policy achieves exploration performance statistically comparable to traditional methods relying on more expensive distance sensors, while delivering a significant 31.40% average reduction in energy consumption. These findings validate an effective and economically viable autonomous control system, establishing a path for deploying highly efficient collective intelligence in real-world engineering applications.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a hybrid AI-driven method combining multi-agent reinforcement learning with neuro-evolutionary strategies (CEM and CMA-ES) to synthesize decentralized swarm robotic controllers for autonomous visual navigation, achieving robust, scalable, and energy-efficient collective exploration.
AI.motivation: Swarm robotics offers a robust and cost-effective paradigm for automation in complex, dynamic environments like search and rescue or environmental monitoring. A fundamental challenge is the data-driven design of decentralized controllers that can generate emergent collective behaviors.
AI.method: A hybrid methodology synergistically combines multi-agent reinforcement learning with neuro-evolutionary strategies, specifically using the cross-entropy method (CEM) and the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES) to optimize a pre-trained individual navigation policy. The deep architecture is a compact neural network relying exclusively on monocular camera imagery, engineered for low-cost, resource-constrained platforms emphasizing computational and energy efficiency.
AI.result: Experiments in a high-fidelity physics simulator show the controllers enable robust and scalable collective exploration of diverse indoor environments. The CEM-trained controller achieved 36.20% higher exploration coverage than CMA-ES. The best vision-based policy achieved exploration performance statistically comparable to traditional methods using more expensive distance sensors, while reducing energy consumption by an average of 31.40%.
AI.conclusion: The findings validate an effective and economically viable autonomous control system, establishing a path for deploying highly efficient collective intelligence in real-world engineering applications.

title: Memory Canonicalization: A Framework and Benchmark for Cross-Model Drift in Persistent LLM Memory
summary: Persistent memory for Large Language Models (LLMs) has matured rapidly: systems such as MemGPT/Letta, Mem0, and Zep now provide agents with tiered, temporally-aware, model-agnostic external storage, while the Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes access to memory servers. A less addressed problem is that an identical stored memory object, retrieved by two different LLMs under otherwise identical conditions, may not be interpreted the same way, factually or emotionally. This paper proposes memory canonicalization: a write-time pipeline that detects ambiguity, conditional structure, and emotional loading in a raw memory object and rewrites it into an explicit, structurally disambiguated canonical form, with emotional valence represented as a separate field rather than inferred from tone. We formalize the pipeline, define a companion Cross-Model Semantic Drift / Emotional Consistency Score benchmark (CMSC-E), and report results from a three-arm pilot using 176 synthetic memory objects and three downstream model families. We find an uncorrected improvement in cross-model emotional consistency for fully canonicalized memory relative to raw memory (+0.050, 95% bootstrap CI [0.013, 0.086], paired t-test p = 0.010), but this result does not survive Bonferroni, Holm, or Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the six comparisons tested. None of the factual-drift (CMSD) comparisons reach significance at any correction level. We report these results as exploratory rather than confirmatory and outline needed follow-up work, including larger samples, independent judge models, human-validated rendering, and preregistration.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes memory canonicalization, a write-time pipeline that rewrites raw memory objects into structurally disambiguated canonical forms with emotional valence stored as a separate field, and introduces a cross-model semantic drift/emotional consistency benchmark (CMSC-E). A 176-object, three-arm pilot found a raw improvement in cross-model emotional consistency (+0.050, 95% CI [0.013, 0.086], p = 0.010) that did not survive multiple-comparison correction, with no significant factual-drift effects.
AI.motivation: LLM persistent memory systems (MemGPT/Letta, Mem0, Zep) and the Model Context Protocol have standardized tiered, model-agnostic external memory access, but a gap remains: the same stored memory object may be interpreted differently—factually or emotionally—by different LLMs under identical retrieval conditions. Existing memory infrastructure addresses storage and access, not cross-model interpretability of the memory content itself.
AI.method: A write-time canonicalization pipeline that detects ambiguity, conditional structure, and emotional loading in a raw memory object and rewrites it into an explicit, structurally disambiguated canonical form, with emotional valence represented as a separate field rather than inferred from tone. The work formalizes the pipeline and defines a companion Cross-Model Semantic Drift / Emotional Consistency Score benchmark (CMSC-E). A three-arm pilot was run on 176 synthetic memory objects across three downstream model families.
AI.result: Fully canonicalized memory showed an uncorrected improvement in cross-model emotional consistency over raw memory (+0.050, 95% bootstrap CI [0.013, 0.086], paired t-test p = 0.010). However, this effect did not survive Bonferroni, Holm, or Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the six comparisons tested. No factual-drift (CMSD) comparison reached significance at any correction level.
AI.conclusion: The authors present these findings as exploratory rather than confirmatory. They outline needed follow-up work: larger samples, independent judge models, human-validated rendering, and preregistration.

title: A Taxonomy on Collective Awareness
summary: As robotic teams tackle increasingly complex tasks in dynamic and unstructured environments, effective coordination requires agents to maintain accurate, aligned representations of their environment, teammates, and mission state. We argue that Mutual Awareness, Shared Situational Awareness, and Team Situational Awareness --- three concepts widely invoked in the multi-robot systems literature --- are not interchangeable: they form a containment hierarchy in which each type subsumes the previous in scope, and span a distribution spectrum from fully individualized understanding (MA) to fully uniform understanding (SSA), with TSA occupying a mixed position. We establish this through a two-dimensional taxonomy organized along the object of awareness and awareness distribution axes. Treating these terms as synonyms obscures the precise coordination requirements each imposes on a robotic system. A Search and Rescue case study with heterogeneous aerial and ground robots grounds each taxonomy position in concrete coordination requirements. These findings provide a conceptual foundation for principled specification, design, and comparison of collective awareness in multi-robot systems.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that Mutual Awareness, Shared Situational Awareness, and Team Situational Awareness in multi-robot systems are distinct concepts forming a containment hierarchy and spanning a distribution spectrum, organized via a two-dimensional taxonomy (object of awareness and distribution), illustrated with a Search and Rescue case study.
AI.motivation: Terms like Mutual Awareness, Shared Situational Awareness, and Team Situational Awareness are often used interchangeably in the multi-robot systems literature, obscuring the precise coordination requirements each imposes on robotic systems operating in dynamic, unstructured environments.
AI.method: The authors propose a two-dimensional taxonomy organized along two axes: the object of awareness and the awareness distribution. They position MA, SSA, and TSA within a containment hierarchy and along a distribution spectrum from fully individualized (MA) to fully uniform (SSA), with TSA in a mixed position, grounding each taxonomy position using a Search and Rescue case study with heterogeneous aerial and ground robots.
AI.result: MA, SSA, and TSA form a containment hierarchy where each type subsumes the previous in scope, and span a distribution spectrum. The case study grounds each taxonomy position in concrete coordination requirements.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide a conceptual foundation for principled specification, design, and comparison of collective awareness in multi-robot systems, clarifying the distinct coordination requirements of each awareness type.

title: AutoSciBench: Autonomous Benchmark Generation for Evaluating Scientific Agents
summary: As agents rapidly evolve, existing benchmarks can become saturated, limiting their ability to distinguish capabilities and reveal remaining failure modes. Particularly in scientific domains, constructing and updating benchmarks requires substantial time, labor, and domain expertise, making it difficult to keep evaluation aligned with advances in agent capabilities. We address this challenge by investigating whether scientific-agent benchmarks can be automatically generated and iteratively adapted as agent capabilities evolve. We introduce AutoSciBench, a framework that represents each task as a high-level concept specifying the scientific domain, data modality, and required reasoning approach, together with a low-level recipe specifying how the question, environment, and ground-truth answer are constructed and verified. Agents attempt to solve each task, producing solver trajectories and corresponding judge feedback which AutoSciBench uses to revise the recipe or concept, closing observed shortcuts and shifting tasks toward raw-data re-examination, interpretation of intermediate results, and evidence integration. Experience distilled from completed refinement trajectories further guides new concept generation, allowing lessons from earlier task refinement to inform subsequent benchmark construction. Starting from existing benchmarks, we evaluate AutoSciBench across computational biology, materials science, and clinical imaging. Generated benchmarks reduce average solver accuracy by 22.4 and 25.5 percentage points relative to the human-curated benchmarks in computational biology and materials science, respectively, while generated tasks receive higher average quality ratings across all three domains, suggesting that scientific-agent evaluation can adapt as agent capabilities advance.

AI.tldr: AutoSciBench is a framework for automatically generating and iteratively adapting scientific-agent benchmarks, where tasks are represented by a high-level concept and a low-level recipe that are revised based on solver trajectories and judge feedback. Applied to computational biology, materials science, and clinical imaging, it reduces average solver accuracy by 22.4 and 25.5 percentage points versus human-curated benchmarks while receiving higher quality ratings.
AI.motivation: Existing agent benchmarks risk saturation, limiting their ability to discriminate capabilities and expose failure modes. In scientific domains, benchmark construction and updating require substantial time, labor, and domain expertise, making it hard to keep evaluation aligned with rapid advances in agent capabilities.
AI.method: AutoSciBench represents each task as a high-level concept (scientific domain, data modality, required reasoning approach) plus a low-level recipe (how the question, environment, and ground-truth answer are constructed and verified). Agents solve tasks, producing solver trajectories and judge feedback, which the framework uses to revise the recipe or concept—closing observed shortcuts and shifting tasks toward raw-data re-examination, intermediate-result interpretation, and evidence integration. Experience distilled from completed refinement trajectories guides new concept generation, transferring lessons from earlier refinement to subsequent benchmark construction.
AI.result: Evaluated across computational biology, materials science, and clinical imaging starting from existing benchmarks. Generated benchmarks reduce average solver accuracy by 22.4 and 25.5 percentage points relative to human-curated benchmarks in computational biology and materials science, respectively, and generated tasks receive higher average quality ratings across all three domains.
AI.conclusion: Scientific-agent benchmarks can be automatically generated and iteratively adapted as agent capabilities evolve, suggesting that scientific-agent evaluation can keep pace with advancing agent capabilities.

title: Odyssey: A Closed-Loop Benchmark for Long-Horizon Real-World Driving with Explicit Navigation Routes
summary: Closed-loop evaluation of end-to-end driving requires continuous rollouts that reveal how earlier decisions affect subsequent driving. However, existing benchmarks evaluate only short segments and fail to capture later consequences. Ambiguous directional commands also obscure the intended navigation objective. We introduce Odyssey, a closed-loop benchmark for long-horizon driving comprising 100 scenarios, each reconstructed from a 100-second nuPlan driving log to preserve the context of navigation maneuvers and traffic interactions. To provide a consistent navigation objective, Odyssey replaces directional commands with explicit standard-definition (SD) map routes that specify which roads to follow, while sensor-based planning determines local driving actions. Throughout these rollouts, diffusion-based refinement of 3DGS-rendered images reduces rendering artifacts along the ego trajectory. To assess how effectively planners follow these routes and prepare for upcoming maneuvers, we introduce SD Route Compliance and Pre-Lane Change Score. These assessments are complemented by RouteDS, which extends the Driving Score with penalties for SD-route deviations and failed lane preparation. We adapt state-of-the-art planners, including vision-language-action (VLA) models, and evaluate their navigation performance using these metrics. Odyssey highlights open questions in route representation and integration for E2E driving. Benchmark code and adapted baselines will be released publicly.

AI.tldr: Odyssey is a closed-loop benchmark for long-horizon end-to-end driving: 100 scenarios reconstructed from 100-second nuPlan logs, using explicit SD map routes instead of directional commands, with new route-compliance metrics (SD Route Compliance, Pre-Lane Change Score, RouteDS) and adapted SOTA/VLA baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing closed-loop benchmarks evaluate only short segments, so they fail to reveal how earlier decisions affect later driving. Ambiguous directional commands further obscure the intended navigation objective, making it hard to assess true route-following and maneuver preparation.
AI.method: Build 100 scenarios, each reconstructed from a 100-second nuPlan driving log to preserve navigation and traffic-interaction context. Replace directional commands with explicit standard-definition (SD) map routes that specify which roads to follow, while sensor-based planning handles local actions. Reduce rendering artifacts along the ego trajectory via diffusion-based refinement of 3DGS-rendered images. Introduce SD Route Compliance and Pre-Lane Change Score, plus RouteDS (extends Driving Score with penalties for SD-route deviations and failed lane preparation). Adapt SOTA planners including VLA models and evaluate them with these metrics.
AI.result: Odyssey enables long-horizon closed-loop rollouts that expose later consequences of earlier decisions, provides a consistent navigation objective, and yields route-following/maneuver-preparation assessments via the new metrics and RouteDS. It highlights open questions in route representation and integration for E2E driving.
AI.conclusion: Odyssey exposes shortcomings of short-segment benchmarks and ambiguous commands, offering a long-horizon closed-loop benchmark with explicit SD routes and route-centric metrics. Benchmark code and adapted baselines will be released publicly.

title: R1A-PC: Physics-Guided Electromagnetic Inversion of Three-Dimensional Human Point Clouds in Complex Static Environments
summary: Recovering three-dimensional human geometry from electromagnetic measure?ments in a complex static environment is difficult because strong multipath responses from walls, floors, and other objects obscure the weak target per?turbation. We propose R1A-PC, a physics-guided method that reconstructs a 2048-point human cloud from paired complex fields measured with and without the target. Complex background subtraction emphasizes target-induced ampli?tude and phase changes, while the background field remains available as an environmental condition. A frequency-balanced discrete Born adjoint produces a three-dimensional spatial knowledge map. At each of two bounded deformation stages, the decoder combines complex measurement features, background fea?tures, and multiscale physical features queried at the current point coordinates; the second stage queries again after the first coordinate update. We analyze the residual of paired subtraction, the weighted normal-operator structure of the raw adjoint, and the feasible set of the predicted cloud. In a held-out background generated by full-wave simulation under a fixed acquisition geometry, R1A-PC obtains a squared Chamfer distance of 0.001434 m2 and an F-score of 0.963080 at 0.05 m. Compared with TopNet, the Chamfer distance decreases by 70.28%. Removing physical guidance or background subtraction increases the Chamfer distance by 242.06% or 241.18%, respectively. Experiments across background layouts and poses support the complementary roles of paired subtraction and position-dependent adjoint features.

AI.tldr: R1A-PC reconstructs a 2048-point human point cloud from paired complex electromagnetic fields (with/without target) in a static cluttered environment, using physics-guided background subtraction and a frequency-balanced discrete Born adjoint in a two-stage deformation decoder.
AI.motivation: Recovering 3D human geometry from electromagnetic measurements in complex static environments is hard because strong multipath responses from walls, floors, and other objects mask the weak target perturbation.
AI.method: Physics-guided pipeline: paired complex-field measurement with and without the target, complex background subtraction to emphasize target-induced amplitude/phase changes while retaining the background field as an environmental condition; a frequency-balanced discrete Born adjoint generates a 3D spatial knowledge map; a two-stage bounded deformation decoder fuses complex measurement features, background features, and multiscale physical features queried at current point coordinates, with re-query after the first coordinate update. Includes analysis of the paired-subtraction residual, the weighted normal-operator structure of the raw adjoint, and the feasible set of the predicted cloud.
AI.result: On a held-out full-wave-simulated background under fixed acquisition geometry: squared Chamfer distance 0.001434 m², F-score 0.963080 at 0.05 m; 70.28% lower Chamfer distance than TopNet. Ablations: removing physical guidance or background subtraction raises Chamfer distance by 242.06% or 241.18%. Experiments across background layouts and poses confirm complementary roles of paired subtraction and position-dependent adjoint features.
AI.conclusion: Paired-field subtraction and position-dependent Born-adjoint physical guidance are both essential and complementary for precise 3D human reconstruction in complex static electromagnetic environments.

title: Traversability-Aware Cooperative Path Planning for Human-UGV Casualty Evacuation
summary: Heterogeneous multi-robot path planning is a well-studied problem in which agents with disparate kinematic and dynamic models must coordinate to achieve shared objectives. These formulations, however, treat all agents as robotic-their cost models are mechanical and their traversability is sensor-derived. In human-robot teaming, the human partner remains relegated to command and supervisory roles rather than being modeled as a physical co-navigator with distinct mobility constraints and dynamic energy reserves. This work investigates joint path planning for a two-agent human-UGV team in search-and-rescue casualty retrieval scenarios. We model the human agent using the Pandolf-Santee metabolic cost model with fatigue-modulated speed, and the UGV using a rolling-resistance energy model with terrain-dependent speed limits. By exploiting the complementary traversability of each agent-the human's ability to traverse dense vegetation and shallow water versus the UGV's superior speed on open terrain and roads-we optimize casualty transfer locations, termed switch points, to minimize total mission time. Evaluated across multiple synthetic 1km2 environments with procedurally generated elevation and land-cover data, the optimized strategy reduces mean mission time by 5.3% relative to a human-only baseline and by 7.0% relative to a naive human-UGV strategy without switch point optimization, while reducing human energy expenditure by 17.8% relative to baseline. Notably, the naive strategy reduces human energy expenditure by a larger margin (22.4%) but incurs a 2% increase in mission time relative to baseline, illustrating that switch point optimization is necessary to realize time savings from human-UGV teaming.

AI.tldr: This work plans joint paths for a human-UGV team in search-and-rescue casualty retrieval, modeling the human with a Pandolf-Santee metabolic cost model and the UGV with a rolling-resistance energy model, and optimizing "switch points" where the casualty is handed off between agents. Across synthetic 1 km² environments, the optimized strategy cuts mean mission time by 5.3% vs. human-only and 7.0% vs. a naive human-UGV strategy, while reducing human energy expenditure by 17.8%.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous multi-robot path planning typically treats all agents as robotic, with mechanical cost models and sensor-derived traversability. In human-robot teaming, the human is relegated to command/supervisory roles rather than modeled as a physical co-navigator with distinct mobility constraints and dynamic energy reserves. This work addresses that gap by modeling the human as a co-navigator with fatigue-modulated mobility in casualty retrieval scenarios.
AI.method: The human agent is modeled with the Pandolf-Santee metabolic cost model with fatigue-modulated speed, and the UGV with a rolling-resistance energy model with terrain-dependent speed limits. The approach exploits complementary traversability (human: dense vegetation and shallow water; UGV: speed on open terrain and roads) and optimizes casualty transfer locations ("switch points") to minimize total mission time. Evaluation uses multiple synthetic 1 km² environments with procedurally generated elevation and land-cover data.
AI.result: The optimized strategy reduces mean mission time by 5.3% vs. a human-only baseline and 7.0% vs. a naive human-UGV strategy without switch point optimization, while reducing human energy expenditure by 17.8% vs. baseline. The naive strategy reduces human energy expenditure more (22.4%) but increases mission time by 2% relative to baseline.
AI.conclusion: Switch point optimization is necessary to realize time savings from human-UGV teaming: without it, a naive cooperative strategy can increase mission time despite greater energy savings for the human.

title: Beyond Instruction Following: Learning Grounded Skill-Following with Skill Contracts
summary: Instruction following typically enforces discrete, response-level requirements, whereas an expert-authored skill prescribes procedural requirements spanning multiple phases and environment interactions. Given such a skill, we train the executor to execute all required phases instead of focusing solely on the final answer. We therefore introduce Grounded Skill-Following, which requires an agent to execute a fixed, expert-authored skill across its required phases by grounding decisions in environment observations. To achieve verifiable procedural execution, we formulate each skill as a skill contract combining visible skill instructions with an explicit contract runtime. The runtime specifies required phases, admissible actions, permitted transitions, and accepted termination. This structure provides a dense, verifiable training signal throughout execution. We leverage this by introducing Verified Progress Credit, which assigns rewards upon the initial completion of contract milestones and aggregates them into the trajectory return to guide policy optimization. During rollout, the contract runtime continuously tracks state transitions to provide Contract-State Feedback, which indicates whether the latest action is accepted and guides the agent toward valid next actions. To measure procedural compliance, we introduce the Protocol Completion Rate (PCR), defined as reaching accepted termination through all required phases, and decouple it from the final Task Outcome. Jointly trained with our framework, Qwen3.5-4B achieves Protocol Completion Rates of 99.27% on Math and 99.96% on Search, while slightly outperforming original baselines in Task Outcome (82.95% and 46.61%, respectively). Controlled studies examine how skill instructions, training signals, and contract-state feedback affect both metrics, while withholding interventions evaluate behavioral dependence on observation content.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Grounded Skill-Following, a task requiring agents to execute expert-authored skills across all required phases by grounding decisions in environment observations, operationalized via skill contracts with a runtime that enables dense verifiable rewards (Verified Progress Credit) and feedback (Contract-State Feedback).
AI.motivation: Instruction following typically enforces discrete, response-level requirements, but an expert-authored skill prescribes procedural requirements spanning multiple phases and environment interactions. Existing training focuses solely on the final answer, ignoring whether the agent executes all required procedural phases. The authors aim to train executors to carry out all required phases grounded in environment observations.
AI.method: Each skill is formulated as a skill contract combining visible skill instructions with an explicit contract runtime specifying required phases, admissible actions, permitted transitions, and accepted termination. This yields a dense, verifiable training signal. Verified Progress Credit assigns rewards upon initial completion of contract milestones and aggregates them into trajectory return. During rollout, the runtime tracks state transitions to provide Contract-State Feedback indicating whether the latest action is accepted and guiding the agent to valid next actions. A new metric, Protocol Completion Rate (PCR), measures procedural compliance (reaching accepted termination through all required phases) decoupled from Task Outcome.
AI.result: Qwen3.5-4B jointly trained with the framework achieves PCR of 99.27% on Math and 99.96% on Search, while slightly outperforming original baselines on Task Outcome (82.95% and 46.61%, respectively). Controlled studies examine how skill instructions, training signals, and contract-state feedback affect both metrics; withholding interventions evaluate behavioral dependence on observation content.
AI.conclusion: Grounded Skill-Following with skill contracts and a runtime enables verifiable procedural execution, providing dense training signals that yield near-perfect protocol compliance without sacrificing task outcome, and offering a principled way to decouple and study procedural compliance versus task success.

title: MarvisNav: Making Memory Visible on Route Choices for Zero-Shot Object Navigation
summary: When searching for an object, people choose their next move by considering both likely target locations and places already explored. The current view can cue place-associated memories, bringing target relevance and prior exploration into the same spatial context. In many zero-shot object navigation (ZSON) methods, however, vision-language models (VLMs) infer promising search areas from egocentric images, while exploration history is represented separately, e.g., as text or maps. This separation either requires an additional fusion step or leaves the correspondence between memory and route choices implicit for the VLM to recover. We instead make exploration memory directly visible on visual route choices. We propose MarvisNav, a ZSON framework that maintains a topological graph and projects candidate nodes together with their exploration states onto egocentric views as memory-bearing visual route choices. These states capture local exploration progress beyond binary visitation. By binding exploration state directly to each visual candidate, MarvisNav enables the VLM to jointly evaluate target relevance and exploration state without a separate post-hoc fusion or reranking stage. Without policy training, MarvisNav achieves state-of-the-art performance on HM3D (81.2% SR and 42.5% SPL), while remaining competitive on MP3D. It also outperforms representative VLM-based methods with far fewer VLM calls (e.g., 7.5% of WMNav). Real-robot experiments across diverse scenes further validate its practical deployability. Beyond MarvisNav, our study shows that memory representation shapes VLM decisions and ZSON performance, highlighting that effective memory use depends not only on its availability, but also on how it is represented. Code and project page will be available at \url{https://wangjincheng1998.github.io/MarvisNav/}.

AI.tldr: MarvisNav is a zero-shot object navigation framework that projects candidate navigation nodes and their exploration states onto egocentric views as memory-bearing visual route choices, enabling VLMs to jointly evaluate target relevance and exploration progress without separate fusion stages.
AI.motivation: In ZSON, humans consider both likely target locations and already-explored places, with views cueing place-associated memories that unify target relevance and prior exploration in one spatial context. Existing VLM-based ZSON methods infer search areas from egocentric images while representing exploration history separately (as text or maps), requiring an extra fusion step or leaving memory-to-route correspondence implicit. This separation motivates binding exploration memory directly to visual route choices.
AI.method: MarvisNav maintains a topological graph and projects candidate nodes together with their exploration states onto egocentric views as memory-bearing visual route choices. These states capture local exploration progress beyond binary visitation. By binding exploration state directly to each visual candidate, the VLM jointly evaluates target relevance and exploration state without a separate post-hoc fusion or reranking stage, and the method requires no policy training.
AI.result: MarvisNav achieves state-of-the-art performance on HM3D (81.2% SR and 42.5% SPL) while remaining competitive on MP3D. It also outperforms representative VLM-based methods with far fewer VLM calls (e.g., 7.5% of WMNav). Real-robot experiments across diverse scenes validate its practical deployability.
AI.conclusion: The study shows that memory representation shapes VLM decisions and ZSON performance, highlighting that effective memory use depends not only on its availability, but also on how it is represented.

title: Memadapter: Counterfactual Adaptation Against Memory-induced Sycophancy
summary: Long-term memory enables LLM-based agents to retain and reuse information across tasks and sessions, supporting personalization and long-horizon interactions. However, persistent memories can also induce sycophancy, causing agents to over-align with users' historical beliefs even when they are inaccurate, outdated, or inconsistent with objective evidence. Existing mitigation methods assume that memory-induced sycophancy originates from biased or incorrect memories and attempt to reduce this risk by filtering such memories at different stages of the memory pipeline. However, in the real world, objective and correct memories can still induce sycophancy, and the same memory can warrant different influence across different contexts. To this end, we propose MemAdapter, a novel framework that adaptively integrates retrieved memories to support objective and reliable reasoning. Specifically, MemAdapter consists of three components: (i) Counterfactual Induction, which leverages counterfactual reasoning to uncover the potential risk of retrieved memories; (ii) Context-Aware Reflection, which calibrates the inferential influence of each retrieved memory in light of the current task via self-reflection; and (iii) Evidence-Based Reasoning, which grounds the final response in appropriate evidence while preserving the legitimate influence of memory. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that MemAdapter consistently improves memory reliability across diverse scenarios. Our code is available at https://github.com/DEEP-JLU/MemAdapter.

AI.tldr: MemAdapter is a framework that adaptively integrates retrieved long-term memories to mitigate memory-induced sycophancy in LLM agents, even when memories are correct, by uncovering risks via counterfactual reasoning, calibrating contextual influence through self-reflection, and grounding responses in evidence.
AI.motivation: Long-term memory enables LLM-based agents to retain and reuse information across tasks and sessions, supporting personalization and long-horizon interactions. However, persistent memories can induce sycophancy, causing agents to over-align with users' historical beliefs even when they are inaccurate, outdated, or inconsistent with objective evidence. Existing mitigation methods assume memory-induced sycophancy originates from biased or incorrect memories and filter such memories at various pipeline stages. Yet in the real world, objective and correct memories can still induce sycophancy, and the same memory can warrant different influence across different contexts.
AI.method: MemAdapter consists of three components: (i) Counterfactual Induction, which leverages counterfactual reasoning to uncover the potential risk of retrieved memories; (ii) Context-Aware Reflection, which calibrates the inferential influence of each retrieved memory in light of the current task via self-reflection; and (iii) Evidence-Based Reasoning, which grounds the final response in appropriate evidence while preserving the legitimate influence of memory.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that MemAdapter consistently improves memory reliability across diverse scenarios.
AI.conclusion: MemAdapter adaptively integrates retrieved memories to support objective and reliable reasoning, addressing the limitation of prior methods that assume sycophancy stems only from biased or incorrect memories. Code is available at https://github.com/DEEP-JLU/MemAdapter.

title: ArtifactArena: Evaluating Models by What They Build in the Physical World
summary: To evaluate the frontier, we must measure models not by what they say, but by what they can engineer and build in grounded physical environments. We introduce \textsc{ArtifactArena}, an open-ended platform where models face a physically grounded hardware-software co-design challenge: engineering fully functional robots to compete in a simulated arena. We evaluate a frontier model's zero-shot, verifier guided refinement, and open-ended physical design capabilities through three harnesses that refine their bot artifacts based on text descriptions, physics simulator feedback, and gameplay data. We benchmark these capabilities with an Elo ranking of frontier models derived from head-to-head tournaments between their artifacts. By releasing this framework and tournament infrastructure for ongoing community submissions, we establish a living, non-saturating testbed to continuously measure the expanding limits of open-ended intelligence in the physical world. Please visit \href{https://artifactarena.ai}{https://artifactarena.ai} for more information.

AI.tldr: ArtifactArena is presented as an open-ended testbed that evaluates frontier models on physically grounded hardware-software co-design by having them engineer functional robots competing in a simulated arena, and ranks model capabilities via Elo from head-to-head tournaments.
AI.motivation: The authors argue that evaluating the frontier of model capability should be based on what models can engineer and build in grounded physical environments, rather than only on what they say.
AI.method: They introduce ArtifactArena, a physically grounded hardware-software co-design challenge where models engineer fully functional robots for a simulated arena, assessed through three harnesses covering zero-shot generation, verifier-guided refinement, and open-ended physical design, using text descriptions, physics simulator feedback, and gameplay data.
AI.result: Frontier model capabilities are benchmarked with an Elo ranking derived from head-to-head tournaments between their produced bot artifacts.
AI.conclusion: The framework and tournament infrastructure are released for ongoing community submissions, forming a living, non-saturating testbed to continuously measure the expanding limits of open-ended intelligence in the physical world.

title: A Safe Action Is Not Enough: Feasible-Future Decoding for Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary:
A safe action is not necessarily a viable one. Under a frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policy, an action can be likely and locally admissible yet leave no policy-supported route to safe task completion. We call this the feasibility-likelihood gap: likelihood ranks the current action, whereas feasibility depends on the futures that remain after it.
  We derive the exact next-block marginal of the history-conditioned policy-environment trajectory law restricted to safe task completion. The derivation exposes a candidate-dependent feasible-future mass with two roles: its support records whether safe completion remains possible under the frozen continuation process, and its magnitude measures how much weighted safe-completion mass is preserved. Exact evaluation is impractical online, so we develop a selective finite-candidate approximation, derive conditions for recovering the best retained viable candidate, and instantiate it as an alarm-triggered, training-free reranker.
  On Safety-CHORES, VICS-G lowers mean cumulative safety cost by 1.9%-57.5% across six settings while remaining within 2.5 percentage points of policy sampling in success and 0.82 steps in mean episode length. The resulting decoder is tied to an exact policy-relative safe-completion target, yet requires neither retraining of the base policy nor online trajectory rollouts.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a feasibility-likelihood gap in frozen VLA policies—actions that are likely and locally admissible may foreclose all safe completion routes—and derives the exact next-block marginal of the safe-completion-restricted trajectory law, approximating it via a training-free, alarm-triggered reranker (VICS-G).
AI.motivation: Under a frozen vision-language-action policy, an action can be probable and locally permissible yet eliminate every policy-supported path to safe task completion. Standard likelihood-based decoding ranks only the current action and ignores the futures remaining after it, creating a mismatch between what is likely and what is feasible for safe completion.
AI.method: The authors derive the exact next-block marginal of the history-conditioned policy-environment trajectory law restricted to safe task completion. This yields a candidate-dependent feasible-future mass whose support indicates whether safe completion remains possible under the frozen continuation process and whose magnitude measures preserved weighted safe-completion mass. Because exact evaluation is impractical online, they develop a selective finite-candidate approximation, derive conditions for recovering the best retained viable candidate, and instantiate it as an alarm-triggered, training-free reranker (VICS-G).
AI.result: On Safety-CHORES, VICS-G reduces mean cumulative safety cost by 1.9%-57.5% across six settings while staying within 2.5 percentage points of policy sampling in success rate and 0.82 steps in mean episode length.
AI.conclusion: The resulting decoder is tied to an exact policy-relative safe-completion target, yet requires neither retraining of the base policy nor online trajectory rollouts, offering an efficient, training-free mechanism that improves safety without materially degrading task performance or efficiency.

title: SimForcing: Distilling Simulation Motion Priors into Real-Domain Robot World Models
summary: Action-conditioned robot world models must respond precisely to robot trajectories while preserving realistic visual dynamics, yet learning both from heterogeneous robot videos remains challenging. Simulation offers structured motion supervision, but appearance differences hinder direct transfer, and inaccurate simulation predictions can misguide real-video generation. We present SimForcing, a simulation-guided framework that uses simulation both as a source of transferable motion knowledge and as a controllable reference for prediction. First, we transfer motion knowledge from a simulation teacher through latent-motion distillation, aligning temporal changes in latent space to internalize motion priors while mitigating the influence of appearance differences. Second, we introduce multi-block simulation conditioning with condition dropout to exploit predicted simulation trajectories without relying excessively on their accuracy. Our simulation-conditioning classifier-free guidance scheme unifies these two ideas by balancing predictions based on internalized motion knowledge with those additionally guided by simulation latents. The jointly trained student generates both simulation conditions and real-domain videos, requiring no additional world model at inference. On Bridge, SimForcing achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and FVD among the compared methods without external embodied pretraining. Evaluation on InternData-A1 further supports its applicability across robot datasets. Moreover, using our trained world model to initialize a vision-language-action model improves LIBERO success, suggesting its utility for downstream policy learning. \url{https://github.com/Wang-Xiaodong1899/SimForcing}

AI.tldr: SimForcing is a simulation-guided framework for action-conditioned robot world models that transfers motion knowledge from a simulation teacher via latent-motion distillation and uses multi-block simulation conditioning with classifier-free guidance, achieving state-of-the-art video prediction on Bridge and improving downstream LIBERO policy learning.
AI.motivation: Action-conditioned robot world models must respond precisely to robot trajectories while preserving realistic visual dynamics, but learning both from heterogeneous robot videos is challenging. Simulation provides structured motion supervision yet suffers from appearance gaps and inaccurate predictions that can misguide real-video generation.
AI.method: SimForcing treats simulation as both a transferable motion source and a controllable reference. It (1) transfers motion knowledge from a simulation teacher through latent-motion distillation, aligning temporal latent changes to internalize motion priors while mitigating appearance differences; (2) introduces multi-block simulation conditioning with condition dropout to exploit predicted simulation trajectories without over-relying on their accuracy. A simulation-conditioning classifier-free guidance scheme unifies these ideas, balancing internally learned motion knowledge against simulation-latent guidance. The jointly trained student generates both simulation conditions and real-domain videos without an additional world model at inference.
AI.result: On Bridge, SimForcing achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and FVD among compared methods without external embodied pretraining. Evaluation on InternData-A1 supports cross-dataset applicability. Initializing a vision-language-action model with the trained world model improves LIBERO success.
AI.conclusion: Simulation can serve simultaneously as a transferable motion prior and a controllable reference to build strong action-conditioned robot world models, yielding superior video prediction and benefiting downstream policy learning.

title: CreativeFlow: A One-to-Many Analogical Relation Transfer Method for 3D Asset Generation
comment: 3 pages. To appear in SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Posters (SA Posters '26), Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, December 2026
summary: Inspired by cognitive science, we present CREATIVEFLOW, an analogical generation framework that explicitly models analogical divergent thinking to mitigate creative homogenization in text-to-3D pipelines. Our method derives a series of meaningful yet relationally similar source-target asset pairs, each featuring distinct geometric configurations. Expert evaluations demonstrate that our framework substantially enhances creative novelty and visual fascination. This workflow and its resulting assets establish a foundational dataset and benchmark for future relation-aware 3D model training.

AI.tldr: CREATIVEFLOW is an analogical generation framework inspired by cognitive science that models analogical divergent thinking to counteract creative homogenization in text-to-3D pipelines.
AI.motivation: Text-to-3D pipelines suffer from creative homogenization, producing repetitive outputs lacking originality. Cognitive science suggests that analogical divergent thinking can drive creative novelty, motivating a framework that explicitly models this process.
AI.method: The framework explicitly models analogical divergent thinking, deriving a series of meaningful yet relationally similar source-target asset pairs, each featuring distinct geometric configurations.
AI.result: Expert evaluations demonstrate that the framework substantially enhances creative novelty and visual fascination.
AI.conclusion: The workflow and its resulting assets establish a foundational dataset and benchmark for future relation-aware 3D model training.

title: Physics Residual Dynamics and Reduced Order Whole-Body Planning for Obstacle Aware Human Robot Cloth CoTransportation
summary: Human--robot co-transportation of deformable objects requires predicting object deformation during motion, since obstacle clearance depends on both the grasp points and the unactuated interior. We present a hierarchical planning framework that combines a learned cloth model with a reduced-order whole-body model of a dual-arm mobile manipulator. A physics-residual conditional recurrent variational autoencoder (p-cRVAE) predicts the full cloth configuration from grasp-point observations by learning a residual correction to a computationally efficient linearized physics model, limiting error accumulation over 40-step planning horizon. The predicted cloth dynamics are embedded in a model predictive path integral (MPPI) planner using a reduced-order representation of a dual-arm mobile manipulator that preserves the non-holonomic base constraint and arm workspace limits. An MPC layer subsequently refines the sampled motion into smooth, executable references for whole-body control. The reduced-order formulation achieves tracking performance comparable to the full 17-DoF model while reducing computation time by approximately 80%. Across four co-transportation scenarios and two carrying speeds, the proposed framework maintains cloth-obstacle clearance where a corner-following baseline results in collisions, while whole-body refinement reduces final cloth deformation from 0.93\,m to 0.28\,m.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical planning framework for human–robot co-transportation of deformable cloth, combining a physics-residual conditional recurrent VAE cloth model with a reduced-order dual-arm mobile manipulator model, integrated into MPPI and refined by MPC, achieving obstacle clearance and reduced deformation at ~80% lower computation.
AI.motivation: Co-transporting deformable objects with a robot requires predicting object deformation, since obstacle clearance depends on both grasp points and the unactuated cloth interior. Accurate yet tractable whole-body planning is challenging due to cloth dynamics and the high DoF of a dual-arm mobile manipulator.
AI.method: A hierarchical planning framework: (1) a physics-residual conditional recurrent VAE (p-cRVAE) predicts full cloth configuration from grasp-point observations by learning a residual correction to a linearized physics model over a 40-step horizon; (2) predictions are embedded in an MPPI planner using a reduced-order dual-arm mobile manipulator model preserving non-holonomic base constraints and arm workspace limits; (3) an MPC layer refines sampled motion into smooth executable references for whole-body control.
AI.result: The reduced-order model matches full 17-DoF tracking performance while cutting computation time by roughly 80%. Across four co-transportation scenarios and two carrying speeds, the framework maintains cloth–obstacle clearance where a corner-following baseline collides, and whole-body refinement reduces final cloth deformation from 0.93 m to 0.28 m.
AI.conclusion: Combining learned residual cloth dynamics with reduced-order whole-body modeling enables efficient, collision-free human–robot co-transportation of deformable objects, with MPC refinement improving deformation outcomes.

title: AECG: Asymmetric Experience Consolidation and Governance In Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems increasingly rely on memory to transform execution trajectories into reusable procedural knowledge. Yet repeated retrieval also makes memory errors persistent: memory pollution arises when outdated, weakly supported, or spuriously successful procedures become recurring components of future reasoning. Multi-agent execution introduces an additional structural risk. Scope collapse occurs when procedural knowledge escapes the coordination scope in which it was shown effective and is repeatedly reused at incompatible decision levels, allowing local errors to influence cascades of downstream decisions. Meanwhile, task-level failures provide ambiguous supervision because they rarely reveal which recalled knowledge was responsible. We introduce AECG, a framework for asymmetric experience consolidation and governance for multi-agent systems. AECG turns memory from static experience storage into a dynamic reliability-governance loop, preserving coordination scope and using multi-scale, confidence-aware reliability to detect degradation. It then combines degradation with downstream impact to prioritize high-risk knowledge under a bounded review budget, applies targeted interventions, and reactivates revised skills only after paired replay. Across three multi-agent frameworks and four benchmarks, AECG achieves the best score in 11 of 12 framework--benchmark settings and improves over the strongest competing memory method by as much as 10.23 percentage points; removing scope preservation reduces accuracy by up to 16.89 points. AECG thereby reframes multi-agent memory from passive accumulation into auditable reliability governance. Code is available at https://github.com/fenhg297/AECG

AI.tldr: AECG introduces asymmetric experience consolidation and governance for LLM multi-agent memory, turning passive storage into a dynamic reliability-governance loop that preserves coordination scope. It detects degradation via multi-scale confidence-aware reliability, prioritizes high-risk knowledge by degradation and downstream impact under a bounded review budget, applies targeted interventions, and reactivates revised skills after paired replay. It wins 11 of 12 framework–benchmark settings.
AI.motivation: LLM-based multi-agent systems rely on memory to turn execution trajectories into reusable procedural knowledge, but repeated retrieval makes errors persistent. Two failure modes motivate the work: memory pollution, where outdated, weakly supported, or spuriously successful procedures recur, and scope collapse, where procedural knowledge escapes the coordination scope where it was effective and is reused at incompatible decision levels, cascading local errors. Task-level failures give ambiguous supervision because they rarely reveal which recalled knowledge caused the failure.
AI.method: AECG is an asymmetric experience consolidation and governance framework. It converts memory from static experience storage into a dynamic reliability-governance loop: it preserves coordination scope, uses multi-scale, confidence-aware reliability to detect degradation, combines degradation with downstream impact to prioritize high-risk knowledge under a bounded review budget, applies targeted interventions, and reactivates revised skills only after paired replay.
AI.result: Across three multi-agent frameworks and four benchmarks, AECG achieves the best score in 11 of 12 framework–benchmark settings, improving over the strongest competing memory method by up to 10.23 percentage points. Ablating scope preservation reduces accuracy by up to 16.89 points.
AI.conclusion: AECG reframes multi-agent memory from passive accumulation into auditable reliability governance, showing that scope preservation and confidence-aware prioritization are critical for reliable multi-agent memory.

title: AffordCraft: Scalable Construction of Task-Ready Simulation Assets from Single Images
comment: 33 pages, 14 figures, 17 tables. Project page: https://affordcraft.github.io Code: https://github.com/AffordCraft/AffordCraft
summary: Robot learning in simulation depends on the objects the simulator offers. Many tasks need objects with separate parts, joints that allow the required motion, and physical properties that remain valid under contact. Existing methods recover this structure anew for every image: generative models predict parts and joints that mostly fail to settle or move in simulation, and general-purpose agents need a long session of model calls for each photograph. AffordCraft builds such an asset from a single RGB image and a task instruction by retrieval instead of generation: it locates the object and the part to operate, selects a matching entry from a library of articulated assets, and fits it to the image while keeping its parts and joints intact. Without any box or mask marking the object, AffordCraft produces a physically valid asset for 1,703 of 2,000 photographs from 31 categories. Five generative methods pass on at most 45% of the same photographs and, at the median, need 10 to 78 times our GPU time per valid asset. On 50 cluttered images, 162 of 237 annotated objects pass the same physical test after automatic detection. Growing the library from 141 to 11,372 entries needs no change to the method and raises category coverage from 46% to 100% and the share of selections with the requested label from 18% to 51%. We also build manipulation tasks from the constructed assets, both with single objects and in composed scenes; policies trained on scripted demonstrations complete both kinds of tasks from initial states unseen in training.

AI.tldr: AffordCraft constructs physically valid articulated assets from a single RGB image and task instruction by retrieving and fitting an entry from an articulated-asset library rather than generating parts and joints, yielding higher physical validity and far lower GPU time than five generative baselines.
AI.motivation: Robot learning in simulation depends on the objects a simulator offers, yet many tasks require objects with separate parts, joints enabling the required motion, and physical properties that remain valid under contact. Existing approaches recover this structure anew per image: generative models predict parts and joints that mostly fail to settle or move in simulation, and general-purpose agents require long sessions of model calls per photograph. This motivates a retrieval-based alternative that preserves articulated structure.
AI.method: AffordCraft takes a single RGB image plus a task instruction as input. It locates the object and the part to operate, selects a matching entry from a library of articulated assets, and fits it to the image while keeping its parts and joints intact. No box or mask marking the object is required. The library can be grown without changing the method.
AI.result: AffordCraft produces a physically valid asset for 1,703 of 2,000 photographs across 31 categories. Five generative methods pass on at most 45% of the same photographs and, at the median, need 10 to 78 times AffordCraft's GPU time per valid asset. On 50 cluttered images, 162 of 237 annotated objects pass the same physical test after automatic detection. Growing the library from 141 to 11,372 entries requires no method change and raises category coverage from 46% to 100% and the share of selections with the requested label from 18% to 51%. Manipulation tasks built from constructed assets, both with single objects and in composed scenes, are completed by policies trained on scripted demonstrations from initial states unseen in training.
AI.conclusion: Retrieval-based asset construction from a single image preserves articulation and physical validity, outperforms generative alternatives in both validity rate and GPU cost, scales naturally with library growth, and yields assets usable for manipulation policies that generalize to unseen initial states.

title: From Scientific Observations to Mechanisms: Benchmarking Hypothesis Generation by AI Scientists
summary: Data-driven mechanistic hypotheses are essential to scientific discovery because they explain how underlying processes produce observed phenomena. AI agents and AI scientists increasingly support scientific data analysis. However, their ability to turn empirical findings into mechanistic hypotheses remains insufficiently examined. To address this gap, we introduce MechHypoBench, the first benchmark for evaluating whether AI agents and AI scientists can generate such hypotheses from empirical data. It combines paper-derived mechanisms from 14 scientific fields with real-world datasets containing 17.98 million records. The construction retains the observational complexity of empirical data while providing a specified underlying mechanism. Agents analyze the observations and propose open-form hypotheses. We develop an evaluation framework that assesses open-form mechanistic hypotheses through their consequences under withheld conditions.
