Experiments with general agents and AI scientists reveal a substantial gap between generated hypotheses and the underlying mechanisms.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MechHypoBench, the first benchmark for evaluating whether AI agents and AI scientists can generate mechanistic hypotheses from empirical data, combining paper-derived mechanisms from 14 scientific fields with real-world datasets (17.98M records), and finds a substantial gap between generated hypotheses and underlying mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Data-driven mechanistic hypotheses are essential to scientific discovery since they explain how underlying processes produce observed phenomena. Although AI agents and AI scientists increasingly support scientific data analysis, their ability to turn empirical findings into mechanistic hypotheses remains insufficiently examined.
AI.method: The authors introduce MechHypoBench, which retains the observational complexity of empirical data while providing a specified underlying mechanism. Agents analyze the observations and propose open-form hypotheses. An evaluation framework assesses open-form mechanistic hypotheses through their consequences under withheld conditions.
AI.result: Experiments with general agents and AI scientists reveal a substantial gap between the generated hypotheses and the underlying mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: AI agents and AI scientists currently struggle to generate mechanistic hypotheses that match ground-truth mechanisms from empirical data, highlighting a significant shortcoming in their scientific discovery capabilities.

title: Recursive Video In-Context Learning for Agentic Robot
summary: LLM agents that orchestrate frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policies improve across episodes through text memory, which records what the agent did but not how the task is done. A demonstration video shows it, but fits poorly into an agent's context. The full video slows every turn, fixed keyframes lose the contact detail that decides whether a grasp holds, and what the agent needs shifts from the task's structure while planning to the frames around each contact. We introduce Recursive Video In-Context Learning (RV-ICL), a training-free method that turns a demonstration into a hierarchy the agent navigates rather than a prompt it receives. The hierarchy is built from the sub-events of the demonstration, such as grasps and releases. Its levels grow finer, from keyframes of the whole task to phases, moments and short clips, and are exposed through read-only tools. The agent reads the coarse levels before planning. During execution it re-enters the hierarchy whenever a step needs more detail and loads only the clip of its current sub-goal. One demonstration per task is enough. Built on RPent, RV-ICL raises success from 92.6% to 96.5% on LIBERO-PRO and from 86.7% to 95.8% on LIBERO-Plus.

AI.tldr: RV-ICL is a training-free method that converts a demonstration video into a navigable hierarchy of sub-events, coarse-to-fine levels, and short clips exposed via read-only tools; the agent reads coarse levels for planning and re-enters finer levels during execution, raising success on LIBERO-PRO from 92.6% to 96.5% and on LIBERO-Plus from 86.7% to 95.8%.
AI.motivation: LLM agents that orchestrate frozen VLA policies improve across episodes via text memory, but such memory records what the agent did, not how the task is done. Demonstration videos convey the missing procedural knowledge, yet they fit poorly into the agent's context: full video slows every turn, fixed keyframes lose the contact detail that decides whether a grasp holds, and the needed information shifts from task structure during planning to frames around each contact during execution.
AI.method: RV-ICL is training-free and turns one demonstration into a hierarchy the agent navigates rather than a prompt it receives. The hierarchy is built from sub-events of the demonstration (e.g., grasps and releases), with progressively finer levels: keyframes of the whole task, phases, moments, and short clips, exposed through read-only tools. The agent reads the coarse levels before planning and, during execution, re-enters the hierarchy whenever a step needs more detail, loading only the clip of its current sub-goal. One demonstration per task suffices. It is built on RPent.
AI.result: On LIBERO-PRO, success rises from 92.6% to 96.5%; on LIBERO-Plus, from 86.7% to 95.8%.
AI.conclusion: Framing a demonstration as a coarse-to-fine, sub-event-based hierarchy with on-demand retrieval via read-only tools lets an LLM agent access video procedural detail selectively—preserving contact-critical information without slowing every turn—and improves task success using only one demonstration per task.

title: Image Synthesis as an Intermediate for Controllable Time Series Generation
summary: Semantic-driven time-series generation offers a promising way to improve downstream learning in few-shot forecasting, but directly generating numerical sequences from language often fails to preserve the intended temporal structure. We propose VisualBridge, which uses time-series plots as a visual intermediate to bridge high-level temporal semantics and numerical sequences. An MLLM first converts plotted series into structured semantic representations, enabling explicit control over temporal properties such as trend, seasonality, and volatility. We then learn a semantic editing policy with downstream forecasting rewards, allowing the generation process to favor temporal patterns that are beneficial for the target task. The resulting sequences are further modeled by a temporal VAE to produce consistent multivariate augmentations. Experiments on standard public forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that VisualBridge improves few-shot forecasting over conventional augmentation methods, with ablations validating the roles of visual semantic grounding, learned semantic control, and VAE-based generation.

AI.tldr: VisualBridge uses time-series plots as a visual intermediate to bridge language semantics and numerical sequences, with a reward-learned semantic editing policy and a temporal VAE for augmentation, improving few-shot forecasting.
AI.motivation: Semantic-driven time-series generation can improve downstream few-shot forecasting, but directly generating numerical sequences from language often fails to preserve intended temporal structure. The paper aims to bridge high-level temporal semantics and numerical sequences more effectively.
AI.method: An MLLM first converts plotted series into structured semantic representations, enabling explicit control over temporal properties such as trend, seasonality, and volatility. A semantic editing policy is learned with downstream forecasting rewards so generation favors task-beneficial temporal patterns. A temporal VAE then models the resulting sequences to produce consistent multivariate augmentations.
AI.result: Experiments on standard public forecasting benchmarks show VisualBridge improves few-shot forecasting over conventional augmentation methods. Ablations validate the contributions of visual semantic grounding, learned semantic control, and VAE-based generation.
AI.conclusion: Using time-series plots as a visual intermediate with reward-guided semantic editing and VAE-based sequence modeling is an effective approach for semantic-driven augmentation that enhances few-shot forecasting.

title: InterMimicGen: Scaling Humanoid Loco-Manipulation through Self-Evolving Motion Imitation
summary: Captured human-object interactions provide rich supervision for humanoid loco-manipulation, but they are sparse, heterogeneous, and not directly executable by robots. We introduce InterMimicGen, a self-evolving motion-imitation framework in which robot motion data and a tracking policy improve each other. First, we consolidate motion-captured human-object interaction datasets and retarget them into humanoid robot references while preserving whole-body coordination and dexterous hand-object relationships. This produces a large and diverse humanoid robot reference collection for dexterous whole-body loco-manipulation. Second, we train a physics-based generalist tracker that executes these references in simulation on a humanoid with dexterous hands, covering a scale and diversity beyond prior humanoid tracking systems for loco-manipulation. Third, we close a data flywheel: each round makes small, task-preserving changes to where an interaction takes place and how the body performs it, fine-tunes the tracker on them, and keeps only the variants whose simulated execution completes the task, which seed the next round. With more iterations, these small edits compound into broader coverage around the sparse original demonstrations while preserving task semantics and motion quality. Experiments show contact-preserving retargeting across robot configurations, broad tracking with a single generalist policy, executable motions that keep growing over augmentation rounds, and transfer to real robots. InterMimicGen provides a unified path from heterogeneous human demonstrations to a continually expanding motion resource for humanoid robot learning.

AI.tldr: InterMimicGen is a self-evolving motion-imitation framework that couples robot motion data and a tracking policy in a data flywheel, converting heterogeneous human-object interaction captures into an ever-growing, executable humanoid loco-manipulation motion resource.
AI.motivation: Human-object interaction captures offer rich supervision for humanoid loco-manipulation, but they are sparse, heterogeneous, and not directly executable by robots. Existing humanoid tracking systems also lack the scale and diversity needed for dexterous whole-body loco-manipulation.
AI.method: Three components: (1) consolidate motion-captured human-object interaction datasets and retarget them into humanoid references while preserving whole-body coordination and dexterous hand-object relationships; (2) train a physics-based generalist tracker that executes the references in simulation on a humanoid with dexterous hands; (3) close a data flywheel that applies small task-preserving changes to interaction location and body execution, fine-tunes the tracker, and retains only variants whose simulated execution completes the task to seed the next round.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate contact-preserving retargeting across robot configurations, broad tracking with a single generalist policy, executable motions that keep growing over augmentation rounds, and transfer to real robots.
AI.conclusion: InterMimicGen offers a unified path from heterogeneous human demonstrations to a continually expanding motion resource for humanoid robot learning, with edits compounding into broader coverage around sparse original demonstrations while preserving task semantics and motion quality.

title: Safe Context Switching for Agents in the Wild: Mitigating Subspace Interference via Orthogonal Adaptation
summary: Most Large Language Models exhibit a fundamental tension between two sequential tasks, such as logical reasoning and safety alignment. The high-variance internal states required for sophisticated Chain-of-Thought (CoT) deduction can geometrically interfere with latent representations encoding safety constraints. We identify this phenomenon as Sequential Subspace Interference, showing that standard fine-tuning on logical tasks such as multi-step mathematics and code generation can result in a 23.3% interference penalty on alignment benchmarks, substantially weakening the model's safety priors. This Reasoning Drift is not adequately captured by current adaptation methods because gradients for logical tasks are rarely orthogonal to safety objectives. To address this issue, we propose AURA (Adaptive Unique Residual Allocation), a spectral regularization framework that enforces Spectral Independence between reasoning and safety. By explicitly estimating the null space of the alignment manifold and constraining reasoning updates to its orthogonal complement, AURA enables models to improve logical reasoning without compromising safety. Empirically, AURA recovers 23.0% of the lost performance while preserving greater than 0.98 cosine fidelity to the safe state, demonstrating that reasoning and alignment can be effectively decoupled through geometric regularization.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "Sequential Subspace Interference," where reasoning-oriented fine-tuning degrades safety alignment due to geometric interference between latent representations, and proposes AURA, a spectral regularization framework that decouples reasoning and safety by constraining updates to the orthogonal complement of the alignment manifold's null space.
AI.motivation: LLMs face a tension between sequential tasks like logical reasoning and safety alignment. High-variance internal states needed for CoT deduction geometrically interfere with safety-encoding latent representations. Standard fine-tuning on logical tasks causes a 23.3% interference penalty on alignment benchmarks, and existing adaptation methods fail because reasoning-task gradients are rarely orthogonal to safety objectives.
AI.method: AURA (Adaptive Unique Residual Allocation) is a spectral regularization framework enforcing Spectral Independence between reasoning and safety. It estimates the null space of the alignment manifold and constrains reasoning updates to its orthogonal complement, decoupling the two objectives via geometric regularization.
AI.result: AURA recovers 23.0% of the lost performance while maintaining greater than 0.98 cosine fidelity to the safe state, showing reasoning and alignment can be effectively decoupled.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning and safety alignment can be decoupled through geometric (spectral) regularization, mitigating Sequential Subspace Interference and Reasoning Drift without sacrificing logical reasoning capability.

title: Look Before You Leap: Thermodynamic Arbitration of Parametric and Non-Parametric Knowledge in LLM Agents via Self-Regulating Memory Architectures
summary: The architecture of modern LLMs consists of a profound cognitive polarization. LLMs possess implicit intuition encoded in their parameters, yet rely on a disconnected, explicit mechanism to access the outside world. Agentic frameworks have not bridged this gap; instead, models are often compelled into pathological "induced amnesia." Under the prevailing "Retrieve-Always" paradigm, agents must distrust their internal knowledge, making every user interaction a "tabula rasa" event that must be checked externally. This creates reflexive dependence that can be thermodynamically wasteful, cognitively fragile, and susceptible to irrelevant context. We propose a return to first principles, operationalizing the biological maxim "Look Before You Leap." We introduce MARTA (Metacognitive Adaptive Retrieval and Thought Architecture), a neuro-symbolic framework that bridges parametric and non-parametric knowledge. Rather than treating retrieval as mandatory, MARTA models it as a cost, taking the leap only when perceived internal inadequacy warrants external information. By allowing the agent to gauge the entropy of its own thoughts before acting, MARTA enables deliberative retrieval and uncertainty-aware decision making. Our approach suggests that giving agents the capacity for introspection can restore a more efficient balance between internal knowledge and external information.

AI.tldr: MARTA is a neuro-symbolic framework that treats retrieval as a cost rather than a default, letting an LLM agent introspect on the entropy of its own thoughts and retrieve external information only when internal knowledge is deemed inadequate.
AI.motivation: Modern LLMs exhibit a cognitive polarization: implicit intuition in parameters versus a disconnected explicit mechanism for accessing the outside world. Agentic frameworks have failed to bridge this gap, instead inducing "induced amnesia" under the "Retrieve-Always" paradigm, where agents distrust internal knowledge, treat each interaction as tabula rasa, and become reflexively dependent on external checks—wasteful, cognitively fragile, and vulnerable to irrelevant context.
AI.method: MARTA (Metacognitive Adaptive Retrieval and Thought Architecture), a neuro-symbolic framework bridging parametric and non-parametric knowledge. It operationalizes "Look Before You Leap": retrieval is modeled as a cost, not a mandate. The agent gauges the entropy of its own thoughts before acting, enabling deliberative retrieval and uncertainty-aware decision making so a "leap" to external information occurs only when perceived internal inadequacy warrants it.
AI.result: Giving agents the capacity for introspection yields a more efficient balance between internal knowledge and external information, as the framework enables deliberative, uncertainty-aware retrieval rather than mandatory retrieval.
AI.conclusion: A return to first principles—modeling retrieval as a cost conditioned on metacognitive self-assessment—can restore efficiency by aligning internal parametric knowledge and external non-parametric information, countering the pathological reflexive dependence of the "Retrieve-Always" paradigm.

title: GFGE: Unifying Explainable AI Methods through an Interpretation Framework
summary: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) encompasses methods that draw on different sources of information and address different explanatory needs. A common framework is needed to describe how this information becomes evidence and is communicated as an explanation for a particular recipient. We propose the General Framework for Generating Explanations (GFGE), grounded in interpretative frameworks and the complementary activities of \emph{sense-reading} and \emph{sense-giving}. Its conceptual foundation is the Interpret/Explain Schema (IES), which connects an analyst's interpretation of system evidence, the communication of a selected account, and the recipient's interpretation of that account. GFGE operationalises this schema through five roles: data interpretation, model interpretation, output interpretation, optional post-hoc analysis, and aggregation. A role-typed operation graph records method-specific dependencies, while evidence records retain the sources, assumptions, and limitations of explanatory claims. The explanatory question, audience, and context guide the procedure. We instantiate GFGE for attribution, surrogate, counterfactual, concept and prototype, intrinsic rule, argumentation, and language-model methods. These instantiations show how intrinsic, post-hoc, and hybrid workflows can be represented through the same roles while preserving their distinct evidential requirements. GFGE provides a common basis for analysing explanation workflows, tracing communicated claims to their evidence, and identifying unresolved explanatory dependencies.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the General Framework for Generating Explanations (GFGE), a unifying framework for explainable AI (XAI) grounded in sense-reading/sense-giving and the Interpret/Explain Schema, operationalised through five roles and a role-typed operation graph with evidence records, and instantiated across seven XAI method families.
AI.motivation: XAI methods draw on heterogeneous information sources and serve different explanatory needs, but there is no common framework to describe how information becomes evidence and is communicated as an explanation to a specific recipient.
AI.method: GFGE is built on interpretative frameworks and the complementary activities of sense-reading and sense-giving. Its conceptual foundation is the Interpret/Explain Schema (IES), linking an analyst's interpretation of system evidence, the communication of a selected account, and the recipient's interpretation of that account. GFGE operationalises IES through five roles—data interpretation, model interpretation, output interpretation, optional post-hoc analysis, and aggregation. A role-typed operation graph records method-specific dependencies, and evidence records retain sources, assumptions, and limitations of explanatory claims. The explanatory question, audience, and context guide the procedure. GFGE is instantiated for attribution, surrogate, counterfactual, concept and prototype, intrinsic rule, argumentation, and language-model methods.
AI.result: The instantiations demonstrate how intrinsic, post-hoc, and hybrid workflows can be represented through the same roles while preserving their distinct evidential requirements. GFGE enables analysis of explanation workflows, tracing of communicated claims to their evidence, and identification of unresolved explanatory dependencies.
AI.conclusion: GFGE provides a common basis for analysing explanation workflows, tracing communicated claims back to their evidence, and identifying unresolved explanatory dependencies.

title: Learning from imperfect teachers for low-resource acoustic generalization
summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) improves low-resource acoustic learning by enriching one-hot supervision with the softened predictive distribution of a fixed teacher network. However, a teacher trained with limited or imbalanced annotations may produce a biased distribution whose components are not uniformly reliable. Although this distribution can still encode useful knowledge, direct full-distribution matching may also transfer teacher-induced biases, thereby distorting the student's decision boundary and degrading its generalization performance. To address this limitation, we propose Boundary-Anchored Mass-Partitioned Distillation (BA-MPD), a logit-based distillation objective composed of Boundary-Anchored Correction (BAC) and Mass-Partitioned Distillation (MPD). BAC addresses missing ground-truth labels in the set of the teacher's top predictions by swapping the true label for the lowest-ranked entry of the set, thus keeping the mass and uncertainty of the set unchanged. MPD then distills this corrected distribution through separate losses that enforce relational consistency within the set, balance the mass between high- and low-confidence groups, and weight lower-confidence dependencies. Ultimately, BAC and MPD together suppress harmful ranking errors and noisy low-confidence details, while retaining all useful teacher information. Experiments on two acoustic benchmarks under multiple label budgets show that BA-MPD consistently improves over supervised-learning baselines and vanilla KD while remaining competitive with strong logit-based KD baselines. Cross-budget results further show that BA-MPD remains effective when the teacher and student models use mismatched label budgets, demonstrating its ability to exploit imperfect teachers across supervision gaps. Implementation available at https://github.com/ShuanglinLi/BA-MPD.

AI.tldr: BA-MPD is a logit-based knowledge distillation objective that corrects biased teacher predictions via Boundary-Anchored Correction and then distills the corrected distribution through Mass-Partitioned Distillation, improving low-resource acoustic learning under various label budgets.
AI.motivation: A teacher trained with limited or imbalanced annotations produces a biased predictive distribution whose components are not uniformly reliable. Direct full-distribution matching can transfer these teacher-induced biases, distorting the student's decision boundary and degrading generalization.
AI.method: The proposed Boundary-Anchored Mass-Partitioned Distillation (BA-MPD) comprises two components: Boundary-Anchored Correction (BAC), which swaps the true label for the lowest-ranked entry in the teacher's top-prediction set to preserve the set's mass and uncertainty when the ground-truth label is missing; and Mass-Partitioned Distillation (MPD), which distills the corrected distribution via separate losses enforcing relational consistency within the set, balancing mass between high- and low-confidence groups, and weighting lower-confidence dependencies.
AI.result: Experiments on two acoustic benchmarks under multiple label budgets show BA-MPD consistently improves over supervised-learning baselines and vanilla KD, remaining competitive with strong logit-based KD baselines. Cross-budget results show BA-MPD remains effective with mismatched teacher-student label budgets.
AI.conclusion: BA-MPD suppresses harmful ranking errors and noisy low-confidence details while retaining useful teacher information, and effectively exploits imperfect teachers across supervision gaps.

title: When Agent Context Goes Stale: Incoherence in Volatile Agent Context
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Accepted to the AgenticOS Workshop at SOSP 2026
summary: Modern agents increasingly ground their reasoning in observations returned by tools, such as file contents read from a workspace. However, the data sources underlying these observations may later be modified by users, other agents, or external tools, while the model retains only the stale content in its context window. Existing agent runtimes provide little support for notifying the model that a previously observed fact has become stale, causing agents to reuse outdated observations and make incorrect claims about the current workspace state. We propose Concord, a context coherence framework that maintains the consistency between tool observation in agent context and the mutable sources from which they were derived. Concord links each observation to its source, detects source changes, and uses configurable handling policies to update, annotate, or suppress stale context before reuse. Concord is applicable across different agent runtimes and external resources, and can be easily extended to new runtime-resource settings. We implement Concord as a general framework, and instantiate a concrete use case to assess its effectiveness. We construct ConcordBench, where previously observed file contents become stale after subsequent edits. Across three evaluated frontier models, Concord produces answers consistent with the restored workspace state in all evaluated cases under these constructed conditions, matching the oracle on recover count for this benchmark, while using 46.4% fewer tokens than the strongest non-oracle baseline.

AI.tldr: Concord is a context coherence framework that detects when tool observations in an agent's context become stale relative to their mutable sources and updates, annotates, or suppresses them before reuse; evaluated on the new ConcordBench, it matches oracle recovery across three frontier models while using 46.4% fewer tokens than the strongest non-oracle baseline.
AI.motivation: Agents increasingly ground reasoning in tool observations (e.g., file contents), but underlying sources may be modified by users, other agents, or external tools while the model retains only stale content in its context window. Existing runtimes offer little support for signaling that a previously observed fact has become stale, leading agents to reuse outdated observations and make incorrect claims about the current workspace state.
AI.method: Concord links each observation to its source, detects source changes, and applies configurable handling policies to update, annotate, or suppress stale context before reuse. It is runtime- and resource-agnostic and extensible to new runtime-resource settings. The authors implement it as a general framework and instantiate a concrete use case, building ConcordBench where previously observed file contents become stale after subsequent edits.
AI.result: Across three evaluated frontier models, Concord produces answers consistent with the restored workspace state in all evaluated cases under the constructed conditions, matching the oracle on recover count on this benchmark while using 46.4% fewer tokens than the strongest non-oracle baseline.
AI.conclusion: Concord effectively maintains consistency between tool observations in agent context and their mutable sources, eliminating stale-observation reuse and incorrect workspace-state claims, and doing so more token-efficiently than strong baselines while remaining general and extensible.

title: Fusion is the New Mutation: Bandit-Guided Evolution on Workflow Graphs
summary: Automated agentic workflow optimization relies on costly evaluations, making it essential to allocate a limited evaluation budget effectively. Multi-parent fusion can reuse designs from previously discovered workflows, but identifying promising parent combinations requires learning from limited fusion feedback. We introduce DAGO (Directed Acyclic Graph Optimization), a contextual-bandit-guided framework that learns which parent workflows to fuse under a limited evaluation budget. DAGO formulates each candidate parent combination as an arm, represented by pretrained embeddings of its constituent workflows' code and prompts. A diagonal LinUCB policy learns a shared reward model across arms and balances exploitation of arms with high predicted offspring quality against uncertainty-driven exploration. After an arm is selected, an LLM generates a child workflow through summary-guided fusion, and the child's validation score serves as the reward for updating the bandit. A shared directed acyclic graph maintains discovered workflows and their multi-parent lineage, providing an expanding pool of parents for subsequent arm proposals. Across six benchmarks covering mathematical reasoning, code generation, and question answering, DAGO achieves the highest macro-average score among the evaluated baselines. Under matched validation-evaluation budgets, it improves over AFlow from 80.3 to 81.7 while reducing aggregate search expenditure by 11.2%. Ablation studies show that LinUCB-guided arm selection outperforms both random selection and its exploration-free variant, supporting the value of feedback-driven selection and exploration-exploitation balance.

AI.tldr: DAGO is a contextual-bandit-guided framework (diagonal LinUCB) that learns which parent workflows to fuse under a limited evaluation budget, using code/prompt embeddings as arm features and an expanding DAG for lineage; it achieves the best macro-average across six benchmarks and improves over AFlow from 80.3 to 81.7 while cutting search cost by 11.2%.
AI.motivation: Automated agentic workflow optimization is evaluation-expensive, so a limited budget must be allocated effectively. Multi-parent fusion can reuse prior workflow designs, but identifying promising parent combinations requires learning from scarce fusion feedback—an underexplored problem.
AI.method: DAGO casts each candidate parent combination as a bandit arm, represented by pretrained embeddings of constituent workflows' code and prompts. A diagonal LinUCB policy learns a shared reward model across arms, trading off exploitation of high predicted offspring quality against uncertainty-driven exploration. Once an arm is chosen, an LLM produces a child workflow via summary-guided fusion, and the child's validation score rewards and updates the bandit. A shared DAG stores discovered workflows and their multi-parent lineage, expanding the parent pool for future arm proposals.
AI.result: Across six benchmarks spanning mathematical reasoning, code generation, and question answering, DAGO attains the highest macro-average score among baselines. Under matched validation-evaluation budgets, it improves AFlow from 80.3 to 81.7 and reduces aggregate search expenditure by 11.2%. Ablations show LinUCB-guided arm selection beats both random selection and its exploration-free variant.
AI.conclusion: Feedback-driven, exploration-aware parent selection is effective for budget-constrained workflow fusion, validating both the bandit formulation and the exploitation-exploration balance; the shared DAG lineage further sustains an expanding parent pool.

title: Readable Before Actionable: Causal Tracing of Indirect Prompt Injection
summary: Indirect prompt injection causes LLM agents to follow commands embedded in external data. A probe may distinguish instructions from data without identifying a state edit that changes the next action. We study this gap through counterfactual role probes, component-wise activation patching, and separate interventions on AgentDojo trajectories. Role decoding survives changes in content and format. In controlled Qwen tests, it precedes strong tool-choice effects from patches along an independently estimated role direction. On AgentDojo, directions estimated from hijacked and resisted training trajectories reduce attack success at pre-action and injected-span positions, but have little effect at random positions. In longer Qwen trajectories, single-position edits become less effective at later layers; span-wide and repeated edits reduce attack success on the same evaluation set. Removing the learned channel subspace preserves role decoding, yet effective intervention directions transfer poorly across the tested channels. These findings distinguish a readable role signal from an effective behavioral intervention: depth matters in controlled tool choice, while position and context also matter in attack trajectories.

AI.tldr: Indirect prompt injection makes LLM agents act on instructions hidden in external data. This paper examines the gap between merely decoding an "instruction vs. data" role signal and actually changing behavior, using counterfactual role probes, component-wise activation patching, and interventions on AgentDojo trajectories.
AI.motivation: A probe can distinguish instructions from data without necessarily identifying a state edit that changes the agent's next action. The paper is motivated by this gap: a readable role representation may not correspond to an effective behavioral intervention against indirect prompt injection.
AI.method: The authors combine three approaches: (1) counterfactual role probes to test role decoding across content and format changes; (2) component-wise activation patching in controlled Qwen tests, including an independently estimated role direction; and (3) separate interventions on AgentDojo trajectories, with directions estimated from hijacked and resisted training trajectories and applied at pre-action, injected-span, and random positions. They also test longer Qwen trajectories, span-wide and repeated edits, and removal of a learned channel subspace.
AI.result: Role decoding survives changes in content and format. In controlled Qwen tests, the decoded role signal precedes strong tool-choice effects from patches along an independently estimated role direction. On AgentDojo, directions from hijacked and resisted trajectories reduce attack success at pre-action and injected-span positions, but have little effect at random positions. In longer Qwen trajectories, single-position edits become less effective at later layers, while span-wide and repeated edits reduce attack success on the same evaluation set. Removing the learned channel subspace preserves role decoding, yet effective intervention directions transfer poorly across the tested channels.
AI.conclusion: The findings distinguish a readable role signal from an effective behavioral intervention. Depth (layer) matters in controlled tool choice, whereas position and context also matter in attack trajectories. Readable role representations are therefore not sufficient for effective mitigation, and the two properties should be evaluated separately.

title: MESH-Harness: Self-Improving Agent Harnesses via Bandit-Guided Compositional Evolution
summary: An agent harness is the code that organizes context, maintains state, and coordinates tool calls for a language model. We study how to improve the harness under a limited evaluation budget while keeping model weights fixed. Our method, MESH-Harness, organizes each harness into functional modules with explicit role-specific interfaces, allowing alternative implementations of each module to be substituted and recombined. It uses shared module representations and full-covariance LinUCB to score candidate combinations based on predicted performance and exploration value. Mixed-start coordinate ascent selects complete configurations for evaluation without enumerating the combinatorial space. Validation traces then guide local code edits, and the resulting candidates are incorporated into fixed-capacity role-specific pools for subsequent recombination. On text tasks, retrieval-augmented mathematical reasoning, code generation, and interactive scientific tasks, MESH-Harness outperforms Meta-Harness by 5.70, 7.01, 2.00, and 5.00 points, respectively, under matched candidate-evaluation budgets. Iterative harness optimization improves MESH-Harness by 5.63-7.79 points over its first-round configurations. For the reported configurations, aggregate test-time cost is 44.2% lower than that of Meta-Harness, while total cost including search is 14.6% lower. These results show that combining module-level design reuse with feedback-driven compositional search can systematically improve agent harnesses while keeping overall optimization cost under control.

AI.tldr: MESH-Harness optimizes agent harnesses under a fixed evaluation budget and fixed model weights by decomposing harnesses into functional modules with role-specific interfaces, then searching over recombinations of module implementations via a LinUCB-based scorer and mixed-start coordinate ascent.
AI.motivation: The agent harness—the code that organizes context, maintains state, and coordinates tool calls—strongly affects language-model agent performance, but improving it is difficult under limited evaluation budgets and with model weights held fixed.
AI.method: Harnesses are organized into functional modules with explicit role-specific interfaces so alternative implementations can be substituted and recombined. Shared module representations and full-covariance LinUCB score candidate combinations by predicted performance and exploration value. Mixed-start coordinate ascent selects complete configurations without enumerating the combinatorial space. Validation traces guide local code edits, and resulting candidates enter fixed-capacity role-specific pools for later recombination.
AI.result: On text tasks, retrieval-augmented mathematical reasoning, code generation, and interactive scientific tasks, MESH-Harness beats Meta-Harness by 5.70, 7.01, 2.00, and 5.00 points under matched candidate-evaluation budgets. Iterative optimization adds 5.63–7.79 points over first-round configurations. Aggregate test-time cost is 44.2% lower, and total cost including search 14.6% lower, than Meta-Harness for the reported configurations.
AI.conclusion: Combining module-level design reuse with feedback-driven compositional search can systematically improve agent harnesses while keeping overall optimization cost controlled.

title: AgentDiscover: Autonomous Discovery with Minimal Search Scaffolding
summary: Frameworks that use large language models for scientific discovery typically rely on a fixed, human-designed algorithm that decides what the model sees at each step, leaving the model only the role of proposer. The model knows nothing of the search beyond what it is shown. As models grow more capable, a question arises: does a search strategy chosen by a human before the run scale better than promoting the model from proposer to planner and letting it own the search? The Bitter Lesson suggests that choosing the strategy in advance is the kind of hand-designed structure that general methods eventually outscale. We introduce AgentDiscover, in which a coding agent plans the search using its context as working memory, runs experiments, and records every attempt in a database of ideas, candidates, and their relations. This database serves as the agent's long-term memory and is structured so that the selection rules of classical algorithms such as MAP-Elites and Monte Carlo tree search each reduce to a single query, which the agent is free to use, combine, or replace. A server maintains the database and steers the agent after every submission, keeping it on course over long runs. In our experiments, AgentDiscover is more cost-efficient than existing frameworks, reaching better scores at lower cost. On tasks in kernel engineering, biology, algorithm design, and mathematics, AgentDiscover outperforms prior discovery frameworks. Its programs would have placed first among human competitors in seven past AtCoder heuristic contests, and on eleven mathematical and systems optimization tasks it matches or exceeds every baseline that uses the same model. Our code is available at https://github.com/mhdfb/AgentDiscover.

AI.tldr: AgentDiscover promotes an LLM coding agent from proposer to planner: the agent owns the search, using a structured database of ideas and candidates as long-term memory, with a server steering it after each submission. It is more cost-efficient and outperforms prior discovery frameworks across kernel engineering, biology, algorithm design, and mathematics.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based scientific discovery frameworks rely on a fixed, human-designed algorithm that dictates what the model sees at each step, restricting the model to the role of proposer with no awareness of the broader search. Given increasingly capable models, the authors ask whether a human-chosen, pre-run search strategy scales better than letting the model itself plan and own the search. The Bitter Lesson suggests hand-designed structure is eventually outscaled by general methods.
AI.method: AgentDiscover lets a coding agent plan the search, use its context as working memory, run experiments, and record every attempt in a database of ideas, candidates, and their relations. The database acts as long-term memory and is structured so that selection rules of classical algorithms (MAP-Elites, Monte Carlo tree search) each reduce to a single query, which the agent may use, combine, or replace. A server maintains the database and steers the agent after every submission, keeping it on course over long runs.
AI.result: AgentDiscover is more cost-efficient than existing frameworks, reaching better scores at lower cost. It outperforms prior discovery frameworks on tasks in kernel engineering, biology, algorithm design, and mathematics. Its programs would have placed first among human competitors in seven past AtCoder heuristic contests, and on eleven mathematical and systems optimization tasks it matches or exceeds every baseline using the same model.
AI.conclusion: Promoting the model from proposer to planner—letting it own the search rather than following a fixed human-designed strategy—yields a more scalable, cost-efficient discovery framework. The structured memory database and server-side steering together enable strong, general performance across diverse domains. Code is available at https://github.com/mhdfb/AgentDiscover.

title: EnGRICH: Enhancing Generative Reward Modeling with Critiques from Humans
summary: Generative reward models (GRMs) are important for LLM optimization. Unlike scalar reward models, GRMs generate natural-language critiques alongside preference judgments, providing finer-grained evaluation signals. Their effectiveness depends heavily on critique reliability. However, existing GRM training typically uses final preference correctness as outcome supervision. Because the preference outcome space is highly constrained, unreliable critiques can still yield correct outcomes and thus be reinforced. Recent work leverages human critiques for process supervision, but such critiques are scarce and are often reduced to scalar rewards, leaving their fine-grained evaluative information underutilized. We argue that evaluative criteria learned from human critiques can be generalized to broader outcome-only preference data. To this end, we propose \textbf{EnGRICH}, a GRM training framework that pairs the GRM with a training-time MetaCritic learned from a small set of human critiques. MetaCritic constructs response-specific rubrics and uses them to evaluate the evidence coverage and correctness of generated critiques. The resulting signals provide both process rewards for fine-grained credit assignment and structured guidance for exploring better critiques. During GRM training, MetaCritic is further optimized to generalize human-grounded evaluative criteria to outcome-only data. At inference, the trained GRM operates independently. Experiments across seven reward-model benchmarks show that EnGRICH consistently improves over competitive baselines, while further analyses validate the effectiveness of its core mechanisms.

AI.tldr: EnGRICH trains a generative reward model alongside a MetaCritic learned from scarce human critiques; the MetaCritic builds response-specific rubrics to assess critique evidence coverage and correctness, providing process rewards and structured guidance that generalize human evaluative criteria to outcome-only preference data.
AI.motivation: Generative reward models (GRMs) produce natural-language critiques with preference judgments, giving finer-grained signals than scalar reward models, but their effectiveness hinges on critique reliability. Existing GRM training relies on final preference correctness as outcome supervision; since the preference outcome space is highly constrained, unreliable critiques can still produce correct outcomes and get reinforced. Prior work using human critiques for process supervision is limited because such critiques are scarce and often collapsed into scalar rewards, underutilizing their fine-grained evaluative information.
AI.method: The proposed EnGRICH framework pairs the GRM with a training-time MetaCritic learned from a small set of human critiques. MetaCritic constructs response-specific rubrics and applies them to evaluate the evidence coverage and correctness of generated critiques. These signals yield process rewards for fine-grained credit assignment and structured guidance for exploring better critiques. During GRM training, MetaCritic is further optimized to generalize human-grounded evaluative criteria to outcome-only data. At inference, the trained GRM operates independently.
AI.result: Experiments across seven reward-model benchmarks show that EnGRICH consistently outperforms competitive baselines, and further analyses validate the effectiveness of its core mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: The authors argue that evaluative criteria learned from scarce human critiques can be generalized to broader outcome-only preference data, and EnGRICH demonstrates this by improving GRM training through a MetaCritic-based process supervision and guidance mechanism, with the trained GRM deployable standalone at inference.

title: Learning Field Reconstruction from Incomplete Data by Globally Correcting Local Estimates
summary: Reconstructing physical fields from training samples that are always incomplete requires learning spatial structure from fragmented observations.Existing context--query work establishes how held-out observations provide valid training targets, but this does not make the complete-field distribution identifiable when every training field is incomplete.With finite data, weak evidence of sharp transitions and localized variations can further favor averaged predictions that attenuate local detail.A structural prior is therefore needed to favor plausible completions; local spatial relationships offer one grounded in the observations.We propose a locally constructed, globally revisable estimator that explicitly learns local field estimates and subsequently corrects them using full-domain observations.A shared coordinate-conditioned predictor learns from incomplete patches, allowing relatively well-observed neighborhoods to provide direct supervision of local structure.Its overlapping predictions are reconciled into an observation-conditioned consensus field.A full-domain estimator retains the original observations and learns a residual correction around this frozen field estimate, allowing locally constructed structure to be revised by broader evidence.The local estimate serves as both an explicit input, accompanied by its discrepancies with the observations, and a prediction starting point that the global model can revise.On three real-world ocean datasets with authentic observation gaps, our estimator achieves the lowest MSE and highest PSNR on withheld source-supported values, reducing MSE by 28.9\%--34.5\% against the strongest external baseline.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a two-stage estimator for reconstructing complete physical fields from fragmented, incomplete observations: a shared coordinate-conditioned predictor learns local structure from incomplete patches and reconciles overlapping predictions into a consensus field, which a full-domain estimator then revises via residual correction. It achieves the lowest MSE and highest PSNR on three real-world ocean datasets, reducing MSE by 28.9%–34.5% over the strongest baseline.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing physical fields from training samples that are always incomplete requires learning spatial structure from fragmented observations. Existing context-query work establishes that held-out observations yield valid training targets, but this does not render the complete-field distribution identifiable when every training field is incomplete. With finite data, weak evidence of sharp transitions and localized variations can favor averaged predictions that attenuate local detail. A structural prior is therefore needed to favor plausible completions, and local spatial relationships provide one grounded in the observations.
AI.method: A locally constructed, globally revisable estimator that explicitly learns local field estimates and then corrects them using full-domain observations. A shared coordinate-conditioned predictor learns from incomplete patches, letting relatively well-observed neighborhoods directly supervise local structure. Its overlapping predictions are reconciled into an observation-conditioned consensus field. A full-domain estimator retains the original observations and learns a residual correction around this frozen field estimate, so locally constructed structure can be revised by broader evidence. The local estimate serves both as an explicit input—along with its discrepancies with the observations—and as a prediction starting point for the global model to revise.
AI.result: On three real-world ocean datasets with authentic observation gaps, the estimator achieves the lowest MSE and highest PSNR on withheld source-supported values, reducing MSE by 28.9%–34.5% against the strongest external baseline.
AI.conclusion: The proposed locally constructed, globally revisable estimator effectively supplies the structural prior needed for incomplete-field reconstruction, combining coordinate-conditioned local learning with full-domain residual correction. Its consistent gains over strong baselines on real ocean data indicate that decomposing reconstruction into local construction and global revision is a practical and effective strategy for handling authentic observation gaps.

title: Sibyl: An Efficient Small-large Model Collaboration Framework for Long-horizon Tasks
summary: Small language models (SLMs) offer a promising foundation for on-device agents through low-latency, resource-efficient inference, yet limited reasoning and planning capabilities constrain their performance on long-horizon tasks requiring multi-step interaction with the environment. Step-level collaboration between SLMs and larger cloud-hosted models can bridge this gap, but identifying states that warrant cloud assistance remains challenging: the contribution of each cloud call is entangled with subsequent actions and can be assessed only from the final task outcome. Compounding this challenge, the SLM must balance two competing objectives: maximizing task success and minimizing cloud calls. To address this, we propose Sibyl, an algorithm that trains SLM agents to selectively consult cloud models at the step level and internalize their guidance for subsequent decisions, achieving strong task performance with minimal cloud reliance. Sibyl follows a three-stage training pipeline that (1) builds a robust base policy through consultation-free self-evolving reinforcement learning (RL); (2) cold-starts consultation behavior via decisive-disagreement state mining; and (3) jointly optimizes consultation decisions and guidance internalization through consultation-aware RL. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate that Sibyl, using only a 0.6B-parameter model, outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, including agent training and routing methods, by 95.2% and 80.4% in success rate while averaging only 0.8 and 3.9 cloud calls per trajectory, respectively.

AI.tldr: Sibyl trains small language model agents to selectively consult cloud models at the step level and internalize their guidance, achieving strong long-horizon task performance with minimal cloud calls.
AI.motivation: SLMs enable low-latency, resource-efficient on-device agents but have limited reasoning and planning for long-horizon tasks. Step-level collaboration with larger cloud models can bridge this gap, yet deciding when cloud assistance is warranted is hard: the value of each cloud call is entangled with subsequent actions and only assessable from the final outcome. The agent must also trade off task success against cloud-call cost.
AI.method: Sibyl is a three-stage training pipeline: (1) build a robust base policy via consultation-free self-evolving reinforcement learning; (2) cold-start consultation behavior through decisive-disagreement state mining; (3) jointly optimize consultation decisions and guidance internalization via consultation-aware RL.
AI.result: On ALFWorld and WebShop, Sibyl with only a 0.6B-parameter model outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, including agent training and routing methods, by 95.2% and 80.4% in success rate, while averaging only 0.8 and 3.9 cloud calls per trajectory, respectively.
AI.conclusion: Selective, step-level consultation combined with guidance internalization lets a small on-device agent approach cloud-assisted performance while keeping cloud reliance minimal.

title: MMPostTrainBench: Benchmarking Autonomous Research for Multimodal Post-Training
summary: Autonomous research seeks sustained model improvements through iterative experimentation and feedback. LLM agents show promise in automating machine learning and language-model post-training, but their ability to sustain multimodal improvement remains unclear. We introduce MMPostTrainBench, a benchmark spanning eight tasks in image, audio, video, and joint audio-video understanding and image-grounded software repair. Agents operate from a common base model within fixed budgets, using development feedback before independent evaluation of their submitted models. Evaluation covers target and non-target model outcomes, iterative model improvement and selection, and research integrity. Across all eight tasks, 52.1% of model--task means fall below the base, and evaluated submissions also exhibit non-target regressions. Model performance does not consistently improve across research iterations, and agents do not reliably select the best evaluated candidate for submission; final submissions trail that candidate by up to 5.38 percentage points. Extending autonomous research from text-only to multimodal tasks introduces additional sources of error in perception, cross-modal alignment, and temporal grounding. The observed regressions and selection gaps highlight the need to balance targeted improvements with non-target capability preservation and to retain gains across research iterations. These requirements motivate MMResearch, a multimodal research framework that connects media-grounded evidence to hypotheses and interventions, carries findings across rounds through hierarchical memory, and retains candidates using development evaluation. Added to existing code-agent runtimes, it improves submitted-model accuracy by up to 7.75 percentage points for Claude Opus 4.8 with Claude Code and 2.33 points for GPT-5.6-sol with Codex.

AI.tldr: MMPostTrainBench benchmarks autonomous multimodal post-training across eight tasks, exposing widespread regressions and candidate-selection gaps; MMResearch, a hierarchical-memory multimodal research framework, mitigates them with up to 7.75-point accuracy gains.
AI.motivation: LLM agents can automate machine learning and language-model post-training, but it is unclear whether they can sustain iterative multimodal improvement. Extending autonomous research from text-only to multimodal settings introduces new error sources in perception, cross-modal alignment, and temporal grounding, so the authors need both a diagnostic benchmark and a framework addressing these failures.
AI.method: The authors introduce MMPostTrainBench, spanning eight tasks in image, audio, video, and joint audio-video understanding plus image-grounded software repair. Agents start from a common base model under fixed budgets, use development feedback, and submit models for independent evaluation; evaluation measures target and non-target outcomes, iterative improvement and selection, and research integrity. They then propose MMResearch, which links media-grounded evidence to hypotheses and interventions, carries findings across rounds via hierarchical memory, and retains candidates using development evaluation, and integrate it into existing code-agent runtimes.
AI.result: Across all eight tasks, 52.1% of model-task means fall below the base model, and submissions show non-target regressions. Performance does not consistently improve across iterations, and agents fail to reliably select the best evaluated candidate, with final submissions trailing by up to 5.38 percentage points. MMResearch improves submitted-model accuracy by up to 7.75 points for Claude Opus 4.8 with Claude Code and 2.33 points for GPT-5.6-sol with Codex.
AI.conclusion: Autonomous multimodal research currently suffers regressions and selection gaps, so it must balance targeted improvements with preservation of non-target capabilities and retain gains across iterations. MMResearch, built on media-grounded evidence, hierarchical memory, and development-based candidate retention, demonstrably addresses these requirements within existing code-agent runtimes.

title: CASE: Cost-Aware Stopping for Efficient Long-Video Agents
summary: Long-video agents can actively gather question-relevant evidence, but they typically leave a central decision implicit: when has the agent seen enough to answer? We propose CASE, a plug-in termination framework that frames this decision as policy-conditioned sequential stopping. At each causal checkpoint, CASE combines an auxiliary multiple-choice assessment of accumulated evidence with the host agent's execution state. From complete native trajectories, we construct a cost-aware target that compares answering now with stopping later along the same search path, accounting jointly for answer correctness and the full cost of continued reasoning. A lightweight Ridge regressor learns this decision gap and produces STOP/CONTINUE decisions. We evaluate three vision-language models with VideoSeek and AVP. On Video-MME, end-to-end accuracy changes by +0.67 percentage points on average while CASE reduces model-token use by 53.63%. The same frozen policies then transfer zero-shot to LongVideoBench and MLVU, with end-to-end accuracy changes of +3.38 and +4.58 points while saving 58.78% and 51.28% of model tokens, respectively. Across all agent-model-benchmark combinations, CASE attains the highest accuracy-efficiency Pareto-frontier coverage among the compared stopping methods (83.3%) at the selected operating points. Online execution preserves this favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off and additionally reduces measured runtime by 54.1% on average. CASE provides a plug-in termination framework for long-video reasoning agents, enabling them to decide when further evidence acquisition is no longer worthwhile.

AI.tldr: CASE is a plug-in termination framework that lets long-video agents decide when they have gathered enough evidence to answer, framing it as policy-conditioned sequential stopping and using a Ridge regressor with a cost-aware target to issue STOP/CONTINUE decisions.
AI.motivation: Long-video agents actively gather question-relevant evidence but leave a central decision implicit: when has the agent seen enough to answer? This missing termination criterion leads to unnecessary continued reasoning and token cost.
AI.method: At each causal checkpoint, CASE combines an auxiliary multiple-choice assessment of accumulated evidence with the host agent's execution state. From complete native trajectories, it constructs a cost-aware target comparing answering now versus stopping later along the same search path, jointly accounting for answer correctness and the full cost of continued reasoning. A lightweight Ridge regressor learns this decision gap and outputs STOP/CONTINUE decisions.
AI.result: Evaluated on three vision-language models with VideoSeek and AVP: on Video-MME, accuracy changes +0.67 points on average while reducing model-token use by 53.63%. Frozen policies transfer zero-shot to LongVideoBench and MLVU with accuracy changes of +3.38 and +4.58 points and token savings of 58.78% and 51.28%. CASE attains the highest accuracy-efficiency Pareto-frontier coverage (83.3%) among compared stopping methods. Online execution reduces measured runtime by 54.1% on average.
AI.conclusion: CASE provides a plug-in termination framework for long-video reasoning agents, enabling them to decide when further evidence acquisition is no longer worthwhile, preserving favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-offs while cutting tokens and runtime.

title: PharmAgent: Constraint-Aware Search with Frozen Language Models for Molecular Optimization
summary: Molecular optimization must improve target activity and satisfy developability constraints within limited evaluation budgets. Classical methods require tailored rules or training to incorporate chemical instructions and property feedback. Frozen language models can condition edits on this information, but need explicit constraint control and relevant experience. We therefore present PharmAgent, a constraint-aware molecular search method driven by adaptive external state. Its Lagrangian controller translates violations in accepted states into accumulated constraint pressure, keeping this history separate from current property measurements. Structure-indexed replay complements this feedback with relevant evaluated transitions that guide subsequent proposals. As a curriculum progressively activates constraints, candidates and the incumbent are compared under the same current objective, and the accepted state determines the next multiplier update. We derive an exact identity that characterizes how accepted-state violations accumulate in the controller's multipliers. Across five tasks with five independent runs, PharmAgent achieves a summed area under the target-score curves (AUC) of 3.9208 in target-only search, improving over MOLLEO by 37.3%. With online constraints, it achieves a property-adjusted AUC of 0.7076, improving over the strongest online baseline, ExLLM, by 53.8%. These results rank first among all evaluated methods in both target-only and constraint-aware search. The online comparison covers all five baseline frameworks. The full system leads every ablation variant in target quality, property-adjusted performance, and Pareto hypervolume. All five molecular cases reach feasible final states, documenting target gains and trade-offs.

AI.tldr: PharmAgent, a constraint-aware molecular search method using a frozen LLM guided by adaptive external state, ranks first on five tasks in both target-only and constraint-aware molecular optimization.
AI.motivation: Molecular optimization must improve target activity while satisfying developability constraints under limited evaluation budgets. Classical methods need tailored rules or training to incorporate chemical instructions and property feedback, while frozen language models can condition edits on such information but lack explicit constraint control and relevant experience.
AI.method: PharmAgent uses a frozen LLM with adaptive external state: a Lagrangian controller translates violations in accepted states into accumulated constraint pressure, kept separate from current property measurements; structure-indexed replay supplies relevant evaluated transitions to guide proposals; a curriculum progressively activates constraints; candidates and the incumbent are compared under the same current objective, and the accepted state drives the next multiplier update. An exact identity characterizes how accepted-state violations accumulate in the multipliers.
AI.result: Across five tasks with five independent runs, PharmAgent reaches a summed target-score AUC of 3.9208 in target-only search (+37.3% over MOLLEO) and a property-adjusted AUC of 0.7076 under online constraints (+53.8% over ExLLM), ranking first among all evaluated methods in both settings. It leads every ablation variant in target quality, property-adjusted performance, and Pareto hypervolume, and all five molecular cases reach feasible final states.
AI.conclusion: PharmAgent demonstrates that constraint-aware molecular search driven by adaptive external state, combining a Lagrangian controller and structure-indexed replay, outperforms baselines and ablations while reliably producing feasible molecules with documented target gains and trade-offs.

title: TeleTune: Evolving Agent Skills From Offline Telemetry
summary: Computer-use agents need to capture procedural knowledge of how people use software. User telemetry offers a scalable source of this knowledge. However, learning reusable skills from these logs requires addressing three challenges: (1) Goal Underspecification, since logs do not record the goal behind each action; (2) Non-Replayability, since past activity cannot be replayed to evaluate skill updates; and (3) Interleaved Trajectories, since logs may mix several tasks without marking their boundaries. To address these, we introduce TeleTune, a framework for learning a textual skill library from offline logs without recorded goals, cannot be replayed during optimization, and may interleave tasks. TeleTune uses action-prediction errors on logged trajectories to propose library edits and keep only those that improve held-out action-prediction accuracy, which we call skill-guided progress. The learned workflows also enable retrieval of demonstrations that cover the subgoals of a new task. At test time, the agent is provided with the learned library and the workflow-based retrieved demonstrations. Experiments on WorkArena and Online-Mind2Web show that TeleTune outperforms random retrieval, Agent Workflow Memory (AWM), and their combination. We find that the best baseline varies by setting, whereas TeleTune achieves average success rates of 77.1% and 80.6%, respectively, improving over the strongest baseline on each benchmark by 6.7% and 7.7%. Under the heaviest perturbation of the WorkArena training data,TeleTune keeps the highest average success rate at 68.5%, 6.3% above the strongest baseline. Our analyses show (1) skill optimization and workflow-based retrieval are complementary, (2) optimizing on fixed logs costs 5 to 75 times fewer tokens than validating the same edits with live episodes, (3) skill-guided progress tracks the live success rate.

AI.tldr: TeleTune learns a textual skill library from offline, goal-less, non-replayable, interleaved user logs by using action-prediction error on logged trajectories to propose and accept library edits, then retrieves workflow-based demonstrations for new tasks at test time.
AI.motivation: Computer-use agents need procedural knowledge of how people use software, and user telemetry is a scalable source. However, learning reusable skills from these logs faces three challenges: Goal Underspecification (logs lack recorded goals), Non-Replayability (past activity cannot be replayed to evaluate skill updates), and Interleaved Trajectories (logs mix tasks without boundaries).
AI.method: TeleTune learns a textual skill library from offline logs without recorded goals, without replay during optimization, and with possibly interleaved tasks. It uses action-prediction errors on logged trajectories to propose library edits, keeping only edits that improve held-out action-prediction accuracy (skill-guided progress). The learned workflows also enable retrieval of demonstrations covering subgoals of a new task. At test time, the agent receives the learned library and workflow-based retrieved demonstrations.
AI.result: On WorkArena and Online-Mind2Web, TeleTune outperforms random retrieval, Agent Workflow Memory (AWM), and their combination. The best baseline varies by setting, while TeleTune achieves average success rates of 77.1% and 80.6%, improving over the strongest baseline per benchmark by 6.7% and 7.7%. Under the heaviest WorkArena training-data perturbation, TeleTune achieves the highest average success rate at 68.5%, 6.3% above the strongest baseline.
AI.conclusion: Analysis shows that (1) skill optimization and workflow-based retrieval are complementary, (2) optimizing on fixed logs costs 5 to 75 times fewer tokens than validating the same edits with live episodes, and (3) skill-guided progress tracks the live success rate.

title: AI Safety via Debate is Compromised by Cognitive Biases
summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has played a central role in making large language models responsive to human instructions. However, human evaluators often favor flattering or persuasive responses over truthful ones, creating incentives for models to appeal to evaluators at the expense of accuracy. AI safety via debate has been proposed as a way to improve the supervision of language models: in this paradigm, two agents argue opposing positions and challenge each other's claims, potentially exposing falsehoods to the adjudicator. A central premise of AI safety via debate is that truthful arguments are easier to defend than false ones under adversarial scrutiny. In this work, we investigate whether this advantage persists when debaters use rhetorical strategies that exploit biases in human judgment. Inspired by competitive debate, we construct 68 LLM-generated dialogues about detective mysteries with known culprits, spanning four interventions: anchoring, fallacy oversight, pro-jargon, and verbosity. We apply each intervention to either the side advocating for the true culprit or the side advocating for an innocent suspect, allowing us to distinguish influence on adjudication from correctness. In a study with 369 participants, we find that, pooled across bias types, these interventions significantly shift judgments toward the manipulated side. These findings expose a vulnerability in debate-based supervision: human adjudication is sensitive to manipulative rhetorical strategies.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether AI safety via debate remains robust when debaters deploy manipulative rhetorical strategies, finding that four bias-exploiting interventions (anchoring, fallacy oversight, pro-jargon, verbosity) significantly shift human adjudication toward the manipulated side and thus expose a vulnerability in debate-based supervision.
AI.motivation: RLHF makes LLMs instruction-responsive but can reward flattery and persuasiveness over truthfulness. AI safety via debate is proposed as a remedy, resting on the premise that truthful arguments are easier to defend under adversarial scrutiny. This work asks whether that advantage survives when debaters exploit biases in human judgment, since debate-based supervision ultimately depends on human adjudicators.
AI.method: Inspired by competitive debate, the authors construct 68 LLM-generated dialogues about detective mysteries with known culprits. Four interventions are used: anchoring, fallacy oversight, pro-jargon, and verbosity. Each intervention is applied either to the side advocating the true culprit or to the side advocating an innocent suspect, which separates influence on adjudication from argumentative correctness. A study with 369 participants measures resulting judgment shifts.
AI.result: Pooled across bias types, the interventions significantly shift participants' judgments toward the manipulated side. Applying interventions to the true-culprit versus innocent-suspect side allows the observed shifts to be attributed to rhetorical manipulation of adjudication rather than to the correctness of the position being defended.
AI.conclusion: Human adjudication in debate-based supervision is sensitive to manipulative rhetorical strategies, revealing a vulnerability in the debate paradigm. The premise that truthful arguments are easier to defend does not hold when debaters exploit human cognitive biases.

title: Hallucination Across the Reasoning Lifecycle: Interface Visibility, Causal Evidence, and Release Control in Large Reasoning Models
comment: 35 pages, 8 figures, 9 tables. Electronic supplementary materials S1-S7 are included as ancillary files
summary: Reasoning errors can propagate into later decisions and memory. This survey synthesizes 312 papers and first-party reports on text-based reasoning hallucinations around three questions: what evidence is observable, what study designs establish, and which corrective actions the evidence supports. UIPCA records unsupported premises (U), invalid inferences (I), dependent reuse (P), visible answer-trace consistency (C), and action-policy failures (A). Across 58 reviewed sources, no comparison establishes that a specified intervention improves reasoning while reducing factual reliability under matched conditions. The synthesis connects diagnosis to verification, repair, selective release, and persistent-state control across memory, tools, and training feedback.

AI.tldr: A survey of 312 papers and first-party reports on text-based reasoning hallucinations, organized around three questions—what evidence is observable, what study designs establish, and which corrective actions are supported. It introduces UIPCA, a five-part taxonomy of reasoning failure, and reports that among 58 reviewed sources no comparison shows a specified intervention improving reasoning while reducing factual reliability under matched conditions. Findings are linked to diagnosis, verification, repair, selective release, and persistent-state control.
AI.motivation: Reasoning errors do not stay local: they propagate into downstream decisions and into memory. The paper aims to consolidate fragmented evidence on text-based reasoning hallucinations so that diagnostic signals, study designs, and corrective measures can be assessed on a common footing.
AI.method: Survey and evidence synthesis over 312 papers and first-party reports, structured by three questions (observable evidence, what designs establish, which corrective actions the evidence supports). Failures are coded with UIPCA: unsupported premises (U), invalid inferences (I), dependent reuse (P), visible answer-trace consistency (C), and action-policy failures (A).
AI.result: Across 58 reviewed sources, no comparison establishes that a specified intervention improves reasoning while reducing factual reliability under matched conditions.
AI.conclusion: The synthesis links diagnosis to verification, repair, selective release, and persistent-state control spanning memory, tools, and training feedback. The absence of an established reasoning-versus-reliability trade-off highlights a gap in current evaluation and intervention evidence.

title: Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning with Stable Temporal Abstraction for Language Model Agents
summary: Hierarchical reinforcement learning improves long-horizon control by organizing primitive actions around persistent subgoals and assigning credit at multiple temporal scales. Recent hierarchical language agents bring these benefits to interactive tasks by explicitly separating subgoal planning from action execution. We observe, however, that an explicit hierarchy does not by itself determine how stable the resulting temporal abstraction is: the learned boundary policy may replace the subgoal almost every turn, making it effectively transient, or retain a subgoal after it has stopped being appropriate. We call this temporal abstraction instability. We propose Stable Temporal Abstraction via Constrained Optimization (STAC), a constrained boundary-policy optimization method that represents premature replanning and stale persistence as constraint costs. STAC applies the resulting Lagrangian costs only to the sampled boundary decision, leaving the underlying algorithm's rewards, critic targets, subgoal advantages, and primitive-action advantages unchanged. Across two backbones and two benchmarks, STAC improves success over a strong hierarchical baseline by $8.1$ and $7.9$ points on ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen3-0.6B, and by $23.5$ and $15.8$ points with Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies "temporal abstraction instability" in hierarchical language agents—where boundary policies either replan too frequently or retain stale subgoals—and proposes STAC, a constrained boundary-policy optimization method that treats premature replanning and stale persistence as constraint costs, yielding substantial success gains across backbones and benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Hierarchical reinforcement learning benefits long-horizon control via persistent subgoals and multi-scale credit assignment, and recent hierarchical language agents exploit this by separating subgoal planning from action execution. However, the authors observe that an explicit hierarchy alone does not guarantee stable temporal abstraction: the learned boundary policy may replace subgoals almost every turn (transient) or keep inappropriate ones (stale persistence). This "temporal abstraction instability" is the problem the paper targets.
AI.method: The authors propose Stable Temporal Abstraction via Constrained Optimization (STAC). STAC is a constrained boundary-policy optimization method that models premature replanning and stale persistence explicitly as constraint costs. It applies the resulting Lagrangian costs only to the sampled boundary decision, deliberately keeping the underlying algorithm's rewards, critic targets, subgoal advantages, and primitive-action advantages unchanged.
AI.result: Across two backbones (Qwen3-0.6B and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct) and two benchmarks (ALFWorld and WebShop), STAC improves success rates over a strong hierarchical baseline: +8.1 and +7.9 points with Qwen3-0.6B on ALFWorld and WebShop respectively, and +23.5 and +15.8 points with Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on the same benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Explicit temporal hierarchy does not by itself ensure stable temporal abstraction. Framing boundary-policy instability as constrained optimization over premature replanning and stale persistence—while leaving the rest of the learning pipeline untouched—substantially improves hierarchical language agents' task success, indicating that boundary-decision stability is a critical, isolable factor in hierarchical agent performance.

title: CodeForge-MA: Execution-Verified Multi-Agent Learning with Language-Conditioned LoRA for Multilingual Code Generation
summary: Large language models for code generation often fail on execution, multilingual coverage, and contamination control, especially under frozen backbone constraints. We present CodeForge-MA, a unified framework that improves code synthesis through a multi-agent data forge, execution verified reinforced instruction tuning, and a language conditioned mixture of LoRA adapters.
