AI.conclusion: Framing text revision as a Nash equilibrium game provides both theoretical justification and a practical decoding algorithm that improves question-answering performance over substantially larger autoregressive baselines, trading extra test-time computation for quality.

title: Data-Driven Personas for Survey Simulation: Insights into Simulation Alignment Across Data-Access Regimes
summary: However, many existing steering approaches rely on target-domain human data for fine-tuning or prompting that is costly to collect and raises privacy concerns. In this paper, we study demographic group-level survey simulation, where personas induced from heterogeneous, anonymized public behavioral data condition agents that simulate responses of individuals from specific demographic groups. We examine whether representative personas can be induced from diverse sources and analyze how the domain, scale, and granularity of the source data affect survey simulation alignment. We find that personas induced from out-of-domain sources rarely outperform simulations conditioned only on basic demographic information, largely due to population mismatch. However, when personas are accurately assigned to the target demographic groups, alignment improves substantially. Finally, personas induced from target-domain survey data generalize better as more survey question history becomes available, suggesting that richer behavioral evidence enables more stable persona trait inference that transfers to better unseen questions simulation alignment.

AI.tldr: This paper studies demographic group-level survey simulation, inducing personas from anonymized public behavioral data to condition agents simulating individual survey responses, and analyzes how source data domain, scale, and granularity affect alignment.
AI.motivation: Existing steering approaches for survey simulation rely on target-domain human data for fine-tuning or prompting, which is costly to collect and raises privacy concerns. The authors aim to avoid this dependency by using heterogeneous, anonymized public behavioral data to induce personas.
AI.method: The authors induce representative personas from diverse, anonymized behavioral data sources and use them to condition agents that simulate responses of individuals from specific demographic groups. They systematically vary the domain (in- vs. out-of-domain), scale, and granularity of source data, and compare personas against conditions using only basic demographic information, evaluating simulation alignment with target survey responses.
AI.result: Personas induced from out-of-domain sources rarely outperform simulations conditioned only on basic demographic information, largely due to population mismatch. When personas are accurately assigned to target demographic groups, alignment improves substantially. Personas induced from target-domain survey data generalize better as more survey question history becomes available.
AI.conclusion: Representative personas can be induced from diverse public behavioral sources, but their effectiveness depends critically on accurate demographic matching and domain relevance. Richer behavioral evidence enables more stable persona trait inference, yielding better alignment on unseen survey questions.

title: Measurement-First Auditing of Agentic Leaderboards: Contamination Susceptibility, Matched-Control Re-evaluation, and Scorer Validation
summary: Agentic leaderboards increasingly evaluate systems on public benchmarks whose task statements and solution-bearing artifacts can remain accessible. We propose a measurement-first audit framework that distinguishes contamination claims according to the evidence required to support them. It separates three channels that require different evidence: training-time exposure, evaluation-time retrieval, and pipeline/scaffold leakage. Each channel is coded as open, partial, closed, or unknown under a fail-closed rule. Across nine Holistic Agent Leaderboard (HAL) configurations, none of the 27 channel assessments was coded closed, but incidents were confirmed in four configurations. We then apply the behavioral component of the framework to a reported file-localization gap on SWE-bench Verified, using an outcome-blind, same-repository matched-control design with symmetric prompt-leakage screening, paired and repository-aware uncertainty analyses, and scorer validation, evaluated on GPT-4.1 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Among the 100 pairs retained after symmetric screening and the pair-integrity exclusion, GPT-4.1 showed a $+10.0$-point pair-weighted Top-3 benchmark-associated gap, but the 95\% intervals from both the prespecified paired-bootstrap procedure and the post-hoc repository-balanced analysis included zero, leaving the benchmark-associated gap inconclusive. The reproduction scorer did not pass its validation gate: against consensus human labels, sufficient scorer sensitivity could not be established for either model, and both DeepSeek-V4-Flash firings on correct-gold comparisons were false positives. Without provenance evidence, appropriate controls, symmetric leakage screening, and validated scorers, stronger contamination claims are not warranted. The results do not establish training-data membership, contamination prevalence, or benchmark-induced score inflation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a measurement-first audit framework for contamination claims in agentic leaderboards, categorizing three leakage channels (training-time exposure, evaluation-time retrieval, pipeline/scaffold leakage) each coded open/partial/closed/unknown under a fail-closed rule. Across nine HAL configurations, no channel was coded closed yet incidents were confirmed in four; a behavioral audit of SWE-bench Verified file-localization found the benchmark-associated gap inconclusive and the reproduction scorer failing validation, so stronger contamination claims are unwarranted.
AI.motivation: Agentic leaderboards evaluate systems on public benchmarks whose task statements and solution-bearing artifacts may remain accessible, raising contamination concerns. Existing contamination claims vary in evidentiary strength, and different leakage channels require different types of evidence, so a structured, evidence-proportionate audit approach is needed.
AI.method: A measurement-first audit framework that distinguishes contamination claims by required evidence and separates three channels: training-time exposure, evaluation-time retrieval, and pipeline/scaffold leakage. Each channel is coded open, partial, closed, or unknown under a fail-closed rule. The framework's behavioral component is applied to a reported file-localization gap on SWE-bench Verified using an outcome-blind, same-repository matched-control design with symmetric prompt-leakage screening, paired and repository-aware uncertainty analyses, and scorer validation on GPT-4.1 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash.
AI.result: Across nine HAL configurations, none of the 27 channel assessments was coded closed, but incidents were confirmed in four configurations. Among 100 retained pairs, GPT-4.1 showed a +10.0-point pair-weighted Top-3 benchmark-associated gap, but 95% intervals from both the prespecified paired-bootstrap and post-hoc repository-balanced analyses included zero, rendering the gap inconclusive. The reproduction scorer failed its validation gate: sufficient sensitivity against consensus human labels could not be established for either model, and both DeepSeek-V4-Flash firings on correct-gold comparisons were false positives.
AI.conclusion: Without provenance evidence, appropriate controls, symmetric leakage screening, and validated scorers, stronger contamination claims are not warranted. The results do not establish training-data membership, contamination prevalence, or benchmark-induced score inflation.

title: Request Order Matters: Cache-History Sensitivity in Selective KV-Cache Reuse for Rolling Agents
summary: Long-running agents repeatedly call an LLM while retaining most of their document window, evicting old documents, and appending new ones. These rolling updates break exact prefix caching and motivate non-prefix KV-cache reuse with selective recomputation. We show that persistent KV-cache reuse with selective recomputation can be history-dependent: in our rolling-agent workload, an unchanged prompt can produce different answers depending on the requests processed before it. At a matched 5% recomputation budget, document-aligned recomputation reduces answer variation across request orders from 69.0% with CacheBlend's token top-$k$ policy to 26.1%. When each prompt is evaluated after a different sequence of preceding requests, document-aligned recomputation improves fidelity to full prefill by 34.5-52.5 percentage points over token top-$k$, while both policies achieve approximately 5.7$\times$ median TTFT speedup. Our ablation study shows that, in our rolling-agent workload, contiguity is the main factor associated with robust selective recomputation.

AI.tldr: Persistent KV-cache reuse with selective recomputation is history-dependent; document-aligned recomputation substantially reduces answer variation across request orders versus token top-k at matched recomputation budgets.
AI.motivation: Long-running agents repeatedly call an LLM while retaining most of their document window, evicting old documents, and appending new ones. These rolling updates break exact prefix caching, motivating non-prefix KV-cache reuse with selective recomputation. The paper investigates whether such reuse is history-dependent and how recomputation policy choice affects answer stability.
AI.method: The authors evaluate persistent KV-cache reuse with selective recomputation in a rolling-agent workload, comparing CacheBlend's token top-k policy against a document-aligned recomputation policy at a matched 5% recomputation budget. They measure answer variation across request orders and fidelity to full prefill when each prompt is evaluated after different sequences of preceding requests, and conduct an ablation study to identify the factor driving robust selective recomputation.
AI.result: At a matched 5% recomputation budget, document-aligned recomputation reduces answer variation across request orders from 69.0% (CacheBlend's token top-k) to 26.1%. When each prompt is evaluated after a different sequence of preceding requests, document-aligned recomputation improves fidelity to full prefill by 34.5-52.5 percentage points over token top-k, while both policies achieve approximately 5.7x median TTFT speedup. The ablation study indicates that contiguity is the main factor associated with robust selective recomputation in this workload.
AI.conclusion: Selective recomputation with persistent KV-cache reuse is history-dependent in rolling-agent workloads. Document-aligned (contiguous) recomputation yields more order-robust and higher-fidelity answers than token top-k at equal recomputation cost, with comparable TTFT speedups, establishing contiguity as the key factor for robust selective recomputation.

title: MiniCorp: The Last Mile of the AI Agent Firm
summary: The last mile toward enterprise AGI is a company that runs itself. Training and adapting such agents require longitudinal enterprise data, which remain scarce, costly to acquire, and often restricted by privacy constraints. Historical archives are also frequently incomplete and record only what actually happened. They cannot show the outcomes of alternative decisions. We introduce MiniCorp, an office simulator for studying how agents can collectively run a company while generating enterprise data at scale. Using an e-commerce company as a demonstration, MiniCorp connects two interacting worlds. The external world models customers, dynamic competitors, and market mechanisms. The internal world consists of agents that observe events, discuss their options, and make strategic decisions. These decisions have lasting effects on the market, and the resulting feedback informs the firm's later decisions. As the firm and market interact, MiniCorp continuously records the agents' communications and decisions. These records preserve the information available at the time and the business results that followed. Checkpointing allows the same situation to be replayed under different decisions, providing comparisons unavailable in static archives. We evaluate end-to-end fidelity against patterns reported in empirical studies of real markets. These evaluations provide agents with realistic market feedback and reduce the risk that they learn to exploit flaws in the simulator. Our experiments show agents coordinating across roles and adapting their decisions to market feedback. With explicit long-term strategic guidance, they also sustain advertising exploration despite weak early returns. MiniCorp thus provides an environment for studying AI-run companies and a scalable source of longitudinal and counterfactual enterprise data for agent training and evaluation.

AI.tldr: MiniCorp is an office simulator that lets LLM agents collectively run a company (demoed as an e-commerce firm) to study AI-run enterprises and generate scalable longitudinal and counterfactual enterprise data.
AI.motivation: The path toward enterprise AGI requires agents that can run a company, but training them needs longitudinal enterprise data that is scarce, costly, privacy-restricted, and often incomplete. Historical archives only record what happened, not the outcomes of alternative decisions, so they cannot support counterfactual learning.
AI.method: MiniCorp couples two interacting worlds: an external world modeling customers, dynamic competitors, and market mechanisms, and an internal world of agents that observe events, discuss options, and make strategic decisions. Decisions affect the market, and the resulting feedback informs later decisions. The simulator continuously records agent communications and decisions along with the information available at the time and subsequent business results. Checkpointing enables replaying the same situation under different decisions. End-to-end fidelity is evaluated against patterns from empirical market studies, providing realistic feedback and reducing the risk of agents exploiting simulator flaws.
AI.result: Experiments show agents coordinating across roles and adapting decisions to market feedback. With explicit long-term strategic guidance, they sustain advertising exploration despite weak early returns. Fidelity evaluations align the simulator with empirically reported market patterns.
AI.conclusion: MiniCorp offers an environment for studying AI-run companies and a scalable source of longitudinal and counterfactual enterprise data for agent training and evaluation.

title: VERA: Scaling Verifiable Environments for Agentic co-Evolution
summary: Competent agents need precise and verifiable environments, such as sandboxes that are resumable at any stage and evolve from observable evidence. However, most long-horizon work exposes how rare these are: for example, an agent in medical research must ground a finding, classify it, and write a report over dozens of dependent steps, yet recent environments score only the outcome. To address the challenges in stable training, we present VERA, which builds such environments at scale and lets agents evolve on them. VERA builds these environments from initial trajectories: an agent writes rubrics, executable checks, a judge verifies each sandbox, and only those that pass enter the training bank. On these environments, VERA alternates between two updates: train the model with rubric rewards, or edit the harness skills. We also create a verifier which gates model checkpoints and harness edits using explicit development-set acceptance criteria. This attribution distinguishes VERA's co-evolution from single-axis baselines: its updates target not only the cause but the outcome. With an open-source corpus of 9,000+ long-horizon verifiable environments, a 9B model paired with its co-evolved agent beats the strongest baseline by 10.3 and 13.0 points in the two domains. At 27B, it surpasses the baseline on AutoCoWorkBench (71.6) and AutoMedBench (80.7), transfers to unseen workflows, and retains general capabilities.

AI.tldr: VERA builds large-scale, resumable, outcome-verifiable sandbox environments from trajectories and co-evolves agents on them via rubric-reward training and harness-skill editing, gated by a verifier; it yields 9,000+ open environments and large gains on two long-horizon domains (e.g., 27B model reaching 71.6 AutoCoWorkBench, 80.7 AutoMedBench).
AI.motivation: Competent agents require precise, verifiable environments that are resumable at any stage and evolve from observable evidence, but such environments are rare. Most long-horizon benchmarks score only the final outcome over dozens of dependent steps (e.g., medical research: grounding a finding, classifying it, writing a report), making stable training and reliable attribution difficult.
AI.method: VERA constructs environments at scale from initial trajectories: an agent writes rubrics and executable checks, and a judge verifies each sandbox so only passing ones enter the training bank. On these environments VERA alternates two updates: training the model with rubric rewards, or editing harness skills. A verifier gates model checkpoints and harness edits using explicit development-set acceptance criteria, enabling attribution that targets both cause and outcome.
AI.result: With an open-source corpus of 9,000+ long-horizon verifiable environments, a 9B model with its co-evolved agent beats the strongest baseline by 10.3 and 13.0 points in the two domains. At 27B, it surpasses the baseline on AutoCoWorkBench (71.6) and AutoMedBench (80.7), transfers to unseen workflows, and retains general capabilities.
AI.conclusion: VERA provides scalable construction of resumable, verifiable long-horizon environments and a co-evolution procedure (rubric-reward training plus harness-skill editing) that improves both task outcome and its cause, outperforming single-axis baselines while transferring to unseen workflows without degrading general capabilities.

title: Process Constitutions and Process Stewards: Towards the Next Generation of BPM for Agentic Organizations
summary: Business Process Management (BPM) was built on a foundational assumption that organizations are populated primarily by human actors whose work can be made visible, governable, and improvable through process models. That assumption is depreciating. AI agent ecosystems increasingly execute, coordinate, and adapt organizational work with limited human direction, challenging not only BPM's methods but its core conception of what a process is. We argue that BPM faces a constitutive shift from modeling human work to governing autonomous agents, for which we propose two new concepts: the \emph{Process Constitution}, a machine-interpretable, value-laden framework that defines the space of admissible agent behavior, and the \emph{Process Steward}, a governance agent that interprets and enforces it. The central value proposition of this new generation of BPM is not efficiency but \emph{organizational legibility}: the capacity to keep agentic organizations accountable, contestable, and humanly understandable. We outline what this means and sketch the research agenda it opens.

AI.tldr: BPM's assumption of visible human-centered work is eroding as AI agent ecosystems execute and adapt organizational work autonomously; the paper proposes a shift from modeling human work to governing autonomous agents via two concepts—Process Constitution and Process Steward—with organizational legibility, not efficiency, as the core value.
AI.motivation: BPM was founded on the premise that organizational work is performed primarily by human actors and can be made visible, governable, and improvable through process models. This premise is depreciating: AI agent ecosystems increasingly execute, coordinate, and adapt work with limited human direction, challenging both BPM's methods and its core conception of what a process is.
AI.method: Conceptual/theoretical argument (research agenda paper) rather than empirical study. The authors propose two new constructs: the Process Constitution, a machine-interpretable, value-laden framework defining the space of admissible agent behavior, and the Process Steward, a governance agent that interprets and enforces that constitution.
AI.result: The paper characterizes the change as a constitutive shift from modeling human work to governing autonomous agents, repositions BPM's central value proposition as organizational legibility—keeping agentic organizations accountable, contestable, and humanly understandable—rather than efficiency, and outlines a corresponding research agenda.
AI.conclusion: A new generation of BPM is needed that governs rather than merely models work, with Process Constitution and Process Steward as foundational mechanisms and organizational legibility as the guiding value; the paper closes by sketching the research agenda this opens.

title: OntoInk: Interactive Ontology Visualization, Validation, and Reasoning
comment: Demo paper at ISWC 2026 Companion Volume, October 25 to 29, 2026, Bari, Italy
summary: Ontology documentation, visualization, and validation are usually carried out with separate tools. This split workflow slows down development and makes knowledge transfer harder. We present OntoInk, an open-source MkDocs plugin that brings these activities together. Within a single documentation-as-code pipeline, OntoInk renders interactive ontology diagrams, validates instance data against SHACL shapes, runs OWL\,DL reasoning, and supports inline Turtle editing. General-purpose diagram plugins for MkDocs cannot parse RDF, dereference IRIs, overlay SHACL constraints, or run OWL reasoning. Compared with standalone ontology visualization tools, OntoInk embeds interactive and editable diagrams directly into documentation pages. A live demo and source code are available at \url{https://ise-fizkarlsruhe.github.io/ontoink/}.

AI.tldr: OntoInk is an open-source MkDocs plugin that unifies ontology documentation, visualization, validation, OWL DL reasoning, and inline Turtle editing within a single documentation-as-code pipeline.
AI.motivation: Ontology documentation, visualization, and validation are typically performed with separate tools, which slows development and hinders knowledge transfer.
AI.method: OntoInk integrates these activities as an MkDocs plugin, rendering interactive ontology diagrams, validating instance data against SHACL shapes, running OWL DL reasoning, and enabling inline Turtle editing within a documentation-as-code workflow.
AI.result: Unlike general-purpose MkDocs diagram plugins, OntoInk can parse RDF, dereference IRIs, overlay SHACL constraints, and run OWL reasoning; unlike standalone ontology visualization tools, it embeds interactive and editable diagrams directly into documentation pages.
AI.conclusion: OntoInk consolidates fragmented ontology workflows into one tool, improving development speed and knowledge transfer. A live demo and source code are publicly available.

title: Grounded Joint-Attention Other-Play for Zero-Shot Coordination
summary: Joint attention - the human ability to share a common visual or cognitive focus with others - enables a meeting of minds that lets us coordinate even with unfamiliar partners. In this work we investigate whether equipping AI agents with a similar mechanism can enable such zero-shot coordination. We introduce Mutual Attention for zero-shot TEaming (MATE): a novel multi-agent reinforcement learning method inspired by human joint attention. MATE encourages agents to coordinate their actions by aligning their visual attention on scene-salient objects during the interaction rather than relying on arbitrary partner-dependent conventions established during training. Unlike symmetry-breaking approaches that merely prevent brittle conventions from emerging, MATE actively promotes coordination through an environment-grounded signal that is naturally shared across partners. We evaluate MATE on three benchmarks: our Card Alignment Game, designed to isolate brittle convention formation, and the more challenging Level-Based Foraging and OvercookedV2 benchmarks. Our experiments consistently show that a joint-attention-inspired signal improves coordination with unknown partners, underlining MATE's potential as a general coordination mechanism that complements and surpasses symmetry-breaking approaches.

AI.tldr: MATE introduces a joint-attention-inspired multi-agent RL method that aligns agents' visual attention on salient scene objects to achieve zero-shot coordination, outperforming symmetry-breaking approaches on three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot coordination with unfamiliar partners is hard because agents tend to rely on arbitrary, partner-dependent conventions learned during training. Existing symmetry-breaking methods only prevent brittle conventions from emerging rather than actively promoting shared coordination grounded in the environment.
AI.method: The authors propose Mutual Attention for zero-shot TEaming (MATE), a multi-agent reinforcement learning method inspired by human joint attention. MATE encourages agents to coordinate by aligning their visual attention on scene-salient objects during interaction, using an environment-grounded signal that is naturally shared across partners.
AI.result: MATE is evaluated on three benchmarks: the authors' Card Alignment Game (designed to isolate brittle convention formation), Level-Based Foraging, and OvercookedV2. Experiments consistently show that the joint-attention-inspired signal improves coordination with unknown partners.
AI.conclusion: MATE demonstrates potential as a general coordination mechanism that complements and surpasses symmetry-breaking approaches for zero-shot teaming.

title: RocketAgent: A Long-Horizon Engineering Agent for Multidisciplinary Design of Liquid-Rocket Thrust Chambers
summary: Liquid-rocket thrust-chamber design involves interdependent analyses in which downstream constraints can require earlier design decisions to be revisited. Managing these dependencies across heterogeneous tools requires consistent design information and coordinated updates throughout the workflow. We present RocketAgent, a long-horizon engineering agent for multidisciplinary preliminary design of liquid-rocket thrust chambers. A single plan-owning Coding Agent coordinates engineering skills for performance sizing, subsystem optimization, geometry generation, and multiphysics assessment. A provenance-aware knowledge graph supports method selection, while a typed Design Intermediate Representation maintains shared parameters, artifacts, and decisions. Revision-aware checks invalidate affected results and block superseded inputs, with consequential changes subject to engineering approval. In a representative simulation-based design, RocketAgent continued from an infeasible cooling search through an engineer-authorized operating-point revision, identified feasible subsystem designs, and coordinated subsequent geometry generation and multiphysics assessment to support final configuration selection. Separate module tests assessed surrogate predictions and nozzle adaptation. A two-configuration comparison across three controlled scenarios verified the expected dependency invalidations and superseded-input blocking before solver execution. The representative case demonstrates sustained coordination across a multidisciplinary design workflow, while the controlled tests establish the behavior of the revision mechanisms supporting that execution.

AI.tldr: RocketAgent is a long-horizon engineering agent for multidisciplinary preliminary design of liquid-rocket thrust chambers. A plan-owning Coding Agent coordinates engineering skills, a provenance-aware knowledge graph supports method selection, and a typed Design Intermediate Representation plus revision-aware checks manage shared parameters, artifact invalidation, and superseded-input blocking under engineering approval.
AI.motivation: Liquid-rocket thrust-chamber design requires interdependent analyses where downstream constraints often force earlier decisions to be revisited. Coordinating these dependencies across heterogeneous tools demands consistent design information and synchronized updates throughout the workflow—an unmet need in preliminary design.
AI.method: RocketAgent uses a single plan-owning Coding Agent that coordinates engineering skills for performance sizing, subsystem optimization, geometry generation, and multiphysics assessment. A provenance-aware knowledge graph supports method selection, while a typed Design Intermediate Representation maintains shared parameters, artifacts, and decisions. Revision-aware checks invalidate affected results and block superseded inputs, with consequential changes requiring engineering approval. Evaluation includes a representative simulation-based design, separate module tests for surrogate predictions and nozzle adaptation, and a two-configuration comparison across three controlled scenarios.
AI.result: In the representative design, RocketAgent proceeded from an infeasible cooling search through an engineer-authorized operating-point revision, identified feasible subsystem designs, and coordinated geometry generation and multiphysics assessment for final configuration selection. Module tests assessed surrogate predictions and nozzle adaptation. The two-configuration comparison across three controlled scenarios verified expected dependency invalidations and superseded-input blocking before solver execution.
AI.conclusion: The representative case demonstrates sustained coordination across a multidisciplinary design workflow, while the controlled tests establish the behavior of the revision mechanisms supporting that execution, indicating RocketAgent's effectiveness for long-horizon, interdependent thrust-chamber preliminary design.

title: Benchmarking Jailbreak Guardrails for Embodied Agents
summary: Embodied agents powered by large language models and vision-language models are increasingly deployed in physical environments, but jailbreak attacks can induce these agents to perform physically harmful actions. A growing number of guardrail methods have been proposed to intercept dangerous behavior before it is executed, yet existing safety benchmarks evaluate the embodied models themselves, leaving it unclear how well these guardrails actually defend an embodied agent in practice. We present the first systematic evaluation of jailbreak guardrails for embodied agents. To compare guardrails under identical conditions, we build a pluggable evaluation framework that treats the embodied agent as a fixed backend and each guardrail as a module that can intervene at the perception, planning, or control stage. We subject six representative guardrails to template-based and automated jailbreak attacks as well as safe instructions, and assess them at the system level along three dimensions: defense effectiveness, measured by the bypass rate and the hazard success rate in the simulator; usability, measured by the false-positive rate and the task completion rate on safe instructions; and efficiency, measured by the latency overhead added at runtime. Experiments on guardrails that span different intervention stages, decision mechanisms, and input modalities reveal a clear trade-off among the three dimensions, and show that no single guardrail dominates in all settings. We further analyze how intervention stage, decision mechanism, and input modality shape safety outcomes, and we offer practical guidance for selecting and designing guardrails for embodied agents.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first systematic evaluation of jailbreak guardrails for embodied agents, using a pluggable framework that fixes the agent as a backend and treats each guardrail as a module intervening at perception, planning, or control stage. Six representative guardrails are tested against template-based and automated jailbreak attacks plus safe instructions, revealing a clear trade-off among defense effectiveness, usability, and efficiency, with no single guardrail dominating.
AI.motivation: Embodied agents driven by large language models and vision-language models are increasingly deployed physically, and jailbreak attacks can induce them to perform physically harmful actions. Although many guardrail methods have been proposed to intercept dangerous behavior, existing safety benchmarks evaluate the embodied models themselves rather than the guardrails, leaving unclear how well guardrails actually defend an embodied agent in practice.
AI.method: A pluggable evaluation framework treats the embodied agent as a fixed backend and each guardrail as a module that can intervene at the perception, planning, or control stage, enabling guardrails to be compared under identical conditions. Six representative guardrails spanning different intervention stages, decision mechanisms, and input modalities are subjected to template-based and automated jailbreak attacks as well as safe instructions, and assessed at the system level along three dimensions (defense effectiveness, usability, and efficiency).
AI.result: Defense effectiveness is measured by the bypass rate and hazard success rate in the simulator; usability by the false-positive rate and task completion rate on safe instructions; and efficiency by the latency overhead added at runtime. Experiments reveal a clear trade-off among the three dimensions, and no single guardrail dominates in all settings. The analysis further shows how intervention stage, decision mechanism, and input modality shape safety outcomes.
AI.conclusion: No single guardrail performs best across all conditions; instead there is a fundamental trade-off among defense effectiveness, usability, and efficiency. The paper offers practical guidance for selecting and designing guardrails for embodied agents, informed by how intervention stage, decision mechanism, and input modality influence safety outcomes.

title: On Impact of Loss Function on the Performance of Neural Networks in Melanoma Diagnosis
comment: Presented at the 30th Conference on Medical Image Understanding and Analysis (MIUA 2026)
summary: Melanoma is the deadliest type of skin cancer, whose early diagnosis is crucial for patients' survival. Image classification using deep learning models has shown promising results for melanoma diagnosis. However, the performance of these models on the melanoma datasets such as SIIM-ISIC melanoma classification dataset is a challenge due to the class imbalance. One of the methods to deal with this challenge is using loss function modifications. In this work, we have investigated the effect of different loss functions on the performance of deep neural networks. We trained these networks using focal loss, logit-adjusted softmax cross-entropy (CE) loss, and weighted softmax CE loss, and we report different metrics for evaluating performance and uncertainty calibration. Our results suggest that focal loss delivers a good combination of performance in terms of AUC and uncertainty calibration in terms of expected calibration error (ECE) simultaneously.

AI.tldr: This work evaluates how different loss functions affect deep neural network performance and uncertainty calibration for melanoma classification under class imbalance, finding that focal loss offers the best joint performance in AUC and ECE.
AI.motivation: Melanoma is the deadliest skin cancer and early diagnosis is critical for survival. Deep learning image classification is promising for melanoma diagnosis, but the SIIM-ISIC dataset suffers from class imbalance, which degrades model performance. Loss function modification is one way to address this, motivating a systematic comparison.
AI.method: The authors trained deep neural networks for melanoma classification using three loss functions: focal loss, logit-adjusted softmax cross-entropy (CE) loss, and weighted softmax CE loss. They then evaluated performance and uncertainty calibration using multiple metrics.
AI.result: Results indicate that focal loss achieves a favorable simultaneous combination of performance in terms of AUC and uncertainty calibration in terms of expected calibration error (ECE).
AI.conclusion: Focal loss is recommended as delivering the best joint performance in AUC and ECE for melanoma classification on the imbalanced SIIM-ISIC dataset, outperforming logit-adjusted softmax CE and weighted softmax CE losses.

title: Impact of Data Augmentation on Confidence Calibration in Melanoma Classification
comment: Presented at the 30th Conference on Medical Image Understanding and Analysis (MIUA 2026)
summary: Accurately quantifying the predictive uncertainty or improving model calibration plays an important role in medical image classification, in particular in melanoma diagnosis, where accurate uncertainty quantification can have significant implications for patient care. One of the methods for calibration improvement is data augmentation. In addition, data augmentation as a method for synthetically increasing the size of the dataset has been proven to improve the performance of models trained on imbalanced datasets. However, the impact of data augmentation, as a transformation of a part of the original data, on calibration of models trained on imbalanced datasets, in particular in melanoma classification is under-explored. We train neural networks on SIIM-ISIC 2020 melanoma classification dataset under two conditions: with and without data augmentation, and compare the differences in AUC and expected calibration error (ECE) in both scenarios. Our results shows improvements in uncertainty calibration using different augmentation methods.

AI.tldr: The abstract examines how data augmentation affects uncertainty calibration and predictive performance of neural networks for melanoma classification on an imbalanced dataset, finding that different augmentation methods improve calibration.
AI.motivation: Accurate predictive uncertainty quantification and model calibration are critical in medical image classification, especially melanoma diagnosis, where they directly impact patient care. While data augmentation is known to improve model performance on imbalanced datasets, its effect on calibration—particularly in melanoma classification—remains under-explored.
AI.method: Neural networks were trained on the SIIM-ISIC 2020 melanoma classification dataset under two conditions: with and without data augmentation. The differences in AUC and expected calibration error (ECE) were compared across both scenarios, and different augmentation methods were evaluated.
AI.result: The results show improvements in uncertainty calibration when using different data augmentation methods.
AI.conclusion: Data augmentation can improve uncertainty calibration for melanoma classification on imbalanced datasets, suggesting practical benefits for reliable medical image classification.

title: MS-Exam-Gen: Source-Grounded Benchmark Construction for Evaluating LLMs on Textual Multiple Sclerosis MRI Knowledge
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures. Accepted for publication to BHI 2026
summary: Biomedical large language model (LLM) evaluation requires auditable assessment of narrow, evolving, source-grounded subspecialty knowledge. Multiple sclerosis MRI (MS-MRI) provides a high-stakes textual-knowledge test case because correct reasoning requires current diagnostic criteria, standardized acquisition and reporting knowledge, longitudinal monitoring concepts, lesion morphology, and recognition of difficult mimics. We present MS-Exam-Gen, a reproducible framework for constructing and auditing a text-based multiple-choice question (MCQ) benchmark for MS-MRI knowledge; it does not evaluate direct MRI image interpretation. MS-Exam-Gen targets source-grounded criteria, protocols, reporting, and differential diagnosis. The framework combines expert-source indexing, exam-oriented topic induction, evidence-grounded MCQ generation, automated quality audits, a same-family consistency screen, and empirical calibration. From a 66-source corpus indexed into 4,289 retrieval chunks, the pipeline produced a locked 3,058-item candidate benchmark spanning 16 topics and 53 subtopics. Evaluation across 12 primary LLM endpoints yielded 36,696 item-level predictions and separated performance over a 42.8-percentage-point accuracy range (89.7% to 46.9%). Across these endpoints, 25.5% of items were missed by at least four. Post-generation audits showed that refreshed construction reduced measurable answer cues, while option-order testing showed that absolute MCQ scores remain position-sensitive. Generated construction labels remain metadata rather than validated psychometric categories. Because expert adjudication and full option-order counterbalancing remain future work, MS-Exam-Gen is not a clinically certified examination. It should be interpreted as an automatically filtered, source-grounded candidate benchmark and reproducible audit workflow for item-level and topic-specific LLM evaluation.

AI.tldr: MS-Exam-Gen is a reproducible framework that builds and audits a source-grounded, text-based MCQ benchmark for multiple sclerosis MRI knowledge, yielding a 3,058-item candidate benchmark that separated 12 LLM endpoints across a 42.8-point accuracy range.
AI.motivation: Biomedical LLM evaluation requires auditable assessment of narrow, evolving, source-grounded subspecialty knowledge. MS-MRI is a high-stakes test case because correct reasoning demands current diagnostic criteria, standardized acquisition and reporting knowledge, longitudinal monitoring concepts, lesion morphology, and recognition of difficult mimics.
AI.method: MS-Exam-Gen combines expert-source indexing, exam-oriented topic induction, evidence-grounded MCQ generation, automated quality audits, a same-family consistency screen, and empirical calibration. It targets source-grounded criteria, protocols, reporting, and differential diagnosis (not direct MRI image interpretation). From a 66-source corpus indexed into 4,289 retrieval chunks, the pipeline produced a locked 3,058-item candidate benchmark spanning 16 topics and 53 subtopics.
AI.result: Evaluation across 12 primary LLM endpoints yielded 36,696 item-level predictions spanning a 42.8-percentage-point accuracy range (89.7% to 46.9%); 25.5% of items were missed by at least four endpoints. Post-generation audits showed refreshed construction reduced measurable answer cues, while option-order testing showed absolute MCQ scores remain position-sensitive.
AI.conclusion: Generated construction labels remain metadata rather than validated psychometric categories. Because expert adjudication and full option-order counterbalancing remain future work, MS-Exam-Gen is not a clinically certified examination; it should be interpreted as an automatically filtered, source-grounded candidate benchmark and reproducible audit workflow for item-level and topic-specific LLM evaluation.

title: Auditable Clinical Timeline Reconstruction with Provenance-Aware Evidence Graphs
summary: A patient-timeline reconstruction system is auditable only if it keeps the mentions behind each answer, records how facts were revised, and declines to answer when the evidence is not in the text. This study tests these three properties on a fully synthetic corpus (1,000 patients, 3,353 notes, 220 revision edges). Two provenance-aware Evidence Graph operators reduced the node-plus-edge count to 67% and 63% (77-78% of serialized size) while preserving every answer and mention link across 6,813 query points answerable by recency; a fixed-window baseline returned no value for 53.4% of points, unflagged. On evidence-unavailable controls that announce the omission, a BioClinicalBERT gate and a zero-shot LLM gate responded mainly to the announcement. On marker-free controls, BERT abstained on 0 of 81 notes while its accuracy fell from 93.8% to 59.3% across all three relation classes; the LLM's coverage fell from 75.6% to 27.7% on notes its own model family judged undeterminable. Against 482 regenerated gold spans, the LLM's cited evidence reached recall 0.850 and precision 0.864; BERT's span head, trained without span labels, did not localize evidence. A temporally versioned provenance graph stored abstentions as typed, queryable edges. The clean task admits a 0.651-accuracy shortcut, and results describe implementation behaviour on synthetic data, not clinical performance.

AI.tldr: On a synthetic patient-timeline corpus, two provenance-aware Evidence Graph operators cut representation size to ~63-67% while preserving all answers and mention links; a fixed-window baseline silently failed on 53.4% of answerable points. Only the LLM gate showed meaningful abstention and evidence localization (span recall 0.850 / precision 0.864), while BERT degraded on marker-free controls and did not localize evidence.
AI.motivation: Auditable timeline reconstruction requires three properties: answer mentions must be traceable (provenance), fact revisions must be recorded (versioning), and the system must abstain when evidence is absent from the text. The study tests whether these properties hold.
AI.method: Fully synthetic corpus: 1,000 patients, 3,353 notes, 220 revision edges. Two provenance-aware Evidence Graph operators (node/edge reduction to 67% and 63%, i.e., 77-78% of serialized size). Evaluated across 6,813 recency-answerable query points against a fixed-window baseline. Evidence-unavailable controls with announced omissions tested BioClinicalBERT and zero-shot LLM gates. Marker-free controls tested abstention and accuracy. Gold-span evaluation against 482 regenerated spans. Temporally versioned provenance graph with typed, queryable abstention edges.
AI.result: Evidence Graph operators preserved every answer and mention link while reducing node-plus-edge count to 67% and 63% (77-78% of serialized size). Fixed-window baseline returned no value for 53.4% of points, unflagged. On announced-omission controls, both gates responded mainly to the announcement. On marker-free controls, BERT abstained on 0 of 81 notes and accuracy fell from 93.8% to 59.3% across all three relation classes; LLM coverage fell from 75.6% to 27.7% on notes its own model family judged undeterminable. LLM cited evidence: recall 0.850, precision 0.864. BERT's span head (trained without span labels) did not localize evidence. Abstentions stored as typed, queryable edges.
AI.conclusion: A temporally versioned provenance graph can store abstentions as typed, queryable edges, supporting auditability. However, the clean task admits a 0.651-accuracy shortcut, and results describe implementation behaviour on synthetic data rather than clinical performance.

title: Bridging the Evidence-to-Execution Gap:A Reflective Agent for Multi-Objective Peptide Design
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can reason over scientific literature to devise design strategies, yet fail to reliably implement them for biological sequences. While protein generative models learn sequence patterns, they lack the capacity to incorporate literature evidence for multi-step reflective reasoning, forming an evidence-to-execution gap between scientific reasoning and sequence manipulation. We present EASER (Evidence-Aware Sequence Engineering with Reflection), a reflective agent bridging reasoning and sequence generation via a learned property interface of offline-trained, fixed low-rank matrices. The agent steers a diffusion generator by combining these matrices, proposing intervention hypotheses (anchors, editable positions, control coefficients) grounded in retrieved evidence, sequence context and past results. A Probe-and-Steer mechanism validates interventions and allocates samples according to predicted property responses, with outcome reflection informing subsequent decisions. Evaluated on multi-objective antimicrobial peptide design (optimizing activity, non-hemolysis and non-toxicity), explicit hypothesis formulation delivers better multi-objective performance than direct action generation under identical decision conditions. Ablation studies verify the importance of evidence retrieval, episodic history, reflection and Probe-and-Steer. Over six repeated trials, EASER obtains the highest mean hypervolume and lowest mean IGD+ on screened candidates compared with competing baselines. Our work demonstrates how an executable property interface and iterative feedback link scientific reasoning to targeted peptide sequence generation.

AI.tldr: EASER is a reflective LLM agent that bridges the evidence-to-execution gap by steering a diffusion-based protein generator through a learned low-rank property interface, achieving top multi-objective performance in antimicrobial peptide design.
AI.motivation: LLMs can reason over scientific literature to devise design strategies but fail to reliably implement them for biological sequences. Protein generative models learn sequence patterns yet cannot incorporate literature evidence for multi-step reflective reasoning, creating an evidence-to-execution gap between scientific reasoning and sequence manipulation.
AI.method: EASER (Evidence-Aware Sequence Engineering with Reflection) uses a learned property interface of offline-trained, fixed low-rank matrices to steer a diffusion generator. The agent proposes intervention hypotheses (anchors, editable positions, control coefficients) grounded in retrieved evidence, sequence context, and past results. A Probe-and-Steer mechanism validates interventions and allocates samples according to predicted property responses, with outcome reflection informing subsequent decisions.
AI.result: On multi-objective antimicrobial peptide design (optimizing activity, non-hemolysis, non-toxicity), explicit hypothesis formulation outperforms direct action generation under identical decision conditions. Ablations confirm the importance of evidence retrieval, episodic history, reflection, and Probe-and-Steer. Over six repeated trials, EASER achieves the highest mean hypervolume and lowest mean IGD+ on screened candidates versus competing baselines.
AI.conclusion: An executable property interface combined with iterative feedback can link scientific reasoning to targeted peptide sequence generation, demonstrating a practical route to closing the evidence-to-execution gap.

title: Judged Useless, Queried Anyway: Tool-Using Agents Rarely Turn Their Own Evidence Judgments into Stopping Decisions
summary: An agent whose tool keeps returning nothing useful should stop relying on it. In a retrieval environment with controlled source failures, we separate how agents judge results from what they do. We compare stopping at the same step after longer and shorter runs of results the agent judged useless; this contrast is zero for clock- or deadline-driven stopping. Where we record their judgments, the seven agents we test call a failing source's results useless 97-100% of the time, yet most of them rarely stop on that judgment. Prompt cues change when they stop but not what they stop on. Permission to answer from memory and a reasoning mode can bring early stops regardless of evidence, a stated budget moves the 7-8B models' stops to the deadline, and a stopping rule or call cost in the prompt is followed at most partly. Stopping follows the evidence only when the harness enforces an integration step that makes the agent answer after five consecutive results it judged useless. This step raises failing-source success for every model, keeps the stopping point fixed when the budget doubles, and needs no extra judgment call when the agent states its judgments. A pre-registered replication on 300 fresh questions confirms the dissociation and the rule's effect.

AI.tldr: Across seven agents in a controlled retrieval environment with failing sources, agents judge useless results as useless 97-100% of the time but rarely act on that judgment; only a harness-enforced integration step aligns stopping with evidence.
AI.motivation: Agents whose tools return nothing useful should stop relying on them, yet it is unclear whether agents fail to recognize useless results or fail to act on that recognition. The paper aims to dissociate judgment from stopping behavior.
AI.method: Controlled retrieval environment with source failures. Stopping behavior is compared at the same step after longer versus shorter runs of results judged useless, a contrast that is zero for clock- or deadline-driven stopping. Prompt manipulations tested include memory-answer permission, reasoning mode, stated budget, stopping rules, and call costs. A harness-enforced integration step requires the agent to answer after five consecutive results it judged useless. A pre-registered replication uses 300 fresh questions.
AI.result: Agents label failing-source results useless 97-100% of the time but mostly do not stop on that judgment. Prompt cues shift when they stop, not what they stop on. Memory permission and reasoning mode induce early stops independent of evidence; a stated budget moves 7-8B models' stops to the deadline; stopping rules or call costs are only partly followed. The enforced integration step raises failing-source success for every model, fixes the stopping point when budget doubles, and requires no extra judgment call when agents state judgments. Replication confirms the dissociation and the rule's effect.
AI.conclusion: Judgment and stopping are dissociated: agents recognize useless results but do not reliably act on that recognition. Stopping follows evidence only when the harness enforces an integration step, which improves success without extra judgment calls.

title: Copies or Sources? Measuring How LLM Aggregators Count Restated Evidence in Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) restate observations as a matter of course: relays forward them, shared boards repeat them and discussion rounds echo them. An aggregator that pools such messages should count sources, not statements. We convert a reported probability into units of independent readings, which assigns every restatement a copy weight, 0 for an aggregator that counts sources and 1 for one that counts every statement, and yields the implied decision under any cost structure. Three testbeds hold the evidence fixed and vary how it is restated: message logs with an exact Bayesian oracle, web documents with appended copies, and logs written by LLM agent teams under four communication protocols. Across four models from three providers, a forwarded copy counts for 0.06 to 0.42 of a new reading, mostly because some replies count every statement. On 5% to 40% of logs that state one reading three times, the reported belief implies an early commitment that the oracle never makes. The models that count copies least and most on controlled logs do so on web copies and agent-written logs as well. A one-paragraph declaration of what a copy contributes brings the copy weight on controlled logs to 0.08 or less. A rule that has agents refer to readings instead of restating them cuts belief-implied early commitment from 11.2% to 1.1% and preserves genuine corroboration.

AI.tldr: LLM multi-agent restatements inflate evidence: a forwarded copy weighs only 0.06–0.42 of an independent reading, causing spurious early commitment on 5–40% of triple-repeat logs; prompt declarations and referential rules largely fix it.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems constantly restate observations—relays, shared boards, discussion rounds—so an aggregator pooling these messages should count sources rather than statements. Existing aggregation appears to double-count paraphrased or forwarded copies as new evidence, and this paper aims to quantify that contamination and its decision consequences.
AI.method: The authors define a copy weight by converting a reported probability into units of independent readings: 0 corresponds to an aggregator counting sources, 1 to one counting every statement, and any value in between yields the implied decision under a given cost structure. They hold evidence fixed while varying restatement across three testbeds: message logs with an exact Bayesian oracle, web documents with appended copies, and logs produced by LLM agent teams under four communication protocols. Experiments span four models from three providers. Two interventions are tested: a one-paragraph declaration specifying what a copy contributes, and a rule requiring agents to refer to readings rather than restate them.
AI.result: A forwarded copy counts for only 0.06 to 0.42 of a new reading, largely because some replies count every statement. On 5% to 40% of logs stating one reading three times, the reported belief implies an early commitment the oracle never makes. Models exhibiting the lowest and highest copy-counting on controlled logs do so consistently on web copies and agent-written logs. The one-paragraph declaration reduces controlled-log copy weight to 0.08 or below. The referential rule cuts belief-implied early commitment from 11.2% to 1.1% while preserving genuine corroboration.
AI.conclusion: Restatement is a systematic, model-consistent source of evidence inflation in LLM multi-agent aggregation, measurable via copy weight and consequential for decisions. Simple prompt-level declarations and referential communication rules substantially mitigate the effect without discarding real corroboration.

title: Do Small Language Models Learn to Negotiate? A Controlled Scaling Study of RL-Trained Sellers
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures, 9 tables. Accepted (poster) at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on SLMs for Agentic Systems (SLM-Agents), Paris
summary: LLM agents are starting to own the full customer experience. Soon, LLMs may be selling and buying on behalf of companies and customers respectively. Small models are more cost-efficient at scale, but can reinforcement learning train them into competent sellers? We train four Gemma 4 checkpoints (2.3B to 31B effective parameters) with GRPO on a programmatic utility reward for bilateral multi-issue bargaining, and evaluate every arm on the same 1,152 negotiations against two frontier buyers it never saw in training. With the same learning rate ($10^{-6}$) for every size, the gain of the RL model over its base rises from $+0.001$ at 2.3B to $+0.078$ at 31B. Each size was trained once and the two smallest checkpoints use a different architecture, so we fit no scaling law. Tripling the learning rate, with the same or fewer training steps, improves on the shared rate at every size by $+0.032$ (2.3B) to $+0.081$ (4.5B). In exploratory comparisons with two frontier models run as sellers, the 12B seller trained at the tripled rate scores above both, though its untrained base already scores as high as they do. The 4.5B seller at that rate shows no detectable difference from either and fits on one 48 GB GPU. A further 2.3B arm at ten times the shared rate raises pooled score, but its gain concentrates on the evaluation buyer that shares a model family with the training pool. These results suggest tuning the learning rate before concluding that a small model cannot learn to negotiate, and testing against buyers from more than one model family.

AI.tldr: Training small Gemma checkpoints with GRPO on a programmatic bargaining reward shows RL gains grow with model size, but learning-rate tuning matters more than size: tripling the LR improves every arm (+0.032 to +0.081), and a 4.5B seller at that rate matches frontier-model sellers while fitting on one 48 GB GPU.
AI.motivation: LLM agents are moving toward owning the full customer experience, potentially selling and buying on behalf of companies and customers. Small models are cost-efficient at scale, but it is unclear whether RL can train them into competent negotiators. The authors question whether apparent failure of small models to learn bargaining reflects a genuine capacity limit or merely suboptimal hyperparameters, and whether evaluation against a single model family inflates results.
AI.method: Four Gemma checkpoints (2.3B to 31B effective parameters) were trained with GRPO on a programmatic utility reward for bilateral multi-issue bargaining. Each arm was evaluated on the same 1,152 negotiations against two frontier buyers unseen during training. All sizes shared one learning rate (1e-6); additional arms tripled the rate (with equal or fewer steps) and, for 2.3B, used ten times the rate. Two smallest checkpoints use a different architecture, and each size was trained only once, so no scaling law was fitted. Exploratory seller-side comparisons were run against two frontier models.
AI.result: At the shared learning rate, the RL gain over base rose from +0.001 (2.3B) to +0.078 (31B). Tripling the learning rate improved every size by +0.032 (2.3B) to +0.081 (4.5B) with the same or fewer training steps. In exploratory seller comparisons, the 12B tripled-rate seller scored above both frontier models, though its untrained base already matched them; the 4.5B tripled-rate seller showed no detectable difference from either and fits on one 48 GB GPU. A 2.3B arm at ten times the shared rate raised pooled score, but gains concentrated on the evaluation buyer sharing a model family with the training pool.
AI.conclusion: Tuning the learning rate should precede conclusions that a small model cannot learn to negotiate, since LR changes dominate reported size effects here. Evaluations should also use buyers from more than one model family to avoid inflating scores through same-family affinity, and no scaling law can be claimed from the current single-seed, mixed-architecture design.

title: AI-Decision Checkpoints for AI-Augmented Business Process Management: Framework and Educational Instantiation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and AI agents are increasingly embedded in operational business processes. Yet Business Process Management (BPM) curricula and frameworks still largely treat artificial intelligence (AI) as an add-on technology, leaving graduates (as potential future process developers) unprepared to reason about AI as a first-class design element of end-to-end processes. This paper addresses that gap by proposing \emph{AI-decision checkpoints}: explicit moments in a process development trajectory where process developers identify AI-candidate sub-processes, assess expected effects on time, cost, quality, and flexibility, consider legal and organisational constraints, and document a reasoned decision to adopt, constrain, or reject specific AI components. The checkpoints are instantiated through a fictitious customer onboarding process as a \textit{BPM Teaching Case}, embedded in a lifecycle-driven framework spanning six modules that combine process modeling, simulation, workflow execution with AI agents, and process mining, with each module's output serving as the next module's input. A preliminary formative reflection draws on instructor observations, submitted artifacts, and discovered process maps from learning-management-system logs. These exploratory observations suggest that the approach supported clearer distinctions between task-level automation and process-level value.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "AI-decision checkpoints"—explicit points in a process development trajectory where developers identify AI-candidate sub-processes, evaluate effects on time, cost, quality, and flexibility, weigh legal/organisational constraints, and record a reasoned adopt/constrain/reject decision—implemented via a fictitious customer onboarding teaching case in a six-module lifecycle framework, with preliminary formative reflection suggesting better distinctions between task-level automation and process-level value.
AI.motivation: LLMs, RAG, and AI agents are increasingly embedded in operational business processes, yet BPM curricula and frameworks still treat AI as an add-on technology. This leaves graduates—future process developers—unprepared to reason about AI as a first-class design element of end-to-end processes.
AI.method: The authors introduce AI-decision checkpoints as explicit moments in a process development trajectory. At each checkpoint, process developers: (1) identify AI-candidate sub-processes, (2) assess expected effects on time, cost, quality, and flexibility, (3) consider legal and organisational constraints, and (4) document a reasoned decision to adopt, constrain, or reject specific AI components. These checkpoints are instantiated through a fictitious customer onboarding process as a BPM Teaching Case, embedded in a lifecycle-driven framework spanning six modules that integrate process modeling, simulation, workflow execution with AI agents, and process mining, with each module's output feeding the next. Evaluation uses a preliminary formative reflection based on instructor observations, submitted artifacts, and process maps discovered from LMS logs.
AI.result: Exploratory observations suggest the approach supported clearer distinctions between task-level automation and process-level value.
AI.conclusion: The paper argues for treating AI as a first-class design element in BPM education via AI-decision checkpoints integrated into a lifecycle-driven, six-module teaching case. Preliminary formative evidence indicates improved learner reasoning about where and whether AI adds process-level value, though findings remain exploratory and warrant further validation.

title: From Papers to Mechanisms: An Evidence-Grounded Knowledge Substrate for Scientific Language Models
summary: Scientific language models often access literature through untyped text chunks, which fragment the functional and evidential structure required for mechanism-rich questions. We introduce an evidence-grounded mechanism knowledge substrate that organizes scientific literature into provenance-linked evidence units, role-typed entities, and directed mechanism paths. We instantiate it as MS$^3$, a Material-Sensor-Signal-System schema for conductive-fiber flexible sensors, over 13,689 papers, 131,083 evidence items, and 26,648 mechanism objects. On in-domain and coverage-shift question-answering benchmarks, we compare closed-book generation, Web search, Raw-PDF RAG, and MS$^3$ retrieval across ten language models. MS$^3$ improves macro-averaged scientific correctness. It also improves citation entailment and answer completeness. These results support mechanism substrates as a reliable representation layer for scientific language models and motivate a source-repair workflow in which insufficient MS$^3$ evidence triggers targeted retrieval from its linked papers rather than assuming that a user has already supplied the correct PDFs.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an evidence-grounded mechanism knowledge substrate for scientific literature, instantiated as MS^3 (Material-Sensor-Signal-System schema) for conductive-fiber flexible sensors, and shows it improves scientific correctness, citation entailment, and answer completeness over closed-book, Web search, and Raw-PDF RAG across ten language models.
AI.motivation: Scientific language models often access literature through untyped text chunks, which fragment the functional and evidential structure required for mechanism-rich questions. There is a need for a representation layer that preserves provenance, entity roles, and directed mechanistic relations.
AI.method: The authors build an evidence-grounded mechanism knowledge substrate consisting of provenance-linked evidence units, role-typed entities, and directed mechanism paths. They instantiate it as MS^3, a Material-Sensor-Signal-System schema for conductive-fiber flexible sensors, covering 13,689 papers, 131,083 evidence items, and 26,648 mechanism objects. They benchmark on in-domain and coverage-shift QA tasks, comparing closed-book generation, Web search, Raw-PDF RAG, and MS^3 retrieval across ten language models.
AI.result: MS^3 retrieval improves macro-averaged scientific correctness, citation entailment, and answer completeness over the baselines.
AI.conclusion: The results support mechanism substrates as a reliable representation layer for scientific language models and motivate a source-repair workflow, where insufficient MS^3 evidence triggers targeted retrieval from linked papers rather than assuming the user has already supplied the correct PDFs.

title: Evolving in Thought Space: Training a Small Model at Test Time Unlocks Better Discoveries
summary: Open-ended scientific discovery often requires repeatedly proposing and evaluating candidate solutions. LLM-based systems can support this process by generating and refining executable solutions from verifier feedback. Methods such as TTT-Discover use test-time training (TTT) to update the solution-generating LLM from verifier feedback, adapting its generation policy to improve subsequent proposals on the target problem. However, this becomes expensive when reliable execution requires a large model, since training must maintain gradients, optimizer states, and policy statistics while repeatedly generating long, structured outputs. It also complicates credit assignment: outcome-level verifier feedback must jointly evaluate the high-level strategy and its low-level implementation. In this work, we introduce Guidance-TTT, which separates these roles. A compact guidance model is trained at test time to propose high-level strategic changes, while a frozen execution model implements them as complete executable solutions. At each step, the system selects a promising previously discovered solution, proposes a change, executes and verifies it, and updates only the guidance model using an adaptive group-relative RL objective. This concentrates test-time learning on short strategic decisions while retaining the implementation capability of a substantially stronger model without adapting it. Without web access, Guidance-TTT produces strong solutions across four distinct domains: combinatorial optimization (Polyomino Packing), heuristic programming (AHC058), machine learning (Lasso), and GPU kernel optimization (TriMul). Across these tasks, it outperforms the best solutions reported in prior work while remaining competitive with state-of-the-art results on public online leaderboards. Code is available at https://github.com/Human-Agent-Society/reef/tree/guidance-ttt-support.

AI.tldr: Guidance-TTT decouples strategy from execution: a compact guidance model is test-time trained via adaptive group-relative RL to propose high-level changes, while a frozen large execution model implements them, yielding strong results across four scientific discovery domains.
AI.motivation: Open-ended scientific discovery requires iterative proposal and evaluation of candidate solutions, and LLM-based systems can generate and refine executable solutions from verifier feedback. Existing methods like TTT-Discover update the solution-generating LLM at test time, but this is expensive when reliable execution demands a large model (gradients, optimizer states, policy statistics, long structured outputs), and it entangles credit assignment between high-level strategy and low-level implementation.
AI.method: Guidance-TTT separates roles: a compact guidance model is trained at test time to propose high-level strategic changes, while a frozen execution model implements them as complete executable solutions. At each step the system selects a promising previously discovered solution, proposes a change, executes and verifies it, and updates only the guidance model with an adaptive group-relative RL objective, concentrating test-time learning on short strategic decisions.
AI.result: Without web access, Guidance-TTT produces strong solutions across four distinct domains: combinatorial optimization (Polyomino Packing), heuristic programming (AHC058), machine learning (Lasso), and GPU kernel optimization (TriMul). It outperforms the best solutions reported in prior work and remains competitive with state-of-the-art results on public online leaderboards.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling strategic guidance from execution enables efficient test-time training that leverages a much stronger frozen model's implementation capability without adapting it, improving over prior verifier-feedback methods across diverse discovery tasks.

title: DPNL: A DPLL-based Algorithm for Probabilistic Neurosymbolic Learning
summary: Probabilistic Neurosymbolic Learning (PNL) combines neural predictions with symbolic reasoning, enabling end-to-end learning from final-output supervision without labels for intermediate concepts. A central challenge is probabilistic inference: state-of-the-art approaches often rely on materializing the logical provenance of a query, which can itself become a major computational bottleneck. We introduce Dynamic Probabilistic Neurosymbolic Learning (DPNL), an oracle-guided framework that avoids requiring complete provenance materialization before inference. DPNL lazily explores the space of intermediate assignments, while oracles resolve entire regions that can already be certified to produce or exclude the target output. We establish conditions ensuring soundness and termination. ApproxDPNL extends the same search with early termination while maintaining certified bounds on the exact output probability, providing controlled approximation guarantees. The oracle interface decouples inference from the representation of the symbolic component, enabling problem-specific reasoning within the same framework. Experiments on several neurosymbolic tasks show that DPNL and ApproxDPNL substantially extend the range of problem instances tractable by probabilistic neurosymbolic inference.

AI.tldr: DPNL is an oracle-guided framework for probabilistic neurosymbolic inference that lazily explores intermediate assignments and avoids full logical-provenance materialization, with ApproxDPNL providing certified bounds via early termination.
AI.motivation: Probabilistic Neurosymbolic Learning (PNL) enables end-to-end learning from final-output supervision without intermediate labels. However, state-of-the-art probabilistic inference often relies on materializing the query's logical provenance, which becomes a major computational bottleneck.
AI.method: DPNL is an oracle-guided framework that avoids complete provenance materialization before inference. It lazily explores the space of intermediate assignments while oracles certify entire regions that can produce or exclude the target output. The authors establish conditions for soundness and termination. ApproxDPNL extends this search with early termination while maintaining certified bounds on the exact output probability, giving controlled approximation guarantees. The oracle interface decouples inference from the symbolic representation, allowing problem-specific reasoning within one framework.
AI.result: Experiments across several neurosymbolic tasks show that DPNL and ApproxDPNL substantially extend the range of problem instances tractable by probabilistic neurosymbolic inference.
AI.conclusion: DPNL and ApproxDPNL provide a scalable, representation-agnostic alternative to provenance-materializing inference, with soundness and termination guarantees as well as controlled approximations, broadening the applicability of PNL.

title: Teaching a Minimalist Machine to Discover Recursive Programs for Arithmetic
comment: 15 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for oral presentation at the 6th International Joint Conference on Learning and Reasoning 2026. Code: https://github.com/cognitive-modeling/minimalist-machine/tree/IJCLR-2026
summary: Humans can often acquire and synthesize complex, recursive concepts from minimal experience. Leveraging cognitive insights, we propose the Minimalist Machine, a framework for inductive program synthesis designed to model such conceptual learning. The system uses a compact relational subset of Prolog: Programs are searched within a fixed schema of body-free facts and two-body conjunctive Horn clauses. Recursion is not defined by a dedicated metarule. Instead, it emerges when a target predicate is reused inside the body of a learned clause. Inspired by a primary school curriculum, the model is taught through a human-curated, sequential introduction of new concepts in arithmetic. Starting from initially empty knowledge base, it first acquires simple structural predicates, then successor-based state transformations, and finally recursive programs for addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. Ultimately, this approach yields the fully transparent, inductive reasoning trace necessary for human-like conceptual learning.

AI.tldr: The Minimalist Machine is a framework for inductive program synthesis that models human-like conceptual learning by searching for compact relational Prolog programs in which recursion emerges naturally rather than from a dedicated metarule, acquiring arithmetic concepts through a sequential curriculum.
AI.motivation: Humans can acquire and synthesize complex, recursive concepts from minimal experience, and the paper seeks to leverage these cognitive insights to model such conceptual learning, aiming for a transparent inductive reasoning trace.
AI.method: The system uses a compact relational subset of Prolog: programs are searched within a fixed schema of body-free facts and two-body conjunctive Horn clauses. Recursion is not defined by a dedicated metarule but emerges when a target predicate is reused inside the body of a learned clause. A human-curated curriculum inspired by primary school introduces new arithmetic concepts sequentially, starting from an empty knowledge base and progressing through simple structural predicates, successor-based state transformations, and recursive addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division programs.
AI.result: Starting from an initially empty knowledge base, the model first acquires simple structural predicates, then successor-based state transformations, and finally recursive programs for addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division, yielding a fully transparent inductive reasoning trace.
AI.conclusion: The approach yields the fully transparent, inductive reasoning trace necessary for human-like conceptual learning.

title: RollPlace: Improving Macro Placement via Monte Carlo Rollout Search
summary: The application of Reinforcement Learning (RL) in Electronic Design Automation (EDA), particularly for chip placement, has attracted considerable attention in recent years. While existing machine learning (ML)-based approaches have achieved notable progress, they predominantly focus on generating optimal layouts in a single attempt, often producing solutions that require subsequent refinement. To address this limitation, we propose RollPlace, a novel and generalized macro placement framework. RollPlace adopts a two-stage optimization strategy: generating initial placement solutions via machine learning methods or heuristic-based strategies, and refining these layouts efficiently by adjusting specific macros derived from the initial stage. This strategy circumvents the sequential generation constraints inherent in traditional RL-based placement methods. Furthermore, RollPlace seamlessly integrates Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to balance exploration and exploitation, and employs a rollout mechanism for efficient local search. Extensive experiments on the ISPD 2005 benchmark demonstrate that RollPlace outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, end-to-end experimental results based on OpenROAD across 19 benchmarks show that RollPlace excels in multiple metrics.
