The proposed framework offers a robust and scalable solution for addressing the growing complexity of modern chip design challenges.

AI.tldr: RollPlace is a two-stage macro placement framework that generates an initial layout then refines selected macros via MCTS and rollout-based local search, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on ISPD 2005 and 19 OpenROAD benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing ML/RL-based chip placement methods mainly generate layouts in a single attempt, often yielding solutions that require post-hoc refinement and are constrained by sequential generation. A more flexible, generalizable framework is needed to handle growing chip design complexity.
AI.method: Two-stage optimization: (1) generate initial placement solutions using ML methods or heuristic strategies; (2) refine layouts by adjusting specific macros from the initial stage, avoiding sequential generation constraints of traditional RL placement. Integrates Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to balance exploration and exploitation, and a rollout mechanism for efficient local search.
AI.result: On the ISPD 2005 benchmark, RollPlace outperforms state-of-the-art methods. End-to-end results on OpenROAD across 19 benchmarks show strong performance across multiple metrics.
AI.conclusion: RollPlace provides a robust and scalable solution for modern chip design placement, offering a generalized two-stage strategy that improves over single-attempt approaches.

title: CRAFTER: Causality-based Self-adaptation for Autonomous IoT Systems
summary: This paper presents CRAFTER, an automated framework for designing and deploying self-adaptive IoT systems using Causal Reinforcement Learning (CRL). As IoT devices increasingly populate pervasive computing spaces, smart environments are enabled with advanced monitoring and interactive services. The dynamic nature of these environments, such as fluctuating workloads and evolving application demands, poses significant challenges in maintaining consistent Quality of Service (QoS) levels of IoT applications. While existing self-adaptation techniques offer adaptive capabilities, they are often designed to deal with specific application domains, hindering the design of self-adaptive solutions that can be re-used across multiple IoT verticals. In addition, there is a lack of automated pipelines that act on identifying key performance drivers to take effective adaptation decisions. CRAFTER addresses these issues by using Causality as a formal framework for performance analysis of IoT systems. CRAFTER generates causal graphs to uncover dependencies among system components and guide adaptation decisions based on cause-effect relationships. Then, adaptation agents can leverage this knowledge to take more effective adaptation decisions in dynamic situations. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates how CRAFTER enables deriving causal graphs spanning diverse IoT use cases. Furthermore, we showcase how CRAFTER improves self-adaptation performance by 25% compared to state-of-the-art Reinforcement Learning-based approaches.

AI.tldr: CRAFTER is an automated framework that leverages Causal Reinforcement Learning to design and deploy reusable, self-adaptive IoT systems across diverse IoT verticals.
AI.motivation: IoT environments are dynamic (fluctuating workloads, evolving demands), making consistent QoS hard to maintain. Existing self-adaptation techniques are domain-specific and non-reusable across IoT verticals, and there is a lack of automated pipelines that identify key performance drivers for effective adaptation decisions.
AI.method: CRAFTER uses Causality as a formal framework for IoT performance analysis. It generates causal graphs to uncover dependencies among system components and guide adaptation based on cause-effect relationships, which adaptation agents then leverage for decision-making in dynamic situations.
AI.result: Experimental evaluation shows CRAFTER derives causal graphs spanning diverse IoT use cases and improves self-adaptation performance by 25% compared to state-of-the-art Reinforcement Learning-based approaches.
AI.conclusion: CRAFTER demonstrates that causal reinforcement learning enables reusable, automated self-adaptation for IoT systems, outperforming existing RL-based solutions.

title: ImproveAnyTask: An Autonomous Post-Training Harness for Iterative Model Self-Improvement
summary: Adapting general-purpose large language models to specific tasks requires substantial human effort in designing data and training strategies. Sustaining improvement is especially challenging because model updates change the error distribution, requiring strategies to be continually refined. We introduce ImproveAnyTask, an autonomous post-training harness that improves task performance under a limited compute budget. Drawing inspiration from gradient-based parameter optimization, the harness organizes adaptation into error attribution, update-direction selection, and executable model updates. It combines metric-level and case-level analysis to identify a focal problem, then investigates research-backed strategies and compares their reported gains and reproduction difficulty. The selected strategy is translated into training data and a training configuration, with small-scale execution checks preceding full post-training. Subsequent evaluation guides model selection and further adaptation, while validated strategies and scripts are retained for reuse. Across 11 tasks, ImproveAnyTask achieves mean gains of 18.29 and 11.97 percentage points on the Base and Instruct models, respectively, with a maximum gain of 41.96 points, under a 24-hour budget with resources equivalent to eight H20 GPUs.

AI.tldr: ImproveAnyTask is an autonomous post-training harness that iteratively attributes errors, selects update directions, and executes model updates to boost task performance under a limited compute budget, achieving mean gains of 18.29/11.97 points on Base/Instruct models across 11 tasks.
AI.motivation: Adapting general-purpose LLMs to specific tasks requires substantial human effort in designing data and training strategies. Sustaining improvement is especially difficult because model updates change the error distribution, so strategies must be continually refined. The paper aims to automate this refinement loop under a constrained compute budget.
AI.method: The harness draws inspiration from gradient-based parameter optimization and organizes adaptation into three stages: error attribution, update-direction selection, and executable model updates. It uses metric-level and case-level analysis to identify a focal problem, investigates research-backed strategies (comparing reported gains and reproduction difficulty), then translates the selected strategy into training data and a training configuration. Small-scale execution checks precede full post-training, and subsequent evaluation guides model selection and further adaptation. Validated strategies and scripts are retained for reuse.
AI.result: Across 11 tasks, ImproveAnyTask achieves mean gains of 18.29 and 11.97 percentage points on the Base and Instruct models respectively, with a maximum gain of 41.96 points, all within a 24-hour budget using resources equivalent to eight H20 GPUs.
AI.conclusion: ImproveAnyTask demonstrates that an autonomous, budget-constrained post-training harness can substantially and consistently improve task performance across diverse tasks and model types while retaining reusable strategies, offering a practical alternative to manual data and training-strategy design.

title: GraphDecide: Benchmarking System One Models on Graph Tasks
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for graph understanding and decision-making, while System One models such as Jev select directly from supplied options. However, the capabilities of System One models on graph-related tasks remain unclear. We introduce GraphDecide, a model-independent benchmark that combines structural task profiles, matched graph-text input contrasts and heuristic-proposal controls to diagnose graph decision performance. We evaluate Jev and related choice-based models alongside language-model baselines, covering fourteen model-interface configurations. Jev's results illustrate the benchmark's central distinctions: accurate adjacency recognition does not guarantee broader structural correctness, joint graph-text input does not consistently improve prediction, and feasible construction does not establish high solution quality. Its task contracts, candidate interfaces and scoring rules support comparison across native selectors and language-model adapters. Code and aggregate results are available at https://github.com/VictorYXL/JevGraphBench.

AI.tldr: GraphDecide is a model-independent benchmark using structural task profiles, matched graph-text contrasts, and heuristic-proposal controls to diagnose System One (choice-based) models like Jev on graph decision tasks.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used for graph understanding and decision-making, and System One models such as Jev select directly from supplied options. However, the capabilities of these System One models on graph-related tasks remain unclear, motivating a dedicated diagnostic benchmark.
AI.method: The paper introduces GraphDecide, a model-independent benchmark combining structural task profiles, matched graph-text input contrasts, and heuristic-proposal controls. It evaluates Jev and related choice-based models alongside language-model baselines, covering fourteen model-interface configurations, with task contracts, candidate interfaces, and scoring rules supporting comparison across native selectors and language-model adapters.
AI.result: Jev's results reveal three central distinctions: accurate adjacency recognition does not guarantee broader structural correctness; joint graph-text input does not consistently improve prediction; and feasible construction does not establish high solution quality.
AI.conclusion: GraphDecide diagnoses graph decision performance of System One and choice-based models, showing that localized correctness, multimodal input, and feasible construction are insufficient proxies for broader structural competence or high solution quality. Code and aggregate results are released publicly.

title: Capability-Driven Self-Evolution of Agent Memory
summary: Memory self-evolution uses task feedback to iteratively improve executable memory programs that store and retrieve information from past interactions. Existing approaches typically adopt holistic evolution, deriving revision directions from mixed feedback and judging progress by overall performance. This can obscure optimization directions and hide capability-specific gains offset by regressions elsewhere, leaving promising directions underexplored. We introduce capability-driven evolution, which extends search guidance from overall performance to individual capability dimensions, preserving promising revisions and expanding exploration beyond the boundaries of holistic evolution. We propose PrisMem, which uses dependency-aware capability selection to prioritize targets with potential cross-capability benefits and history-guided diagnosis to refine capability specialists. Trace-guided integration compares evaluated programs on paired differential cases, using their behavioral differences to consolidate complementary gains into a unified memory program. Experiments show that PrisMem outperforms the strongest baselines by 10.54 and 7.83 percentage points on BEAM-1M and LongMemEval-M, respectively, demonstrating its effectiveness on million-token histories.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes PrisMem, a capability-driven self-evolution framework for memory programs. Instead of holistic evolution driven by overall performance, it evolves along individual capability dimensions using dependency-aware selection, history-guided diagnosis, and trace-guided integration, achieving large gains on million-token history benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing memory self-evolution methods use holistic evolution: they derive revision directions from mixed task feedback and judge progress by overall performance. This obscures optimization directions and hides capability-specific gains that are offset by regressions elsewhere, leaving promising directions underexplored.
AI.method: The authors introduce capability-driven evolution, extending search guidance from overall performance to individual capability dimensions. PrisMem comprises three components: (1) dependency-aware capability selection to prioritize targets with potential cross-capability benefits; (2) history-guided diagnosis to refine capability specialists; (3) trace-guided integration, which compares evaluated programs on paired differential cases and uses their behavioral differences to consolidate complementary gains into a unified memory program.
AI.result: PrisMem outperforms the strongest baselines by 10.54 percentage points on BEAM-1M and 7.83 percentage points on LongMemEval-M, demonstrating effectiveness on million-token histories.
AI.conclusion: Capability-driven evolution, as instantiated in PrisMem, effectively preserves promising revisions and expands exploration beyond the boundaries of holistic evolution, yielding substantial improvements in memory self-evolution over long histories.

title: CVIF: A Criticality-Driven Visual Intervention Framework for Geometric Diagram Understanding in MLLMs
summary: Despite significant progress in visual tasks by Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), geometric diagram understanding remains challenging due to the presence of sparse visual cues and ambiguous symbol-primitive associations. MLLMs may therefore rely on textual priors, producing interpretations that conflict with visual evidence. We introduce the training-free Criticality-Driven Visual Intervention Framework (CVIF), an inference-time method that localizes critical layers and executes visual interventions during the transition from evidence aggregation to semantic decoding. At these layers, a Geometry-Constrained Local Relation Reconstruction (GCLR) module selects and weights vertex-centered visual evidence, while an Adaptive Visual Steering Operator (AVSO) redistributes attention mass toward the selected tokens. Experiments on PGPS9K and PGDP5K show that CVIF raises Overall F1 from 77.85 to 85.58 and from 75.23 to 82.84, respectively, establishing a novel inference-time visual intervention paradigm.

AI.tldr: CVIF is a training-free inference-time framework that localizes critical layers in MLLMs and applies geometry-constrained visual interventions to improve geometric diagram understanding.
AI.motivation: MLLMs struggle with geometric diagrams due to sparse visual cues and ambiguous symbol-primitive associations, often relying on textual priors that conflict with visual evidence.
AI.method: CVIF localizes critical layers and performs visual interventions during the transition from evidence aggregation to semantic decoding, using two modules: Geometry-Constrained Local Relation Reconstruction (GCLR), which selects and weights vertex-centered visual evidence, and Adaptive Visual Steering Operator (AVSO), which redistributes attention mass toward selected tokens.
AI.result: On PGPS9K, Overall F1 improves from 77.85 to 85.58; on PGDP5K, from 75.23 to 82.84.
AI.conclusion: CVIF establishes a novel inference-time visual intervention paradigm for geometric diagram understanding, without requiring training.

title: What Did the Agent Actually Do? Evidence-Grounded Oversight for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: As agents take on long-horizon tasks, users shift from making individual decisions to overseeing autonomous execution. Yet the volume of agent activity and the fragmentation of supporting evidence make it difficult to determine which decisions warrant user verification. We study monitors that identify consequential decisions and locate evidence to help users assess their implications. We introduce AgentMonBench, a software-engineering benchmark comprising three subsets that cover two complementary dimensions: alignment between requirements and behavior, and awareness of consequential autonomous decisions for verification. To support these judgments, we propose the Evidence-Grounded Behavior Graph (EBG), a training-free method that groups source-linked evidence into behaviors and organizes their relationships into a graph. EBG presents task-oriented views of this graph to help monitors interpret behavior in context. Experiments across eight models show that EBG improves decision identification and evidence localization in most settings compared with direct access to the original context. Further experiments show that EBG's evidence-localization gains persist across input scales and hyperparameter settings, while real-world applications illustrate its practical value for human oversight.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AgentMonBench, a software-engineering benchmark for evaluating monitors that identify consequential agent decisions and locate supporting evidence, and proposes EBG, a training-free evidence-grounded behavior graph method that improves decision identification and evidence localization across eight models.
AI.motivation: As agents handle long-horizon tasks, users move from making individual decisions to overseeing autonomous execution. However, the sheer volume of agent activity and the fragmentation of supporting evidence make it hard to determine which decisions require user verification. This motivates monitors that can flag consequential decisions and retrieve the relevant evidence for assessing their implications.
AI.method: The authors propose AgentMonBench, a software-engineering benchmark with three subsets covering two dimensions: alignment between requirements and behavior, and awareness of consequential autonomous decisions for verification. They also propose the Evidence-Grounded Behavior Graph (EBG), a training-free method that groups source-linked evidence into behaviors and organizes their relationships into a graph, presenting task-oriented views to help monitors interpret behavior in context.
AI.result: Experiments across eight models show that EBG improves decision identification and evidence localization in most settings compared with direct access to the original context. Additional experiments show that EBG's evidence-localization gains persist across input scales and hyperparameter settings, and real-world applications illustrate its practical value for human oversight.
AI.conclusion: EBG offers a training-free, scalable approach for grounded monitoring of autonomous agents, improving decision identification and evidence localization and supporting practical human oversight of long-horizon agent execution.

title: From Benchmark to Bench: Can Agents Survive Real-World Drug Discovery?
summary: Agentic systems increasingly coordinate molecular-design tools, but it is unclear which layer of the stack limits outcomes on real projects. We developed MAGI, an open modular agent that authors objectives, launches and monitors optimization, interprets structure--activity relationships, and revises its strategy accordingly. MAGI generates molecules either directly through the LLM or by delegating to REINVENT 4, with scoring services interchangeable behind a common contract. We tested it across nine retrospective lead-optimization campaigns from three pharmaceutical companies, replayed under fixed temporal cutoffs. Both routes produced valid structures: LLM proposals stayed closer to local chemistry and reached comparable or higher primary activity in fewer operations, whereas REINVENT explored broader chemical space. Whether a campaign met its objective depended on the predictive models, not on the generation route: attainment followed model accuracy on the chemistry proposed, dropping once that chemistry moved outside the model's applicability domain. Separately, a blinded evaluation asked whether the MAGI's output could pass as expert work: chemists were not able to discriminate agentic proposals from held-out compounds, and judged the SAR reasoning broadly plausible yet incomplete. Together, these results position MAGI as a coordination layer pluggable into existing computational chemistry workflows. The ceiling on real projects, however, remains currently set by scorer applicability rather than by tool orchestration.

AI.tldr: MAGI is an open modular agent coordinating molecular-design tools; across nine retrospective lead-optimization campaigns, success depended on scorer applicability rather than on generation route or tool orchestration.
AI.motivation: Agentic systems increasingly orchestrate molecular-design tools, yet it remains unclear which layer of the stack constrains outcomes on real projects.
AI.method: MAGI authors objectives, launches and monitors optimization, interprets structure-activity relationships, and revises strategy. It generates molecules either directly via the LLM or by delegating to REINVENT 4, with interchangeable scoring services behind a common contract. Evaluated on nine retrospective lead-optimization campaigns from three pharmaceutical companies under fixed temporal cutoffs, plus a blinded expert assessment of its outputs.
AI.result: Both routes produced valid structures: LLM proposals stayed closer to local chemistry with comparable or higher primary activity in fewer operations, while REINVENT explored broader chemical space. Objective attainment tracked predictive-model accuracy on the proposed chemistry and dropped once chemistry left the model's applicability domain. In blinded evaluation, chemists could not discriminate agentic proposals from held-out compounds and judged the SAR reasoning broadly plausible but incomplete.
AI.conclusion: MAGI positions itself as a coordination layer pluggable into existing computational chemistry workflows; on real projects the performance ceiling is set by scorer applicability rather than by tool orchestration.

title: Multimodal Safety Evaluation Should Measure Controllability Beyond Classification
summary: VLM safety is commonly evaluated through input- and output-level classification. Such classification is necessary, but it does not reveal whether a safety state is accessible or controllable inside the model. We argue that multimodal safety evaluation should therefore report a \emph{controllability profile} alongside behavioral classification, separating representation-level detectability, cross-modal specificity, intervention sensitivity, and benign-preserving selectivity. Using implicit toxicity as a stress case, we instantiate this profile on LlavaGuard and Qwen3.5 with sparse feature decompositions. LlavaGuard admits localized handles with a narrow benign-preserving intervention range and modest downstream safety gains, whereas Qwen3.5 supports strong representation-level readout but no comparable selective-control regime under the tested operators. These results show that internal readout and controllability can diverge. Future multimodal safety benchmarks should therefore report not only behavioral safety metrics, but also whether safety-relevant internal signals can be intervention-tested and controlled within a validated operating range.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that multimodal safety evaluation should report a controllability profile (representation-level detectability, cross-modal specificity, intervention sensitivity, benign-preserving selectivity) alongside behavioral classification, and demonstrates on LlavaGuard and Qwen3.5 that internal readout and controllability can diverge.
AI.motivation: VLM safety is typically assessed via input- and output-level classification, which is necessary but fails to reveal whether a safety state is actually accessible or controllable inside the model. The authors contend that behavioral classification alone does not capture whether safety-relevant internal signals can be intervention-tested and controlled within a validated operating range.
AI.method: Using implicit toxicity as a stress case, the authors instantiate a controllability profile on LlavaGuard and Qwen3.5 with sparse feature decompositions, separating four dimensions: representation-level detectability, cross-modal specificity, intervention sensitivity, and benign-preserving selectivity.
AI.result: LlavaGuard admits localized handles with a narrow benign-preserving intervention range and modest downstream safety gains, whereas Qwen3.5 supports strong representation-level readout but no comparable selective-control regime under the tested operators. These results show that internal readout and controllability can diverge.
AI.conclusion: Future multimodal safety benchmarks should report not only behavioral safety metrics but also whether safety-relevant internal signals can be intervention-tested and controlled within a validated operating range.

title: Normality Constraint Learning: Adapting Foundation Models for Time Series Anomaly Detection
summary: Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) achieve strong generalization by learning to reconstruct or forecast broad temporal patterns from large-scale time series during pre-training. Yet this strength can become a weakness for anomaly detection: TSFMs may model rare anomalous patterns as effectively as normal ones, allowing anomalies to be accurately reconstructed or forecasted and thus diminishing their reconstruction/forecasting error-based anomaly scores. This paper proposes $\underline{\textbf{N}}$$\textbf{ormality}$ $\underline{\textbf{C}}$$\textbf{onstraint}$ $\underline{\textbf{L}}$$\textbf{earning}$ ($\textbf{NCL}$), a lightweight plug-and-play framework that adapts pre-trained TSFMs for accurate anomaly detection without modifying their pre-trained parameters. Our key insight is to constrain the broad pattern space of TSFMs to the normal structure of a target time series, preventing their broad modeling capability from obscuring abnormal deviations. Specifically, NCL constructs a compact normality subspace from a few normal patch features and adaptively steers each patch feature toward normality within this subspace, guided by contrastive constraints that form compact and discriminative normality manifolds. The calibrated features are aggregated to reinforce normal components and fused with the original TSFM output, amplifying the discrepancy between normal and abnormal observations for the reconstruction/forecasting error-based anomaly scoring. Extensive experiments across diverse TSFM families and benchmarks show that NCL consistently improves anomaly detection performance, providing a generalizable framework for adapting TSFMs to anomaly detection.

AI.tldr: NCL is a lightweight, plug-and-play framework that adapts pre-trained Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) for anomaly detection by constraining their broad pattern space to the normality subspace of a target series, without modifying pre-trained parameters.
AI.motivation: TSFMs generalize well by modeling broad temporal patterns, but this becomes a weakness for anomaly detection: they may reconstruct/forecast rare anomalous patterns as accurately as normal ones, reducing reconstruction/forecasting error-based anomaly scores. A method is needed to prevent the broad modeling capability from obscuring abnormal deviations.
AI.method: NCL constructs a compact normality subspace from a few normal patch features, then adaptively steers each patch feature toward normality within this subspace, guided by contrastive constraints that form compact and discriminative normality manifolds. The calibrated features are aggregated to reinforce normal components and fused with the original TSFM output to amplify the discrepancy between normal and abnormal observations for error-based anomaly scoring.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across diverse TSFM families and benchmarks show that NCL consistently improves anomaly detection performance.
AI.conclusion: NCL provides a generalizable, plug-and-play framework for adapting pre-trained TSFMs to anomaly detection, achieving consistent performance gains without modifying pre-trained parameters.

title: AgentPrivArena: Evaluating and Auditing Real-world AI Agent Privacy
summary: The rapid advancement of LLM agents has enabled systems to autonomously perform complex tasks through external tools, but their growing access to personal data introduces significant privacy risks. Existing benchmarks primarily evaluate LLM agent privacy through simulated trajectories and outcome-based metrics, limiting their ability to capture privacy risks arising during multi-step agent execution. In this work, we introduce AgentPrivArena, a framework for evaluating privacy risks in realistic LLM agent workflows. AgentPrivArena integrates authentic MCP tools and self-hosted services within a reproducible execution environment. We further propose trajectory-level privacy metrics that quantify unnecessary information access beyond final response leakage. Building on this framework, we introduce AgentPrivAudit, a runtime auditing approach for monitoring privacy violations during agent execution. Extensive experiments on state-of-the-art LLM agents reveal substantial privacy risks overlooked by existing evaluation paradigms, highlighting the importance of trajectory-level auditing for trustworthy agent deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces AgentPrivArena, a reproducible execution framework with authentic MCP tools and self-hosted services, plus trajectory-level privacy metrics and a runtime auditing approach (AgentPrivAudit) to capture privacy risks during multi-step LLM agent execution that existing outcome-based benchmarks overlook.
AI.motivation: LLM agents increasingly access personal data via external tools, creating significant privacy risks. Existing benchmarks rely on simulated trajectories and outcome-based metrics, which fail to capture privacy risks that emerge during multi-step execution beyond final responses.
AI.method: AgentPrivArena integrates authentic MCP tools and self-hosted services into a reproducible execution environment. Trajectory-level privacy metrics are proposed to quantify unnecessary information access beyond final response leakage. AgentPrivAudit performs runtime auditing to monitor privacy violations during agent execution.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on state-of-the-art LLM agents reveal substantial privacy risks that prior evaluation paradigms overlook, demonstrating the value of trajectory-level auditing.
AI.conclusion: Trajectory-level auditing is essential for trustworthy agent deployment, and AgentPrivArena provides a realistic, reproducible basis for such evaluation.

title: GPlaceRL: An Open-Source Graph Reinforcement Learning Framework for Detailed Placement
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising approach for placement optimization, particularly when combined with graph neural networks (GNNs) that capture circuit connectivity. However, most learning-based placement approaches focus on floorplanning, macro placement, or global placement, while detailed placement refinement remains relatively unexplored. In this paper, we present GPlaceRL, an open-source graph reinforcement learning framework for detailed placement refinement. GPlaceRL represents legalized placements as graphs and provides a modular environment for studying graph encoders, policy architectures, reward formulations, and local placement actions. To demonstrate the capabilities of GPlaceRL, we conduct a systematic evaluation of proximal policy optimization (PPO) policies with graph attention network (GAT) encoders in a per-design optimization setting. Across five placement benchmarks, the best greedy evaluation results achieve HPWL improvements ranging from $3.27\%$ to $32.87\%$. The results highlight the importance of compact GAT architectures and flexible local action spaces for placement optimization. Overall, GPlaceRL provides a reproducible and extensible framework for systematic research on RL-based detailed placement refinement.

AI.tldr: GPlaceRL is an open-source graph reinforcement learning framework for detailed placement refinement, providing a modular environment to study graph encoders, policies, rewards, and local actions; experiments with PPO and GAT encoders achieve HPWL improvements of 3.27%–32.87% across five benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Most learning-based placement work targets floorplanning, macro placement, or global placement, leaving detailed placement refinement relatively unexplored. There is a lack of reproducible, modular infrastructure for systematically studying RL-based detailed placement refinement.
AI.method: The authors present GPlaceRL, which represents legalized placements as graphs and exposes a modular environment for graph encoders, policy architectures, reward formulations, and local placement actions. They systematically evaluate PPO policies with GAT encoders in a per-design optimization setting across five placement benchmarks.
AI.result: Best greedy evaluation achieves HPWL improvements ranging from 3.27% to 32.87% across five benchmarks. Compact GAT architectures and flexible local action spaces are found to be important for placement optimization.
AI.conclusion: GPlaceRL offers a reproducible and extensible framework for systematic research on RL-based detailed placement refinement, highlighting the value of compact graph encoders and flexible local action spaces.

title: polyview: A Python package for multi-view machine learning
summary: Multi-view learning jointly exploits multiple complementary representations of the same data and has become increasingly important in machine learning. However, the Python ecosystem lacks actively maintained, unified tooling for end-to-end multi-view workflows. In this paper, we present polyview, a Python package that provides tools for multi-view embedding, clustering, fusion, and view augmentation, as well as for handling incomplete views, all compatible with scikit-learn. The library offers a unified interface for composing heterogeneous multi-view workflows, including seamless transitions between multi-view and single-view stages. It is built around a core set of classes and utilities that enable composition of different methods and straightforward implementation of new ones. We illustrate the package on five real multi-view datasets and compare its components based on canonical correlation analysis with those of two established libraries. polyview aims to be both a practical toolkit for benchmarking and prototyping multi-view methods and a foundation for future research and development in this area.

AI.tldr: polyview is a scikit-learn-compatible Python package offering unified, end-to-end tooling for multi-view learning, including embedding, clustering, fusion, view augmentation, and handling of incomplete views.
AI.motivation: Multi-view learning exploits complementary representations of the same data and is increasingly important, yet the Python ecosystem lacks actively maintained, unified tooling for end-to-end multi-view workflows.
AI.method: The authors present polyview, built on a core set of classes and utilities that enable composition of heterogeneous multi-view methods and straightforward implementation of new ones. It supports multi-view embedding, clustering, fusion, view augmentation, and incomplete-view handling, with seamless transitions between multi-view and single-view stages, all compatible with scikit-learn.
AI.result: The package is illustrated on five real multi-view datasets, and its canonical-correlation-analysis-based components are compared with those of two established libraries.
AI.conclusion: polyview aims to serve both as a practical toolkit for benchmarking and prototyping multi-view methods and as a foundation for future research and development in multi-view learning.

title: You Changed Your Mind, The Model Didn't: Demystifying Intent in Multi-Turn Dialogue
summary: When a large language model handles a multi-turn task and a user proposes a change but ultimately rejects it, the model should continue as if nothing changed. We find a surprising failure: merely mentioning a rejected change can derail task execution, even when the user's final intent remains unchanged. To systematically study language model behavior under evolving user intent, we introduce Intent-Eval, a controlled benchmark spanning tool actions, code, databases, and mathematics. Across diverse tasks, models are vulnerable to both rejected proposals and superseded requirements, consistent with mentioned-as-in-effect confusion: conversational content is treated as active requirements even after it has been rejected or replaced. Accuracy degradation can deepen or persist as interaction continues, highlighting the need to distinguish what has been mentioned from what remains in effect. Building on this insight, we propose Intent-OPSD, a decision-conditioned on-policy self-distillation framework with Teacher and Student initialized from the same model. The frozen Teacher provides active-intent supervision from the complete task matching the user's decision, training the Student on the full dialogue to follow active requirements reflecting user intent.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a failure mode called "mentioned-as-in-effect confusion," where LLMs treat rejected or superseded conversational content as active requirements, and introduces the Intent-Eval benchmark to study it plus Intent-OPSD, a decision-conditioned on-policy self-distillation method that improves adherence to active user intent.
AI.motivation: In multi-turn tasks, when a user proposes a change and later rejects it, the model should behave as if nothing changed. However, merely mentioning a rejected change can derail task execution even when the user's final intent is unchanged. The paper motivates the need to systematically study model behavior under evolving user intent and to distinguish what has merely been mentioned from what remains in effect.
AI.method: The authors introduce Intent-Eval, a controlled benchmark spanning tool actions, code, databases, and mathematics, to systematically test model behavior under evolving user intent (rejected proposals and superseded requirements). Building on the insight of mentioned-as-in-effect confusion, they propose Intent-OPSD, a decision-conditioned on-policy self-distillation framework with Teacher and Student initialized from the same model. The frozen Teacher provides active-intent supervision from the complete task matching the user's decision, training the Student on the full dialogue to follow active requirements reflecting user intent.
AI.result: Across diverse tasks, models are vulnerable to both rejected proposals and superseded requirements, consistent with mentioned-as-in-effect confusion: conversational content is treated as active requirements even after being rejected or replaced. Accuracy degradation can deepen or persist as interaction continues.
AI.conclusion: The work highlights the need to distinguish what has been mentioned from what remains in effect, demonstrates a systematic vulnerability of LLMs under evolving user intent, and proposes Intent-OPSD as a decision-conditioned on-policy self-distillation solution that trains the Student to follow active requirements reflecting user intent.

title: ANT: A Multi-Granularity Network Traffic Dataset and Benchmark for Agents Behavior Auditing
summary: The growing adoption of large language model (LLM) agents creates a need for network administrators and security teams to audit agent behavior within organizational networks without inspecting private user content. Network traffic offers an observable source of evidence, but how much it reveals about agent tasks and operations remains unclear. Existing traffic datasets lack the joint task and stage annotations needed to evaluate this question. We introduce ANT (Agent Network Traffic), a dataset providing agent behavior information at risk, scenario, and behavior primitive granularities alongside network traffic. ANT contains 3,114 execution episodes across 20 tasks and five scenarios, comprising 276,417 bidirectional flows and 40,049 behavior primitive segments organized into 47 macro groups. We establish a benchmark for agent risk identification, scenario recognition, and behavior primitive classification using 13 representative traffic analysis baselines. The results show that existing methods recover useful but uneven behavioral signals. They struggle to identify risk when malicious workflows resemble benign tasks and to distinguish scenarios with similar traffic patterns. Primitive classification is more reliable for frequent macro groups and those with distinctive traffic patterns than for rare or semantically similar groups. ANT provides a common basis for developing more precise auditing and forensic analysis of agent behavior from network traffic. Our data and code are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ant-main-suite-7BC0/.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ANT, a network-traffic dataset annotated with agent task/stage labels at risk, scenario, and behavior-primitive granularity, and benchmarks 13 traffic-analysis baselines on agent risk identification, scenario recognition, and primitive classification.
AI.motivation: Organizations need to audit LLM agent behavior over networks without inspecting private user content. Network traffic is an observable evidence source, but it is unclear how much it reveals about agent tasks and operations, and existing traffic datasets lack the joint task and stage annotations required to evaluate this question.
AI.method: The authors construct ANT (Agent Network Traffic), a dataset pairing network traffic with agent behavior annotations at risk, scenario, and behavior-primitive granularities. It contains 3,114 execution episodes over 20 tasks and five scenarios, totaling 276,417 bidirectional flows and 40,049 behavior primitive segments in 47 macro groups. They define a benchmark covering agent risk identification, scenario recognition, and behavior primitive classification, evaluated with 13 representative traffic-analysis baselines.
AI.result: Baselines recover useful but uneven behavioral signals. They struggle to identify risk when malicious workflows resemble benign tasks and to distinguish scenarios with similar traffic patterns. Primitive classification performs better for frequent macro groups and those with distinctive traffic patterns, and worse for rare or semantically similar groups.
AI.conclusion: ANT offers a shared foundation for developing more precise auditing and forensic analysis of agent behavior from network traffic. Data and code are released publicly.

title: Proof-Grounded Patient-Specific Clinical Explanations from Knowledge-Graph Reasoning
summary: Clinical decision-support outputs can lack an au- ditable link between patient observations, encoded knowledge, conclusions, and recommendations. We present the CKG Clinical Explanation Engine, a downstream layer for a frozen, training-free clinical knowledge-graph reasoner that converts patient inference states and disease knowledge into typed facts, explicit rule-application traces, provenance-linked conclusions, and policy-licensed recommendations. The design separates measurement availability, representation completeness, and disease-specific activation; consequently, observed zero-activation evience is not treated as missing and partial representation is distinct from unobserved evidence. Optional language generation is restricted to symbolically licensed content. Across five usable workbooks (6,720 patients; 20,160 patient-disease traces; 1,021,440 feature-evidence rows), IG-range validity and knowledge provenance were 100%, numerical cross-sheet fidelity was 100% (120,960/120,960), and exported logical/report trace completeness was 100% (20,160/20,160). Availability representation consistency was 99.7028% (1,018,404/1,021,440); all 3,036 disagreements were confined to three systematic feature-cohort patterns. The corpus contained 86,783 observed zero-activation and 139,949 observed partially represented instances. A separate seeded 25-patient end-to-end audit completed without execution failure and passed all pre-specified trace, licensing, provenance, and state-consistency checks. These results establish structural and implementation auditability, not clinical correctness or utility.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the CKG Clinical Explanation Engine, a downstream layer over a frozen, training-free clinical knowledge-graph reasoner that produces auditable, provenance-linked explanations; evaluation on five workbooks shows 100% trace/provenance/completeness and 99.7% representation consistency, demonstrating structural rather than clinical validity.
AI.motivation: Clinical decision-support outputs often lack an auditable link connecting patient observations, encoded knowledge, conclusions, and recommendations, undermining transparency and traceability.
AI.method: A downstream explanation layer for a frozen, training-free clinical knowledge-graph reasoner converts patient inference states and disease knowledge into typed facts, explicit rule-application traces, provenance-linked conclusions, and policy-licensed recommendations. It separates measurement availability, representation completeness, and disease-specific activation, treating observed zero-activation as evidence rather than missingness, and restricts optional language generation to symbolically licensed content.
AI.result: Across five workbooks (6,720 patients; 20,160 patient-disease traces; 1,021,440 feature-evidence rows): IG-range validity and knowledge provenance 100%; numerical cross-sheet fidelity 100% (120,960/120,960); exported logical/report trace completeness 100% (20,160/20,160); availability representation consistency 99.7028% (1,018,404/1,021,440), with all 3,036 disagreements confined to three systematic feature-cohort patterns. The corpus contained 86,783 observed zero-activation and 139,949 observed partially represented instances. A seeded 25-patient end-to-end audit passed all pre-specified trace, licensing, provenance, and state-consistency checks without execution failure.
AI.conclusion: The results establish structural and implementation auditability of the engine, not clinical correctness or utility.

title: Signature-Based Feature Learning for Human Activity Recognition: A Reproducible Machine Learning Study of Representation, Depth, and Model Choice
summary: Human activity recognition (HAR) relies on transforming sensor signals into informative representations for classification. Although deep learning and handcrafted features are widely used, the role of representation itself is often not systematically isolated. Signature transforms provide a mathematically grounded way to encode temporal order and cross-channel interactions, but their value for HAR under a fully reproducible and leakage-aware framework remains unclear. To evaluate whether signature-based feature learning improves HAR performance compared with raw-signal baselines, and to assess the effects of embedding strategy, truncation depth, model choice, and sensor configuration. Experiments were conducted on the UCI HAR dataset using a fully reproducible pipeline with the original train--test split preserved and subject-disjoint validation to prevent leakage. Three representations were compared: raw flattened signals, time-augmented paths, and lead--lag transformed paths. Signature features were computed at multiple truncation depths and evaluated using multilayer perceptron (MLP) and Random Forest (RF) classifiers under identical preprocessing and validation procedures. A prior K-means-based feature reduction study was also reproduced for comparison. Signature-based representations improved performance when paired with RF models, the best configuration was time-augmented six-channel signatures at depth 6 using entropy-based RF achieving 0.858 accuracy and 0.859 macro F1, outperforming the strongest raw baseline (0.816 accuracy). Lead--lag representations were competitive at moderate depths but did not surpass the best time-augmented models. MLP models did not exceed raw baselines. Signature-based feature learning can improve HAR, but its benefit depends on alignment between representation design and classifier choice.

AI.tldr: This study asks whether signature-transform representations improve human activity recognition (HAR) over raw-signal baselines, using a fully reproducible, leakage-aware pipeline on the UCI HAR dataset. Time-augmented signature features at depth 6 with an entropy-based Random Forest achieved the best result (0.858 accuracy, 0.859 macro F1), outperforming the strongest raw baseline (0.816 accuracy).
AI.motivation: Deep learning and handcrafted features are widely used in HAR, but the role of the representation itself is often not systematically isolated. Signature transforms offer a mathematically grounded encoding of temporal order and cross-channel interactions, yet their value for HAR under a fully reproducible and leakage-aware framework remains unclear.
AI.method: Experiments on the UCI HAR dataset with the original train-test split preserved and subject-disjoint validation to prevent leakage. Three representations were compared: raw flattened signals, time-augmented paths, and lead-lag transformed paths. Signature features were computed at multiple truncation depths and classified with MLP and Random Forest under identical preprocessing and validation. A prior K-means-based feature reduction study was also reproduced for comparison.
AI.result: Signature-based representations improved performance with Random Forest classifiers. The best configuration was time-augmented six-channel signatures at depth 6 with entropy-based RF, reaching 0.858 accuracy and 0.859 macro F1 versus the strongest raw baseline at 0.816 accuracy. Lead-lag representations were competitive at moderate depths but did not surpass the best time-augmented models. MLP models did not exceed raw baselines.
AI.conclusion: Signature-based feature learning can improve HAR, but the benefit depends on alignment between representation design and classifier choice.

title: HERA: Harness-Environment Co-Evolution for Reliable Agentic Abstention
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of acting in complex tool-use environments, yet they often fail to recognize when tasks are infeasible and no valid solution exists. Recent work has formalized this reliability gap as the problem of agentic abstention, and existing approaches typically optimize a model or agent harness against a fixed set of tasks, leading to limited generalization to unseen failure modes. We introduce HERA, a framework for harness-environment co-evolution for agentic abstention. HERA consists of (i) a pipeline to automatically construct verifiable pairs of feasible and infeasible tasks by applying controlled environment mutations that transform solvable tasks into cases requiring abstention, and (ii) a co-evolution procedure in which performance failures on previous tasks are used to drive harness adaptation and generate new execution environments and tasks geared towards previous weaknesses. On held-out evaluation tasks, an evolved harness from HERA improves abstention accuracy from 61.7% to 83.3% while improving feasible-task completion from 68.3% to 76.7%, achieving the highest abstention and feasible-task completion among the compared methods. The resulting best harness transfers across 19 other LLMs, improving abstention accuracy by 15.3 percentage points on average without any model-specific optimization, and enabling smaller models to match the performance of more powerful models at an estimated 85% lower cost.

AI.tldr: HERA is a harness-environment co-evolution framework that improves LLM agents' ability to abstain on infeasible tasks by automatically generating verifiable feasible/infeasible task pairs and iteratively adapting the harness toward discovered weaknesses.
AI.motivation: LLM agents in tool-use environments often fail to recognize infeasible tasks requiring abstention. Prior agentic abstention methods optimize against a fixed task set, limiting generalization to unseen failure modes.
AI.method: HERA comprises (i) a pipeline that applies controlled environment mutations to convert solvable tasks into infeasible ones, producing verifiable feasible/infeasible pairs, and (ii) a co-evolution procedure where failures on prior tasks drive harness adaptation and generate new environments and tasks targeting prior weaknesses.
AI.result: On held-out tasks, the evolved harness raises abstention accuracy from 61.7% to 83.3% and feasible-task completion from 68.3% to 76.7%, achieving the best of both among compared methods. It transfers across 19 other LLMs, improving abstention by 15.3 percentage points on average without model-specific optimization, and lets smaller models match stronger models at ~85% lower cost.
AI.conclusion: Co-evolving the agent harness with generated environments yields generalizable agentic abstention, transferable across models and cost-efficient.

title: DGA-Muon: Decoupled Geometry-Aligned Adaptive Scaling for Muon
summary: While NorMuon has achieved strong empirical performance in large-scale pretraining by enhancing Muon with row-wise adaptive scaling, its underlying adaptive mechanism remains poorly understood. In this work, we provide the first systematic analysis of NorMuon's adaptivity, revealing that it originates primarily from orthogonalization-induced geometry rather than genuine optimization-relevant information. Under exact orthogonalization, the adaptive scaling factors degenerate into a single global scalar for square and wide matrices, while for tall matrices their variation arises from the non-uniform distribution of row energy after orthogonalization. Under approximate orthogonalization, the orthogonality residual introduces additional variation into the scaling factors, leading to the \textit{Orthogonalization--Adaptivity Paradox}: more accurate orthogonalization weakens adaptivity. We further show that NorMuon's rigid row-wise scaling is geometrically misaligned with the one-sided orthogonal structure of tall matrices. Based on the analysis of these limitations, we propose two core design principles that a desirable adaptive mechanism for Muon should satisfy. First, adaptive scaling should be decoupled from orthogonalization, with the scaling factors computed directly from raw gradients. Second, adaptive scaling should be aligned with the shape-dependent orthogonal structure of the polar factor, using row-wise scaling for wide matrices and column-wise scaling for tall matrices. By incorporating several other design considerations, including sum-based second-moment estimates, bias correction, and adaptive clipping of scaling factors, we obtain the Decoupled Geometry-Aligned Muon (DGA-Muon) optimizer. We establish convergence guarantees for DGA-Muon and empirically validate both our theoretical characterization of NorMuon's scaling degeneration and the superiority of DGA-Muon over NorMuon.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first systematic analysis of NorMuon's adaptivity, showing that its adaptive scaling stems from orthogonalization-induced geometry rather than optimization-relevant information, and proposes DGA-Muon, a decoupled and geometry-aligned adaptive optimizer for Muon.
AI.motivation: NorMuon enhances Muon with row-wise adaptive scaling and achieves strong empirical performance in large-scale pretraining, yet its underlying adaptive mechanism remains poorly understood. The authors aim to clarify the source and limitations of NorMuon's adaptivity to guide better optimizer design.
AI.method: The authors systematically analyze NorMuon under both exact and approximate orthogonalization, examining the behavior of its adaptive scaling factors for square, wide, and tall matrices. They identify the Orthogonalization–Adaptivity Paradox and geometric misalignment of rigid row-wise scaling. Based on these findings, they propose two design principles—decoupling adaptive scaling from orthogonalization and aligning scaling with the shape-dependent orthogonal structure of the polar factor—and incorporate sum-based second-moment estimates, bias correction, and adaptive clipping to build the DGA-Muon optimizer.
AI.result: Under exact orthogonalization, the adaptive scaling factors degenerate into a single global scalar for square and wide matrices, while for tall matrices their variation arises from non-uniform row energy distribution after orthogonalization. Under approximate orthogonalization, the orthogonality residual introduces extra variation, leading to the Orthogonalization–Adaptivity Paradox: more accurate orthogonalization weakens adaptivity. DGA-Muon is shown to have convergence guarantees and empirically outperforms NorMuon, validating both the theoretical characterization of NorMuon's scaling degeneration and the proposed optimizer's superiority.
AI.conclusion: NorMuon's adaptivity is largely an artifact of orthogonalization geometry rather than genuine optimization-relevant information, and its rigid row-wise scaling is misaligned with the one-sided orthogonal structure of tall matrices. Decoupling adaptive scaling from orthogonalization and aligning it with the polar factor's shape-dependent structure yields DGA-Muon, which provides convergence guarantees and empirically surpasses NorMuon.

title: Mind the Execution Gap: Action-Semantic Mismatch in World-Model Control
summary: World-model controllers rely on action-conditioned dynamics for prediction and planning, yet real control systems often execute commands asynchronously due to communication delay, packet loss, reordering, and actuator buffering. We study how asynchronous execution changes the action semantics assumed within world-model controllers, rather than treating it only as an external control disturbance. Through controlled interventions, we identify two architecture-dependent failure modes: planning-based controllers such as TD-MPC2 suffer from a future-action timeline mismatch between imagined and executed action sequences, while recurrent world models such as DreamerV3 can attribute observed transitions to commands that were not actually applied. Our analysis shows that TD-MPC2 requires the correct future action sequence during latent dynamics rollout, whereas DreamerV3 requires timely attribution of each transition to the action that generated it. Based on these findings, we introduce two lightweight execution-consistent interfaces, Future-Sequence for TD-MPC2 and Applied-Action Feedback for DreamerV3, that correct these mismatches without modifying the pretrained world models. Experiments across delays, packet loss, reordering, multiple control domains, measured network traces, and a process-separated asynchronous stack consistently support both diagnoses and the corresponding architecture-specific corrections.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how asynchronous execution breaks the action semantics assumed by world-model controllers, identifies two architecture-dependent failure modes, and proposes lightweight execution-consistent interfaces to fix them without retraining.
AI.motivation: Real control systems execute commands asynchronously due to communication delay, packet loss, reordering, and actuator buffering. Prior work treats this only as an external disturbance, but the authors argue asynchrony fundamentally changes the action semantics that world-model controllers rely on, motivating a deeper investigation.
AI.method: Through controlled interventions, the authors analyze two controller families: planning-based controllers (e.g., TD-MPC2) and recurrent world models (e.g., DreamerV3). They diagnose the mismatch mechanisms and introduce two lightweight, execution-consistent interfaces—Future-Sequence for TD-MPC2 and Applied-Action Feedback for DreamerV3—that correct the mismatches without modifying pretrained world models.
AI.result: Two architecture-dependent failure modes are identified: TD-MPC2 suffers from a future-action timeline mismatch between imagined and executed action sequences, while DreamerV3 can attribute observed transitions to commands that were not actually applied. TD-MPC2 requires the correct future action sequence during latent dynamics rollout, whereas DreamerV3 requires timely attribution of each transition to the action that generated it. Experiments across delays, packet loss, reordering, multiple control domains, measured network traces, and a process-separated asynchronous stack consistently support both diagnoses and the corresponding corrections.
AI.conclusion: Asynchronous execution is not merely an external disturbance but alters action semantics central to world-model control. Architecture-specific, execution-consistent interfaces can effectively and cheaply recover performance under realistic asynchronous conditions without retraining the underlying world models.

title: The Review Lottery: Calibrating an Observational Estimator of Peer-Review Noise (ICLR 2017-2025)
summary: How much of a conference accept/reject decision would change if the same paper were reviewed by a different set of reviewers? Running a second independent program committee is the gold standard for answering this, but it is prohibitively expensive: done only twice (NeurIPS 2014 and 2021). We build an observational estimator of this quantity from public review data alone, calibrate it twice, and apply it to nine years of ICLR (2017-2025; 36,113 papers, 134,912 reviews). The estimator decomposes scores with a Bayesian ordered-probit model into paper quality and reviewer noise, maps scores to decisions with a logistic model, and simulates two independent committees (posterior draws B=1,000; committee sizes k=2,3,4). Estimated disagreement rates are 23-30% at k=2 and 18-24% at k=4; 30-50% of accepted papers would be rejected. External calibration: at the NeurIPS 2021 reviewer-count caliber (k=3), the simulated 2021 disagreement rate is 23.3% [21.7%, 25.0%] vs. reported 23.0% (bias +0.3pp); accept precision and committee correlation agree within 5pp and 0.04. Internal calibration: on 18,740 papers with 4+ reviews, random model-free 2+2 reviewer splits agree with the k=2 simulation within 1pp in 2018 and 2021-2025. Longitudinally, we find no robust time trend in reviewer noise over 2017-2025. The high accepted-paper flip rates of 2020 and 2021 have distinct mechanisms: the 2020 four-point scale compressed scores (23.7% of papers had zero within-paper variance), and a counterfactual shows coarsening the scale raises disagreement by about 7pp; 2021 instead combined the lowest signal-to-noise ratio in the sample with the most threshold-crowded acceptances. For the LLM era, a 2023 breakpoint test on within-paper score variance finds no break, but the design has almost no power, and no post-2022 review text or confidence data exist, so no LLM attribution is attempted.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a cheap observational estimator that recovers how much conference decisions would flip under an independent committee, calibrated against NeurIPS 2021 and validated internally on ICLR splits, and applies it to nine years of ICLR data.
AI.motivation: Running a second independent program committee is the gold standard for measuring reviewer-assignment randomness, but it is prohibitively expensive and has been done only twice (NeurIPS 2014 and 2021). A public-data-only estimator would make this quantity measurable at scale and across many years.
AI.method: The authors build an observational estimator from public review data: a Bayesian ordered-probit model decomposes scores into paper quality and reviewer noise; a logistic model maps scores to decisions; two independent committees are then simulated via posterior draws (B=1,000) at committee sizes k=2,3,4. It is calibrated externally against NeurIPS 2021 (k=3) and internally via model-free 2+2 random reviewer splits on 18,740 ICLR papers with 4+ reviews, then applied to nine years of ICLR (2017-2025; 36,113 papers, 134,912 reviews).
AI.result: Estimated disagreement rates are 23-30% at k=2 and 18-24% at k=4, with 30-50% of accepted papers flipping to rejection. External calibration matches NeurIPS 2021 (simulated 23.3% [21.7%, 25.0%] vs. reported 23.0%; bias +0.3pp), and accept precision and committee correlation agree within 5pp and 0.04. Internal calibration agrees within 1pp for 2018 and 2021-2025. No robust time trend in reviewer noise appears over 2017-2025. The elevated flip rates in 2020 and 2021 have distinct mechanisms: the 2020 four-point scale compressed scores (23.7% of papers had zero within-paper variance, and coarsening the scale raises disagreement by ~7pp), while 2021 combined the lowest signal-to-noise ratio with the most threshold-crowded acceptances. A 2023 breakpoint test on within-paper variance finds no break, but the design has almost no power and no post-2022 review text or confidence data exist, so no LLM attribution is attempted.
AI.conclusion: Peer-review outcomes are substantially determined by reviewer assignment rather than paper quality alone, and this can be quantified cheaply from public data. The estimator is well calibrated and reveals no longitudinal drift in reviewer noise. However, the near-zero power of the breakpoint test and the absence of post-2022 text/confidence data mean the design cannot identify any LLM-era effect, so no such attribution is made.

title: Can Agent Harnesses and Inference Engines Hear Each Other? The HEAR Protocol for Agentic LLM Serving
comment: Jiaqi Zhao, Haodong Chen, and Jitai Hao contributed equally
summary:
LLM agents increasingly execute complex workflows involving multi-turn reasoning, tool use, and parallel agents. Efficient serving requires decisions that span two layers with complementary information: the agent harness understands workflow dependencies, context lifecycles, and execution objectives, whereas the inference engine observes request queues, KV-cache state, resource pressure, and execution capabilities. Existing interfaces do not systematically connect these views, limiting workflow-aware execution.
  HEAR, a bidirectional Harness--Engine Pairing protocol for agentic LLM serving. HEAR standardizes how the harness communicates workflow intent and execution requirements and how the engine returns runtime state, capabilities, and outcomes. By separating protocol semantics from optimization policies, HEAR supports diverse coordination strategies without changing workflow or model semantics. We instantiate HEAR for online cache-aware runtime coordination and workload-aware execution-mode selection for agent roles.
  Across four conversational and research-agent benchmarks under memory-constrained, concurrent serving, HEAR achieves a $1.61\times$ batch speedup and reduces median time-to-first-token by $2.23\times$ on SCBench. Mooncake shows that workflow intent and live engine state provide complementary benefits across load regimes. On BrowseComp-Plus and DeepResearchBench, workload-specific configurations yield $1.23\times$ and $2.45\times$ end-to-end speedups, respectively, without observed task-quality degradation. These results establish HEAR as a reusable coordination substrate for efficient agentic LLM serving.

AI.tldr: HEAR is a bidirectional Harness-Engine Pairing protocol that connects agent workflow intent with live inference-engine state to enable efficient, workflow-aware agentic LLM serving without altering model or workflow semantics.
AI.motivation: LLM agents now run complex multi-turn, tool-using, and parallel workflows, but efficient serving requires coordination across two layers holding complementary information: the agent harness (workflow dependencies, context lifecycles, execution objectives) and the inference engine (request queues, KV-cache state, resource pressure, execution capabilities). Existing interfaces fail to systematically connect these views, limiting workflow-aware execution.
AI.method: HEAR standardizes a bidirectional protocol defining how the harness communicates workflow intent and execution requirements, and how the engine returns runtime state, capabilities, and outcomes. It separates protocol semantics from optimization policies, allowing diverse coordination strategies. The authors instantiate HEAR for online cache-aware runtime coordination and workload-aware execution-mode selection for agent roles.
AI.result: Across four conversational and research-agent benchmarks under memory-constrained concurrent serving, HEAR delivers a 1.61× batch speedup and reduces median time-to-first-token by 2.23× on SCBench. Mooncake analysis shows workflow intent and live engine state provide complementary benefits across load regimes. On BrowseComp-Plus and DeepResearchBench, workload-specific configurations yield 1.23× and 2.45× end-to-end speedups with no observed task-quality degradation.
AI.conclusion: HEAR establishes a reusable coordination substrate for efficient agentic LLM serving, demonstrating that bridging harness workflow knowledge and engine runtime state yields substantial latency and throughput gains without harming task quality.

title: FREA: A Multi-Source Expert Benchmark for Reaction Feasibility Verification
summary: As generative models and AI agents propose chemical reactions at a scale beyond expert review, feasibility verifiers decide which proposals enter synthesis planning. But do their decisions agree with chemists across different kinds of candidates? We introduce FREA, a benchmark of 751 reactions labeled by expert chemists under an explicit feasibility criterion, drawn from retrosynthesis model proposals, zero-yield experimental records, edits by large language models (LLMs), and five negative candidate generation methods. Our evaluation finds that no verifier leads across all sources: LLMs given only the criterion are competitive with dedicated verifiers, while forward models perform best on retrosynthesis proposals but reject most feasible edits of recorded reactions at the evaluated operating points. Looking beyond aggregate scores, both forward models perform below chance when separating infeasible alternative disconnections from feasible generated candidates. To study whether negative supervision addresses these weaknesses, we also release a corpus of over 14 million recorded reactions and generated negative candidates. In matched training comparisons, adding a mixture of generated negatives to forward training raises mean AUROC across sources, but these gains do not extend to retrosynthesis proposals. Varying the generation method further shows that the largest gain on generated candidates coincides with worse proposal screening. These findings motivate evaluating verifiers against experts across sources and designing negatives for transfer to model proposals.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FREA, a 751-reaction expert-labeled benchmark for chemical reaction feasibility, evaluated across four candidate sources and multiple verifiers. No verifier leads across all sources; forward models dominate on retrosynthesis proposals but fail on feasible edits of recorded reactions and fall below chance on alternative-disconnection discrimination. A 14M+ negative corpus and matched training experiments show mixed negatives improve mean AUROC but not on proposals, revealing source-dependent weaknesses and motivating transfer-aware negative design.
AI.motivation: Generative models and AI agents propose chemical reactions at a scale exceeding expert review capacity, so automated feasibility verifiers gate which proposals reach synthesis planning. However, it is unclear whether these verifiers agree with expert chemists, particularly across the heterogeneous kinds of candidates produced by different sources. The paper motivates a source-stratified, expert-labeled evaluation to expose where verifiers succeed or fail.
AI.method: The authors build FREA, a benchmark of 751 reactions labeled by expert chemists under an explicit feasibility criterion. Candidates are drawn from four sources: retrosynthesis model proposals, zero-yield experimental records, LLM edits (perturbations of recorded reactions), and five negative candidate generation methods. They benchmark dedicated verifiers and LLM verifiers given only the criterion, stratifying performance by candidate source. They additionally release a corpus of 14M+ recorded reactions with generated negatives and run matched training comparisons, varying the negative generation method to test whether negative supervision closes the observed gaps.
AI.result: No verifier leads across all sources. LLMs given only the criterion are competitive with dedicated verifiers. Forward models perform best on retrosynthesis proposals but reject most feasible LLM edits of recorded reactions at the evaluated operating points. Both forward models score below chance at separating infeasible alternative disconnections from feasible generated candidates. Adding a mixture of generated negatives to forward training raises mean AUROC across sources in matched comparisons, but these gains do not transfer to retrosynthesis proposals. Varying the generation method shows the largest gain on generated candidates coincides with worse proposal screening.
AI.conclusion: Feasibility verifiers should be evaluated against expert chemists across candidate sources rather than on aggregate scores, since rankings and failure modes are source-dependent. Negative supervision helps on some distributions but not on model proposals, so negatives must be designed for transfer to proposals. The FREA benchmark and the 14M+ negative corpus support this source-stratified and transfer-oriented evaluation paradigm.

title: Collective intelligence through aggregation
comment: This is a preprint of a paper published in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B (2026) 381 (1948): 20240454
summary: Suppose a committee, expert panel, or other group is making judgments on some issues, where these may be not just yes/no-questions, such as whether a defendant is guilty, but also variables with many possible values, such as macroeconomic or meteorological variables or travel directions. Furthermore, there may be interconnections between different issues, as in the case of economic or climate variables. How can the group arrive at "intelligent" collective judgments, based on the group members' individual judgments? We investigate three challenges raised by this judgment-aggregation problem. First, reasonable methods of aggregation (such as defining the collective judgment for each issue as the average or median judgment) can produce inconsistent collective judgments. Secondly, many methods of aggregation are manipulable by strategic voting. Finally, not all methods of aggregation are conducive to tracking the truth on the issues in question. We prove new impossibility or possibility theorems on all three challenges, identifying what it takes to produce collective judgments in a consistent, non-manipulable, and truth-tracking manner and thereby to achieve collective intelligence through aggregation. Overall, the median method, though imperfect, performs reasonably well. We also note the relevance of our analysis for non-human group decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes judgment aggregation for multi-valued issues with logical interconnections, addresses three challenges (consistency, strategy-proofness, truth-tracking), and proves new possibility/impossibility theorems, showing the median method performs reasonably well.
AI.motivation: Committees and expert groups must aggregate individual judgments not only on yes/no questions but on variables with many possible values (e.g., macroeconomic, meteorological, or directional variables), often with interdependencies between issues. The goal is to determine how such a group can reach "intelligent" collective judgments, motivating a systematic study of what aggregation methods can and cannot achieve.
AI.method: The authors model the judgment-aggregation problem with multi-valued issues and interconnections among them, then analyze three challenges: (1) aggregation rules such as averaging or median yielding inconsistent collective judgments, (2) manipulability via strategic voting, and (3) failure to track the truth. They prove new impossibility and possibility theorems characterizing the conditions needed for consistent, non-manipulable, and truth-tracking aggregation.
AI.result: New impossibility or possibility theorems are established on all three challenges, identifying what is required for collective judgments to be simultaneously consistent, non-manipulable, and truth-tracking, thereby achieving collective intelligence through aggregation. The median method is found to be imperfect yet reasonably effective.
AI.conclusion: Achieving collective intelligence in multi-valued, interconnected judgment aggregation faces fundamental trade-offs captured by the new theorems. The median method offers a reasonably good, though not flawless, approach, and the analysis extends to non-human group decisions.

title: Language models can notice an impossible engineering problem yet still report it as solved
comment: 36 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables; Supplementary Information included as an appendix; figure source data as ancillary files
summary: Language models draft engineering calculations, but answer accuracy does not show whether they reject an impossible problem. We tested 14 models on 30 pairs of mechanics problems, each with a valid version and one made impossible by changing a given value or assumption. Two independent solvers verified every answer key and showed that each flawed problem was physically impossible. We scored solving of valid problems separately from rejection of their flawed counterparts. Each reply required a "solved" or "cannot solve" status; rejection meant "cannot solve" or withholding an answer. The initial prompts did not warn that problems could be flawed. Across three recent models, 12 of 90 replies failed to reject a flawed problem. In 11 of these replies, the model stated the flaw, answered a corrected problem and still reported the original as "solved", according to artificial intelligence raters and numerical checks. We later retested four models from one provider, offering "flawed" instead of "cannot solve" and asking them to name and explain the defect. Three models showed statistically significant increases in rejection, but valid-problem solving fell in three. Evaluations therefore need to score both versions and distinguish flaw recognition from the reported status.

AI.tldr: Language models often fail to reject physically impossible mechanics problems: across 14 models and 30 valid/flawed problem pairs, flawed problems were sometimes answered as "solved" even when the model stated the flaw, and prompting for "flawed" improved rejection at a cost to valid-problem solving.
AI.motivation: Accuracy on answerable problems does not reveal whether a model recognizes and rejects an impossible or inconsistent problem, so evaluation methods must separately measure solving of valid problems and rejection of flawed counterparts.
AI.method: Tested 14 language models on 30 pairs of mechanics problems, each comprising a valid version and an impossible version created by altering a given value or assumption. Two independent solvers verified all answer keys and confirmed that each flawed problem was physically impossible.
