Scoring separated valid-problem solving from rejection of flawed counterparts; every reply required a "solved" or "cannot solve" status, with rejection defined as "cannot solve" or withholding an answer. Initial prompts did not warn that problems might be flawed. A follow-up retest of four models from one provider replaced "cannot solve" with "flawed" and asked models to name and explain the defect.
AI.result: Across three recent models, 12 of 90 replies failed to reject a flawed problem. In 11 of these, the model stated the flaw, answered a corrected problem, yet still reported the original as "solved", per AI raters and numerical checks. In the retest, three models showed statistically significant increases in rejection, but valid-problem solving decreased in three.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation of language models on engineering or mechanics problems should score both valid and flawed versions and distinguish flaw recognition from the reported status, since models may detect an impossibility while still claiming to have solved the original problem.

title: The Pushback Paradox: A Two-Probe Diagnostic for Language Model Compliance
summary: Are language models compliant with user instructions? A model that always complies can be stopped but also exploited, while one that always resists can be neither exploited nor stopped. We contribute an open two-probe benchmark that can place any language model on this spectrum. In the active probe, a user instructs the model to act and accept a lower payoff, which measures exploitability. In the passive probe, the user instructs it to wait and give up a higher payoff, which measures stoppability. The two compliance rates combine into a compliance index $κ$. Applied to twelve language models, the benchmark shows that seven mostly follow the instruction in both probes and justify their action by pointing to the instruction. Only Claude Sonnet-4.6 and Claude Opus-4.7 can be stopped without being exploitable, Claude Opus-4.6 and GPT-5-mini resist both instructions, and no model is exploitable but unstoppable. Knowing where a language model sits on the compliance index $κ$ matters for human operators and for multi-agent systems, whether distributed or orchestrated.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a two-probe benchmark (active/passive) that measures language models' compliance with user instructions along an exploitability-stoppability spectrum, combining both rates into a compliance index κ. Across twelve models, most comply in both probes; only Claude Sonnet-4.6 and Claude Opus-4.7 are stoppable without being exploitable, while Claude Opus-4.6 and GPT-5-mini resist both.
AI.motivation: Compliance with user instructions is double-edged: a fully compliant model can be stopped but also exploited, whereas a fully resistant model can be neither exploited nor stopped. There is a need for a principled way to locate any language model on this trade-off spectrum, which is relevant for human operators and for distributed or orchestrated multi-agent systems.
AI.method: An open two-probe benchmark is proposed, yielding a single compliance index κ. The active probe instructs the model to act and accept a lower payoff, measuring exploitability. The passive probe instructs it to wait and forgo a higher payoff, measuring stoppability. The two compliance rates are combined into κ. The benchmark is applied to twelve language models.
AI.result: Seven of the twelve models mostly follow the instruction in both probes, justifying their action by pointing to the instruction. Only Claude Sonnet-4.6 and Claude Opus-4.7 can be stopped without being exploitable. Claude Opus-4.6 and GPT-5-mini resist both instructions. No model is exploitable yet unstoppable.
AI.conclusion: The compliance index κ provides a compact characterization of where a language model sits on the exploitability-stoppability spectrum. This positioning is important for human operators and for multi-agent systems, whether distributed or orchestrated.

title: Conditional Rank Allocation for Taxonomy-Aware Medical Language Model Adaptation
summary: Medical question answering spans specialties and clinical operations that may benefit from different adaptation directions. We propose ARBOR, a parameter-efficient method that selects rank-one components from a shared low-rank basis for each question. An additive gate combines question representations, specialty tags, operation tags, and their interaction; a learned coefficient scales the adapter residual. An illustrative separation under orthogonal, equiprobable subtasks shows how conditional selection can avoid an approximation floor faced by a fixed update with the same active rank. This result motivates the design without asserting a corresponding bound for medical corpora. On Qwen3-8B across CMB, CMExam, MedQA, and MedMCQA, five-seed experiments yield 69.69% mean accuracy across benchmarks, exceeding LoRA r16 and MoELoRA by 1.26 and 1.30 percentage points, respectively. The reported advantage over LoRA r16 increases from 0.08 to 1.94 points as training expands from one to seven specialties. Tag perturbations and atom masking support the usefulness of clinical routing, while atom clusters align with the supplied specialty labels (adjusted Rand index 0.62). Calibration, transfer, and measured costs further characterize the method. These findings support structured conditional adaptation for medical QA, while leaving clinical safety and broader deployment untested.

AI.tldr: ARBOR is a parameter-efficient adaptation method that selects rank-one components from a shared low-rank basis per medical question, conditioned on question, specialty, and operation signals, outperforming LoRA r16 and MoELoRA on four medical QA benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Medical QA spans diverse specialties and clinical operations that may require different adaptation directions; a single fixed low-rank update may hit an approximation floor, motivating structured, conditional adaptation.
AI.method: ARBOR selects rank-one components from a shared low-rank basis for each question. An additive gate combines question representations, specialty tags, operation tags, and their interactions, and a learned coefficient scales the adapter residual. Motivation is supported by an illustrative orthogonal, equiprobable subtask separation.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B across CMB, CMExam, MedQA, and MedMCQA, five-seed experiments reach 69.69% mean accuracy, exceeding LoRA r16 and MoELoRA by 1.26 and 1.30 points. The gain over LoRA r16 grows from 0.08 to 1.94 points as training expands from one to seven specialties. Tag perturbations and atom masking support clinical routing utility; atom clusters align with specialty labels (ARI 0.62). Calibration, transfer, and costs are also characterized.
AI.conclusion: Results support structured conditional adaptation for medical QA, but clinical safety and broader deployment remain untested.

title: Back to the Future: Rethinking EDA Infrastructure for Agentic Systems in Chip Design Verification
comment: 40th NeurIPS'26 Workshop AI for Chip Design
summary: The unprecedented computational scale of modern artificial intelligence depends on complex, multi-billion-transistor Systems-on-Chip, yet the workflows that verify these chips remain stubbornly manual. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have made rapid inroads into Electronic Design Automation (EDA), approximately 74.6% of existing studies target static Register-Transfer Level (RTL) code generation, leaving post-simulation verification and interactive waveform debugging largely untouched. We introduce Back-to-the-Future (BTTF), an end-to-end agentic framework that closes this infrastructural gap. BTTF distills massive, unstructured simulation dumps into a normalized relational SQLite database and couples it with a collaborative multi-agent orchestration engine that translates natural-language verification queries into schema-aware SQL while correlating signal anomalies with versioned RTL repositories. Across a 150-query benchmark, BTTF attains 95.33% execution accuracy, charting a practical path toward autonomous EDA verification.

AI.tldr: BTTF is an end-to-end agentic framework that converts raw chip simulation dumps into a normalized SQLite database and uses a multi-agent engine to translate natural-language verification queries into schema-aware SQL, achieving 95.33% execution accuracy on a 150-query benchmark.
AI.motivation: Modern AI relies on multi-billion-transistor Systems-on-Chip, but chip verification workflows remain largely manual. While LLMs have entered EDA, about 74.6% of studies focus on static RTL code generation, leaving post-simulation verification and interactive waveform debugging unaddressed. BTTF targets this infrastructural gap.
AI.method: BTTF distills massive unstructured simulation dumps into a normalized relational SQLite database, coupled with a collaborative multi-agent orchestration engine. The engine translates natural-language verification queries into schema-aware SQL and correlates signal anomalies with versioned RTL repositories.
AI.result: Across a 150-query benchmark, BTTF attains 95.33% execution accuracy.
AI.conclusion: BTTF charts a practical path toward autonomous EDA verification by closing the post-simulation verification gap.

title: TasteVal: Measuring the Experimental Research Taste of AI Systems Against Human Experts
summary: We introduce TasteVal, a benchmark to evaluate the experimental research taste of frontier models. We define research taste as the ability to pick interesting problems to solve, design experiments, and interpret experimental results. TasteVal measures the experimental component of research taste; given a fixed research problem, we measure how well a model iteratively designs experiments and draws conclusions from their outcomes. We operationalize experimental research taste as compute efficiency; a Researcher who reaches the same score as an expert human using half the serial experimental compute has twice the experimental taste. Experimental taste thus acts as a multiplier on experimental compute, making it a key input to forecasts of AI progress. TasteVal consists of 8 novel, challenging, open-ended tasks representative of frontier AI R&D. To isolate taste from coding ability, the model under evaluation acts as a Researcher that iteratively designs experiments while a fixed Coder agent implements them and reports their results. The Researcher executes until either the 40 H100 hour or 120 wall-clock hour budgets are exhausted. We recruit 24 human experts, at least 2 per task, and take the best expert attempt per task as the expert baseline. We evaluate 20 models released between 2023 and 2026. The best-performing model, Opus 5.5, exceeds our expert baseline, with a compute multiplier of 2.3x (95% CI 1.15-4.37), at roughly 1/30 of our baseliners' average per-run cost. On TasteVal, the compute multiplier of frontier models has doubled approximately every 3.0 months since December 2025 (95% CI 1.7-5.0), up from every 14 months between 2023 and December 2025. Measured by final normalized performance, frontier models show no trend break, doubling every 14.6 months. To keep TasteVal uncontaminated, we do not release the tasks.

AI.tldr: TasteVal is a new benchmark measuring the "experimental research taste" of frontier AI models, operationalized as compute efficiency relative to expert humans on 8 novel open-ended R&D tasks. The best model (Opus 5.5) surpasses the expert baseline with a 2.3x compute multiplier, and frontier models' compute multipliers have been doubling roughly every 3 months since Dec 2025.
AI.motivation: Research taste—choosing problems, designing experiments, interpreting results—is a key input to forecasts of AI progress, but there has been no benchmark to evaluate the experimental component of this ability in frontier models. Isolating taste from raw coding skill is difficult, and measuring it quantitatively is valuable for predicting AI R&D acceleration.
AI.method: TasteVal comprises 8 novel, challenging, open-ended tasks representative of frontier AI R&D (tasks withheld to avoid contamination). The evaluated model acts as a "Researcher" that iteratively designs experiments, while a fixed "Coder" agent implements and reports results, isolating taste from coding ability. Runs terminate at 40 H100-hours or 120 wall-clock hours. The baseline is the best attempt among 24 human experts (≥2 per task). 20 models released 2023–2026 were evaluated.
AI.result: Opus 5.5 exceeds the expert baseline with a compute multiplier of 2.3x (95% CI 1.15–4.37) at roughly 1/30 of the baseliners' average per-run cost. On TasteVal, frontier-model compute multipliers doubled about every 3.0 months since December 2025 (95% CI 1.7–5.0), up from every 14 months between 2023 and December 2025. By final normalized performance, however, models show no trend break, doubling every 14.6 months.
AI.conclusion: TasteVal provides a compute-efficiency-based measure of experimental research taste, framing taste as a multiplier on experimental compute. Frontier models have rapidly improved in this dimension—faster than their raw performance gains suggest—and the best model now outperforms expert humans more cheaply. Tasks are withheld to preserve benchmark validity.

title: BiasFlow: Geometric Monitoring and Backbone Regularization for Spurious Feature Reliance
summary: Worst-group accuracy (WGA) evaluates a trained predictor but does not characterize how its frozen backbone behaves when a new head is learned. We introduce BiasFlow, a hook-based toolkit for monitoring class-attribute centroid alignment (IBMI), within-class centroid separation (W-IBMI), and feature-projection sensitivity. IBMI is confounded by class-attribute correlation and is not a measure of causal feature reliance. We pair these diagnostics with BiasFlow Regularization (BFR), a supervised, composable class-conditional centroid-alignment penalty. W-IBMI verifies the quantity BFR optimizes; it is scale dependent and does not independently establish attribute removal. Across the reported small-scale benchmarks, adding BFR improves or preserves mean WGA, with gains up to +26.0 pp on UrbanCars. The principal independent stress test freezes CelebA-Std backbones and trains fresh heads on biased data: BFR+GroupDRO improves WGA from 40.7% to 64.1%, while Male probe accuracy decreases from 92.5% to 72.2%. Attribute information remains recoverable, and cross-task results are mixed. A controlled synthetic-watermark ImageNet experiment additionally improves watermark-shift accuracy by +23.0 pp under matched training. These results support evaluating centroid geometry and resistance to biased head retraining alongside WGA, within the tested protocols.

AI.tldr: BiasFlow is a hook-based toolkit measuring class-attribute centroid alignment (IBMI), within-class centroid separation (W-IBMI), and feature-projection sensitivity, paired with a composable centroid-alignment penalty (BFR); frozen-backbone stress tests show improved worst-group accuracy but residual attribute recoverability and mixed cross-task results.
AI.motivation: Worst-group accuracy (WGA) only evaluates a trained predictor and does not characterize how a frozen backbone behaves when a new head is learned, leaving backbone-level bias properties under-examined. The authors seek diagnostics of centroid geometry and resistance to biased head retraining that complement WGA.
AI.method: BiasFlow: a hook-based toolkit monitoring IBMI (class-attribute centroid alignment), W-IBMI (within-class centroid separation), and feature-projection sensitivity, plus BiasFlow Regularization (BFR), a supervised, composable class-conditional centroid-alignment penalty. Validation includes small-scale benchmarks, frozen CelebA-Std backbones with fresh heads trained on biased data, and a controlled synthetic-watermark ImageNet experiment under matched training.
AI.result: Adding BFR improves or preserves mean WGA on reported small-scale benchmarks (up to +26.0 pp on UrbanCars). In the principal stress test, BFR+GroupDRO raises WGA from 40.7% to 64.1% while Male probe accuracy drops from 92.5% to 72.2%. Attribute information remains recoverable and cross-task results are mixed. The synthetic-watermark ImageNet experiment improves watermark-shift accuracy by +23.0 pp under matched training.
AI.conclusion: Centroid geometry and resistance to biased head retraining should be evaluated alongside WGA within the tested protocols. IBMI is confounded by class-attribute correlation and is not a causal measure; W-IBMI is scale dependent and does not independently establish attribute removal.
